comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2019-08818  -- This is a duplicate posting.
comments.comment_text:
Thank you for the opportunity to respond to this important NIST endeavor. The Executive Order on U.S. Leadership in Artificial Intelligence is an important step forward in providing clarity on this rapidly trending and evolving topic. NISTs work on standards for the domain of Cyber and Cybersecurity (as well as other matters) have been extremely impactful in the world community and demonstrate clear American thought leadership. Important elements of AI standards promulgated by NIST should address parameters of
trust in AI
security and resiliency of AI data sets
general classification of sectors of AI activities (e.g. space, air traffic, national security, ground transportation, consumer activities, etc.)
role and depth of human involvement in decisions
human-machine interfaces
transparency on AI algorithms
data visualization and depictions generated from AI data analysis
privacy and civil liberty aspects of AI data sets and algorithms
framework for trusted AI validation and verification to include test environment concepts.

We look forward to further engagement on these matters and are excited by NIST leadership on establishing AI Standards.

comments.organization_name: CITRIS Policy Lab, CITRIS and the Banatao Institute, UC Berkeley
comments.comment_text:
The CITRIS Policy Lab (https://citrispolicylab.org/), headquartered at UC Berkeley, supports interdisciplinary technology policy research in the interest of society. The Center for Information Technology Research in the Interest of Society (CITRIS, https://citris-uc.org/), located on the campuses of UC Berkeley, UC Davis, UC Merced, and UC Santa Cruz, creates information technology solutions to societys most pressing challenges.

Recommendations

1.In addition to development of FDA-like regulation and clinical trials (with well-defined standards) for AI systems within critical applications, we also need the equivalent of an NTSB investigation process to learn from AI failings, and ensure that these learnings are captured, widely disseminated, and play a role in informing a well-defined process for influencing policy and regulation and technical development standards.

2.The existing body of technical work in improving AI explainability should be leveraged and supported in order to develop practical explainability/accountability standards.

3.Items #1 and #2 above should be used to support a certification process, a certain level of certification being mandatory for critical applications (i.e. in medical diagnostics, non-discriminatory hiring and lending, various critical decision support systems, etc).

4.Since testing of AI algorithms for various traits is highly dependent on well-curated reference datasets, reference datasets should be maintained and made available to the public for those purposes.

5.A significant challenge exists in translating values-based principles for AI into sound development and deployment practices. Significant research support is needed to operationalize values of fairness, accountability, and transparency in public and private sector AI strategies. Federal agencies can play a significant role in supporting and facilitating this research and disseminating standards.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2019-08818
comments.comment_text:
AI must be held to standards documenting effectiveness and freedom from bias.

Artificial intelligence shapes everything from the music we hear, to the web pages and news stories suggested to us, to whether taxis are nearby, to the way our cars drive, to the way we work. So how AI develops is more than a computer science issue. Its an issue for humans to grapple with.

Now an initiative between the MIT Media Lab and the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society at Harvard University seeks to ensure AI develops for the public good. It will collaborate on unbiased, evidence-based work on AI across disciplines and sectors, says Albert Ibargen, president and chief executive officer of the Knight Foundation, which is one of the efforts funders.

Even when we dont know it, artificial intelligence affects virtually every aspect of our modern lives. Technology and commerce will ensure it will impact every society on earth, Ibargen says. Yet, for something so influential, theres an odd assumption that artificial intelligence agents and machine learning, which enable computers to make decisions like humans and for humans, is a neutral process.

comments.title: Comment from Georges Le Nigen
comments.comment_text:
For the first time in history, computing power, big data and algorithms are simultaneously available - enabling the FDA and the food industry to be more predictive and save time on alerting and cause determination. The era of AI for Food Safety is coming!

However, a big question remains in the possible biases an AI solution could create- by flagging certain types of ethnic foods because of the prejudices of some consumers, or creating alerts based upon fake news aimed to impact company reputation.

At AIFS, a AI-centric company focused on delivering augmented intelligence solutions for food safety, we believe that software vendors should disclose their algorithms in full transparency and present the countermeasures taken to prevent the biases presented above.

Future regulation should impose vendors to disclose their data models upon request to warrant full transparency and accountability.

Traceability will improve and deficiencies in the safety of the food chain may become easier to identify and predict.

comments.title: Comment from David Bergman
comments.comment_text:
Food traceability is paramount to consumer safety. Currently, outbreaks lead to recalls which lead to weeks or months of attempting to trace back where the infection originated. Incompatible systems, paper documents, forged documents, and more lead to issues regarding where to identify exactly which products are contaminated and who to blame for that contamination. This leads to food wastage by throwing out perfectly good food and it wastes manhours trying to track down where things went wrong. A better system would ensure the authentication of hand off between distinct parties, allow customers to track their food from farm to store, and provide a secure immutable database to cut down on paper waste and inefficiencies.

One company I know of that is rather mature in providing a solution to these issues is DNV-GL with their product MyStory. It is based on the blockchain VeChain.

comments.title: Comment from Izzi
comments.comment_text:
A New Era of Smarter Food Safety seems like an effective step working towards a safer public and a more informed FDA.Engaging the community and bringing conversation to the people is never a bad idea. The registration webpage for the meeting is easy to navigate and has clear instructions.

There are some questions the Agency may want to consider asking at the meeting. For instance, in addition to collaboration between FDA and industry, how can the FDA work with other government agencies to address potential challenges to creating a more digital, traceable global food supply? It also may be worthwhile to take into account potential economic effects of developments in food safety technology and how that may affect various markets. Similarly, in addition to asking "How can FDA encourage and support companies in the development of food safety cultures throughout the supply chain?", receiving feedback about potential repercussions for companies that demonstrate poor food safety practices may be helpful.

comments.title: Comment from Jonathan Sierra
comments.comment_text:
Fast testing results before product release, and data generated by novel testing technology, as part of the new tools for the New Era of Smarter Food Safety.

Fast testing of produce and food products before release must be considered and adopted as an integral part of the New Era technology-empowered food process and supply chain.

Obtaining in-shift reliable microbial testing results -as well as generating new valuable data from novel testing technologies- is now possible. Testing results obtained before the product release are the best validation of the preventive measures adopted during cultivation or production, enabling timely decisions, to stop possibly contaminated fresh food, avoid outbreaks, protect consumer health and industry interests.

A novel technology for fast-testing produce and other food products, able to detect and count within 45 minutes dangerous bacteria as E.coli, Listeria, Salmonella and more, has been developed by startup Yarok Microbio. This technology has been validated in Israel and is already in use.

Based on proprietary reagents and AI-driven software, used with a few affordable off-the-shelf laboratory tools, the Yarok method is CFU-focused, counting only live dangerous bacteria. It's easy to learn and simple to use, aimed at staff with no testing background.

Yarok fast testing results serve as an active component in blockchain-empowered traceability, documenting in real-time the product conditions before and after delivery, i.e. from field to handler, or from manufacturer to retailer, etc. Recorded data dynamically transforms into actionable information to safeguard all supply chain stakeholders so that immediate preventative measures can be taken before an outbreak might occur.

In addition to fast detection as a proactive measure, to detect and stop a clear and present danger, Yaroks new testing method generates unique datasets that describe tested produce and food under unique parameters: microbial specific metabolic and chemo-reactive behaviors, structural and morphological characteristics, collateral contamination in the internal environment of the tested sample, and more.

Aligned with complementary data generated by other new technologies, such as Whole Genome Sequencing, the Yarok data can be used to extend the New Era knowledge base, empowering current and future predictive analytical tools.

Yarok Microbio would be honored to support the Food & Drug Administration in creating a hardened preventive controls system, armed with innovative technologies, that will usher in a truly new era in food safety for the United States, and for the world.

Docket No. FDA-2019-N-4187

comments.title: Comment from Ian Duffield
comments.comment_text:
An increasing number of organizations and businesses are now concluding that the only real solution to improving food safety (of perishable food) is a universally implemented traceability system. This has recently been the conclusion supported in numerous FDA presentations, as well as the principle conclusion from the Romaine Task Force led by the Produce Marketing Association and United Fresh.
There have several noble efforts to do this during the past 10 years particularly, each of which failed due to lack of support from one or more elements of the complex perishable supply chain.
This comment is not intended to negate the tremendous improvements that have occurred in related areas such as improved farming practices, micro-biology, pathogen analysis and more.
However, these related improvements are unable to provide the critical support towards the goal of safer food, without comprehensive traceability.
Traceability technology has evolved in recent years and today offers cost-effective options to growers, shippers and producers to initiate the traceability data stream. As food moves through the multitude of hands and business from farm to fork, all players must play their part, for the total system to be effective. This includes wholesalers, retailers and food service outlets. This has been a challenge in past efforts.
A single technology platform makes the solution easier to use in the event of an outbreak, but it is not necessary, or indeed the most important aspect of future initiatives. The most critical factor in the process of food safety is that the data stream is complete from farm to fork.
Previously, the Produce Traceability Initiative, for example, set out with a goal of one step forward, one step back. This would have resulted in a perfectly viable system, had all parties implemented it.
One of the newer technologies being hailed as a panacea, is blockchain. It is dangerous to expect that any technology will solve the food safety problem without active participation of all parties. Blockchain is just a different type of database to store the data. It will be as useless as prior technologies, if data is not collected at each step of the journey from farm to fork.
We can all look forward to a New Era of Smarter Food Safety if each party in the perishable supply chain contributes to collecting and maintaining the appropriate traceability data, as food moves from farm to fork. This will provide a more rapid start to limiting the impact of food safety outbreaks, while increasing consumer confidence that their food is safe.

Retail Data Trust is enabling our existing grocery back office and point of sale software to better manage recalls at consumer checkout, our software (patents pending) is applicable to most retail systems. The team has spent the past decade managing billions of transaction scans at retail checkout. Earlier this year we began augmenting our software to monitor FDA and USDA recall lists and notify cashiers at checkout. When a recalled product is scanned, the cashier can verify the product information (lot number and other), or the system can be configured to lock out the sale of most any item thus better managing a product recall and better protecting the buying public. We believe that a proactive approach must be taken to manage recalls and any viable service should think of the consumer first. Retailers are required to remove items in a timely manner, they should have the ability to automatically restrict the sale of known recalled products. We can take this response from days to seconds.

We also share your excitement in the opportunities blockchain brings to food safety networks and are developing blockchain adaptors to remain interdependent to the various leaders in the industry. As brands align with various blockchains, our solution ensures monitoring at the checkout can write to any of them, real-time, and close the last mile or blocks in the network. Finally, we will contact consumers that have purchased recalled foods the moment a recall happens. Some recalls happen after the product has already been purchased thousands or millions of consumers. Retail Data Trust is developing a solution that enables private communications to 80-90% of consumers who have purchased recalled products.

Currently we are leveraging the FDA and USDA website recall announcements; however, are hoping to automate this process. Is there an API we can integrate into to access real-time recall announcements? Our hope is to eliminate human error in the recall process. The technology exists to monitor and alert consumers on other events, we believe it should also be used in consumer safety. comments.organization_name: Japan Electronics and Information Technology Industries Association (JEITA)
comments.comment_text:
Japan Electronics and Information Technology Industries Association (JEITA) is Japans leading ICT and electronics association, with around 400 member companies from Japan and abroad. JEITA serves as a platform for connecting industries such as electronic components and devices, electronic equipment, and IT solutions and services as well as stakeholders in those industries.

First of all, allow us to express our gratitude for an opportunity to submit our comments on a Draft Memorandum to the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies, Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications.

JEITA welcomes the Draft Memorandum of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), as it aims in the same direction in line with the JEITA Technology Strategy Board recommendation "Toward Social Implementation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Realize SDGs and Society 5.0," released in May 2018
(https://home.jeita.or.jp/press_file/20181002154214_5ArIOKGNLH.pdf), and our key messages that "AI exists for the sake of society and should be actively used" and "Importance of wide and accurate understanding of AI by the general public". In particular wed like to emphasize the following points.

1) We highly appreciate the fact that this Draft Memorandum clearly indicates that the United States is trying to avoid the introduction of excessive regulations on the use of AI that could impede innovation, and that it establishes the principles for the development, operation and use of AI applications, rather than simply opposing the introduction of regulations. We also highly appreciate that these principles take into account the specific aspects of safety, fairness and non-discrimination as well as the economic and business aspects.

2) Currently, AI is still in the early stages of deep learning technology, and it is very difficult to predict the trend of technological development and its social implementation in the near future. Therefore, it is also important to ensure participation of various stakeholders, including AI researchers and other experts as well as businesses that develop and provide AI, rather than only seeking specific perspectives from regulatory authorities and technology users when discussing regulations on the use of AI. Transparency in these discussions is indispensable. In this regard, we appreciate the OMBs recommendations for such multi-stakeholder consultation.

In the course of discussions with stakeholders from various standpoints, we believe it is important to develop and implement policies to improve AI literacy of each citizen in order to promote the relationship with the public mentioned in the principles 1. Public Trust in AI and 2. Public Participation of the Draft Memorandum.
In addition, it is important to enhance social acceptability of AI. When considering 5. Benefits and Costs, we believe that principles 6. Flexibility, 7. Fairness and Non-Discrimination, 8. Disclosure and Transparency, and 9. Safety and Security of the Draft Memorandum should be fully taken into consideration.

Finally, we expect that the policies to be developed in accordance with the Draft Memorandum will be consistent with the international policy guidelines on the subject such as the OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2020-00261
comments.comment_text:
On behalf of PATH we appreciate the opportunity to comment on the draft Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications.

We commend the agency for the content of the draft. Our major comments are to address a broader scope of needs for the federal government to advance AI in healthcare. More specifically, we urge agency guidance to (1) promote artificial intelligence (AI) research and development and (2) increase federal adoption of AI to address federal needs and responsibilities and (3) place a major priority to accelerate the development and deployment of AI applications to support public health such as the current crisis with covid-19. We urge that as much as possible such topics be included in a timely final version of this guidance with more extensive issues addressed soon in more sufficient guidance.

We believe that AI should be addressed as one of the top national priorities. The federal government has unmatched expertise and resources to assist. In the federal realm, there are massive opportunities to improve federal programs and conserve spending. There are several pending Congressional proposals that could be a basis for more expeditious Administration action.

Responding to the coronavirus epidemic utilizing advanced technology to help diagnose, develop vaccines, treat infected patients, and assist populations that are in isolation or quarantine should be a major priority. Given the large numbers of affected people and the pressure placed on existing healthcare workers, the use of emerging AI applications can be of great benefit both currently and for any future public health crisis. Results of such an effort can serve as a great opportunity for America to boost its reputation and advance the country's leadership around the world.

Further, the U.S. faces significant international competition on AI. Aggressive federal leadership is urgently needed for substantial federal benefits as well as stimulate additional private sector actions.

AI needs a moonshot-like agenda and urgency.

PATH recommends three basic ways that this guidance be begin to meet such a broader scope:

1.Each parent agency leader should be directed to designate an agency employee as the AI lead for the agency. Keys task for such designee should be collecting and reporting agency AI information and coordinating agency AI research, development, procurement and use.

2.OMB should create an AI-specific website for agencies to report AI actions and interests.

3.Each agency should be directed to identify the top priorities for further agency use of AI. For health-related agencies, such priorities could be about improving customer services, improving the cost and quality of services, and controlling waste, fraud, and abuse

About PATH

PATH is a membership-based, mission-driven alliance to ensure the integration of advanced technologies with the many components that comprise global healthcare. PATH's forward-thinking directives help to ensure that expertise critical for decision-making and funding makes its way into healthcare settings. PATH members include health care providers, health system executives in industry, public policy, academia, finance, and government - all of whom have a stake in the delivery of effective healthcare around the world in both on-site and remote care environments.

comments.comment_text:
On behalf of Amnesty International and our more than seven million members and supporters worldwide, we hereby submit this statement in response to the request for information on the "Draft Memorandum to the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies, Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Application" (henceforth "AI Memorandum"). Amnesty International ("Amnesty") is an international human rights organization with national Sections in more than 70 countries, including the United States (U.S.)
AMNESTY'S ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ("AI") AND HUMAN RIGHTS INITIATIVE
Amnesty's Artificial Intelligence ("AI") and Human Rights Initiative tackles human rights challenges posed by AI technologies. A core part of the initiative is the enforcement of human rights law to ensure that the development and use of AI does not undermine human rights standards, and instead strengthens such standards where possible.

OVERVIEW
1.AI has the potential to bring positive change for human rights. As noted in the Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications, the deployment of AI technology "holds the promise to improve safety, fairness, welfare, transparency and other social goals." However, Amnesty believes there are key issues with AI systems that urgently need to be addressed to respect human rights.
2.Global innovation and development of AI technology is being substantially driven by major U.S.-based companies in Silicon Valley. The U.S. is one of a handful of countries that has experienced significant economic gain linked to the development of AI. The U.S. Government therefore has a critical role to play in adopting robust regulatory measures and accountability mechanisms to ensure that AI advances rather than undermines human rights. For the purpose of this paper, Amnesty adopts the definition of artificial intelligence as codified in Section 238(g) of the John S. McCain National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2019, Pub. L. No. 115-232, 132 Stat. 1636, 1695 (August 13, 2018), and also understands that the scope of the potential regulation covered by these regulations applies to "narrow" AI.
3.Amnesty's chief concerns with current AI systems are that:
AI technology is predicted to fuel significant changes to employment in the U.S., particularly through automation of jobs, which will require governmental action to protect U.S. workers' rights.
AI systems collecting and processing vast amounts of personal data create new threats to human rights, notably to the right to privacy on both an individual and societal level.
A growing body of research demonstrates that AI systems are already contributing to discrimination - for example, in policing and criminal justice systems in the U.S. The Toronto Declaration underscores the risks to the right to equality and non- discrimination that are inherent to machine learning, and outlines means of protecting and promoting this right.
The impact of AI on policing and conflict could have extremely dangerous and irreversible implications on international human rights and humanitarian law.
A lack of transparency and accountability in current systems denies those harmed by AI-informed decisions adequate visibility of harms and access to effective remedy.
Innovation in AI technology is being led by powerful corporate actors and has rapidly advanced before appropriate state-based regulatory safeguards have been put in place.

comments.comment_text:
From the Office of Karl Kochendorfer, Associate Vice Chancellor for Health Affairs and Chief Health Information Officer at the University of Illinois at Chicago

As artificial intelligence applications continue to become more popular, we appreciate the commitment from the Office of Management and Budget, the Office of Science and Technology Policy, the Domestic Policy Council, and the National Economic Council to providing guidelines for federal agencies who are interested in expanding and establishing best practices. We concur that there are opportunities to improve usage of technology and simultaneously stress the importance of preventing harm to individuals and groups through the use of these potential advancements.
There are a few points which we feel would benefit from clarification or revision.

The scope of this document is unclear. As this has potential impact on healthcare, insurance, federal housing, the justice system, research, etc, we would appreciate further clarification as to which specific federal agencies this applies to and if any agencies are exempt.

In Item 2: Public Participation, on page 3 of the draft, the call for public participation is primarily aimed at the rulemaking process rather than throughout the implementation and use of AI. This may result in applications of AI which, while meeting the defined rules, do not meet the needs of the population or which have unanticipated impact without mechanism for active public participation or removal of their own data. Ongoing and active participation of members of the public in the entire process remains critical for the ability of citizens to fully participate in the democracy.

In Item 5: Benefits and Costs, the clause when consistent with law risks allowing agencies to ignore potential harm of AI particularly for minority and protected communities who may be overly impacted by introduction of these techniques. By removing that clause, agencies are more obligated to consider both immediate and downstream effect. This is in greater alignment with the requirements stated in Item 4: Risk Assessment and Management.

In Item 7: Fairness and Discrimination, on page 5 of the draft, the guidelines says that Applications can, in some instances, introduce real-world bias. This does not recognize the inherent biases that already exist in the data that has been captured and on which. As has been detailed by Safiya Noble[1], Cathy ONeil[2], and Virginia Eubanks[3] the datasets captured historically and currently, the reasons for those datasets, and ignoring the biases in those datasets have already created harm. Further use of AI without acknowledging these issues will not only introduce greater bias but will perpetuate harm along economic, race, religious, ethnic, insurance status, and other lines. Additionally, silence in the datasets, areas where data has not been captured can create harm. Obermeyer, et al described an example of this missing data in Science in October 2019, which found that a healthcare algorithm categorized black patients as less ill and at lower risk than white patients due to reliance on a flawed health care cost model,
leading to them receiving poorer care.[4] Without the acknowledgement of historical bias in the data to begin with, AI will perpetuate the structural bias for generations to come.

On Page 12 under the Assessing Risk heading, we are concerned that this does not account for natural data drift or other evolution of data over time. Thus algorithms could be built based on current data without understanding or anticipating future changes in data, which may create additional issues for privacy, bias, and other unexpected outcomes and harms.

On Page 13 under the Managing Risk heading, we are concerned that appropriate management of risk at each individual agency and the department under them will require extensive development of technical expertise and analytical capacity to determine both the risk of immediate usage of AI as well as future impact. This could serve as a regulatory burden to individual agencies as well as creating large variances between agencies in what is considered appropriate risk. It is recommended that national expertise or centralized vetting processes are developed in order to fully comprehend and anticipate risk.

1.Noble SU. Algorithms of Oppression: How Search Engines Reinforce Racism.; 2018.
2.ONeil C. Weapons of Math Destruction: How Big Data Increases Inequality and Threatens Democracy. Great Britain: Penguin Books; 2017.
3.Eubanks V. Automating Inequality: How High-Tech Tools Profile, Police, and Punish the Poor.; 2018.
4.Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations. Science. 2019;366(6464):447-453. doi:10.1126/science.aax2342

I recommend two classifications of artificial intelligence applications:
1) applications that guide the operation of machinery to reduce error and increase efficiency, and
2) applications that are intended to support or replace human decision making.

Examples of type 1 are AI that supports automated steering in vehicles, packing in factories, and storage/retrieval in warehouses. Examples of type 2 are AI that powers policy advice (e.g. financial or medical) or human surveillance.

Type 1 applications should require less strict regulation than type 2, as the success parameters are easier to measure and the symptoms and consequences of application failure are generally clear. In contrast, type 2 applications are more prone to have hidden complications and major negative social side effects that are hard to foresee. The testing and approval processes for type 2 AI applications should therefore be more deliberate and more rigorous.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2020-00261
comments.organization_name: The Hastings Center and Harvard Kennedy School
comments.comment_text:
At a time when delivery robots block the sidewalks, leaving wheelchair users stuck, when navigation apps create neighborhood traffic nightmares, when department stores secretly track customers' movements and sell the data, and when angry residents throw rocks at autonomous cars and throw scooters into the sea, it's tempting for Washington to override state and local laws on AI. In fact, the White House's draft memo on Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications seems designed to preempt state action. But the administration's statements about over-regulation suggest this is a call, not for a federal answer to these problems, but for the destruction of local solutions.

That would be a mistake.

In the absence of federal action, U.S. cities and states have been regulating facial recognition, autonomous vehicles, rideshare companies, and consumer data collection and sale, offering their residents additional protections and creating environments to test new ideas. As quickly changing technology creates new models and markets, local action offers a natural way to experiment with regulatory environments on a smaller scale before national policies are finalized.

However, even the biggest cities and states cannot do what the federal government can.

The federal government is in the best position to identify and address some kinds of AI risk, including those which come from cumulative or widespread use or which are threats to or through national infrastructure and networks. It can implement solutions that require significant financial resources, political power, collaboration across governments or with industry, or which might require rethinking common regulatory frameworks or creating national standards. It can take a broader view, offering protection across the U.S. and far beyond.

Congress and the White House should use local and international experience to help inform U.S. federal AI policy, provide protection for all residents by creating minimum national standards, and make limited use of federal preemption, at least for now. They should also work to build deep AI technical and policy capacity across all levels and sectors of government.

It's hard for governments to compete with AI industry salaries and there are great inefficiencies in each city or state or even each country separately building technical capacity and trying to think through all the societal implications of artificial intelligence and its applications. Many don't have the internal resources to do it well or even at all, leaving industry, academia and nonprofits filling the void: convening city and state leaders, providing tech education for policymakers and building and deploying AI and algorithms for city, state and federal services. Those organizations should all continue to contribute their expertise, but governments should not have to rely on it.

The federal government should create a national AI research and policy office, as a resource for local and federal agencies and policymakers, recruiting top talent and encouraging collaboration across all levels of government and across all sectors, providing a cost efficient way to develop, access and share unbiased AI technical and policy expertise. It should be done very quickly, this year. It might only be needed for a limited period, less than 20 years, but there's a pressing need right now.

The substantive work could be undertaken in collaboration with existing agencies or national research labs including the United States Digital Service, the Office of Science and Technology Policy, the national transportation lab Volpe, and the DOE's new Office of Artificial Intelligence. Each holds some of the resources that are needed, but none holds the mandate.

Governments across the world are trying to figure out what the benefits and risks of AI are, what safeguards should be in place and how high-level principles about trustworthy, responsible, or ethical AI or international human rights should translate to specific action or law about AI. We don't know how AI's unprecedented ability to autonomously pull together data, find patterns and make inferences online and in the physical world, cheaply, quickly and at a massive scale is affecting and will affect societies globally. We don't know how we want it to, or how to get there.

The administration's hands off approach to regulation won't answer these questions. Neither will regulations, not on their own.

Answering these questions will require significant investments in research and development, collaboration, negotiation, and experimentation, deep and careful thought across many fields, and leadership at all levels, across and between governments. But we can't wait until we have perfect answers to start to respond to the risks we see now.

The U.S. federal government is well positioned to lead, but if it won't, it should at least stay out of the way.

Request for Comments on a Draft Memorandum to the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies, "Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications," (Federal Register Doc. 2020-00261)

Dear Mr. Ray:

The U.S. Council for International Business (USCIB) is pleased to participate in this call for public comments concerning the Office of Management and Budget's draft "Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications." USCIB is a U.S.-based business association composed of U.S. multinational companies, law firms, and trade associations from every sector of the economy. Importantly, our membership includes a cross-section of leading global companies in the information and communications technology (ICT) sector as well as a diverse array of leader users of ICT technologies and emerging innovations, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI). We appreciate the opportunity to offer both a cross-sectoral and tech-informed perspective on proposed policies or regulations related to AI applications.

As the sole U.S. affiliate of Business at OECD, USCIB members played leading roles shaping the OECD's landmark AI Principles and subsequent OECD Council Recommendation on Artificial Intelligence. USCIB member experts from leading AI innovators such as IBM, Microsoft, Google, and Facebook were tapped to advise development of these principles, which the G20 Trade and Digital Economy Ministers subsequently endorsed at the June 8-9, 2019 meeting in Tsukuba, Japan. Although OMB's proposed AI regulatory guidance is outlined a bit differently from the OECD principles, USCIB members note with favor the high degree to which the OMB proposal aligns substantively with the OECD principles. This constitutes a solid foundation to build upon in considering appropriate policies and regulations for ever-evolving technology.

Key Alignments between OMB Proposed Guidance and OECD AI Principles

We would like to highlight elements of the OMB proposed guidance that are closely aligned with what we developed in the OECD and would like to see implemented in the United States.

Discouraging Premature Regulation - USCIB agrees that pre-emptive regulation risks hampering innovation that ultimately could contribute to economic development, commercial and employment opportunities, and societal well-being. We feel there is great potential for the application of AI in healthcare, "smart city" applications, optimizing and securing telecommunications networks, fraud prevention, financial services, transportation, agriculture, and enabling disabled individuals to become active participants in the digital economy, to name a few. We further concur that a "light touch" approach to regulation of AI is preferable until we develop a clear understanding through further research of how it may be applied beneficially to a variety of use cases, while at the same time addressing privacy, security, and other challenges.

Flexibility - We note that OECD AI Principle 2.3 urges development of a policy environment for AI that supports an "agile transition" from R&D to deployment. OMB's call for performance-based flexible frameworks when developing regulatory and non-regulatory approaches that can adapt to rapid changes and updates to AI applications is in the same spirit.

Safety and Security - USCIB commends OMB for highlighting the need for public trust in AI by designating this as the first principle. We share OMB's view concerning the importance of safety and security issues throughout the AI design, development and operation lifecycle.

Risk Assessment - USCIB strongly agrees that policy and regulatory approaches to AI should be based on consistent application of risk assessment and risk management practices. This concept is the cornerstone of the OECD's 2015 Digital Security Risk Management for Economic and Social Prosperity, which USCIB members also actively shaped as Expert Group participants.

Public Participation - OMB's proposed principles underscore the importance of the public comment process throughout the rulemaking process. They also urge agencies to inform the public and promote awareness of AI standards through the creation of informative documents. This is consistent with OECD's emphasis on initiating public dialogue to enhance understanding of AI and to debate AI-related opportunities and challenges for the economy, society, and the workplace to inform policymakers.

Please see the attached PDF for our comprehensive comments.

Sincerely yours,


Barbara P. Wanner
Vice President, ICT Policy

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2020-00261
comments.comment_text:
Regulation is going to get stuck. Because of how AI works, accuracy and fairness compete. An AI will be racist or sexist or unfair simply as a natural by-product of optimizing for accuracy or profit. It won't deliver "fair" or "trust" or "non-discriminatory" on its own. What makes AI regulation so difficult is that, although in theory, many existing laws can work just fine for AI, in practice there's a missing piece.

AI outpaces humans. It takes time for people to see that damage has been done and it's not possible to see the harm as it's happening. Reactive regulation will be ineffective because it leaves regulators without any technical way to regulate. All they have are organizational and human responses - oversight committees and corporate processes.

The regulation needs to be proactive. Here are two ways that can happen.

Real-time monitoring

We need humans to be able to understand what machines are doing, even if they can't match their speed and scale, or understand the deep complexity of the algorithms, data, and models. The financial industry has largely solved this problem. FINRA, the industry's self-regulatory agency has direct access to highly granular trading data with sensors placed directly into data feeds.

In a recent Brookings article, the authors of The Ethical Algorithm, explain how the financial industry uses technology to monitor technology. The solution is to monitor selectively; placing sensors where the most important algorithmic decisions are made and knowing what to looking for. This same idea could be applied to big tech AI - the science is understood, the measures are known and the techniques are available. Monitoring could theoretically be run completely from the outside, perhaps using composite systems or only at specified times. It could be built off to the side and never deployed in production. It could, in short, be non-intrusive.

Fairness by design

The behavior of an AI system relies to some extent on its post-design experience. In AI design, more effort has to go in upfront to define intent, anticipate consequences and uncover sources of bias. Fairness has to be designed in from the beginning.

Today, the problem is that it's an afterthought, if at all. Fairness slows down development. Most engineers and project managers have no experience with AI design and don't think about fairness. Many companies avoid fairness design and testing because of the legal liability of discovering that their AI is, in fact, unfair. Discovering discrimination leaves the company in a worse position.

Privacy-by-design is the precedent for fairness-by-design. Privacy-by-design was first thought of in the 1970s and was then incorporated in the 1990s into the data protection directives. Privacy-by-design principles are fundamental to GDPR and, although, in need of a refurb for the age of AI, they have had a meaningful impact in advancing better regulation.

In AI we need fairness-by-design in regulation because it's probably one of the best ways to have people think about the unique requirements of AI design. A mindset where speed and MVP (minimum viable product) is more important than fairness and MVD (minimum viable data) is a tough mindset to break. The market rewards the former and there are no guard rails to argue for the latter. No mal-intent is required for AI to be unfair.

We need regulation because we need people to start thinking more about what goes into AI; the people, the data, the design. In much the same way as regulation of food safety includes employees' hygiene ("employees must wash their hands before returning to work") we need regulations in AI that focus on the quality of the inputs.

We need to take a proactive rather than a reactive approach. Machines are too fast, are too big and do too much damage before anyone notices. Don't believe the story that AI regulation is a tweak on what we have in telecoms or utilities or media. We know the underlying science, which tells us how we can make use of intentional design principles and real-time monitoring in market-oriented ways so that we do not reveal proprietary intellectual property or stifle innovation.

The draft document states, "public trust" seven (7) times, yet the draft. which states, the policy of the United States Government [is] to sustain and enhance the scientific, technological, and economic leadership position of the United States in AI appears to contradict the very intent of standards, formalized processes that are utilized, very successfully and widely, in industries.

One of the first paragraphs in the draft, "Principles for the Stewardship of AI Applications" has a clearly misleading statement: AI applications do not necessarily raise novel issues. This is completely incorrect as professional conferences over the past 36 months talk about novel issues, novel opportunities. The IEEE Ethically Aligned by Design (IEEE EAD) authored formal documents that address the novel issues that AI is bringing to developers and consumers.

Paragraph 2, Public Participation, the draft provides not guiding principles on implementation as transparency is a must for AI to be realized in the market for Public use. Public trust and confidence can only be realized using formal standards that describe transparency, ethics and ethical behavior, privacy, and address bias.

Paragraph 4, Risk Assessment and Management, lacks substantive guiding principles that describe what this means and how to management; no oversight so no Public Trust. The implementation of Risk Assessment and Management can only be realized using standards, such as IEEE P7000, P7002, P7003, P7007.

Specifically calling out formal standards is the only ethical and practical way to implement AI in solutions that consumers, the People; trust in using, but only with formal standards. This draft document is not even a starting point. The draft fails to inspire, motivate, stipulate, communicate any formal mechanism related to "pubic trust" as it applies to AI. The development of Artificial Intelligence applications must be undertaken in a way that does not hinder the pace or originality of AI but also assures that AI applications have appropriate protections from improper use of data, risk of failure due to AI approaches, discrimination or improper applications of algorithms to violate personal protection, and lack of ability to interact with systems partially based on aI in order to correct, edit, or improve government systems partially based on AI.

That is, both weak and strong aI must allow agencies, individuals responsible for programs, Congress, affected individuals, and the public to understand how the AI program in question 1. Gathers data 2. Manipulates or collates date 3. Utilizes data to reach conclusions 4. Modifies use of data in subsequent iterations based on prior use and results, and 5. Achieves the intended policy, mathematical, program, and agency desired result as the purpose of introduction of AI into the federal agency.

For example, there have been examples of colection of dual data from HHS, unemployment, GI Bill, and VA data to assure appropriate levels of reimbursement for Veterans receiving certain benefits. If AI were introduced to attempt to duplicate or improve these functions, there should be clear understanding of how any AI system gathers, utilizes, and revises its use of data. Self-documentation of algorithms within AI systems, with archiving of previous versions and indication of changes to future versions would help such understanding, similar to the Clinical Trials.gov system of noting changes in clinical trials by date and areas changed.

It is not an impossibly high standard to require that AI systems be well understood, documented, and subject to audit for changes and differences in outcomes or use of data over time. A benefit risk framework similar to that adopted by the FDA for analyzing new drugs and therapies could be a useful analog for assessing aI implementation. This structure would be something like:

Process or Data Function Needing to Be Address (Decribe)
Significance or Importance of the Function to Which AI is to be ADDED (High, medium, low)
Existing systems and alternatives (Existing system, non-AI improvements, AI role in improving)
Benefits of Introduction of AI ( Speed, efficiency in data analysis, improved outcomes)
Risks of AI introduction (Discrimination, Errors in results, lack of understanding, System failure throug aI)
Conclusion on Benefit Risk of AI Process Introduction -net benefit in view of identified risks and alternatives.

As the example of recent failure of Boeing aircraft due to misunderstanding of systems to prevent stalls, leading
to crashes when data were improperly interpreted shows, the are significant risks to automated systems which are not well understood and cannot be adequately controlled by users. Captain Sully Sullenberger has often spoken of the paradox of automation, meaning that as automated systems take over pilot controls, failures of the automated system may produce unrecoverable accidental results, and inadequate human attention to systems and their operation. The possibility of failure of Artificial Intelligence can be mitigated by informed, documented implementation of systems wherein all users are fully aware of the processes and underlying algorithms which are being used.

The tone of the general memorandum is to suggest that agencies should not over regulate AI, but it should also provide that in terms of public participation, agencies should provide information about changes in AI systems as they develop (2. Public Participation, p. 3 and the Risk assessment, p. 4 would be improved by referring to Benefit-Risk assessment as discussed above. The benefits to be achieved should be weighed along with the risks resulting.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2020-00261
comments.comment_text:
Dear OMB members,

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on Draft Memorandum to the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies, Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications. This letter is a joint submission from four members of the Fort Collins MIRIx group, which is an AI safety meeting group connected to the Machine Intelligence Research Institute and is comprised of university and industry members based in Fort Collins, Colorado. The authors collectively have nearly 100 years of industry and academic experience in the fields of computer design, software engineering, artificial intelligence, computer security, machine learning, and computer graphics. Three of us contributed to the AI Race Safety through Agile Risk Management (https://www.cs.colostate.edu/~steveko/wp/publications/FCMIMLAIRiskMitigation.pdf ) proposal written in 2018 as part of an international effort to discuss methods to reduce risks related to international competition to develop AI. That document expands on the Memorandum section Non-Regulatory Approaches to AI and we encourage you to read, leverage, and reference it in the Memorandum.

Collectively we applaud the general tone and approach taken by the Memorandum encouraging agencies to avoid overly restrictive regulations and work with standards committees and the scientific community to establish best practices.

In cases where an AI application may have some risk indicating oversight is important, we feel that explicitly encouraging 3rd party reviews of the application and testing would be good to include (in the section on Non-Regulatory Approaches). Such reviews could be used to reduce legal or regulatory penalties in a way similar to GDPR guidelines in Europe (in which corporate fines are limited to 2% of annual revenues instead of 4% if GDPR practices were followed). Working to establish non-governmental review companies or organizations (akin to Underwriters Labs for electronics) could help with the Memorandums stated goals of providing flexible oversight.

With respect to international efforts, the United States can help lead the world in safe use of AI and also maintenance of personal and data privacy. While the Memorandum references such goals, it does not set explicit guidelines. Rules related to video and audio data gathered from homes or on private property should be considered.

The 2 best papers from ICML 2018 are relevant to the Memorandum and provide background for key points. Obfuscated Gradients Give a False Sense of Security: Circumventing Defenses to Adversarial Examples (https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.00420) deals with the challenge of insuring that a machine learning algorithm cannot be fooled by malicious attacks; while this gets a bit specific, adding the phrase well considered training cases for learning algorithms to insure correct generalizations into the Memorandum could be valuable. Delayed Impact of Fair Machine Learning (https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.04383) deals with the optimal point to set a machine learning algorithm when trying to address historical discrimination against a protected demographic group; again, a take-away for the Memorandum could be to add a note about adjusting learning algorithms to appropriately benefit protected and historically disadvantaged groups.

In relation to bias, we feel image recognition or other datasets should strive to have fair representations of key demographics in the population (in relation to race, sex, age, etc). Voice recognition should include representative accents from the population (Hispanic, indian, southern, Boston, etc).

Thank you for reading our feedback, and feel free to contact us if you have further questions.

Regards,
Steve Kommrusch (steve.kommrusch@gmail.com )
Ahmed Alawami
John Diamant
Dan Yee

DLA Piper Global Law Firm is pleased to provide a beta version of its Artificial Intelligence Scorebox in response to the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s RFI (NIST-2021-0004-0001) to help inform the development of a framework for managing risks associated with artificial intelligence.

DLA Piper built its AI Scorebox as a means to help organizations and businesses assess AI adoption readiness and governance maturity based on a series of questions and criteria. DLA Piper’s global team assessed various approaches to AI regulation being developed by governmental organizations including the G20, OECD, European Commission, Council of Europe, White House Executive Order 13859 and many others. This “common ground” analysis led to the synthesis of key concerns and risks for the deployment of complex AI technology use cases in an ethical and legally compliant way.

For all organizations we would suggest the involvement of legal, technical, financial, ethics, and senior leadership since the deployment of AI is something that needs to be assessed from many perspectives within an organization. By utilizing this AI Scorebox, organizations around the world can prepare and position themselves in the best way possible for adopting sustainable AI technologies into their business models.

We believe our AI Scorebox is consistent with NIST’s intent to frame the development of new approaches to address characteristics of trustworthiness, including accuracy, reliability, privacy, security and safety.

To access the beta version of DLA Piper’s AI Scorebox, please use the following address: http://ai-scorebox.opencms.co.za/index.html.

DLA Piper is a global law firm with lawyers located in more than 40 countries throughout the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia Pacific. DLA Piper established its Artificial Intelligence practice in May 2019.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2021-16176
comments.comment_text:
NIST is requesting information related to the following topics:
1. The greatest challenges in improving how AI actors manage AI-related risks—where “manage” means identify, assess, prioritize, respond to, or communicate those risks;
*Voluntary Participation and Reporting is likely insufficient. Mandatory reporting must be required.

2. How organizations currently define and manage characteristics of AI trustworthiness and whether there are important characteristics which should be considered in the Framework besides: Accuracy, explainability and interpretability, reliability, privacy, robustness, safety, security (resilience), and mitigation of harmful bias, or harmful outcomes from misuse of the AI;
*A Complete Standard for Hazard Identification and Mitigation, Threat Identification and Risk, and Specific Scoped Vulnerability must be created and maintained for all eternity.

3. How organizations currently define and manage principles of AI trustworthiness and whether there are important principles which should be considered in the Framework besides: Transparency, fairness, and accountability;
*Project Motivation and Specific, Issue-Based, Moral Value Statements with Proof-of-No-Conflict documents must be recorded.

4. The extent to which AI risks are incorporated into different organizations' overarching enterprise risk management—including, but not limited to, the management of risks related to cybersecurity, privacy, and safety;
*At last, Enterprise must formally be welcomed into the fold of Managed Risk, just as Infrastructure and others have before it. There are classifications, Tiers, and Strategies.

5. Standards, frameworks, models, methodologies, tools, guidelines and best practices, and principles to identify, assess, prioritize, mitigate, or communicate AI risk and whether any currently meet the minimum attributes described above;
*Start with the basic inclusions of RAMCAP, and work your way out.

6. How current regulatory or regulatory reporting requirements (e.g., local, state, national, international) relate to the use of AI standards, frameworks, models, methodologies, tools, guidelines and best practices, and principles;
*I envision something like the current practices of Building Planning, with the ongoing practices of Emissions Monitoring, with similar penalties and practices.

7. AI risk management standards, frameworks, models, methodologies, tools, guidelines and best practices, principles, and practices which NIST should consider to ensure that the AI RMF aligns with and supports other efforts;
*Existing Hazard, Threat, Risk, Vulnerability and Resource-Use Planning methods should be used and expanded upon.

8. How organizations take into account benefits and issues related to inclusiveness in AI design, development, use and evaluation—and how AI design and development may be carried out in a way that reduces or manages the risk of potential negative impact on individuals, groups, and society.
*Once again, Mandatory reporting of project Motivations into the public record, with customer/stakeholder accountability from the project owners, is the best and only perceived way.

9. The appropriateness of the attributes NIST has developed for the AI Risk Management Framework. (See above, “AI RMF Development and Attributes”);
10. Effective ways to structure the Framework to achieve the desired goals, including, but not limited to, integrating AI risk management processes with organizational processes for developing products and services for better outcomes in terms of trustworthiness and management of AI risks. Respondents are asked to identify any current models which would be effective. These could include—but are not limited to—the NIST Cybersecurity Framework or Privacy Framework, which focus on outcomes, functions, categories and subcategories and also offer options for developing profiles reflecting current and desired approaches as well as tiers to describe degree of framework implementation; and
*Understanding the existence of AI Agents/Entities as primarily a “Risk to be Reduced with Untold Benefits” drives the contriving of a Risk-Mitigation-First Framework. (please see my attached comments)

11. How the Framework could be developed to advance the recruitment, hiring, development, and retention of a knowledgeable and skilled workforce necessary to perform AI-related functions within organizations.
*(please see my attached comments)

12. The extent to which the Framework should include governance issues, including but not limited to make up of design and development teams, monitoring and evaluation, and grievance and redress.”
*(please see my attached comments)

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2021-16176
comments.comment_text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is not only advancing fast, but it has also been a rapidly accepted technology that is currently being utilized throughout various industries to increase effectiveness, understand processes, provide insight, and alleviate burden from workers in order to allow them to focus on higher cognitive loading tasks. However, regulatory and security understanding has not kept up with this advance in technology and therefore has not changed to incorporate fairness, security, explainability, or proper reporting measures into the development and usage of these tools. Therefore it is with great pleasure that I respond to this RFI as the Principal Researcher of Rotunda Solutions, Inc, so that we may provide our understanding of this field into this very important work.

Rotunda Solutions is a Systems Engineering and Data Analytics firm with clients throughout the Federal Government, as well as the commerical, academic, and non-profit sectors. Rotunda provides consulting services to these entities and regularly engages with its academic and industrial colleagues through publication, conference presentation and attendance, and assistance in the development of policy related to these fields. A key pillar of the Rotunda Analytics and Innovation Lab (RAIL)—the research wing of Rotunda Solutions—revolves around AI security and fairness. In addition, Rotunda prides itself on the usage, research, and development of explainable AI technologies, as well as its ability to explain these technologies to both technical and non-technical audiences. Pertaining to this RFI, employees of Rotunda Solutions have actively served on various efforts with clientle, research, and policy regarding AI security, fairness, and ethics.

The development of a Risk Mitigation Framework (RMF) must consider methodologies which incorporate current industrial and academic understanding of security vulernabilites and mitigation techniques, inherent bias and fairness concerns, ethical considerations, and the ability to understand how a particular tool arrived at its conclusion. This includes not only the development of the algorithms and models themselves, but also the collection, storage, transfer, and sharing of datasets utilized to develop such technologies. Current efforts at Rotunda Solutions are focused on the research and development of methodologies within fields of AI Security in order to provide users with the ability to understand not only the vulnerability of their assets to various adversarial attacks, but also to understand the origin of these vulnerabilities and how to mitigate their affect without degrading the effectiveness of developed AI techniques. This is a core area in which effort must be focused: how can AI be made secure, explainable, and fair, while remaining effective. These areas can often be seen in competition. Often, the more secure an AI tool becomes, the less effective it can be. In addition, fairer tools tend to be more complex whether through extensive data collection or extensive model development. The construction of an RMF which encorporates such a fast-paced technology can only be done through consensus and the ability for evolution of the RMF as the technology advances.

comments.comment_text:
The AI Village* welcomes the NIST RFI on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework. Such a framework is long overdue to confidently adopt AI in production systems, including mission-, security- and safety-critical applications.
Our response is articulated on five axes: (i) concrete and current risk, (ii) actionability, (iii) organizations focus, (iv) case specific and (v) existing and upcoming standards.

More specifically each of those five axes tries to answer a specific need of the framework:

Concrete and current risk: This addresses the lack of adequate and easily manipulable risk definition in the case of AI systems and the current divide between risks faced today in production by organizations and the hypothetical and future risks considered in a number of Reliable AI academic publications. As a strongly industry focused organization, we believe the former should be given immediate priority and the latter should be used primarily as a support vector for threat anticipation.

Actionability: This axis addresses the current difficulty in making AI risk assessments and mitigation operational including both the methodological and tooling gaps in conducting end-to-end AI risk assessments. We identify gaps in enforceability as well as current risk and testing methodologies that will need to be filled ahead of proper AI risk assessment engagements.

Organizational focus: By this axis we address the incentives, budget obtention, team reorganizations, business integration and related organizational challenges that implementers will eventually face in their respective organizations. The framework will need to provide answers on those points to ease its deployment in complex governance schemes.

Case specific: By this axis we seek to address specific challenges that will arise on a case by case basis and which a generic framework might be incapable of covering. In our response, we take specific attention in addressing both large and small organizations, specific industries like finance, ICS and pharmaceuticals etc.

Existing and upcoming standards: Our submission draws heavily from a number of existing and upcoming security, privacy and AI regulations that are listed in appendix A. We curated this list based on their relevance and implementation likelihood in target organizations. The upcoming AI Risk framework should tightly integrate with those to limit conflicts and necessary additional work, thereby facilitating adoption.

Our full response is included in separate file.

*The AI Village is a community of hackers and data scientists working to educate the world on the use and abuse of artificial intelligence in security and privacy. We are academics, IT specialists, security experts, students, philosophers, and concerned citizens.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2021-16176
comments.comment_text:
Consider aligning with CAN/CIOSC 101:2019, Ethical design and use of automated decision systems.

In October 2019, the CIO Strategy Council published a National Standard of Canada for automated decision systems — the world’s first consensus-based standard helping organizations design and implement responsible artificial intelligence (AI) solutions.

The CIO Strategy Council engaged over 100 thought leaders and experts from governments, industry, academia and civil society groups from coast-to-coast-to-coast in developing the National Standard of Canada, CAN/CIOSC 101:2019, Ethical design and use of automated decision systems.

CAN/CIOSC 101:2019 specifies the minimum requirements in protecting human values and incorporating ethics in the design and use of artificial intelligence (AI) using machine learning for automated decisions.

This national standard goes beyond a common set of aspirational principles. It provides a framework and process that can be both measured and tested for conformity, providing consumers with confidence in the technologies that are providing information, recommendations, or making decisions using AI and machine learning.

The national standard applies to all organizations including public and private companies, government entities, and not-for-profit organizations, and helps organizations address AI ethics principles, such as those described by the OECD:

AI should benefit people and the planet by driving inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being.

AI systems should be designed in a way that respects the rule of law, human rights, democratic values and diversity, and they should include appropriate safeguards – for example, enabling human intervention where necessary – to ensure a fair and just society.

There should be transparency and responsible disclosure around AI systems to ensure that people understand AI-based outcomes and can challenge them.

AI systems must function in a robust, secure and safe way throughout their life cycles and potential risks should be continually assessed and managed.

Organizations and individuals developing, deploying or operating AI systems should be held accountable for their proper functioning in line with the above principles.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2021-16176
comments.comment_text:
NIST-2021-0004 National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework

I thank the NIST on the development of an AI risk management framework and the opportunity to provide input.

ENCOURAGE MODERN INNOVATION
Creating boundaries is a great way to spur true innovation. In an environment with little regulation or oversight, the market - in particular - will take the path of least resistance to reach their primary objective(s) which are generally: capturing market share, being the first to market, and maximizing shareholder value. Rules of the road will challenge the AI ecosystem to also take into consideration external factors such as societal and ethical impacts that should be a prerequisite for modern innovation.

PRESERVE EXISTING CONSUMER PROTECTIONS
Quickly evolving AI makes regulation a challenge. However, the AI ecosystem should still abide by existing consumer protection laws that address traditional human activity, particularly in aspects where augmented by automated-decision-making technology.

ACCOUNTABILITY ALONG THE VALUE CHAIN
With an ever-growing market for white-label products, considerations should be taken in providing guidance for white-label AI providers, including prevention of unauthorized use and accountability along the value chain. Because product liability laws are sparse in this area, guidance should be welcomed.

ENCOURAGE INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION
As a code of ethics and self-regulation will not be enough, the AI ecosystem should be open to independent testing and verification. Right now, the AI industry is rife with overpromising or mis-representing capabilities. There should be a mechanism to verify claims of AI capabilities and limitations.

BE TRANSPARENT AND PROVIDE DISCLOSURES
Generally, consumers are unaware that they interact with AI when they receive advertising, information, prices, or decisions made about them. As such, consumers cannot view, correct or opt-out of automated systems. The AI ecosystem should be transparent and upfront about the use of AI. As appropriate, disclosures should include what data is used and how that data is used to arrive at decisions.

OFFERING GUIDANCE FOR RECOURSE
It is not sufficient for the AI ecosystem to be transparent and provide disclosures. Opportunities for recourse should be provided, such as an ‘adverse action’ notice. This is of particular importance with the rise of the use of AI - and personal data - for surveillance by governments and the private sector. The AI ecosystem should move in the direction of proactively balancing the advancement of AI while protecting basic rights like privacy.

Thanks,

Yadi

8. How organizations take into account benefits and issues related to inclusiveness in AI design, development, use and evaluation – and how AI design and development may be carried out in a way that reduces or manages the risk of potential negative impact on individuals, groups, and society.

Answer: Organizations should provide continuous investment in the growth and maturation of AI engineering by engaging the broader AI research community through academic partnerships, providing specific opportunities for early-career researchers, and safely and responsibly integrating AI technology into larger, complex engineered system. They should establish a program for training and education that is relevant to the respective AI-related skills and knowledge required of personnel who develop, use, or manage AI solutions. Various AI training programs tailored to the specific roles and responsibilities should be made widely available. Communities of Practice (CoPs) should be established to promote engagement and information exchange, as well as to ensure that wide range of practitioners understand the potential adversary impact AI may have on tasks, individuals, groups, or society as a whole and monitor and reduce the associated risks.

11. How the Framework could be developed to advance the recruitment, hiring, development, and retention of a knowledgeable and skilled workforce necessary to perform AI-related functions within organizations.
Answer: Organizations should consider relying on innovative companies and academic partnerships to develop cutting edge AI methods, since they are better positioned to retain R&D talent. In addition, there is a need for specific guidance and tools for project managers to balance explainability, accuracy, repeatability, potential biases and their tradeoffs and make the appropriate decision for a project. Areas for increased focus should include AI competitive and escalatory dynamics and avoiding “black box” problem with AI. Organizations should provide training to the employees at the appropriate levels to create understanding of the technology, development processes, and operational methods of its AI, including transparent and auditable methodologies, data sources, design procedure, and documentation.

comments.comment_text: While the federal government should take action to prevent the theft of sensitive data and intellectual property, as it is within the role of the federal government to protect critical U.S. infrastructure, it is unclear whether the proposed rule will accomplish that goal. Some of the language of the proposed rule is vague and allows for significant bureaucratic discretion, such as the requirement for IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) firms to adopt and adhere to "security best practices". The lack of direction in the development of "security best practices" is concerning because firms or bureaucrats can define said practices in whatever manner they deem appropriate with little to no oversight. Another area of concern is the lack of methods for implementation of the requirements in the proposed rule. For example, the Department is still looking for recommendations on the implementation of the ID verification of foreign actors attempting to use U.S. IaaS services. This seems like a relatively basic aspect of securing IaaS services from foreign cyber attacks that ought to be defined in the proposed rule. The federal government should pursue the goal of protecting intellectual property and critical U.S. infrastructure from malicious cyber attacks, but the methods for implementing said goal should be more clearly defined witht he assistance of relevant stakeholders and experts in the cybersecurity community.

The following information is contained in the 2021 Technology In Industry Report, compiled and published by Automation Alley in Troy, MI. It is distributed to the members of Automation Alley for their education and benefit.
Foreword
After years of stagnation, punctuated by a global health crisis, the manufacturing sector is poised for a boom—and Industry 4.0 technologies are leading the way.

While the COVID-19 pandemic exposed manufacturing supply chain vulnerabilities, it also demonstrated the power of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, as digital technologies played a critical role in the pandemic response for many companies. It was also a wake-up call to the world that resiliency and agility must have an equal seat at the table to efficiency. These realizations are now placing new pressures on manufacturers to innovate.

Emerging tech continues to transform the world of production—creating competitive advantage for companies and unlocking new value for industry, society and our environment. However, it is also creating profound uncertainty for small and medium-sized manufacturers (SMEs), as well as the global workforce.

Automation Alley, the Industry 4.0 knowledge center, exists to help companies of all sizes navigate the digital transformation. Our annual Technology in Industry Report, a collaboration between regional academic and industry leaders, provides a deep dive into smart technology trends, case studies that demonstrate technology adoption and ROI and action items designed to guide businesses to strategic success.

What we have learned from our collective 2021 research, and through conversations with SMEs, is that their roadblocks to Industry 4.0 adoption are extraordinarily similar. Companies consistently report 1) a lack of technology knowledge and expertise, 2) a lack of financial resources, 3) a lack of awareness of the need and/or relationship to the bottom line, and 4) a lack of visionary leadership and/or cultural appetite for adoption.

Though these roadblocks exist, and they present real challenges for SMEs, we have seen remarkable progress and change over the last several years when it comes to Industry 4.0 awareness and adoption. Here in Michigan, SMEs are much more aware today of Industry 4.0 and the benefits of digital transformation. In addition, SMEs are no longer intimidated by technology, and are becoming much more comfortable with technologies like 3D printing, collaborative robotics and artificial intelligence (to name a few); and more importantly, experimenting with ways these technologies can work together.

The journey ahead will not be smooth sailing, as we adjust to continued pandemic challenges. And as Industry 4.0 accelerates, what you know may or may not be valid going forward. Technology will change the business model in which you’ve always operated.

Success will be measured by how companies large and small commit to building a culture where people feel free to create change; where technology isn’t something we fear, but something we embrace. We applaud the early adopters. Will you be a fast follower?
