comments.title: Comment from Anonymous
comments.comment_text:
While the memo is well-structured, the most likely outcome is that agencies ignore parts of it. It strikes of being balanced, but adds too much overhead. Some simple fixes, and a recognition of existing policy (PIAs, ATOs) would make this policy more implementable, as opposed to forcing agencies to pretend to comply. A few points:
1. The requirement that "Evaluation of a potential vendor, commercial capability, or freely available AI capability that is not otherwise used in agency operations, solely for the purpose of making a procurement or acquisition decision;" should be changed to "solely for the purpose of making a procurement or feasibility decision" This relies on the antiquated notion that all systems development occurs through the procurement avenue, where, even if teams tend to be contractors, they are often functioning as staff augmentation, not as "products." No federal technology team would go through a compliance effort like this (public consultations, testing and evaluation, opt-out, etc.) without having shown to leadership that the solution has the potential to be feasible. It is too great an overhead risk to do otherwise. To be clear, agencies will conduct feasibility testing anyway (and without the minimal practices), whether the memo sanctions it or not. It would be productive to call it out so it is clearly documented and grassroot agency initiatives are not squashed where individuals don't have enough political capital to ignore this memo while they perform essential feasibility testing (in non-production contexts).
2. Giving until August 1, 2024 is not realistic for waivers. Given that the memo is likely not to be finalized until early 2024, you are providing agencies 6 months to do significant overhauls of potential hundreds (thousands?) of systems. While a waiver is a good flexibility, even having agencies get organized around this and hire compliance staff (it won't be CAIOs doing it themselves), will take longer than 6 months from time of the memo release.
3. The data reporting requirement is a poison pill for generative AI applications. For example, OpenAI is extremely unlikely to provide "how errors from data entry, machine processing, or other sources are adequately measured and limited, to include errors from relying on AIgenerated data as training data or model inputs." Has the White House/OMB consulted with Microsoft/Anthropic/OpenAI on whether they would ever consider providing this type of documentation to agencies? This seems unreasonably heavy-handed and is unclear what actionable information would come from some of these requirements. If errors sometimes slip through, but the system has been rigorously tested and evaluated and shows no discernible bias and is subject to human oversight, opt-out, and intervention, is this really so important? A simple fix would be to build in flexibility, for example rewriting the data reporting "to include, as appropriate..."
4. Maintain human consideration and remedy processes. Human consideration makes sense but the remedy process will inevitably lead to huge build-ups in the number of people seeking remedy. If you receive an adverse outcome from the government and are notified that AI was used, why wouldn't you try to seek remedy regardless of merit? Stronger would be to add "agencies may consider combining the remedy process with existing appeal or secondary review processes, where present, provided that there are clear instructions or options to denote the affected individual's concern about the impact of AI on the decision."
5. The opt-out language "An opt-out mechanism must exist where the affected people have a reasonable expectation of an alternative" is very weak and is likely to cause many many challenges with internal agency counsel teams who are not tech savvy and value human consideration highly. Why not just keep it to "where lack of an alternative would meaningfully limit accessibility or create unwarranted harmful impacts"? Since AI, especially more advanced AI implementations are newer, in *most* cases people reasonably expect there to be a human process, so this makes this section apply to almost everything. The reality is often AI will be put in place as an automation vehicle for cost-savings and streamlining processes. It is a problem of the masses where if every AI system has opt-out available, even where all the other strong practices in this memo are in place, individuals will still choose to opt-out so they get the full human review negating the point of doing AI in the first place. Please consider a few scenarios: license plate readers...would anyone not choose to opt out of that, given that it is likely to give you a ticket if you go a couple above the speed limit? Systems to detect cheating, even if you are not cheating, wouldn't you opt-out of a system that to make sure the AI system doesn't accidentally flag you, what incentive do you have to opt-in? And many more. Please consider refining this section.

comments.title: Comment from Stephen Lawton
comments.comment_text:
Please see the enclosed PDF with 8 questions answered. I concluded my answers with the following:

I support the overall goals of the draft memorandum, which are to advance responsible AI innovation and to manage the risks associated with the use of AI by federal agencies. I believe that the memorandum provides a good framework for agencies to develop and implement effective AI governance programs.

With that being said, my key concern is who Nvidia is allowed to do business with.

Here are some factors to consider when making this decision:
•The entity's track record of responsible AI use.
•The entity's commitment to human rights and ethical values.
•The potential for the entity to use NVIDIA products for malicious purposes.
•The benefits of allowing the entity to use NVIDIA products, such as the advancement of scientific research or the development of new products and services.
It is also important to note that NVIDIA has a number of policies and procedures in place to mitigate the risks of its products being used for malicious purposes. For example, NVIDIA has a Code of Conduct that prohibits its employees and customers from using NVIDIA products for illegal or unethical purposes. NVIDIA also has a number of technical safeguards in place to prevent its products from being used for malicious purposes, such as encryption and authentication.
Ultimately, the decision of whether or not to allow NVIDIA to do business with a particular entity is a complex one that must be made on a case-by-case basis. There is no easy answer, and there will always be some risk involved. However, by carefully considering the factors discussed above, decision-makers can help to ensure that NVIDIA products are used for good and not for harm.
In the specific case of Del Complex, I would recommend that OMB carefully consider the company's plan to develop AI offshore with lax regulations or no regulations at all. This raises concerns about the company's commitment to responsible AI use and human rights. Additionally, Del Complex's plan to launch barges into international waters beginning next year to develop AI outside of the reach of regulators is concerning. This plan could make it more difficult to oversee and mitigate the risks associated with Del Complex's use of AI.
Overall, I believe that the risks of allowing NVIDIA to do business with Del Complex outweigh the benefits. I urge OMB to disallow NVIDIA from providing H100 GPUs to Del Complex.

comments.title: Comment from Joshua Brown
comments.comment_text:
Proper security controls should be placed on any AI system that interacts with data flows, both inbound and outbound, to and from an agency. There will not be tools of high quality to support defending an AI system nor filtering its outputs, whether they be actions or information, for a very long time. It would be concerning for agencies to build support onto AI systems that do not have strong mitigations for threats and risks from using these systems.

Training should be a top priority for agencies. The expectation is that all agencies will need to embrace and utilize the power of AI and AI like systems. Education needs to be treated with urgency. Safety and bias are commonly known risks; as well as ways to leverage the technology. Currently, training and education is going to technical engineering teams and some people tinkering, motivated by the hype. However, it's critical that we train all staff to understand the bias, limitations, hallucinations, trustworthy answers, and answer validation. To draw a comparison, I use the example of a statistics course. Understanding statistics and when false attributions are made with them is an important skill set that the whole workforce should understand and avoid.

Proposal:
1. Build a baseline AI Policy for all agencies to follow.
2. Scope should include private or SaaS based AI systems.
3. Build a list of technical controls for the strong authZ+MFA/authN of an AI system.
4. Implement secure data transmission protocols for both inbound and outbound data flows.
5. Use data loss prevention (DLP) tools to monitor and control data transfer.
6. Employ network segmentation and firewall rules to regulate data access and flow.
7. Deploy intrusion detection and prevention systems (IDPS) to detect and prevent malicious activities.
8. Regularly update and patch AI systems to mitigate vulnerabilities.
9. Develop and implement algorithms for output validation to detect and filter out biased or incorrect outputs.
10. Use anomaly detection systems to identify unusual AI behaviors or outputs.
11. Conduct regular risk assessments to identify and mitigate potential threats.
12. Implement incident response plans specifically tailored for AI systems.
13. Use threat intelligence to stay informed about emerging risks related to AI.
14. Develop training modules focusing on AI safety, bias recognition, and ethical use.
15. Include training on understanding AI limitations, hallucinations, and trustworthy answer validation.
16. Extend AI education beyond technical teams to all staff, similar to foundational statistics training.
17. Implement tools and practices for continuous monitoring of AI decisions for bias.
18. Establish ethical guidelines for AI use and ensure compliance through regular audits.
19. Use explainable AI (XAI) frameworks to make AI decision-making processes transparent.
20. Document AI models and their decision-making processes for review and validation.
21. Conduct periodic audits of AI systems for security, compliance, and ethical adherence.
22. Review and update AI models regularly to ensure they reflect current data and ethical standards.

Other points to consider:
1. Implement techniques like differential privacy to protect individual data within datasets used by AI.
2. Use homomorphic encryption to enable computation on encrypted data, enhancing privacy.
3. Develop AI systems to be resilient against adversarial attacks (e.g., input data designed to trick the AI).
4. Regularly test AI models against adversarial examples and update them to handle such scenarios.
5. Beyond transparency, ensure that AI decisions can be interpreted and understood by non-technical stakeholders.
6. Use tools and frameworks that provide insights into how and why decisions are made by AI models.
7. Implement continuous monitoring systems to track AI performance and behavior over time.
8. Establish feedback mechanisms to learn from AI decisions and improve models iteratively.
9. Establish a governance framework and team to oversee AI ethics, including fairness, accountability, and societal impact.
10. Regularly review and update AI policies to align with evolving ethical standards and societal values.
11. Engage with various stakeholders, including legal, regulatory, and domain experts, to ensure comprehensive AI governance.
12. Foster a culture of collaboration and transparency in AI development and deployment.
13. Stay informed about and comply with relevant AI regulations and standards, both locally and globally with corresponding SLAs.
14. Conduct legal reviews to ensure AI applications meet all regulatory requirements and ethical standards.

comments.comment_text: It is extremely unclear what authority OMB has to insist that "By August 1, 2024, agencies must implement the minimum practices in Section 5(c) of this memorandum for safety-impacting or rights-impacting AI, or else stop using any AI that is not compliant with the minimum practices, consistent with the details and caveats in that section." The AI in Government act does not appear to give OMB specific abilities to do this and while I know that OMB is interested in having additional oversight of individual system authorizations, it is not clear that they can actually prevent an agency head from launching a system. This should be rectified by using "should" language as strong encouragement, as opposed to must, for which no citation of OMB's authority is provided. While I am commenting anonymously, since I am affiliated with an agency but not yet authorized to speak directly on its behalf, I can say that OMB insisting it has this authority does not appear to be in the text of the law which simply states that OMB will "IDENTIFY [emphasis added] best practices for identifying, assessing, and mitigating any discriminatory impact or bias on the basis of any classification protected under Federal nondiscrimination laws." This does not appear to empower OMB, at all, to block system deployment. If there are other authorities being used, it is frankly irresponsible for OMB to issue this memo without citing that authority so that agencies can provide that context to their appropriate counsel if escalation is needed. Though it is more likely that we will simply ignore OMB policies that are not grounded in statutory authority.

comments.title: Comment on OMB-2023-0020-0001
comments.comment_text:
The City of San José Information Technology Department appreciates the opportunity to submit comments in response to the request for comment on the proposed draft memorandum titled “Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence” by the Office of Management and Budget (the OMB Memo).

In late 2022, the Digital Privacy Office (DPO) began the initial governance of AI systems as a natural extension of governing data policies and data processing. Starting with procurement reviews, the City’s AI governance has evolved into Generative AI initiatives, and impact assessments. Recently, San José began a coalition of over 100 state and local agencies to build a standardized approach to AI governance, policy, and vendor accountability. We hope to connect the Coalition’s work with the efforts at OMB and the broader Federal government.
Summary of Comments
We celebrate the OMB memo as a vital step towards comprehensive AI policy for U.S. public agencies.

•Chief AI Officer (CAIO): Our experience at San José has demonstrated the need for a designated lead on AI policy and governance. The CAIO needs to lead across AI governance, procurement, and technical projects. This ensures all AI projects follow responsible AI governance and fosters mutual maturity between policy and practical implementation of technology. The City’s CAIO function is currently served by technical and project management leads with the Digital Privacy Officer, but may vary based on where technology policies are managed in an agency.

•Leveraging existing governing bodies: The City has leveraged its Digital Privacy Officer and existing privacy and data governing bodies to handle AI governance. The City found that stakeholders for both Privacy and AI overlapped considerably, and we recommend exploring if the same is true at your agencies to minimize additional overhead.

•Vendor accountability: When implementing our impact assessment framework at the City of San José, we experienced varying levels of cooperation across vendors in obtaining information around the “nutrition facts” of their AI systems. Larger vendors were often unresponsive or unwilling to provide us information about the AI system. Having a standardized “nutrition facts” requirement for all AI systems enforced at the federal level would solve this problem.

•Generative AI: Agencies should leverage generative AI tools for creating initial drafts of content while establishing safeguards to ensure responsible use. To promote the responsible use of generative AI tools, the City of San José and many others have released Generative AI Guidelines to help City employees leverage the benefits of generative AI tools while understanding and mitigating its risks.

•Minimum practices: The minimum practices outlined in the memo may be too aggressive for agencies to implement by the desired timeline. Agencies with a lower AI maturity may struggle to successfully implement all minimum requirements by the deadline.

Our detailed comments can be found in the attached document titled "231205 OMB Public Comment City of San José". Additional attachments are explained in our detailed comments.

comments.title: Comment on OMB-2023-0020-0001
comments.comment_text:
Attached are comments from CAP, Public Citizen, Public Knowledge, and numerous other organizations in response to the Request for Comments: Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence Draft Memorandum.

Throughout 2023, numerous civil, technology, and human rights groups called for the Executive Branch to take immediate executive action on artificial intelligence (AI)i and to center the White House Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights. The President’s Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI EO) represents a strong start on the guidance needed to ensure the development of safe and effective AI.iv The accompanying draft OMB guidance, “Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence,” represents essential and needed guidance for federal agencies, contractors, and grantees that are already using AI systems.

We believe it is essential to meaningfully center civil rights and equity in the implementation of these executive actions. Most centrally, that means building on the AI Bill of Rights and requiring that AI systems be shown to be effective, safe, and nondiscriminatory before use; further enumerating rights-impacting and safety-impacting uses that inherently pose the greatest risk; ensuring a broad scope by strengthening procurement language and increasing specificity around waivers and exemptions; ensuring adequate resourcing for implementation; and publishing guidance prior to using generative AI. Agencies should also consider alternative solutions when evaluating AI systems and continue to inventory their AI regulatory authority. Attached, we provide brief comments on each of these elements.

comments.title: Comment from Fred Oswald
comments.comment_text:
This brief comment is to emphasize worker, workforce, and organization-relevant implications of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) draft memorandum, "Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)." In particular, AI and machine learning in all their various forms:

* will likely accelerate in their abilities (a) to create opportunities for new jobs and entire occupations, (b) to alter required job skills for existing jobs fundamentally, and (c) to replace certain jobs or essential job tasks (Selenko et al., 2022);

* require a continuous re-examination of the knowledge, skills, abilities, and other essential worker requirements across occupations (National Center for O*NET Development, 2023), with wide-ranging implications for both workers and the workforce;

* carry major implications for both technical and socio-technical aspects of AI-specific education and workforce training (NAIAC, 2023), as well as the reskilling of existing worker skills that have been fundamentally altered by AI tools and systems;

* alter the nature of organizational systems of recruiting, hiring, training, and promoting, and the manner in which these functions will be conducted.

OMB guidance will stand to benefit from considering all these interrelated points above and how they can lead to tangible actions for assessing, forecasting, intervening, and improving the AI workforce across federal agencies. The end goal is to improve AI infrastructure within federal agencies and in their relationships with one another. This not only means increasing workers' AI-related capabilities and capacities in terms of their own functioning; it also means equipping workers with the ability to assess the nature and balance of AI benefits and risks adequately, taking into account the broader sociotechnical work environment in which AI and machine learning systems operate.

In closing, please note that I am a member of the National Artificial Intelligence Advisory Committee (NAIAC), but I speak here in my own personal capacity.

Best regards,
Fred Oswald
Professor and Herbert S. Autrey Chair in Social Sciences
Rice University

References

National Artificial Intelligence Advisory Committee (NAIAC, 2023). Recommendations: National campaign on lifelong AI career success. https://ai.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Recommendations_National-Campaign-on-Lifelong-AI-Career-Success.pdf

Re: Request for Comments: Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence Draft Memorandum; FR Doc. 2023-24269, 23 Nov. 2023.

Dear Ms. Martorana,

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has the potential to dramatically impact nearly all the federal government’s operations and engagement with the American people. The opportunities and risks of AI, combined with the power of the state, places an even greater burden on the federal government to ensure its ethical use of AI, especially when AI is used for purposes that impact safety or rights. The federal government, its contractors, and its grantees’ use of AI should only be allowed if those AI systems are effective, safe, and nondiscriminatory.

The Center for American Progress (CAP) has called for the Executive Branch to take immediate action on AI and has joined the civil rights community and other allies in advocating for centering the White House Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights (AI Bill of Rights) in any AI executive order (EO) and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) guidance. The President’s Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI EO) represents a strong start on the guidance needed to ensure the development of safe and effective AI.

The accompanying draft OMB guidance “Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence” is essential guidance for federal agencies and contractors that are already using AI systems. Particularly worthy of praise is the draft guidance’s definition of safety-impacting and rights-impacting AI and purposes that are presumed to be safety-impacting and rights-impacting. These thoughtful definitions are an important step forward in outlining the conditions in which the use of AI requires extra attention and caution.

Below CAP provides the following response to the Request for Comments: Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence Draft Memorandum; FR Doc. 2023-24269. Please contact Adam Conner (aconner@americanprogress.org) with any questions.

Sincerely,

The Center for American Progress

comments.title: Comment on OMB-2023-0020-0001
comments.comment_text:
Muse Technologies Inc., a woman-owned small business, is an IT consulting firm located in Lanham, Maryland. We were founded in 2013 by Dr. Linda Cureton, the former NASA CIO, and offer a range of services, including program/project management, organizational development, IT strategy and governance, facility management, property management, and strategic communication.

The "AI in Government Memo" is a critical step towards harnessing the potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) while safeguarding the public against its risks. It proposes comprehensive guidelines for advancing governance innovation and managing risks associated with AI deployment in federal agencies, emphasizing the necessity of balancing the technological boon of AI with the imperative to protect the safety and rights of citizens. The memo mandates the designation of Chief AI Officers in agencies, reflecting a commitment to high-level accountability in AI governance.

The requirements for AI governance include enhanced accountability and oversight, improved risk management, operational efficiency and innovation, and a balance between innovation and regulation. However, the effectiveness of these requirements depends on their implementation, particularly if agencies lack the necessary expertise, resources, or infrastructure to support advanced AI systems and governance structures.

Balancing innovation with regulation requires flexibility in the governance framework, as different AI applications may pose varying levels of risk and require different management strategies. Effective regulation should minimize risks and encourage responsible innovation, promoting ethically designed, transparent, and accountable AI applications while also effectively and efficiently addressing government objectives.

Collaboration with stakeholders, including AI experts, ethicists, and the public, is essential for formulating guidelines that are both innovative and ethically grounded. Continuous evaluation and revision of regulations and guidelines can ensure that governance keeps pace with technological advances while maintaining necessary safeguards.

Suggestions for improving accountability and effectiveness in AI governance include continuous education and training for agency heads and Chief AI Officers, instituting ethics and organizational leadership in executive capacity building, involving a broader range of stakeholders in AI governance decisions, developing clear performance metrics and reporting, and establishing feedback loops and continuous improvement mechanisms.

The evolving nature of AI technology necessitates ongoing education, adaptation, and improvement of risk management strategies. Public and private organizations should stay informed about emerging, ethical, and regulatory standards and continuously assess and enhance their approaches to AI implementation. By prioritizing ongoing education and staying abreast of evolving standards, organizations can foster an environment that embraces innovation and upholds ethical considerations and regulatory compliance.

Continuous assessment and enhancement of risk management strategies are imperative in navigating the dynamic landscape of AI. As technology evolves, so do potential risks related to data security, privacy, bias, and legal compliance. Proactive measures, such as robust governance structures, regular performance reviews, and stakeholder engagement, are critical to mitigating these risks.

The synergy between education, adaptation, and risk management is pivotal for responsibly harnessing AI's full potential. Public and private entities that commit to a culture of continuous improvement will optimize their AI implementations and contribute to the responsible advancement of AI technology on a broader scale. As we navigate the future of AI, the commitment to ethical practices and regulatory compliance will be the compass guiding organizations toward sustainable and impactful AI integration.

Muse would like to acknowledge the invaluable involvement of:

•Dustin S. Sachs, Senior Manager, Information Security Risk Management, World Kinect Corporation
•Joyce Hunter, CEO, Vulcan Enterprises, LLC

Respectfully Submitted,
Dr. Linda Y. Cureton

comments.organization_name: Citizens and Technology Lab, Cornell University
comments.comment_text:
The Citizens and Technology Lab (CAT Lab) of Cornell University is pleased to provide input in response to the request for comment (RFC) on OMB’s draft memorandum on Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence. These comments respond to questions 2, 3, 5, and 8 of the RFC, and provide additional feedback. With our attached supporting materials we:

- Encourage the OMB to acknowledge and support the role of community/participatory science in the oversight of AI tools.
- Urge the OMB to develop guidelines for soliciting and supporting participation in AI innovation and governance from underrepresented groups who have been historically excluded from AI research and development - and who face disproportionate risks from AI systems.
- Advise the OMB to account for the labor, rights, and mental health consequences for volunteer and professional communities whose work is used to train AI systems and manage AI safety.

About the Citizens and Technology Lab

The Citizens and Technology Lab (CAT Lab) at Cornell University works alongside the public to discover effective community ideas for change in ways that advance scientific knowledge. CAT Lab has worked with communities of tens of millions of people on reddit, Wikipedia, and Twitter to study socio-technical safety and reliability questions, including online safety and discrimination.

CAT Lab is led by Dr. J. Nathan Matias, Assistant Professor at Cornell in the departments of Communication and Information Science. In 2010, he developed one of the first socio-technical testing systems for a generative language model in his capacity at one of the earliest neural network predictive text software companies (SwiftKey).

CAT Lab has particular expertise with AI systems that are built on adaptive algorithms: systems that train on their outputs such as systems for ranking and sorting, resource allocation, logistics management, and generative AI. As Dr. Matias has outlined in a recent article in Nature, the creators of these systems cannot currently make reliable assurances about the performance and safety of systems that adapt to their human environments. He outlines the needed scientific work of testing, forecasting, and preventing harms from this kind of collective AI and human behavior, including the essential role of community/citizen science. When AI systems adapt to widely different contexts, attempts at AI transparency, accountability, and regulation will grossly fail the most vulnerable in society without significant support for community/participatory science on AI and its social impacts.

Coordination mechanisms and OMB’s role advancing responsible AI innovation (questions 2, 3, 8)

OMB should direct agency heads to establish a task force to build community/participatory science-based review of AI tools.
OMB should include indicators in any system it develops to inventory AI use cases (pursuant to section 7225 of the Advancing American AI Act) to seek clarity from Federal agencies on the diversity of analysis in safety-impacting and rights-impacting AI.

To engage the public in responsible AI innovation, federal agencies should consider the roles of access to data, ethics, and volunteer labor that make up the governance systems of digital decision-making.
CAT Lab recommends that the OMB reflect on how federal agencies can approach AI governance with the role of semi-professional moderators in mind, and designate a person to lead in advancing our understanding of the role of volunteer moderators in advancing responsible AI innovation.
OMB should direct agency leads to support the work of developing best standards and practices for mitigating the mental health and secondary trauma of trust and safety teams and moderators working with AI systems.

Use cases for presumed safety-impacting and rights-impacting AI (Section 5 (b)) that should be included, removed, or revised (question 5)

Harms from human-algorithm interaction in AI systems should be considered to develop and change both in their harms and benefits over time. OMB should consider expanding the list of safety and rights impacting AI to specify arenas where the initial effect may not yet be easily observed, but where research has shown initial effects, specifically:
-The chilling effect on freedom of speech that emerges from the use of AI to establish automated law enforcement to deter behavior. This includes systems of legal action in which a computer is responsible for unsupervised decision-making, which distributes or outsources surveillance and enforcement to parties that are not governments.
- The potential for such automated law enforcement tools to be deployed in requirements to watermark generative AI content. Early research has shown that receiving takedown notices from copyright enforcement bots drives down individuals’ rate of posting, on average, regardless of whether the takedown notice was legitimate or not.

comments.title: Comment from Freeman Jackson
comments.comment_text:
1.Flexibility and Achievability of Roles for Chief AI Officers: The memorandum outlines that each covered agency is responsible for pursuing AI innovation and ensuring compliance with AI requirements, including risk management. It mandates the designation of a Chief AI Officer (CAIO), who bears primary responsibility for AI issues within the agency. This directive appears to offer flexibility suitable for different agencies, considering that the range of agencies is broad and includes various executive departments, military departments, government corporations, and other establishments in the executive branch. The requirement for a CAIO ensures a focused and accountable approach to AI governance, adaptable to each agency's specific needs and structures.
2.Coordination Mechanisms for AI Governance Body: Effective coordination mechanisms could include a centralized governance structure or a federated model, depending on the size and nature of the agency. Public sector models like inter-agency working groups or committees have effectively coordinated across different government entities. In the private sector, cross-functional teams or AI ethics boards are standard. The benefit of establishing a new body specifically for AI governance is its focus on AI-related issues, ensuring dedicated resources and expertise. However, expanding the scope of existing groups might be more efficient and leverage existing structures and knowledge, especially in agencies where AI intersects significantly with existing domains like IT or data management.
3.Advancing Responsible AI Innovation: To advance responsible AI innovation, OMB can focus on creating clear guidelines and standards for ethical AI use, promoting transparency in AI operations, and ensuring robust public engagement and feedback mechanisms. Supporting educational initiatives and research in AI ethics and governance and providing resources for agencies to build AI expertise can further this goal. Collaboration with industry, academia, and international partners to share best practices and develop common standards can also be beneficial.
4.Generative AI in Agency Missions and Operations: Agencies should leverage generative AI to automate and improve efficiency in data processing, analysis, and decision-making processes, where appropriate. Adequate safeguards could include rigorous testing and validation processes, transparency in AI decision-making, continuous monitoring for biases or errors, and ensuring human oversight of critical decisions. Generative AI could be beneficial in areas like predictive analytics, natural language processing, and pattern recognition, enhancing agencies' capabilities in fulfilling their missions.
5.Use Cases for Safety-Impacting and Rights-Impacting AI: The current categories of use cases seem comprehensive. However, ongoing review and revision might be necessary as AI technology evolves. Specific use cases might need to be added, especially those emerging from new AI applications not currently envisioned. Regular consultation with AI experts, ethicists, and the public can inform these revisions.
6.Minimum Practices for AI Use: The minimum practices set a baseline for responsible AI use, but they should be dynamic and evolve with technological advancements. Agencies must be given the flexibility to implement context-specific risk mitigations. Regular reviews and updates of these practices, informed by the latest research and industry standards, would ensure they remain relevant and effective.
7.Materials and Resources for Incorporating Requirements into Contracts: Guidance documents, best practice manuals, checklists, and templates would be valuable for agencies. Training workshops and webinars can also help in understanding and implementing the requirements. Collaboration platforms for sharing experiences and challenges among agencies could provide practical insights.
8.Public Information on Agencies' AI Use: The annual AI use case inventory should include types of AI used, purposes, benefits, risk assessments, ethical considerations, and any incidents or challenges encountered. Transparency is crucial, so non-sensitive summaries of AI impact assessments and performance metrics could also be included. This transparency promotes public trust and accountability in government use of AI.

comments.title: Comment from Caryn DiMarco
comments.comment_text:
Thank you for laying out a comprehensive plan to address AI/ML. I'm glad to see the government taking a strong stand for the rights of Americans. This policy should be strengthened by requiring all federal contractors or other recipients of government money to abide by the same rules.
I would also like to see language addressing privacy threats like facial recognition and "predictive policing". We've already seen these practices used to infringe upon Americans' civil rights; it's past time to create federal guidelines that rein in these unlawful uses of AI/ML. In fact, the guidance on "acceptable risks" does not define what level of risk is acceptable. We've seen tech companies play fast and loose with customer data in extremely harmful ways, so it's obvious their level of "acceptable" will result in high levels of community harm. The limit for "acceptable risk" needs to be clearly delineated and it must apply to all AI/ML—no opt outs just because an agency (or contractor) doesn't see the need for a risk assessment.
Another concern of mine that this guidance touches on, but doesn't fully address, is the potential for huge data privacy violations. There is currently no way for any of us to opt out of having our data used to train an AI/ML system. At the very least, the government must ensure training data is protected against internal and external threats.
Finally, the public needs (and deserves) full transparency in the government's use of AI/ML. In the few years these types of tools have been around, we've seen police base their enforcement decisions on biased data (https://themarkup.org/prediction-bias/2021/12/02/crime-prediction-software-promised-to-be-free-of-biases-new-data-shows-it-perpetuates-them), schools unfairly label students as "dropout risks" thanks to racially biased systems ( https://themarkup.org/machine-learning/2023/04/27/false-alarm-how-wisconsin-uses-race-and-income-to-label-students-high-risk), and healthcare systems bypass patients who live in poorer states (https://themarkup.org/organ-failure/2023/03/21/poorer-states-suffer-under-new-organ-donation-rules-as-livers-go-to-waste). These abuses were only uncovered thanks to the relentless work of investigative journalists. If AI/ML is going to become a part of our everyday society, everyday people need to have access to data about how it's used and what the results are. AI/ML itself is built to be somewhat of a black box, a fact many companies working with this tech have used to avoid scrutiny. The only way to balance out such a barrier to transparency is to share the outcomes in a way that protects citizens' privacy, yet would reveal the kind of worrisome trends that we've seen in other situations.
It would be foolish at this point to suggest that the government not use AI/ML; it's already happening, and I don't foresee that changing. I strongly urge the OMB to strengthen its guidance on the use of these tools to further protect our civil rights and liberties.

comments.commenter_name: Center for AI and Digital Policy
comments.organization_name: Center for AI and Digital Policy
comments.comment_text:
We write to you, on behalf of the Center for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP), in response to the request for public comments on the draft memorandum titled Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The Notice seeks comments on the Proposed Memorandum for the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies (hereinafter the “OMB AI Guidance”).

CAIDP wrote to OMB on April 24, 2023 and October 19, 2021, regarding the need for OMB to establish regulations for the use of AI by federal agencies. We applaud the Biden-Harris Administration’s Executive Order on AI (hereinafter the “AI Executive Order”) and support the OMB AI Guidance as a critical step in the implementation of the AI Executive Order.

We welcome OMB’s publication of the draft memorandum addressing the pressing concerns of the use of AI by federal agencies. We commend the detailed and pertinent recommendations to address responsible use of AI by federal agencies based on the principles of democratic values, human rights, and the rule of law. We believe the provisions on minimum practices for “rights-impacting” and “safety-impacting” are foundational requirements for the government’s use of AI and will serve to increase public trust of AI systems.

In our detailed comments attached we provide consolidated/combined responses to questions 3, 5, 6, and 8 with reference to specific provisions of the draft memorandum. Our key recommendations in brief are:

1. Establish redline prohibitions across all agencies for systems without scientific validity and which fundamentally undermine human rights, rule of law and democratic process
2. Amend OMB AI Guidance section 5(c)(iii), “Waivers from Minimum Practices” to include strict objective criteria and a disclosure process for waiver
3. Require minimum practices for rights and safety in AI Systems to be applied “during the procurement phase” for procurement regulation with the minimum practices

As in our earlier statements to the OMB, CAIDP reiterates that the public and the Congress must be able to hold federal agencies the for procurement of AI systems and 1) alignment of policies and goals with the tools, 2) effective use of taxpayer funds, 3) alignment between administrative law and AI system design, 4)mission effectiveness, and 5) quality and safety of public services, and 6) dependency on major vendors. We have set out recommendations and amendments to the proposes OMB AI Guidance to achieve these goals. We also underscore the need to ensure that agencies rules are established in regulation, published in the Federal Register with opportunity to public comment, and subject to judicial review as the Administrative Procedure Act requires.
We support the OMB’s effort to undertake rulemaking for the deployment and use of AI systems in federal agencies. For transparency, public trust, and promotion of safe and trustworthy AI, we urge the OMB to incorporate our recommendations. Thank you for your consideration of our views.

comments.title: Comment from Anonymous
comments.comment_text: Section 5 (d)(v)(B) about generative AI for content provenance really runs the risk of incentivizing the heavy us of text information as images - probably mostly PDF- greatly limiting the accessibility and quality of government provided information. Given that there are no proven text-based generative AI content techniques, you are risking that individual users of AI in agencies with have to argue with attorneys in the agency about why they shouldn’t make all generative AI output in a PDF, since attorneys will note that PDFs are a technically feasible way of reliably labeling AI in future dissemination. The policy should be updated to include a few caveats including, “At the time of writing this policy, many text-based labeling techniques are still developmental and text-based labeling should focus on technologies at the point of interaction with the government as opposed to future dissemination such as posting information only on government websites or verified accounts.” Alternatively make it clear that this should not be accomplished by converting to PDF, such as writing “where technically feasible and does not require converting information to proprietary or image-based formats.” I am quite concerned this will also cause no end of headaches once Microsoft includes generative AI into their office suite in the summer of 2024. Please be very wary of further entrenching a PDF and anti-user experience culture in the government.

comments.title: Comment from Beth Noveck
comments.comment_text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is not just transforming economies and industries; it holds the key to revolutionizing public engagement with the federal government. The potential for AI to bridge communication gaps, streamline feedback, and foster inclusion is immense, yet unrealized.

Front and center in the guidance is the requirement for each agency to appoint a Chief AI Officer (CAIO) whose primary responsibility is “coordination, innovation, and risk management” of their agency’s uses of artificial intelligence.

The establishment of a senior AI role in every department underscores the importance of technology in governance. However, the role of the CAIOs should be explicitly linked to innovating public engagement through AI, ensuring that every voice is heard and accounted for in the policymaking process.

In order to take advantage of AI’s unmatched potential to analyze public sentiment, manage feedback, and scale engagement across diverse demographics, OMB’s guidance must evolve to explicitly require federal agencies to implement AI solutions that facilitate and enhance public consultations.

While the proposed guidance calls for “consult[ing] affected groups, including underserved communities, in the design, development and use of the AI, and use [of] such feedback to inform agency decision-making,” the guidance calls for doing so by means of antiquated methods, including:

User testing
Soliciting comments via the Federal Register
Customer feedback
Public hearings, or meetings, such as listening sessions, or
Any other transparent process

Noticeably absent is any injunction to take advantage of AI to make such consultations easier, faster and more equitable than the above methods.

While traditional methods of public participation are valuable, they are often limited by scale, speed, and accessibility. People might talk but it is very difficult for either the agency or the public to hear them because of the volume of comments.

Integrating AI can overcome these limitations, offering real-time analysis and broader inclusivity, particularly for underrepresented communities.

The guidance should be amended to require that the CAIO consults regularly with the public and use AI to make those consultations more effective and equitable.

There is a wide array of tools already in use by other governments. Over 500 governments use the Citizen Lab platform, which incorporates AI to cluster, group and organize public comments. AI is much faster than humans at making sense of large quantities of text and can automate the process of summarizing what people are saying, classifying submissions by topic and sorting them into categories to make it easier for governments and the public to read.

Your Priorities, a free, open source tool for public engagement from Citizens Foundation and used in thousands of online engagements globally, uses AI to scan incoming postings for toxicity. AI automates the process of spotting offensive speech that violates terms of service and community norms, bringing such language to the attention of moderators and reducing the cost of organizing engagements. Your Priorities uses AI to offer a “chatbot” so that the public and government organizers can get answers to questions such as “show me all the comments on Topic X” or “summarize the best comments on Topic Y.”

At MIT, Deb Roy’s Cortico uses machine learning to synthesize comments in live, face-to-face discussions. Remesh leverages artificial intelligence to rapidly make sense of answers to live questions in online sessions, making it possible to extract insights even from spoken conversations such as with communities that are low literacy.

AI translation tools like Facebook’s open source SeamlessM4T make it possible to translate writing into 100 languages and speech into 35 languages, creating avenues for non-native English speakers to participate in conversations on a level playing field.

If OMB amends the guidance to mandate that federal agencies use AI to enable broader, deeper, more meaningful and equitable engagement, innovators will produce even more such tools and agencies will learn how to use them.

Instead of telling agencies, as the guidance does, that they only have to engage “to the extent practicable,” OMB’s guidance should embrace the use of artificial intelligence to foster equitable engagement. It is time for federal agencies to lead by example, leveraging AI to ensure that participatory democracy is not just a principle but a daily practice.

We offer free, independent, evidence-based research on how to use AI for public engagement at https://rebootdemocracy.ai, including a chatbot (coming in early December 2023) to provide answers to questions about effectively using AI for engagement.

comments.title: Comment from Deepti Kannapan
comments.comment_text:
Artificial intelligence is an emerging technology with enormous potential for both positive and negative impact, so I applaud the Biden-Harris administration for taking this step toward setting the direction of its future development. Preventing harm to the rights and safety of individuals is an important priority.

This executive order encourages agencies to implement AI only when doing so has benefits that outweigh the risks, and to manage the risks that occur from its use.

As an engineer with professional experience in automating physical systems, I have two comments on the role of non-AI automation (which the executive order describes as "systems whose behavior is defined only by human-defined rules"), alongside AI.

1. Need to incentivize other forms of automation over AI when it is better fit for purpose
Automation has considerable potential in improving the effectiveness of agencies. Agencies are instructed to assess the potential benefits of using AI automation. This assessment should not evaluate AI solutions in isolation, or only against legacy systems. AI solutions must be evaluated relative to non-AI automation solutions, which can provide many of the same benefits of increasing effectiveness and efficiency.

When a non-AI auotomation system provides comparable benefit to an AI system, agencies should be incentivized to use the non-AI automation system if it can be more rigorously tested, validated, and explained. Mature engineering and mathematical techniques exist for guaranteeing safety of non-AI automated systems.

AI systems are harder to validate for all conditions, since their ability to learn may cause them to depart from their test conditions. They also frequently lack explainability, which can hinder rigorous analyses.

I support the development of AI expertise by agencies and evaluating of automation solutions, but the evaluation of systems should include the full range of automation types, including non-AI, to find the most suitable solution.

2. Safety-impacting AI must have non-AI fail-safes
The executive order acknowledges the possibility of erroneous or harmful results from a rights-impacting AI system, and hence requires periodic human review and the provision of escalation mechanisms. For safety-impacting AI, especially those controlling physical systems, harmful AI actions may require a response too rapid for a human escalation system.

Fail-safes (such as limits on system variables like as the amount of kinetic force delivered) must be implemented. These fail-safes must be able to be rigorously analyzed and validated, and troubleshot in case of emergencies. Non-AI automation may suit this purpose because it is explainable. In general, fail-safe mechanisms are a teaming of AI, humans, and non-AI automation.

I urge the Biden-Harris administration to require the use of automated and human fail-safes for safety-impacting AI.

Thank you,
- Deepti Kannapan
M.S. Mechanical Engineering (University of California)

comments.title: Comment on OMB-2023-0020-0001
comments.comment_text:
We write to share comments regarding OMB’s proposed memorandum titled ‘Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence’ (OMB Proposed AI Memorandum).

OMB is taking an important step to ensure that federal agencies can procure, deploy, and use AI responsibly. Your efforts appropriately reflect the serious, comprehensive cross-sector approach needed to address the broad implications of artificial intelligence (AI). The federal government plays a critical role in signaling to the marketplace what standards and frameworks are deemed to be best practice with respect to responsible innovation.

In this respect we urge OMB to consider how the directives set forth in future OMB guidance can best support and advance America’s vital startup ecosystem.

We believe that America’s technological and economic leadership in AI will depend upon innovation driven by startups. The transformative benefits of AI will not accrue to the American people from an uncompetitive marketplace walled off from new innovators. We appreciate your recognition of this critical fact in the OMB Proposed AI Memorandum and strongly encourage it going forward.

We offer our full comments in the attached letter.

Sincerely,

Gaurab Bansal
Executive Director, Responsible Innovation Labs

comments.title: Comment from Anonymous
comments.comment_text:
The OMB draft guidance provides visionary, consequential, and much needed guidance to federal agencies on the use, deployment, and procurement of AI. Congratulations on releasing the draft and allowing the opportunity for members of the public to submit comments.

I make the following recommendations for your consideration:

1. Please address in more detail how the Chief AI Officer will work with Chief Data Officers, and their potentially conflicting roles and obligations arising under the Foundations of Evidence Based Policy Making Act. For example, page 9 refers to data governance and curation. That is usually the role of the CDO. Chief data officers have to assess all legal risks and conduct a data inventory to assess copyright and patents and other requirements.
2. Please include legal perspectives consistently and comprehensively, throughout. For example, 3(c)(II) should require a legal officer as part of the AI governance board. An example of a “rights-impacting purpose” on pg. 12 should include the use of AI to generate regulatory language, statutory text, judicial opinions, or equivalent uses that may impact someone’s legal rights. Consider consulting with different agency legal subject matter experts on his draft before finalizing.
3. Please insert more references to intellectual property rights. Copyright is mentioned only in the procurement space, and intellectual property as part of the safety purpose. However, the use of people’s images, names, signatures, likenesses, etc.. or “persona” rights is an important issue that Congress is looking at. Deepfakes of people, passing off someone’s content as their own (trademark), and possible ip and privacy violating uses to get training datasets are relevant issues.Government employees should be able to prevent their likenesses from being used by their employer without permission. It is possible that copyright is only mentioned in procurement because agencies may be liable for intellectual property infringement (patents, copyright) under 28 USC1498, but if the goal is to respect rights than
4. Please consider whether “procurement” is sufficiently broad. Is it possible agencies will seek to avoid obligations by acquiring AI through other means: other transaction authorities (OTAs)? This focus on procurement and not other ways agencies obtain technologies could be a loophole.
5. Please consider using the OECD definition for AI system, and other ways these initiatives can more clearly pave the way for international collaboration and harmonizations. Please consider including a reference to international engagement plans in the required strategy on pg. 8 for agencies that have such equities.
6. Please consider requiring multi stakeholder engagement (including SLATTs, other government agencies, industry, and civil society) as part of the AI strategy development and implementation processes.
7. Consider requiring agencies to make data available for ai training datasets, and using machine readable licenses that clearly specify how data can be used and for what purposes,possibly creating an interagency task force, especially if this requires standards.
8. The EO refers to safe, secure, and trustworthy AI. This only refers to impacting safety and rights. Consider whether this is the correct framing, or whether responsible AI, trustworthy ai, or other terms should be used.

Thank you for considering these points as you finalize the guidance.

comments.title: Comment from Anonymous
comments.comment_text:
I am a private citizen and an open-source artificial intelligence research collaborator with an interest in AI policy – while I have done reading on the use of AI in governments as well as legal issues related to AI, I come from a mostly technical perspective, aiming to increase the depth of the current regulatory response to AI.
As an individual interested in the potential of this technology, I believe the Office of Management & Budget’s (OMB) plan is a great first step toward incorporating AI in the federal government – however, the devil lies in the details. My concerns are fourfold:
(a) how to build up AI expertise and coordination in the government to meet the ambition of these proposals as well as the proposed laid out in Biden’s recent executive order,
(b) the lack of adequate coverage on the topic of cybersecurity throughout the document,
(c) the lack of technical, specific guardrails for risk management, and
(d) miscellaneous related investments and initiatives that I believe would support the intent behind the OMB Draft Memorandum.

To that, I propose:
(1) A coordinated, centralized AI governance body – especially around expert advice. These AI governance bodies should ideally be modeled after successful public-private collaborations, comprising a mix of technical experts, policy makers, and diverse stakeholder representatives.
(2) Stronger investments in federal cybersecurity and critical infrastructure security are made, given the reliance of agencies on AI and digital services post-implementation.
(3) Rigorous evaluations for risk management with regard to algorithms in use by the federal government.
(4) Investments in AI ethics & safety
(5) Regular communication with peer governments on implementation of AI in analogous agencies/ministries in other countries

I'm not too confident in these proposals, but these represent my perspectives in the present moment. I hope you find these helpful, and I'd be happy to play a role in the future with regard to AI uptake in the federal government.

comments.title: Comment from Deelip Mhaske
comments.comment_text:
Here are specific suggestions for improvement, including the United Nations’ guidance on communities discriminated against due to work and descent:

Explicit Inclusion of United Nations Guidelines: The document should explicitly incorporate the United Nations' guidelines regarding the protection of communities discriminated against due to work and descent. This can ensure that AI applications are developed and used in ways that do not perpetuate or exacerbate discrimination against these communities.

Detailed Framework for Bias Mitigation: The document should provide a more comprehensive framework for identifying and mitigating biases in AI systems, especially those impacting communities discriminated against due to work and descent. This could include guidelines for data collection, algorithm development, and regular bias assessments.

Engagement with Impacted Communities: There should be a mandate for agencies to actively engage with communities that have historically been discriminated against. This engagement could involve consulting with community representatives during the AI system development process to understand their specific needs and concerns.

Training and Awareness Programs: Implement training programs for government employees and AI developers to increase awareness about the challenges faced by communities discriminated against due to work and descent. This training should focus on understanding cultural sensitivities and the potential impacts of AI on these groups.

Monitoring and Reporting Mechanisms: Establish robust monitoring and reporting mechanisms to track the impact of AI systems on underserved communities, including those discriminated against due to work and descent. This could involve regular audits and public reporting on the findings.

Accessibility and Language Inclusion: Ensure that AI systems are accessible to all communities, including providing multilingual support and considering different levels of digital literacy.

Legal Compliance and Ethical Considerations: Strengthen the sections on legal compliance and ethical considerations, emphasizing the need for AI systems to adhere to laws protecting the rights of communities discriminated against due to work and descent.

Research and Development Inclusivity: Encourage research and development efforts that focus on addressing the unique challenges faced by these communities, fostering innovation that benefits a broader spectrum of the population.

By integrating these suggestions, the document can more effectively guide federal agencies in developing and using AI in a manner that is inclusive, equitable, and respectful of all communities, particularly those facing discrimination due to work and descent.

comments.title: Comment from Anonymous
comments.comment_text:
Please reconsider why you are even using the term Artificial Intelligence. What does it mean? I say it is a marketing term that effectively encapsulates the idea that our computing power has reached new levels. People in general are too easily convinced that it means more than that, and they can't understand it. Worse yet, it becomes another thing to be worried about! Maybe make up a new acronym like ACSO for Ambitious Computing Systems Overhaul. The goals seem laudable though vague. I am perturbed by the use of that ridiculous term (A.I.) which may be nothing more than an attempt by profiteers to put advanced computing into a kind of conceptual black box so citizens and consumers (and bureaucrats) can get steam-rolled and fleeced yet again.

A government should at least try to lead with good language and clear thinking. Instead, I feel, the US government prefers to abdicate that responsibility and lets itself get pushed around by other interests and the whims of billionaires and popular culture. The explosion in computing power is nothing new, though some of the effects on us are absolutely new, but we can still try to think clearly about how and why we use computers.

Unlike the explosions in fossil fuel use and population in the last 100 years, the computing power spike is not going to reverse it's course and diminish. The technical advances may be slowing, particularly in miniaturization, but the gains are permanent and continue at a slower rate. The population is expected to start shrinking and may diminish rapidly in several generations. The fossil fuel use is of course self limiting based on supply (not that we shouldn't reduce emissions). My point is that this third incredible spike, all the incredible feats of technical quasi-magic involving electrons (and photons) are only going to continue to amaze us and hopefully help us to be better human beings (and not just make elites richer). How we talk about these phenomena is critical, so I hope I can help to nip this mistake in the bud. Artificial Intelligence is a sloppy term that leads to sloppy thinking. I appreciate the opportunity to comment.

Why should DeFi and FinTech and CryptoCurrency be able to consume so much of our Federal Agencies time? A much cleaner and simpler way to regulate the chaotic mess of financial transactions would be to clarify that only real investments qualify for the tax benefits of being an "investment" (and not personal use for tax purposes). Speculators who love to gamble have a regulated industry (casinos etc.) where they can play. History has proved that Brooksley Born was right about unregulated derivatives trading. The massive computing power has led to massive trading (with strategies and algorithms galore), and the challenges to regulators are huge, but entrepreneurs have no right to start making up there own crazy schemes involving currencies. Only sovereign states have currencies. The legitimacy of purely speculative bets on commodities and derivatives as "investments" needs to be challenged as well. Not trying to outlaw all crazy schemes is laudable. Why not just take away the abused tax advantages instead? Defining an "investment" as something that has tangible benefits is the type of work the Federal financial agencies should be doing. Computers at an advanced level could certainly help once a list is drawn up (and maintained) to help the IRS determine where taxpayers err in assuming that just because they spent money they had made an "investment". Sloppy thinking about easy money is causing social problems, which is an insight I gathered by working as a tax preparer for 25 seasons.

comments.title: Comment from Christopher Lish
comments.comment_text:
Sunday, December 3, 2023

Clare Martorana,
Office of the Federal Chief Information Officer
Office of Management Budget.
1600 Pennsylvania Ave NW
Washington, DC 20500

Subject: Protect Civil and Human Rights When the Federal Government Uses Artificial Intelligence -- Request for Comments: Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence Draft Memorandum (Document ID: OMB-2023-0020-0001)

To OMB Director Shalanda Young, Director and U.S. Federal Chief Information Officer Clare Martorana:

I strongly urge the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and other federal agencies to use all of their powers and resources to ensure that the harmful effects of artificial intelligence (AI) are limited when developed, procured, or used by the federal government—and that the government provides meaningful transparency and publicly available information about the ways our government uses AI so that we have more power to regulate, push back on harmful uses, and limit AI use in the future. In every use case, protecting civil rights must be the top priority.

There are some strong pieces of the OMB guidance that I urge you not to rollback as this process moves forward. The requirement that agencies meet minimum practices for rights-impacting and safety-impacting AI is very important in addressing my concerns around bias and discrimination in AI, and I urge you to keep these strong requirements and ignore pressure to weaken this guidance.

There are a number of areas where this guidance, and future AI policy documents, must be improved:

* The Executive Order on AI did not do enough to address law enforcement agencies and the use of AI on immigrant communities, which are some of the spaces where AI has already been shown to have serious negative impacts. I was glad to see that the OMB guidance did include law enforcement under the covered agencies, and strongly urge you not to change this. We must establish strong policies to address law enforcement use of AI, and to limit use to mitigate harms.

* Some AI is too dangerous to be used, and any possible benefits are outweighed by known harms. Facial recognition is an AI-enabled biometric technology that infringes on the right to privacy to such a degree that it should not be used at all by the government, and this guidance should ban its use by government agencies.

* The guidance does not establish enough data privacy protections. Because AI is reliant on data the opportunity for data abuses is high, and ensuring strong privacy protections must be a top priority. While there is a need for Congress to pass comprehensive data privacy protections, the OMB should use this guidance to establish data privacy policies when government agencies develop, procure, or use AI.

* The minimum practices for safety-impacting and rights-impacting AI require agencies to stop using an AI when the “risks to rights or safety exceed an acceptable level,” but the guidance both gives agencies an option to skip determining an AI system’s risk, and also doesn’t specify what an “acceptable level” is. In these safety- and rights-impacting cases the consequences of the use of AI are so high that the OMB must set a very limited acceptable level of risk and ensure that all agencies using AI comply with this requirement.

* The minimum practices should also apply in cases where federal funds are used to purchase AI systems, including government grants. This would better protect civil rights in even more situations, including at the state and local levels.

* All information reported by agencies in their annual use case inventory should be made publicly available, to allow for as much public scrutiny and transparency as possible. This is critical for ensuring that the public, as well as experts in civil rights, have the opportunity to critically assess the use of AI by the government.

While there may be uses of AI that can benefit the federal government, I call on the OMB to focus on protecting against the harms of AI your top priority in this guidance.

Thank you for your consideration of my comments. Please do NOT add my name to your mailing list. I will learn about future developments on this issue from other sources.

Sincerely,
Christopher Lish
San Rafael, CA

comments.title: Comment from Karriem Perry
comments.comment_text:
Utility of the Document

Governance and Accountability: The document emphasizes the establishment of AI governance structures within agencies, including the designation of Chief AI Officers (CAIOs). This is crucial for ensuring responsible AI use and aligning AI initiatives with broader agency objectives.

Risk Management: The focus on risk management, particularly for AI applications impacting public safety and rights, is vital. The detailed guidelines for managing these risks show a deep understanding of AI's potential adverse impacts.

Innovation and Capacity Building: Encouraging agencies to develop AI strategies and remove barriers to responsible AI use fosters innovation. This is beneficial for harnessing AI's potential to improve government operations and services.

Probable Future Implications

Enhanced AI Adoption: The memorandum could lead to broader and more effective adoption of AI across federal agencies, potentially transforming government operations and public services.

Increased Public Trust: By mandating risk management and transparent governance, the strategy could enhance public trust in government use of AI.

Technological Advancements: This approach could spur advancements in AI technologies and practices, particularly in areas like risk assessment and ethical AI use.

Probability of Fulfillment by Federal Agencies

The probability of successful implementation largely depends on:

Resource Allocation: Adequate funding and resources are crucial for agencies to meet these requirements.

Training and Expertise: The success of this strategy hinges on the availability of trained personnel and AI expertise within agencies.

Inter-agency Collaboration: Effective implementation will require cooperation and knowledge sharing among different agencies.

Recommendations for Improvement

Enhanced Focus on Ethical AI: While the document addresses AI risks, it could benefit from a more pronounced focus on ethical AI principles.

Flexible Frameworks: Given the fast-evolving nature of AI, the strategy should incorporate flexible frameworks to adapt to technological advancements.

Stakeholder Engagement: Encouraging broader stakeholder engagement, including public participation, in AI governance can provide diverse perspectives and enhance trust.

Implementation Support: Providing agencies with more detailed guidance or support mechanisms, like shared services or centers of excellence, can aid in the practical implementation of these strategies.

Continuous Evaluation: The strategy should include provisions for regular evaluation and revision of AI governance frameworks to align with emerging global best practices and standards.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2023-28232
comments.comment_text:
4.1: There needs to be clear linkage and delineation on dual use foundation models regarding the use of parameters and floating point operations from section 4.2b that specifies: any model that was trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 1026 integer or floating-point operations, or using primarily biological sequence data and using a quantity of computing power greater than 1023 integer or floating-point operations. AI model weight adjustment through forward pass/back propagation, tokenization, loss calculation, regularization, batch normalization and evaluations all necessitate floating point operations (FLOPs). And that is before you get into the language of whether you're using Floating Point (FP) 32, FP16 for training or choosing to quantize models. So while this qualifier of floating point operations and tens of billions of parameters exists in section 4.2b, it directly addresses sections 4.1 (guidelines- standards and best practices) 4.5 (synthetic content generation relative to methods that implement different variations of FLOPs) and 11 (standardization for global engagement).
4.5: Identifying synthetic data generation is a tough one as that is the proverbial cat and mouse. I would submit for consideration that much like NIST has developed standards for post quantum security with the FIPS, that similar methods be established for synthetic data generation that are approved and implemented. Chasing down every new way of beating detectors is an ongoing battle that is necessary- but to be effective without being overly labor intensive it needs to be paired with synthetic data generation standards that are applied to the most high value use cases (training medical ai systems, cybersec etc) that has a seal from the government of authenticity. It is most likely this industry standard seal of authenticity will need to be post quantum secure or at least post quantum resistant to bridge the gap until full migration to post quantum security on hardware and software is set.

11: The reality is small language models (SLMs) and Small Multimodal models (SMMs) are already becoming the standard as well as the "mixture of experts" training process and implementation. In this case the answer is the development of small models (1-5 billion parameter considered small as of Feb 2 2024) that can then be compiled into a mixture of experts configuration with other small models based on use cases. Like clinical subspecialists working together on one patient with multifactorial pathologies, this model of training small domain specific models that can be combined as needed can help to focus data collection/development and training protocols. For red teaming, the most promising outside of post quantum secure FIPs is the cyberseceval from Meta with LLaMA guard and purple llama. Pushing that forward and implementing it as standard rather than recreating the wheel from scratch is the right call.

I have attached a proposal aligned the intersection of the domains of medicine and education addressing these same three subdomains of the EO.
