comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2023-28232
comments.comment_text:
I write today as a person who uses or is impacted by AI or an end user of such systems, and in my personal capacity as a career Federal employee whose use of AI will be ultimately enabled or constrained according to the guidance that NIST publishes about AI safety. In the discussion of AI actors such as myself within the framework provided in NIST AI 100-1, I would be under “People and Planet”, and appear to be regarded as something of an afterthought. This is a grievous mistake.

While it may appear that NIST AI 100 and Section 4.1 of EO 14110 have focused the attention on the development and deployment of AI systems, the paradigm of development and deployment in the case of what we consider to be generative AI – which presumes highly complex end user interactions with the software – fails to account for the fact that end users are no longer merely reacting to deployed software but crossing the boundary into development. That envelope is increasing, and can be expecting to increase further, as AI tools further bridge the gap between programming languages at various levels of abstraction and human language.

If the closing divide between end user and developer / deployer is not promptly addressed, the NIST project to provide risk management best practices will be certain to face a significant decrease in effectiveness, as well as an increasing risk that the project will entirely fail to produce an increase in AI safety.

The end user, moreover, lacks the time, resources, and interest in accounting for the many broad-based risk management issues that NIST AI 100-1 describes. Like travelers at an airport – or participants in a hackathon or conference – end users require signposts and streamlined procedures that enable them to customize a range of activities for which the general outline is known in advance.

To that end, I encourage NIST to develop a supplement to its risk management framework that provides a framework for end user training around current major use cases, as well as examples and explanations serving to increase end user awareness of common risks and common use cases and end user association of risks with a given use case. Such a supplement could also further the cause of Section 10 of EO 14110 by helping to identify beneficial shortcuts to AI project development, allowing Federal employees evaluating new AI projects to rapidly greenlight projects that meet certain criteria for low risk while identifying common pitfalls for other projects.

Such a supplement would ideally be task specific. For example, the supplement could be expected to have separate chapters for computer vision / identification problems, filtering or proximity / nearest neighbor searching, and resource allocation and other optimization problems. Ultimately, end users trained on such supplemental materials could be expected to assist in developing and using AI across these distinct tasks in a manner than supports the goals of the risk management framework, and to engage with additional caution or experimentation as appropriate to the use case and information available about the AI.

comments.comment_text:
I would like to address the issue of integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into accounting within the framework of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). IFRS introduces a transformative potential for enhancing the accuracy, efficiency, and comprehensiveness of financial reporting. However, this integration also brings forth significant security concerns that must be addressed to protect sensitive financial data and ensure compliance with regulatory standards. To mitigate these risks, it is essential to implement robust security measures tailored to the unique challenges posed by AI applications in accounting. This includes adopting advanced encryption techniques to safeguard data in transit and at rest, deploying anomaly detection systems to monitor for suspicious activities indicative of potential security breaches, and ensuring that AI algorithms are transparent and explainable to facilitate audits and compliance checks.

Moreover, it is crucial to foster a culture of security awareness among all stakeholders involved in the AI-driven accounting processes. Training programs should be instituted to equip employees with the knowledge and skills necessary to recognize and respond to security threats. Additionally, organizations should establish clear policies and procedures for data governance, access control, and incident response, specifically designed to address the nuances of AI applications in accounting. Collaboration with regulatory bodies and industry experts can also provide valuable insights into best practices and emerging threats, enabling continuous improvement of security measures. By prioritizing security in the deployment of AI within accounting practices, organizations can leverage the benefits of technology while minimizing risks, thereby enhancing trust and reliability in financial reporting under IFRS.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2023-28232
comments.comment_text:
As you move forward in this process, I urge you to avoid examination of issues presented by AI in a silo, and resist decontextualization that would undermine the ability to address the broader risks posed by inadequately regulated machine learning/artificial intelligence. Governance is anything but a technical issue, and “alignment” in far too much of the discussion of AI ethics is entirely circular and self-referential. As such, please don’t limit yourselves to discussions with technical experts. Take the path less traveled. Pay attention to the voices of those marginalized in current discussions, and who consequently are those for whom risks are greatest. Center the voices of women, of people of color, of poets & other artists. Artificial intelligence promises to remake a new society. We owe it to ourselves to build a better one than the one we currently inhabit. Technical architectures & systems must avoid reifying current biases & injustices. We must focus on establishing radical transparency and effective accountability in an environment that empowers rather than diminishes the role of consent. We have an opportunity and an obligation to establish governance in the public interest. I hope you will seize it.

Some specific thoughts on copyright/artists’ rights below:

An even more fundamental starting point for consideration of AI and copyright should be to unpack some of the words used in this exercise. Artificial intelligence. Machine learning. There is no artificial intelligence — only intelligence, and computers are not capable of possessing it — at least not in the way that we generally associate intelligence with reference to judgment. Computational efficiency — the ability to discern patterns through mountains of data so as to be able to predict outcomes, or to generate new patterns based on the past, is not an exercise in intelligence, and the anthropomorphism employed here affects the way we think about these issues. We need to exercise great care at the outset. Intelligence isn’t reducible to stimulus-response, regardless of the sophistication and complexity of the experiment. Aggregations of data can tell us where we’ve been. Perhaps also where, based on the past, we are likely to go. They can find patterns that may escape human perception that can inform future decision-making, but they necessarily are engaged in measuring the past, not dreaming about the future. They’re incapable of being inspired. So let’s be really careful here and not entrust our future to the guardians of the past. I will leave it to philosophers to debate the metaphysics of the meaning of intelligence — I think it will suffice here to observe that it involves more than mere computation, thus we employ the adjective “artificial.” But here, the adjective actually negates the thing it’s supposed to be modifying and therefore philosophically defines a null set. That must be borne in mind as we proceed.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2023-28232
comments.comment_text:
As generative AI continues to expand into mainstream use, the need for regulation is urgent. AI-generated media itself is not only poisoning the information ecosystem, but the mere presence of AI makes it harder to trust what one is seeing or hearing, even when the media in question is real. For a while now, there has been a slow erosion of trust in institutions and among society generally; AI will exacerbate this problem many times over if guardrails are not put into place. Additionally, unregulated AI has made it trivially easy for bad people to cheat, steal, propagandize, and harm others.

However, moral responsibility should not lie only with the users, but with the AI companies who have created commercial models using data scraped from the internet--including private, copyrighted and illegal material--and at inordinate energy costs.

Data transparency and a basic respect for privacy and copyright should be the standard for all AI training--especially when used for commercial intent; and on the user end synthetic media should be clearly labeled as AI-generated so as to disempower scammers, fraudsters, plagiarists, and bullies. Dire legal consequences should be brought upon those who would knowingly circumvent such regulations.

We want better technology, but it should not be at the expense of copyright, a trustworthy media, or the well-being of the most vulnerable among us--most especially kids. Ethics with technology should be the goal, not "Technology no matter the costs".

I don't work in the tech industry, but as a U.S. citizen deeply concerned about the state of current generative AI, I just wanted to add my voice to those urging for reasonable AI regulations, and I appreciate you giving the chance to do so. Thank you and God Bless.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2023-28232
comments.comment_text:
To ensure safe and trustworthy AI that is beneficial to every member of society, including those from underrepresented groups and the Global South, it’s important a responsible AI framework is adopted. In Toju Duke’s book “Building Responsible AI Algorithms - a framework for transparency, fairness, safety, privacy and robustness ”, she explains the foundations of developing safe and responsible AI focused on the following:
1. AI Principles, 2. Data ethics 3. Fairness 4. Safety 5. Human-in-the-loop 6. Explainability 7. Privacy 8. Robustness 9. Ethical Considerations / AI Ethics. The principles outlined in this book form the basic foundation for ensuring the safe development and deployment of AI.

Following on from the above work, Toju Duke is partnering with Paolo Giudici in authoring a book titled “Responsible AI in practice” which introduces an additional Responsible AI framework called SAFE-HAI (Safe Human-centered AI). The focus of this work is on the safe and accurate AI development across AI models and applications. We propose risk management frameworks across the following Responsible AI principles: AI governance, robustness, security and safety (which includes red-teaming), accuracy, privacy and data, explainability, fairness and human rights, sustainability, and human-centered AI. Using several statistical metrics such as Area Under Curve (AUC) and Shapley values, we explain the application of Lorenz curves to measure risk and inequality across the different principles and a taxonomy/scoring rubric to identify and mitigate identified risks.

To ensure a Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of AI, we believe the above principles are necessary for adoption during the ML lifecycle and development of AI systems. These principles are applicable to all AI modalities including generative AI.

comments.comment_text:
February 2, 2024

Laurie E. Locascio
Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and
Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology
100 Bureau Drive
Gaithersburg, MD 20899

Submitted electronically via www.regulations.gov

Re: Request for Information (RFI) Related to NIST's Assignments Under Sections 4.1, 4.5 and 11 of the Executive Order Concerning Artificial Intelligence (Sections 4.1, 4.5, and 11); Docket Number: 231218–0309, December 21, 2023

The development of artificial intelligence (AI), and in particular the public availability of generative AI and the widespread ability to automatically generate images, audio, and video, is already having a significant impact on society. The development and deployment of generative AI is happening at a speed and scale that is likely to exceed previous technological deployments. Unfortunately, this rapid deployment has meant the risk management and trust and safety features that would traditionally have time to develop do not currently exist.

On October 30, 2023, President Biden signed the Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI EO) which directed NIST to undertake several tasks including “developing a companion resource to the AI Risk Management Framework, NIST AI 100-1, for generative AI.”

As CAP has previously stated, voluntary risk management frameworks are not a sufficient substitute for needed AI regulations and legislation. Scholars have noted the shortcoming of a risk management framing for AI.

However, as AI legislation or regulation faces an uphill battle in the United States in the immediate future, voluntary frameworks like the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI RMF) can be a first step in helping to identify and potentially mitigate harms from Generative AI. As NIST carries out the mission assigned to it by the AI EO, the NIST AI RMF generative AI companion and any updated NIST AI RMF should:
- Incorporate the White House Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights (AI Bill of Rights).
-Define and include requirements for the responsibilities and risk management for developers of AI models and first- and third-party deployers of those AI models.
- Adopt the categories from the draft OMB AI guidance where AI use is presumed to be Safety-Impacting or Rights-Impacting and craft risk mitigations for these categories.
- Prioritize recommendations to address generative AI’s risks to the integrity of elections and democratic processes given the historic number of elections taking place in 2024.

Below CAP provides the following response to the Request for Information (RFI) Related to NIST's Assignments Under Sections 4.1, 4.5 and 11 of the Executive Order Concerning Artificial Intelligence (Sections 4.1, 4.5, and 11); Docket Number: 231218–0309, December 21, 2023. Please contact Adam Conner (aconner@americanprogress.org: 202-669-5671) with any questions.

Sincerely,

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2023-28232
comments.comment_text:
To the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST),

Thank you for the opportunity to respond to the Request for Information (RFI) concerning the management of risks and harms of generative AI, as outlined in Sections 4.1, 4.5, and 11 of the Executive Order on Artificial Intelligence. We at Swear would like to provide insights on the roles different AI actors can play in this landscape and discuss the current techniques for content authentication, provenance tracking, and synthetic content detection.

Roles of AI Actors in Managing Risks and Harms of Generative AI:
-AI Developers: The primary responsibility of AI developers is to incorporate ethical considerations and risk mitigation strategies during the development phase of AI technologies. This includes embedding mechanisms for content authentication and traceability within the AI systems, especially those capable of generating synthetic content.
-AI Deployers: Deployers should ensure that AI systems are used within ethical boundaries and comply with existing regulations. They are responsible for implementing content labeling and detection mechanisms to distinguish between authentic and synthetic content.
-End Users: The end user’s role involves being vigilant and informed about the potential risks associated with AI-generated content. They should be equipped with tools to verify content authenticity and be aware of the implications of sharing unverified information.

Current Techniques for Content Authentication and Provenance Tracking:
-Swear's approach to content authentication and provenance tracking involves real-time digital watermarking and cryptographic signatures. This method ensures that any piece of digital content is authenticated at its point of creation and its journey is traceable throughout its lifecycle. (Please see Attachment 1_Swear Explainer.pdf)
-The feasibility of this approach lies in its seamless integration into existing content creation and sharing platforms, requiring minimal behavioral change from end users.
-Regarding validity and fitness for purpose, real-time watermarking and cryptographic techniques offer a robust solution against sophisticated AI-generated forgeries, ensuring the integrity of digital media.

Techniques for Synthetic Content Labeling and Detection:
-Current techniques involve AI-driven algorithms that analyze visual and audio content for signs of manipulation. However, these techniques often lag behind the rapidly advancing synthetic content creation technologies.
-Swear proposes a preventive approach where content is authenticated at the source, thus reducing the reliance on post-hoc detection methods. This method is more efficient in preventing the spread of synthetic content.

Reducing the Risk of Synthetic Content:
-The key to reducing the risk lies in a proactive strategy where content is authenticated at the source rather than relying solely on detection after the content has been disseminated.
-This approach involves a trade-off: while it is highly effective in preventing the spread of deepfakes, it requires direct consumer opt-in or integration into content creation tools and platforms.

Opposing Views:
-Some may argue that real-time authentication could potentially infringe on privacy or creative freedom. However, Swear's method prioritizes user privacy and data security, ensuring that the content remains in the user's control.
-Another opposing view is the reliance on AI for detection of synthetic content. While AI detection is a valuable tool, it should be complemented with proactive measures to ensure a comprehensive approach to content integrity.

Swear's approach to managing risks associated with generative AI involves a combination of real-time content authentication, ethical AI development practices, and informed use by end users. This approach not only addresses current challenges but is scalable and adaptable to future advancements in AI technology.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2023-28232
comments.comment_text:
Submitted Comment:
My response relates to responsible AI risk management for accounting and finance industry. For responsible AI risk management, the implementation of specific control activities is essential to ensure that AI systems are developed and used in a safe, ethical, and compliant manner. Here's a list of recommended control activities tailored for managing risks associated with Artificial Intelligence:
1. Ethical and Legal Compliance Reviews:
- Conduct regular reviews to ensure AI systems comply with ethical standards and legal regulations.
- Implement control mechanisms to monitor changes in laws and ethical guidelines relevant to AI.
2. Data Quality and Privacy Controls:
- Establish protocols for data accuracy, completeness, and relevance.
- Implement robust data privacy controls, including data anonymization and encryption
3. Bias Detection and Mitigation:
- Regularly test AI models for biases (gender, racial, or otherwise).
- Implement procedures to mitigate and correct detected biases
4. Model Validation and Verification:
- Conduct thorough testing and validation of AI models for reliability and accuracy.
- Implement version control and approval processes for model updates.
5. Security Measures for AI Systems:
- Implement cybersecurity measures to protect AI systems from unauthorized access and tampering.
- Conduct regular security audits and vulnerability assessments.
6. Transparency and Explainability Measures:
- Ensure AI decisions and processes are transparent and understandable to relevant stakeholders.
- Implement control activities like logging and reporting mechanisms to track AI decision-making processes.
7. Human Oversight and Intervention:
- Establish processes for human oversight of AI decision-making.
- Develop mechanisms for manual intervention and override of AI decisions where necessary.

comments.comment_text:
From the Center for AI and Digital Policy (“CAIDP”) in response to the request for information (“RFI”) issued by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (“NIST”) relating to NIST’s assignments under section 4.1, 4.5, and 11 of President Biden’s Executive Order concerning Artificial Intelligence (hereafter “EO 14110”). Our overarching recommendations to NIST to fulfill its mandate under EO 14110 are as follows:

1. Use a human-rights based approach to AI governance
2. Clearly recommend and establish the obligation to terminate
3. Recommend human rights impact assessments
4. Recommend continual and open monitoring and contestability of outcomes
5. Recommend “no-go” decisions for pseudo-scientific and human rights violating systems
6. Recommend transparency mechanisms including ‘white-box’ and ‘out-of-the box’ auditor access, use of public model cards, training set documentation
7. Intended use cases and exclusion criteria should be aligned with OMB’s guidance on “rights-impacting” and “safety-impacting” AI systems

In the Comments below, we provide the following recommendations in response to the specific issues identified in the RFI:

1.On the “Best practices regarding data capture, processing, protection, quality, privacy, transparency, confidentiality, handling, and analysis, as well as inclusivity, fairness, accountability, and representativeness (including non-discrimination, representation of lower resourced languages, and the need for data to reflect freedom of expression) in the collection and use of data;” [3.a]: NIST must account for the lack of underrepresented groups in AI development and how their absence is inconsistent with existing laws and international best practices on inclusivity and representation in AI. Best-practices and standards should guide development of AI tools/systems which are traceable, contestable, and contribute to accountability by their design.

2.On “[how to develop standards for] AI risk management and governance, including managing potential risk and harms to people, organizations, and ecosystems” [3.a]: NIST should account for the growing environmental implications of the AI supply chain as a part of its standard development process and consider existing obligations towards reducing carbon emissions and other environmental harms arising out of the development of AI systems.

3.On the “Risks and harms of generative AI, including challenges in mapping, measuring, and managing trustworthiness characteristics as defined in the AI RMF, as well as harms related to repression, interference with democratic processes and institutions, gender-based violence, and human rights abuses” [1.a.1]: we present a catalog of risks, the urgency in addressing them, and supply recommendations of standards that advance a rights-based approach to AI governance.

4.On the “Forms of transparency and documentation (e.g., model cards, data cards, system cards, benchmarking results, impact assessments, or other kinds of transparency reports) that are more or less helpful for various risk management purposes” [1.a.1]: we urge NIST to require ex-ante human rights impact assessments, advance a transparency and disclosure framework, and continue an open public comment process.

We are conscious that NIST’s framework is not mandatory and does not create enforceable rights and obligations for private actors. However, NIST must be mindful that the approach and elements of its risk management framework will inform ongoing discussions on regulation and should be human-centered, designed to proactively set a robust floor for transparency, accountability, safety, and fairness obligations for the industry.

Our attached file provides details of these recommendations in response to the specific questions/items in the RFI.

The American Bankers Association (ABA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the request for information (RFI) related to National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) assignments under sections 4.1, 4.5 and 11 of the October 30, 2023 Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence as published in the Federal Register on December 21, 2023 (EO). NIST is uniquely positioned to build upon the success of its AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) by developing a complement to address the unique opportunities and challenges presented by generative AI (GenAI) and prompt-based large language models (LLMs).
In our attached comment letter, the ABA:

- Encourages NIST to consider the banking industry’s approach as a possible solution for other industries given that banks are at the forefront of the responsible AI movement due to the mature and flexible risk management framework at its core, which is subject to oversight by industry-focused regulatory agencies;

- Requests NIST to develop voluntary standards in harmony with regulatory requirements given that financial institutions are subject to numerous regulatory requirements with respect to the use of AI, including third party risk management, model risk management and cybersecurity;

- Requests NIST to clarify what outputs need to be subject to AI governance;

- Encourages NIST to define “red-teaming” given that the term is used in many ways and lack of clarity could raise concerns;

- Applauds efforts to reduce the risk of synthetic content given GenAI can generate synthetic content leading to the creation of deepfakes that can be used to perpetrate fraud and causing mis- and dis-information but also encourages NIST to recognize the positive uses of synthetic data to advance privacy and trade secrets protection and ensure it does not inadvertently prevent its development; and

- Generally supports efforts to advance global technical standards that accommodate the risk management needs (including regulatory compliance requirements), that are technology neutral, risk-based, and tailored to use cases.

comments.comment_text:
Developing a companion resource to the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) for generative AI involves addressing several critical areas. Based on the non-exhaustive list of possible topics provided, here are key points and recommendations for each area:

Risks and Harms of Generative AI
Mapping and Managing Trustworthiness: Establish methodologies for assessing trustworthiness in generative AI, including transparency, reliability, and fairness metrics.
Addressing Specific Harms: Develop guidelines to mitigate risks such as repression, interference with democratic processes, gender-based violence, and human rights abuses. This may include strict protocols for content generation and distribution, as well as monitoring mechanisms.
Standards, Norms, and Practices
Existing Standards and Gaps: Evaluate current standards and identify gaps, particularly in governance, risk mapping, measurement, and management specific to generative AI.
Industry Best Practices: Document and promote industry best practices, encouraging standardization across different sectors utilizing generative AI.
Governance Practices
Recommendations for AI Actors: Suggest updates in governance models to include risk assessment procedures specific to generative AI, emphasizing ethical considerations and stakeholder impacts.
Inclusive Governance Models: Encourage inclusive models that incorporate feedback from diverse stakeholders, including marginalized and impacted communities.
Professions, Skills, and Disciplinary Expertise
Interdisciplinary Teams: Advocate for the formation of interdisciplinary teams comprising experts in AI, ethics, law, sociology, and other relevant fields.
Roles and Responsibilities: Define clear roles and responsibilities for various team members in managing and governing generative AI systems.
Roles of Different AI Actors
Developers, Deployers, and End Users: Outline distinct roles and responsibilities for developers, deployers, and end users, ensuring each group contributes to risk management.
Collaborative Frameworks: Encourage collaborative frameworks where different actors work together to identify and mitigate risks.
Techniques and Implementations
Model Validation and Verification: Develop robust model validation and verification protocols, including red-teaming exercises tailored to generative AI.
Impact Assessments: Implement comprehensive human rights and ethical impact assessments as standard practice in generative AI development.
Content Authentication and Provenance Tracking: Promote the development and use of technologies for content authentication, provenance tracking, and synthetic content detection.
Effectiveness Assessment Mechanisms: Establish mechanisms to assess and verify the effectiveness of implemented techniques, ensuring they are scalable and fit for purpose.
Additional Considerations
Continuous Monitoring and Adaptation: Emphasize the importance of ongoing monitoring and adaptation of strategies as generative AI technologies evolve.
Stakeholder Engagement: Foster a culture of continuous engagement with various stakeholders, including policymakers, civil society, and the general public.
Public Awareness and Education: Develop public awareness campaigns and educational programs to inform about the potentials and risks of generative AI.
By addressing these areas comprehensively, the companion resource to the AI RMF for generative AI can provide valuable guidance in managing the unique challenges posed by these technologies, ensuring their development and deployment are aligned with ethical principles and societal values.

The concept of Artificial Intelligence currently functions as a linguistic ensnarement for social imagination, transcending its strict association with computer science terminology. Dr. Son Pham (2022), within the pages of his booklet "On Artificial Intelligence: A Poetic Definition," currently accessible on Amazon and Kindle Prime, delves into the amalgamation of technology and linguistic creativity. In a pivotal section, he presents an alternative definition of AI as either the Automated Intent or the intent of automation.

"Artificial Intelligence, a concept profound,
Born of automation, in intent it's found.
A synergy of minds, silicon and thought,
In the dance of algorithms, a connection sought.

Automated intent or intent of automation,
The essence distilled, in clear formation.
AI, a creation of human design,
A marvel that transcends the confines of time.

So let us ponder, with minds wide and free,
The fusion of technology and humanity.
In the tapestry of progress, where dreams are sown,
Artificial Intelligence, a definition known."

My comment is to incorporate, right at the outset of the policy, a clear articulation of the social imagination surrounding the concept of AI through this poetic definition.

Given that AI is fundamentally driven by "intent," a heightened focus on K-12 education becomes imperative. This educational stage is pivotal for nurturing the next generation of AI scientists across various fields, while also laying the essential groundwork for our democracy and ethical standards.

The establishment of safe, secure, and trustworthy AI systems hinges on the bedrock of democracy and ethical standards. It is therefore paramount to cultivate a collective understanding among policymakers and other stakeholders that AI fundamentally operates as an "automated intent." This recognition will fortify our efforts to shape policies that ensure responsible AI deployment and contribute to the broader societal good.

Furthermore, it is essential to integrate the viewpoints of 21st-century post-foundational scholars in education when addressing matters of democracy and ethical standards. Scholars who draw upon research from the 20th century and earlier, along with ancient philosophies, should reassess and modernize their arguments to align with contemporary advancements and insights.

Thank you for granting me the opportunity to share my insights and address concerns regarding the Executive order on the Safe, secure, and trustworthy development and use of artificial intelligence. I am hopeful that we can effectively tackle the challenges ahead by developing a comprehensive understanding of the associated risks and taking necessary actions.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2023-28232
comments.comment_text:
This comment is pertaining to the best practices of AI Safety and Security.

The rapid advancement of AI brings immense potential for improving our lives, from healthcare and education to entertainment and business. However, this progress also demands careful consideration of safety and security. This is where psychologists play a critical role in shaping the future of AI, and their collaboration with AI developers is crucial for developing safe and responsible AI products. Here are some key reasons why:

1. Mitigating Human Biases in AI: AI algorithms are built on data, and human bias can easily creep into this data, leading to discriminatory or unfair outcomes. Psychologists have the expertise to identify these biases and develop methods to mitigate their impact. They can analyze the training data, the algorithms themselves, and the potential biases that users might bring to their interactions with the AI, ensuring fairer and more ethical algorithms.

2. Understanding Human-AI Interaction: Psychologists understand how humans perceive information, make decisions, and interact with technology. This expertise is essential for designing AI systems that are user-friendly, intuitive, and promote trust. They can help developers understand how people will react to different AI behaviors, anticipate potential misunderstandings or frustrations, and design interfaces that foster positive and productive interactions.

3. Addressing the Psychological Impact of AI: As AI becomes more sophisticated and integrated into our lives, it's crucial to understand its potential psychological impact. Psychologists can study the effects of AI on mental health, social dynamics, and human behavior. This knowledge can inform the development of AI systems that are mindful of these impacts and minimize potential harm, for example, ensuring AI companions are emotionally supportive or avoiding AI systems that exacerbate anxiety or social isolation.

4. Promoting Explainability and Transparency: A major concern with AI is the lack of transparency in its decision-making processes. This can lead to distrust and fear among users. Psychologists can advocate for explainable AI systems that users can understand, allowing for informed interaction and building trust. They can also help developers communicate the capabilities and limitations of AI effectively, managing expectations and preventing misunderstandings.

5. Developing Ethical Guidelines and Regulations: Designing ethical AI requires a thorough understanding of human values and social context. Psychologists can contribute to the development of ethical guidelines and regulations for AI development and use. They can help identify potential ethical pitfalls, guide discussions on acceptable and unacceptable applications of AI, and ensure that AI serves the greater good while respecting human rights and dignity.

Collaboration, not isolation, is key. By working together, psychologists and AI developers can create safer and more beneficial AI products for everyone. Psychologists bring their expertise in human behavior and ethics to the table, while developers provide the technical know-how to build the tools. This collaboration is essential for ensuring that AI continues to advance responsibly and ethically, maximizing its potential while minimizing its risks.

The future of AI is in our hands. By fostering effective collaboration between psychologists and AI developers, we can ensure that AI becomes a force for good, improving our lives while safeguarding our well-being and ethical principles.

Plan International is a global development NGO focused on girls' rights. Plan partners with US Government entities including USAID, State and DOL. Plan is not an expert on the workings of AI, but rather on the impact of AI and social media on the lives of girls and women in the United States and globally. The attached research report summarizes the key findings from scientifically representative surveys that Plan conducted in more than two dozen nations regarding the impacts of social media on women and girls. The data and qualitative interviews clearly demonstrate that girls and women are seeing their educational, employment, social and political roles heavily compromised due to the hostile and unregulated environments on social media, which have only been further exacerbated and accelerated by AI. Plan was therefore dismayed to find that the impacts of AI on girls and women were largely ignored in the text of Executive Order 14110. Plan fully supports the addition of a gender lens and of gender analysis to these regulations as they are developed by the NIST for sections 4.1, 4.5 and 11. Plan fully supports the comments by Vice President Harris that underlined the importance of addressing gender-based violence and other human rights abuses through these regulations.

Such consideration is especially relevant to the AI Risk Management Framework, to Biases in Data, Models and AI Lifecycle Practices and to Impacts on Equity. It also must be addressed through regulations to prevent generative AI from producing child sexual abuse material or producing non-consensual intimate imagery of real individuals (to include intimate digital depictions of the body or body parts of an identifiable individual). Most girls and women do not have an army of followers to protect them (as Taylor Swift does) and are relying on the government to provide that security.

As an international NGO, Plan has worked with State and USAID to include the issue of technology-facilitated gender-based violence through social media and AI in their program strategies. Plan has also worked with USUN to successfully include language on the impact of online abuse on adolescent girls in the Agreed Conclusions at the UN Commission on the Status of Women. Plan has also worked with the White House Gender Policy Council on these issues and is a member of the advisory council for the Global Partnership for Action on Online Harassment and Abuse, which the United States and Denmark co-chair. Plan's work in these forums and the attached research demonstrate that girls and women around the world are facing essentially one global culture of abuse online. With the European Union, UK and Australia already years ahead of the US in regulating these social ills, we believe there is fertile ground for advancing global standards, as mandated by section 11 of the EO.

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2023-28232
comments.comment_text:
Recommendations on Generative AI risk management and AI evaluation
Author: Gautam Jain
linkedin.com/in/gautamjain

Thoughts expressed are original views of the author. Submission is in personal capacity and does not represent the views of the author’s employer
Preface
These recommendations are created in response to National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) RFI (Request For Information) as per executive order 14110 Sections 4.1(a)(i)(A) and (C) which directs NIST to establish guidelines and best practices in order to promote consensus industry standards in the development and deployment of safe, secure, and trustworthy AI systems.
Recommendations
Specific and actionable best practices that should be part of AI RMF 2.0 and were missing in AI RMF 1.0 are listed below. To promote a safe, secure and trustworthy AI system in the future, there are 6 unique recommendations namely Disclaimer, Source and Transparency, Human-led testing, Pre-launch readiness, Post-launch feedback and Independent 3rd Party auditor ecosystem. The following section describes each recommendation further:
Disclaimer
Every output from a generative AI based product or feature must have a disclaimer which is specific to the intent of the query or the subject within reasonable human understanding. For e.g. if a human requests for financial investment advice to an AI model, it’s output must contain a standard alert message or disclaimer related to the risk associated and that the output is not a legal financial advice and the end user is requested to exercise caution and avail professional financial advice from a registered, professional advisor, tax consultant or accountant - as the case may be. AI developers, deployers and auditors must all adhere to the provision (to be added to AI RMF 2.0) that each response has an associated disclaimer which is relevant within reasonable understanding of the intent of the query.

Source & Traceability
In the AI RMF 1.0, it is mentioned that Accountability and Transparency will lead to Trustworthiness. However, there is no mention of Source and Traceability of the generated content or output. If auditors were to pass an AI model for a public launch and wider-availability beyond safe-environment testing, the AI models must be able to either probabilistically or deterministically share the source(s) in creating the output i.e articles read, authors quoted, web pages crawled, systems used, websites referred, books studies, data analyzed, countries associated. In case multiple generic data sets are used to generate the output, the AI model must be able to trace the top ‘n’ contributing data sets which had the highest percentage role to play in algorithmic learning in the process of generating output.

Human-led Testing
Create a community of Trusted Testers.
An AI model, to be publicly available in the hands of humans, or affecting their day-to-day lives, must pass rigorous testing standards
AI models or algorithms, train on data sets and have the computational ability to learn and bypass a test, thus NIST or Secretary of Commerce must actively invest in creating a thriving community of human testers representing different races, regions, religions, ages, genders, IQs, EQs etc. respecting aspects of diversity, equity, inclusion and belonging.
Create a repository of basic, intermediate and advanced test cases which can be used by the human testers to get started with an AI-model audit, but do maintain > 51% of the tests to be impromptu, human-created, unguided cases

Pre-launch readiness
Checklist requirements for a public launch of an AI model should include a Safety score. Based on the human-led testing, each AI model must be given a safety score on a scale of 0-100, which should help the end users of the system to understand directionally how safe it might be to use a particular generative AI based solution

Post-launch feedback
NIST must direct AI developers and deployers to continually accept, process, action and inform on each and every piece of feedback received from human interactions. This will help in improving the models based on human expectations of a particular result and maintain a sustainable way to keep AI models in check
The end user must be entitled to receive an update or resolution within reasonable time (SLAs) as is possible for the creators and maintenance personnel of the AI solution

Independent 3P audits
The AI RMF 2.0 should have a certification of the highest standard, issued by NIST or other leading regulators to create a 3rd party auditors ecosystem. The auditors may charge a fee for each evaluation based on the AI RMF 2.0 and render an algorithm as safe or unsafe (pass or fail) to be launched
These auditors should be independent entities, not having any vested interests in the companies they are auditing for a given framework
Public launch of AI solutions which do not have a valid certification must be illegal under cybersecurity laws.

I also recall university professors at that time working on neural nets and other early forms of AI, which have made enormous advances. We struggle today with the knowledge that software - even without AI - can be harmful and potentially life-threatening. We have convened multiple time in our effort to define practices and standardized rules to follow for developing 'safe' code.

Unfortunately, AI development can be very costly. We should predict that much like the condition of bridges in the 19th century, there will be people who cutting corners (whether deliberately or through ignorance is not stipulated) in their personal path to completing AI projects. Perhaps there are corner cases without adequate training data. As with financial investments, there will be bad actors. As such, our collective contributions to recommended practices are helpful, but may be of only modest benefit for those are willful, or willfully ignorant. Let's remember the role of software in the 737MAX crashes - and Boeing's stated intent to commercialize without the user-cost of pilot retraining.

For this simple too-human reason, we must have an expectation of a methodical process of both target performance and guardrails for any potentially life-threatening software application. We must remember that people have already died - in the case of autonomous vehicles (Uber in Arizona). That is, requirements must be explicit and coders and manager will need to authenticate their work - regardless of conformance to recommended coding methodologies.

Most importantly, there must be a way to audit the process of the development and certification of both low level algos and higher level functions. Today's applications have hundreds of individual code blocks - some being open-source or software of unknown provenance. The audit function must also satisfy release and edit processes supporting near-term and long-term software lifecycle management (See PATCH-Act). Following a decade of internal development, the FDA has finally iterated toward a methodology of supporting software audits, AI inclusive. (See Software as a Medical Device.) It's is defined extensively for the condition of potentially life-threatening applications. As implemented in industry today it is both tedious and laborious for coders and front line managers to execute to this standard; however, it need not be given the very recent expansion of automated tools to both ensure requirements compliance and track versions, tests, certifications and approvals. (See Ketryx.)

In conclusion, while it's clear that the audit function is not explicitly part of the current NIST effort, it is likely short-sighted to ignore the need for any useful standard to be auditable by government employees who may not have the time/ability to read code blocks at a detailed level.
To paraphase the nineteenth century riddle, "What is it the less of it there is, the more it is dread?," if coders built bridges the way they write software, no one would cross them.

Ken Harvey
Retired CEO/Entrepreneur

comments.title: Comment on FR Doc # 2023-28232
comments.comment_text:
Generative AI Risk Management

a. Risks and Harms of Generative AI: The potential for generative AI to cause harm is significant, especially in relation to misinformation, deepfakes, and other forms of synthetic media. The development of a companion resource to the AI RMF for generative AI should prioritize the identification of these risks, with a clear mapping of trustworthiness characteristics, to ensure robust risk mitigation strategies are in place. It is essential to consider both technical and non-technical harms, including the impacts on democracy, privacy, and human rights.

b. Standards and Practices: There is an apparent gap in standardized practices for managing generative AI risks. The AI RMF core functions should be expanded to include specific guidance tailored to generative AI, with a focus on governance structures that incorporate multi-stakeholder perspectives, including those from civil society and affected communities.

AI Red-Teaming

a. Guidelines for Red-Teaming: Red-teaming exercises are essential for identifying and mitigating unforeseen risks in AI systems. Guidelines for red teaming should consider the various stages of the AI lifecycle and provide a structured approach to identifying potential threat models and harmful capabilities.

b. Capabilities and Limitations: Understanding the capabilities and limitations of AI red-teaming is vital for its effectiveness. The guidelines should provide clarity on the scope and scale of red-teaming exercises, ensuring that they are comprehensive enough to reveal significant risks without compromising the security or intellectual property of the AI systems.

c. Best Practices and Information Sharing: Establishing best practices for red teaming is necessary to ensure consistency and effectiveness across different organizations and sectors. These practices should include mechanisms for information sharing that balance the need for collaboration with the protection of sensitive information.

comments.title: Comment from Lopin, Lennart
comments.comment_text:
Dear Department of Commerce,

I write to express my profound concern over the direction of regulatory focus amid pressing national security issues. The prevailing situation at our national borders remains unaddressed, with the administration and Congress seemingly indifferent to the consequences of unchecked immigration, which, as reported, has led to severe criminal activities affecting American citizens. This disregard is juxtaposed with an apparent preference for instituting additional regulatory burdens, reminiscent of the Patriot Act's encroachment on civil liberties—a legislation that, in my view, necessitates reevaluation and repeal for its infringement on personal freedoms.

Presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy's critique of the federal government as excessively expansive and detrimental to our nation's foundational principles resonates deeply with me. His call for a substantial reduction in the federal workforce underscores a critical need for reformation, suggesting that the current proposal to regulate Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) products and foreign transactions involving large AI models is misplaced. It is imperative to recognize that the resources dedicated to such regulations might be more effectively allocated towards securing our borders and investing in crucial infrastructure projects that directly benefit the public welfare.

The proposed regulations, aimed at verifying the identity of foreign IaaS customers and monitoring transactions related to the training of large AI models, overlook the inherently open-source nature of AI research and scientific literature. This oversight not only hinders scientific progress but also fails to address the root issues of intellectual property theft, particularly from international actors. The focus on bureaucratic expansion through regulation serves to encumber American scientists and innovators, without offering a tangible solution to the pressing problem of intellectual theft, notably from China.

In light of these considerations, I urge a reevaluation of regulatory priorities, emphasizing the immediate need to fortify our national borders and invest in infrastructure that directly contributes to the nation's prosperity and security. Let us redirect our focus towards measures that genuinely safeguard the interests of American citizens and uphold the values of freedom and innovation that define our great nation.

comments.title: Comment from American Institute of Noncompliance
comments.comment_text:
Inclusion is a fundamental principle that should be considered when implementing identification methods for technology services. By imposing strict identity verification requirements, there is a risk of limiting people's ability to use the technology and excluding certain individuals from accessing essential services. This can disproportionately impact marginalized communities, including individuals without official identification documents, immigrants, and those from low-income backgrounds. It is important to ensure that identification methods are inclusive and accessible to a wide range of individuals.

Identification services can be seen as an invasion of privacy for individuals. The collection and verification of personal information can lead to the potential misuse or mishandling of sensitive data. With the increasing prevalence of data breaches and cyber threats, there is a legitimate concern about the security and privacy of individuals' personal information. The implementation of identification services may expose individuals to greater risks of identity theft, surveillance, and unauthorized access to their personal data. It is crucial to strike a balance between national security and protecting individual privacy rights.

Furthermore, it is important to critically evaluate the effectiveness of identification services in addressing national security threats. While the intention behind these methods is to enhance security and combat malicious cyber activities, there are doubts about their efficacy. Sophisticated cyber actors may find ways to circumvent these identification measures, rendering them ineffective in deterring potential threats. Additionally, the focus on identification services may divert resources and attention away from other crucial aspects of national security, such as investing in robust cybersecurity measures and promoting international cooperation in combating cyber threats.

Instead of solely relying on identification methods, a more comprehensive approach to national security should be adopted. This approach should include a combination of measures such as strong encryption, multi-factor authentication, and continuous monitoring of network activities. By focusing on these proactive security measures, the risks associated with identification services can be mitigated, while still ensuring the protection of individuals' privacy rights.

For small businesses, these compliance costs can be particularly challenging to manage. Limited financial resources and personnel may make it difficult for small businesses to allocate the necessary funds and manpower to meet these requirements. The costs associated with understanding and implementing the proposed regulations can potentially strain their operational budgets and hinder their ability to invest in other areas of their business

The risk of individuals at the state level can be abused due to several factors. First, the collection and storage of personal information for risk assessment purposes can be vulnerable to unauthorized access or misuse. If this sensitive data falls into the wrong hands, it can be exploited for various malicious activities, such as identity theft, fraud, or surveillance. Additionally, the subjective nature of risk assessment can lead to biases and discrimination. If the criteria used to determine an individual's risk are flawed or influenced by personal biases, it can result in unfair treatment and stigmatization of certain individuals or communities. Moreover, the abuse of individual risk assessments can lead to the violation of privacy rights and civil liberties, as excessive monitoring and surveillance measures may be imposed on individuals without proper justification.

In conclusion, the implementation of identification methods should be approached with caution. While national security is important, it should not come at the expense of inclusivity, privacy, and the potential limitations of technology usage. It is crucial to strike a balance between security and individual rights, and to explore alternative methods that are more inclusive, privacy-enhancing, and effective in addressing national security threats.

comments.title: Comment from Toscano, Lorenzo
comments.comment_text:
Dear Department of Commerce,

As an individual that works in the cybersecurity department of a U.S. company with foreign customers I wanted to comment in response to the proposed regulation regarding the verification of foreign customers by U.S. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) providers, it is important to highlight the nuanced landscape of cybersecurity and digital service provision. The regulation, motivated by the need to catch potential misuse by foreign cyber-enabled adversaries, casts a broad net that might not differentiate adequately between malicious actors and legitimate customers of IaaS services.

While recognizing the intent behind requiring an identification processes for all foreign nationals utilizing IaaS services from U.S. providers, it is crucial to acknowledge the complexity of digital identification. The digital space, characterized by rapid innovation and diverse international standards, presents a dynamic challenge in verification processes. Notably, any identification method, regardless of its sophistication, is susceptible to falsification, especially in the cyber-enabled foreign adversaries countries. This inherent vulnerability highlights the importance of not penalizing IaaS providers for fraudulent activities perpetrated with falsified identification methods beyond their control.
Adopting digital identification methods as part of the verification process represents a step forward in addressing this challenge. However, this approach necessitates a deep understanding of international trends in digital identification and an adaptive framework that respects global privacy norms.
I recommend to concentrate "Red Flags" reporting to the Department or related agency, on entities from countries with a high risk of cybercrime. Additionally, I would recommend the requirement for annual self-attestation by IaaS providers to compliance with the regulation to introduce a layer of accountability while maintaining operational flexibility. Audits and investigations may be conducted on providers suspected of non-compliance. For non-complying providers, utilizing the distinction between civil and criminal penalties based on the intent behind non-compliance is another positive aspect of the proposed regulation. While intent may be hard to prove, the review of documents drafted while creating the CIP program might shine light on their intent.

However, the broader implications of these regulations on the economic viability of U.S. IaaS providers, and consequently on the cost to consumers, including those in the U.S., warrant careful consideration. Increased regulatory burdens could inadvertently raise service costs, affecting accessibility and fostering a shift towards non-U.S. providers driven by privacy concerns and data handling perceptions.

In conclusion, while the drive to regulate foreign access to U.S. IaaS services stems from a valid concern over cybersecurity threats, the regulation must balance security objectives with the realities of digital identification and the operational dynamics of IaaS providers. Emphasizing that providers should not be penalized for activities conducted using falsified identification methods beyond their control is essential. Finally, the Department may consider only applying this rule for high-risk countries, as the operational expense would be justified by the higher risk of cybercrime offenders using the IaaS services defined by the regulation.

Best regards,
Lorenzo

I am writing to express my concerns regarding the proposed rule titled "Taking Additional Steps To Address the National Emergency With Respect to Significant Malicious Cyber-Enabled Activities" as outlined in the Federal Register on January 29, 2024¹[1].

comments.comment_text:
The proposed regulations requiring identity verification for foreign customers of U.S. cloud providers and reporting on foreign entities training large AI models are deeply troubling from a civil liberties, privacy, and human rights perspective. These regulations would create a chilling effect on free expression, open access to information, and technological innovation globally.
By forcing cloud providers to collect and verify the identities of foreign customers, it would make it far more difficult for activists, journalists, researchers, and others abroad to privately and securely access cloud computing resources. This could expose them to retaliation from authoritarian regimes for simply storing data or hosting websites. It also creates significant privacy risks if this personal data is mishandled or breached.
The requirement to report on foreign entities training large AI models is equally concerning. While the government claims this is to detect potential malicious cyber activity, it seems more aimed at giving authorities широкого surveillance over a key emerging technology. AI training involves ingesting and processing huge corpuses of data, including personal information, copyrighted works, and sensitive materials. Mandating reporting on this private activity raises major censorship and intellectual property risks.
Moreover, these rules would put U.S. cloud providers at a major disadvantage globally. If other nations adopt similar data localization and AI monitoring rules, it could lock American companies out of foreign markets. The impact on the competitiveness of the U.S. tech industry could be severe.
From a technical standpoint, the definitions and criteria in the proposed rules also appear vague and unworkable. What constitutes a "large" AI model or "potential malicious cyber capabilities" is highly subjective. Implementing such ambiguous standards would be extremely difficult and likely overly censorious.
Beyond pragmatic concerns, the underlying premise of these regulations - treating foreign access to common computing resources as a national security threat - is misguided and counterproductive. The open, decentralized nature of the internet has been a tremendous engine of economic growth, cultural exchange, and human empowerment globally. Erecting digital borders and scrutinizing routine online activities will only breed distrust, fragment the internet, and cut off America's own access to global innovation.
Rather than unilaterally clamping down, the U.S. should be leading efforts to establish clear international norms and safeguards around technology governance through multilateral cooperation. Hasty, knee-jerk regulations like these will simply encourage other nations to pursue tit-for-tat restrictions, stifling the cross-border data flows critical to AI development and modern economic prosperity.
In summary, these well-intentioned but heavy-handed and shortsighted rules would significantly undermine core American values of free expression, privacy, and innovation leadership. A more nuanced, collaborative approach respectful of civil liberties is needed.

Expansion of Government Surveillance: Enforcing KYC on internet connections extends government surveillance beyond reasonable limits. This expansion undermines civil liberties and contributes to distrust between citizens and authorities.
Limitations on Online Education and Information Access: Mandating KYC for internet access can impede online education initiatives and restrict access to essential information, especially in regions with limited educational resources.
Global Regulatory Complexity: KYC implementation for internet connections may result in regulatory fragmentation across jurisdictions. This can impede cross-border internet access and disrupt the free flow of information internationally.
Unintended Cybersecurity Risks: KYC requirements may inadvertently weaken cybersecurity measures. Requiring personal information increases the attack surface for cybercriminals exploiting vulnerabilities in identity verification systems.
Impact on Online Expression and Creativity: Heightened surveillance due to KYC measures can stifle online discourse and creative expression. Users may self-censor or refrain from engaging in online activities due to fear of monitoring or identification.

Ineffectiveness Against Cybercrime Root Causes: KYC for internet connections fails to address the underlying causes of cybercrime and online misconduct. Instead of monitoring individuals, efforts should focus on proactive measures to enhance cybersecurity and digital literacy.
In summary, implementing KYC for internet connections poses significant threats to digital rights, disproportionately impacts vulnerable populations, and imposes regulatory burdens and costs on ISPs and online platforms. Moreover, it extends government surveillance, restricts access to information and education, and introduces unintended cybersecurity risks while failing to address the root causes of online misconduct. Alternative strategies should be explored to enhance online security without compromising individual rights and freedoms.

comments.title: Comment from Esposito, Matthew
comments.comment_text:
The proposed regulations outlined in the Executive orders of January 19, 2021, and October 30, 2023, certainly aim to address significant threats posed by foreign malicious cyber actors. However, while the intentions may be noble, the implications of these regulations on privacy and the openness of the internet raise serious concerns.

1. **Privacy Infringement**: Requiring U.S. Infrastructure as a Service
(IaaS) providers to verify the identity of foreign customers and to submit reports on transactions involving AI training runs encroaches upon individuals' privacy rights. Such measures essentially introduce a form of surveillance, where every interaction with IaaS providers becomes subject to scrutiny. This blanket surveillance undermines the principles of privacy and anonymity that have long been cherished on the internet.

2. **Chilling Effect on Innovation and Freedom of Expression**: By imposing stringent verification requirements and reporting obligations, the proposed regulations may deter legitimate users, including researchers, developers, and entrepreneurs, from accessing IaaS products. Fear of being subjected to scrutiny or mistakenly flagged as engaging in malicious activity could stifle innovation and limit the free exchange of ideas and knowledge. An internet landscape where individuals fear constant surveillance is antithetical to the principles of a free and open society.

3. **Overreach and Lack of Proportionality**: While combating cyber threats is undoubtedly crucial, the proposed regulations appear disproportionate to the problem at hand. Mandating identity verification for all foreign users and imposing reporting requirements on AI training runs casts too wide a net, potentially ensnaring innocent users in bureaucratic red tape. Such measures should be carefully tailored to target specific threats without unduly burdening legitimate users.

4. **Erosion of Trust in U.S. Tech Companies**: Imposing onerous regulations on IaaS providers could erode trust in U.S. tech companies and drive users towards less regulated alternatives. Foreign customers may seek out services from jurisdictions with less stringent oversight, thereby circumventing the intended security measures and undermining the effectiveness of the regulations.

5. **Unintended Consequences and Security Risks**: Heavy-handed regulations could inadvertently create new security vulnerabilities.
Forcing IaaS providers to collect and store sensitive personal information increases the risk of data breaches and unauthorized access.
Moreover, the diversion of resources towards compliance could divert attention and resources away from more effective cybersecurity measures.

In conclusion, while the need to address cyber threats is undeniable, the proposed regulations represent a heavy-handed approach that threatens to undermine privacy, innovation, and the openness of the internet. A more balanced approach, which prioritizes targeted measures to address specific threats while safeguarding fundamental rights and freedoms, is necessary to preserve the integrity of the internet as a platform for communication, collaboration, and innovation.

comments.title: Comment from Anonymous, Anonymous
comments.comment_text:
I have been working IT for decades now, and I currently work in the field of machine learning - or, simply, AI.

I understand the extreme risks that could be posed by future AI systems, and I do agree that steps should be taken to mitigate those risks.

However, I cannot in my right mind agree to the measures proposed.

The "KYC" requirements across the industry already border on overreach, and this proposal takes them well past. The proposed KYC measures are applied to areas that are only tangentially relevant to cybersecurity, in no way at all relevant to AI development, and instead serve to impose burdens on service providers, and threaten the privacy of regular users.

KYC requirements impose a burden on every service provider. KYC data is, for the lack of a more concise term, "radioactive". Any leak or breach involving such data has dire and far-reaching user privacy implications - and thus, well meaning industry actors have to take costly security measures when collecting, handling and storing such data. But, as decades of industry experience show, there is NO way to avoid data breaches altogether. The only way to prevent critical user data from being leaked is to never collect or store it in the first place. Not collecting any unnecessary data is the cheapest, simplest and by far the most foolproof solution to mitigate data breach risks. It's the best solution industry has. This proposal goes directly against that.

Furthermore, KYC measures have privacy implications for the end users. VPS and VPN are two types of services typically used by individuals, often with the goal of protecting their privacy specifically, and uses of such services have no relevance to AI development. CDN services have no relevance to either cybersecurity or AI development whatsoever. Targeting users of VPS, VPN and CDN systems with KYC measures only serves to threaten their privacy, and for no benefit.

To me, the KYC requirements proposed resemble ones imposed by authoritarian countries of Iran, China and Russia. The goal there is not to protect the country, or the users, but to threaten dissent and enable authoritarian control. This is the only context in which measures so severe and far-reaching would make sense.

If you truly seek to stop threat actors from using cloud services for developing advanced AI capabilities, you should instead implement measures targeted to counter that specifically. Advanced AI development requires specialized computational capabilities, and massive amounts of such.

Thus, you should only target transactions with relevant capabilities (primarily GPU or NPU machine-hours), and bulk amounts of that (transactions in hundreds of thousands of dollars at the minimum). By its very nature, this kind of large transaction is already likely to be KYC verified - and thus, the extra burden imposed on service providers would be minimal.

Conversely - no one is going to develop bleeding edge AI by using a $8 VPN, an $50 VPS, or by renting 10 machine-hours worth of NVIDIA A100.

Please, take care to target the right actors - and to avoid hitting service providers and users instead.

The proposed requirement for Know Your Customer (KYC) regulations for internet users raises significant concerns regarding the potential infringement of fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and privacy. The internet has played a pivotal role in facilitating the free flow of information and ideas, and any attempt to curtail this freedom should be scrutinized under the lens of constitutional protections.

The First Amendment of the United States Constitution guarantees the freedom of speech and expression, which includes the right to communicate anonymously and without undue government interference. The Supreme Court has consistently upheld this principle in various cases, such as McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission (1995), where the Court ruled that the freedom to publish anonymously is protected by the First Amendment.

Furthermore, the right to privacy is recognized as a fundamental liberty under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, as established in the landmark case of Griswold v. Connecticut (1965). This right has been extended to protect various forms of personal information, including online activities and communications, as outlined in cases such as Riley v. California (2014) and Carpenter v. United States (2018).

Imposing KYC requirements on internet users could potentially violate these constitutional protections by compelling individuals to disclose personal information and potentially chilling their willingness to engage in online speech and expression. Such a measure could also enable the government to monitor and track individuals' online activities, raising significant privacy concerns.

It is important to engage in a robust public discourse and carefully consider the potential implications of such regulations on the open and free nature of the internet, while also addressing legitimate concerns related to online security and public safety.

Personally, I believe that the rights and freedoms enjoyed by the majority of people should not be impinged by the rather sparse and sporadic actions of the few.

comments.title: Comment from kkn, ri
comments.comment_text:
The concept of KYC (Know Your Customer) is primarily associated with the financial industry, where businesses are required to verify the identity of their clients to prevent services from being used for money laundering, terrorism financing, or other illegal activities. When the concept of KYC is applied to internet connections, it suggests a scenario where users would have to verify their identity to access the internet. This idea raises several concerns about privacy, freedom, and potential misuse of data. Here’s why KYC'ing internet connections could be considered detrimental to society:

1. Privacy Concerns
Requiring identity verification for internet access could lead to significant privacy invasions. The internet is a fundamental tool for personal expression and information gathering. KYC mandates would mean that users' online activities could be easily linked to their real-world identities, potentially leading to surveillance and a lack of anonymity online.

2. Freedom of Expression
Anonymity and privacy are often vital for freedom of expression, particularly under oppressive regimes or in sensitive situations. If users know that their identity is linked to their online activities, they may self-censor or avoid discussing or researching certain topics. This could stifle free speech and inhibit the free flow of information.

3. Access and Inclusivity
The internet is a critical resource for education, communication, and commerce. Requiring identity verification could create barriers to access for those without the means to prove their identity through official documents, which disproportionately affects marginalized and lower-income individuals. This could widen the digital divide and reinforce social and economic inequalities.

4. Potential for Misuse
Centralizing identity and access data could make this information a target for cybercriminals. If breached, the consequences could be severe, exposing virtually every aspect of an individual's digital life. Additionally, there is the risk of misuse by governments or private entities, leading to increased surveillance or discriminatory practices based on monitoring internet access.

5. Impact on Innovation
The general openness and pseudo-anonymity of the internet have been significant drivers of innovation. Requiring KYC could dampen entrepreneurial activities, as creators may feel inhibited by surveillance or privacy concerns, thus slowing technological advancement and the free exchange of ideas.

6. Regulatory and Implementation Challenges
Implementing a KYC requirement for internet access would be technically and administratively burdensome. It would require building and maintaining secure, sophisticated systems capable of handling a massive amount of sensitive data. The cost and complexity of such systems could lead to higher costs for consumers and might be impractical for smaller internet service providers.

7. International Implications
The internet is a global network without borders, but different countries have varying standards for privacy and data protection. Implementing KYC on internet connections would require navigating these diverse legal frameworks, potentially leading to conflicts of law and concerns over sovereignty and jurisdiction.

In summary, while the intention behind KYC'ing internet connections might be to enhance security, the potential negative impacts on privacy, freedom of expression, inclusivity, and innovation could have far-reaching consequences for society. The debate around such a policy would need to carefully consider these factors against the perceived benefits of reduced anonymity online.
