Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

I am a professional programmer in the video game industry. I have worked at Activision on the largest projects in the industry, and at startups on the smallest projects. I have worked with the sorts of individuals in the tech industry hyping up technologies like blockchain, NFTs, and now "generative AI".

It is simply unacceptable to allow companies to bypass copyright restrictions, period. Companies like OpenAI, Microsoft, Google, Adobe, and Apple are engaging in blatant theft to create technologies that do not create value for the world. An OpenAI representative has already stated in plain English that their products cannot exist without the use of copyright materials without permission -- we have a word for this: "stealing".

Furthermore, these companies have demonstrated time and time again that they will engage in anti-competitive business practices that hurt Americans. It is unthinkable to trust them with unprecedented copyright privilege. In fact, they are already engaging in untrustworthy tactics, claiming that they are creating "ethical" AI models, when they are in fact using billions of copyright works without permission as we speak. They are not seeking permission to gather more data, they are seeking pardons for the data they have already illegally gathered.

For example, when Adobe introduced generative AI features in Photoshop, they claimed they were trained only on the stock photo library that they own (while quietly announcing a partnership with OpenAI). However, AI image generators require billions of images to function, far more images than Adobe's stock photo library contains. It is obvious that Adobe's claim is a lie, and that they are gaslighting Americans about the nature of their products. It is gut-wrenching to think that a company engaging in such untrustworthy behavior could be granted special privileges.

It is important to understand that despite the newly-granted name "AI", machine learning is not "artificial intelligence". Machine learning encompasses algorithms that produce outputs that are a function of their input. Fundamentally, machine learning does not invent new outputs. If an LLM can output a corporate email, it's because millions of similar corporate emails were taken without permission as training data. If an "AI" image generator can produce a picture of Mickey Mouse, it's because millions of images of Mickey Mouse were taken without permission. Moreover, these models require TENS OF BILLIONS of such training data to function at the level they current do.

An economy cannot function when theft is rampant. Allowing this to continue is a bad idea for Americans, and a bad idea for the American economy.

Finally as a personal note, the fact that my work and the work of my friends is already being stolen at-scale is profoundly troubling and insulting. I don't know if I could ever support a politician or political party that sides with the thieves.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

While I understand the concern with international developments on this technology, the current approach is being done with a very shortsighted view. The original developers and researchers of what we call artificial intelligence have long warned us against using it without much restriction. There are better approaches that can be done to continue development without harming American people and American culture.

We need to keep things that involve and require human experiences and judgement to humanity. We are already seeing negative impacts against Americans by using this technology to circumvent processes that need human judgement. This is seen in many jobs right now where Americans are getting automatically rejected regardless of whether they qualified or not, since these applications are being processed as variables rather than for qualifications.

We will also be degrading American culture by leaving everything to computerized ideas, which cannot live full lives as Americans to enrich us and show the world who we are. Everything that defines us will be jumbled into a game of telephone by a computer based off of calculated inputs, rather than have us defined by Americans with rich and different lives that can bring pride to our country. A computer can be completely copied while a skilled American cannot.

Because these are computers as well, they can easily be manipulated and worked around and we are haphazardly leaving judgement onto these devices. We have already faced great cyberattacks in our country with data breaches, who is to say our Artificial Intelligence cannot be tampered with by another country to harm us? We are already having issues protecting our systems and this technology is far too new to rely on it.

However, This is to not say we do not need Artificial Intelligence whatsoever and that we need to handicap ourselves based off of these concerns. There is ways it can still be develop and I urge the United States to take some time to think about their strategy thoroughly rather than with haste. There is a long history with this technology that is being overlooked that should be a factor into this decision.

I believe as a way to continue development and to use this technology to its full, true potential, we need to be focused on its use mathematically, just like any other computer technology. We can greatly use this technology to speed up progress in other developments in other industries, without completely replacing those jobs. For example some industries require very lengthy calculations as a part of the job, which can be sped up greatly with the assistance of AI. We can use this technology to enhance our current algorithms in our infrastructure, which wouldn't affect jobs as those algorithms are already written down and tend to be set in stone.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

America does not need a stronger generative AI policy - generative AI programs are a massive waste of resources, being inefficient and producing mediocre to bad results, and gutting copyright to allow generative AI companies to steal data and creative works at will is a great way to chill actual scientific and artistic progress in the United States. The reality of generative AI is that it's a probability machine, a stochastic algorithm that generates a series of words, images, music, etc. that are related to some input. If I'm working on a paper about a scientific field, and I ask a generative AI program to make a bibliography, it'll throw out the names of papers, researchers, and journals that are associated with the field I'm interested in. Whether or not those words make any sense together, whether or not the thing those words are describing actually exists, is an entirely different question. There is no "mind" behind a generative AI program that knows the difference between a truth and a lie, and generative AI programs are by nature uncreative. As such, putting these programs in charge of national security and database management is incredibly dangerous, and has the potential to do lasting damage to America's stability and security. Furthermore, the companies pushing generative AI programs have massive financial investments in those programs, and it frankly seems like they're trying to use the United States government as a piggy bank to line their pockets. Even in calling these programs AI, when there's nothing intelligent, no "mind" behind these programs, it's obvious that this is a scam. I'm also worried about the scientists, artists, engineers, and entrepreneurs who will have their copyrighted work stolen by these for-profit companies. How are we supposed to create anything, why would we want to create anything, if our work is just going to be used by companies who'll sell it off to the highest bidder? This policy seems to be a great way to strangle real creativity in the cradle, while driving up utility costs due to the massive amounts of electricity and water that generative AI programs need to function to badly ape that creativity. We need better policy than this.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

The methods in which OpenAI and Google plan to collect training data is absurdly anti-competitive and generally unethical. This proposal is effectively granting these companies special exception to blatantly violate copyright law and fair use. Even if other AI companies were allowed to freely use copyrighted materials in their training models, the lack of compensation for the original creators of the training materials would disincentivize creating any further material at all. AI models cannot create new material in the same way humans can and must constantly rely on a continuous source of data. The quality of their models will decay over time without this.

Should Google and OpenAI be granted this exception, it would lead to them becoming a large scale monopoly, stifling any further innovation in not just the field of artificial intelligence but in all creative media. It is a blatant double standard as well. I'm certain both Google and OpenAI would take issue to their own data being used for training by a rival AI company.

If these companies need to gain an unfair advantage in order to remain competitive, then they need to reconsider how they are running their business in the first place. OpenAI and Google is effectively asking all creatives across the United States of America to work for free. That does not exactly sound like a free market capitalist society. This is made worse so as these companies do not necessarily have the best interests of the American people in mind when they are depriotizing quality of service.

Google in particular is already making Internet searches difficult by limiting the results you want to see as well as giving incorrect, biased information as well as prioritizing advertisements over accurate information. Effectively, they are also limiting free speech and a person's right to public information.

Future AI laws need to prevent this disastrous scenario from happening.

Experts in AI safety, including those from OpenAI, DeepMind, and leading universities, have warned that misaligned AI systems could surpass human intelligence and become uncontrollable. Scenarios such as AI-driven economic disruption, autonomous weapons escalation, and loss of human oversight in critical systems are no longer speculative—they are real risks that could destabilize our societies.

Moreover, a poorly regulated AI race between nations and corporations could push safety considerations aside, leading to catastrophic consequences. We need proactive governance, international cooperation, and strict regulatory frameworks to ensure AI remains aligned with human values. The choices we make today will determine whether AI becomes humanity's greatest ally or its gravest threat.

I appreciate your attention to this urgent matter.

## **General Comment**

AI does not & should not have a future in the United States - the energy costs are disasterous for our grid & natural resources. That alone should be enough -- it is simply not sustainable. All the creative enterprises that this nation is known for, from cinematic masterpieces to the "next great American novel" -- gone, mashed into a bland paste. Eventually, the only companies that will be able to compete at all will be those driven by human artists -- the extra time it takes to produce the art by hand is less the manual labor, and more due to the deliberate intention, research, attention to detail, and inspiration it takes to make products that resonate with a wide audience.

As a highly successful artist that creates wholly original content by hand and has made millions for corporations & big box stores without the assistance of AI, who happily made a typical office worker's wage & was grateful for it, I promise you the affordable, creative powerhouses you seek are already present en masse in highly trained, specialized human beings and is FAR more worth the investment than any flash-in-the-pan technology ever will be. ## **General Comment**

I am a programmer. I work with AI as part of my job, at the insistence of my superiors. The current most popular branches of AI development produce shoddy output, sometimes even dangerously so depending on what it's being used for, are over-promised on what they can reliably accomplish or what they could ever hope to reliably accomplish, leading to many users and investors putting unwarranted faith and sometimes money into the products. This shoddy output is on top of training via rampant copyright infringement and a complete disregard for intellectual property, sometimes purposeful and targeting in attempts to infringe on a particular creator's unique style. They're anti-competitive, as they produce low-quality output at a subsidized and unsustainable cost, using predatory pricing practices to force the creatives that they stole their training materials from to either also drop to unsustainable prices or fold. They're harmful to the environment, wasting large amounts of natural resources to accomplish tasks that could've been accomplished much more simply and with much fewer resources by paying a human to do so. I believe there are valid and useful places for AI to be used, but at present the most "lucrative" options, which are only lucrative thanks to a bubble, falsified advancement trajectory, and lax government oversight, are a scam in progress, with creatives already feeling the burn and the collapse inevitably soon to reach executives. AI should be more strictly regulated to ensure these companies aren't scamming investors and consumers alike by over-promising or promising things their product can't accurately accomplish, that their training is done ethically, and that the pricing accurately reflects the cost of business; that they're not using anti-competitive pricing strategies with plans to increase prices once they achieve market dominance.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

While AI technology is helpful for some tasks there should be an extreme degree of consideration taken for data privacy in the training of these models. Up to this point it has been clear that AI companies have no concern for the ethics of the data they have. Many AI companies have swept the entirety of the internet and ingested nearly all accessible data to train their models giving no concern for the legality of the data they ingest or the copyright protections of said data. Now with this further order there is a great concern that people's private data will be used for training. It is not surprising that people do not want large corporations with no concerns for data privacy having access to information about them. If data ingested is retained without censorship it would in theory be possible to get the AI model to regurgitate part of said data as was done at a hacking convention with a car company's public chat bot instance of an AI model which was able to be tricked into revealing customers credit card numbers. In the rush to get investor money based on innovation in AI many companies have disregarded the ethics of what they do in favor of speed, we should not allow them access to private data as a reward for their actions.

Furthermore there are massive concerns as to the energy efficiency of these models. While our electricity infrastructure and generation ability continues to age we are developing technologies that require an extraordinary amount of power to perform basic tasks that AI was not previously used for. For example almost every basic google search now pops up Google's AI suggestion, because of this every google search now requires much more electricity to perform as well as more water to cool the computers. It is worth remembering that the resources used for things like this are limited to the electricity we can generate, the more we buy into it the more infrastructure will need to be generated making life more expensive for everyday Americans.

AI models can be useful, I do agree with that. Alphafold 2 (the AI model that has been able to compute hundreds of millions of protein structures easily) has been revolutionary the past 2 years in Biology and we are making advances because of it. But these models are not ingesting private data, they only use known protien models and chemical information to train their system of calculators, and have real uses that benefit every human. It is dangerous to use successes like these to justify handing people's private information to a model for unknown benefits that would likely not help anybody and actively harm some people.

## **General Comment**

The privacy and intellectual property rights of private citizens must be of utmost importance regarding AI policy. Already, we have seen that AI companies have little regard for copyright protections, harvesting mass amounts of copyrighted work (e.g. writing, artwork, etc) from the internet to develop their models without any permission from the owners of said works, thus directly profiting off their work.

Additionally, mass amounts of personal data and information are harvested by tech corporations to be sold off to advertisers or other 3rd parties; for AI companies to do the same would be a similarly massive breach of privacy for the American public. Already we have seen propositions to use AI to predict human behavior: who is best to let out of jail and who should stay, who should be deported for their potential to commit future crimes, who should be hired and who should be fired. Such uses are incredibly inappropriate to downright dangerous: a computer program with zero accountability should not be trusted to make potentially life-altering decisions regarding our lives.

President Trump's executive order makes it clear that this administration prioritizes the profit of tech corporations above the safety and security of the American people. Removing safeguards to AI development will not make us safer; it will only lead to increased surveillance and give us less control over our own lives. I am wholeheartedly opposed to the idea.

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-3255

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

# **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

# **General Comment**

Reading through the executive order regarding A.I., one cannot help but notice a distinct lack of understanding in what A.I. is or what viable use cases there are. The niche use cases for purpose built A.I. in medical analysis and other scientific fields can be valuable in the hands of experts and those who understand the fundamental limitations of A.I. The A.I. referred to in common parlance and the executive order is a different matter, and the methods to create or "improve" it have proven to be inefficient and unethical. Big technology companies already have outsized influence and power over us and they do not need even more power and influence. The government should not allow them to disregard existing intellectual property laws for the sake of "global AI dominance". People are the true innovators and creators; thus the encouragement for creation and innovation must be directed toward the people, not A.I. or its facilitators.

If A.I. is to be used, there must be barriers and policies in place to prevent mishandling of that tool. Below are guardrails that I think most living the the United States would find reasonable and essential to protect our rights.

#### COPYRIGHT:

Copyrighted material or creative commons licensed works must not be used for any artificial intelligence purposes unless written consent is given by the original creator(s) of the works. Failure to obtain consent must be considered a violation of the law and the entity operating or training the A.I. must remove the data from the training data set and pay restitution to the original creator(s) as applicable.

## OPT-IN AND OPT-OUT RIGHTS:

All individuals, companies, or organizations have a fundamental right to not have their works, likenesses, information, et cetera, used in training artificial intelligence by default. Any service that uses A.I. or may use A.I. in the future, must allow users to opt-in if they want to allow their data to be used in this manner. It is not acceptable for users to be automatically opted-in or retroactively opted-in. Any user must be allowed to opt-out if they so choose and have their data removed from the data training set. Software or services that offer A.I. must allow that set of features or options to be permanently removed at the client level.

### WATERMARKING & METADATA:

Generative A.I. outputs must have conspicuous watermarks indicating that the output was A.I. made. Metadata must include and not be limited to: A.I. model(s) used, creation timestamps, and platform or service used. This is a must for transparency and integrity of accurate information.

This document is approved for public dissemination. The document contains no business-proprietary or confidential information. Document contents may be

reused by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.

## Good day to you!

I wanted to reach out and ask you to consider a logical and moral fallacy of cutting down regulations to further innovation in AI in competition with countries such as China.

To my knowledge, Google and OpenAI wish to train their models on intellectual property and other data not under their ownership; ergo, scraping from people regardless of their consent or not.

Is this not a violation of United States Copyright law? And a bare-faced one at that? Some random YouTuber under 500 subscribers can get copyright striked for including a half-second clip from a Warner Brothers movie, but two of the largest tech companies of today can leech off of people's creative work (of which those people sacrifice a lot of time, energy, and in several cases money to craft) and train their AI on them with intent to replace human effort for lower costs and newer heights at the expense of the livelihoods of the artists they scrape with no fear of repercussions?

If such is allowed, then piracy is an endeavor that need not be a crime. What is the point of copyright if intellectual property can be used to train a robot to replace it whether the owner of said property is on board with such or not?

I do not presume that any of this might sway you completely, however, I hold a tiny bit of hope that you might take what I said into consideration. At least, some of it. So many people are done with the absurd medical expenses and student loan debt, the broken education system, the rapidly rising rent prices and cost of living, and so much more. By giving the green light, you will not only alienate artists and other creatives but also many ordinary people whose personal photos and other information will be used without permission for tech that can and has been used for malicious purposes before. Eventually, their patience will run dryer than the Atacama. The first stone will be thrown, and the gates will fly open and right off their hinges. And nothing will put them back on.

Please make the right decision. Don't handicap the people even more.

## **General Comment**

Ai is theff of copyrighted materials and negatively impacts the livelihoods of the people it has stolen from. Individuals should have the same copyright protection that big companies like Disney receive for their copyright. If I can't take mickey mouse and do what I want with him, AI companies should also not be allowed to take my and other artists' copyrighted materials to do with as they please, especially for profit. Please do not allow AI companies to steal from artists for their own profit or fun. AI exists to replace artists and steal their jobs and their works. It is not fair use or transformative because a machine can not add any of their own experience or self into the 'new' art, which is really just an amalgamation of copyrighted material rather than something actually new. It simply regurgitates what it has been trained on and there is a risk of it outputting copyrighted ideas or images that are nearly identical to the work it has been trained on. It does not learn or create like a person who adds their own experiences into the transformative art. AI has no place competing in the market with artists whose copyrighted material it uses, either. A human that takes a few days to complete a work at best can not compete fairly with a machine that can output images and material instantly. It is unfair to allow a machine to use copyrighted material to compete in the same market as the people whose copyrighted material it is using when the humans have no hope of being able to compete with them.

## AI should be required to

- A) delete training data that uses copyrighted material that they did not gain implicit consent for
- B) Be required to obtain explicit consent for future training data via an OPT IN, not an OPT OUT system. An OPT OUT system allows them to train on data of artists who for one reason or another are unable to opt out, whether because they no longer have access to the account, or they have passed away, etc. it should NOT be default that they are allowed to use it unless you say no.
- C) They should have to compensate the artists that they have already made a profit off and required to compensate artists in the future if they are using their materials via the opt in system.
- D) There needs to be a watermark necessity for materials that are AI generated showing that they are AI generated as a disclaimer to stop the spread of potential mis and dis information.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

It is easy to pretend, especially if one likes to listen to popular people who call themselves intelligent, that Large Language Models ("AI") are to the modern day what factory industrialization was two hundred years ago. And they do share a commonality; the complete deskilling, atomization, and immiseration of artisans can be easily likened to the possible fates of artists, authors, engineers, musicians, and critical-thinking-enjoyers at large. But the industrial revolution lead to wealth, products, economic possibility—for all its human and environmental cost, it \*gave\* us something concrete. The investors behind LLM startups promise to do the same, to broaden the scope of society beyond whatever could be previously imagined.

They are lying.

By their construction, LLMs can give us nothing humans already do—they merely plagiarize, remix, and hallucinate a possible data point between what it has already devoured. LLMs train on other LLMs, creaing feedback loops of inaccuracies all citing each others' lies as proof. Primarily, "AI" has enriched a group of wealthy few who speculate on the future of our society. By smoothing over the promising and complicated technology of LLMs into a shiny project, these hucksters has created an underclass of impoverished moderators desperately steering the model away from regurgitating racist lies, environmental devastation while our planet tumbles toward irreversible climate damage, and a frustrated consumer adrift on a sea of shiny falsehoods made by no human hand which can ever be held to account. There is no soul, no promise to AGI—merely a sequence of snake oil billionaires so full of their own success they neglect the input of intelligent and measured critique. Use of LLMs has been demonstrated to erode the critical thinking of its users—there is no promise of a transformative future here. There is only billions of dollars to be lost on wisps of dreams.

This technology—and its many promises, amidst its woeful modern implementations—is best left regulated and studied carefully, its great power guarded behind human-first interface design, its many possibilities kept as tools first and economically-destructive-pseudo-humanreplacements second.

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-3461

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

While it is undeniable at this point in history that development of AI technology will be ongoing and it is necessary that the United States of America maintain its ability to compete if not lead in this field with other world powers, it absolutely must be done with the protection of the citizen in mind.

AI technology has proven its ability to assist in amazing ways in the fields of medicine, technology, and even entertainment. However it can easily be used by corporations and the government to push the ordinary citizen out of positions that could be deemed unnecessary or redundant in the path of such advances without providing necessary alternatives for those who could be displaced from jobs or even careers.

Intellectual properties must also be considered. Many AI farming sites and technology centers consider it priority to use anything that they can find, regardless of consent, in order to train their AI models to becomes more powerful. Copyright protections and artistic licenses are an important step to ensure that individual artists, authors, filmmakers and creators do not find their creations taken by AI programs and used without their consent to create derivative works that may blatantly take or even potentially steal from them with no legal recourse to protect their rights as creators. If an individual agrees to allow their creations to be used to train AI or as part of a larger program, then that is of course a transaction up to the artist to engage in. But artists, performers and creators must be given full copyright protections to ensure that AI programs or users of the technology cannot simply take their work because it was posted onto the internet. See Italy's views on the treatment of artists and AI.

The final consideration is the protection of the individual's own appearance. AI technology has the capability of creating accurate deepfakes of people, both visually and auditorily. These AI recreations of people have been used in creative parodies online, but there is an underlying threat that they could be used to falsely incriminate innocent people or even be used to manipulate footage of people to endorse ideals, movements, etc. that the individual does not endorse. These are concerns that have existed since the creation of video and audio technology, but never has the threat of technology being used to weaponize a person's very appearance and sound been so prevalent. It may be considered common sense that a person has the right to their own appearance and voice, but we are on the precipice of a time when even that could come under threat because of the demand for advancing this new, powerful technology.

In closing, AI has the potential to launch humanity into a new age. But we must take steps now to ensure that this new age will be one that enhances the life of the individual, not one that threatens the rights and securities of the people if AI and the people who program it are given unchecked power to do as they please with the technology. If we wait to try and work these protections out after the technology has already been advanced to the point we wish it to be, then it will be far more difficult if not impossible to ensure the protection of the very people those developing these programs desire to help.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

The "Development of an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan" must not go through, as the current state of "AI" is nothing more than deception, theft, and an environmental and humanitarian disaster.

"AI" has been deceptively marketed as being similar to, or is an Artificial General Intelligence. Which is far from the case, as current models are do not "think", they utilize tokens, a weighted value to generate imagery, text, and now video. Zero "thought" or "reasoning" is used in this process, nor is any truly novel technology being used.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) as it stands, is nothing more than a marketing term for weighted Markov Chains fed with massive amounts of data, using inordinate amounts of power for results that are often incorrect, outright disinformation, or manipulated to achieve the creator's goals. AI, which often refers to Large Language Models are an extrapolation of previous machine learning algorithms with the operational idea behind them being that "more data is better" when it comes to accuracy and flexibility, which is not the case.

Current "AI" schemes are fed data in ways that violates all known national and international copyright laws. Crawling websites, literature, imagery, and software and collecting and copying all the data within without permission of the users or creators. Often, this involves violation of "robots.txt", a file which says to crawlers that the site is not to be indexed. In order to prepare the data to make it useful for the model, unpaid or minimally paid workers in the US and abroad to achieve this goal cheaply. And the end result is the wholesale copying of unlicensed works utilizing borderline slave labor.

Each "AI" processor utilizes 1200 watts of power, in data farms that have dozens of thousands of them per facility. Utilizing inordinate amount of power to generate middling, incorrect results that most LLM's and other "AI" even admit to. And to cool all of this, 20 gallons of groundwater are used per minute in evaporative cooling systems. Even if said data farm is in the drought-stricken southwest US.

And all of this mass data gathering is carte blanche for a setup for a surveillance state. Instead of having a human in the middle, it liberates malicious actors within the government and corporations from having to deal with manpower needed behind national and local surveillance. Without the accuracy or second guessing of a human operator.

Needless to say, "AI" should not be confused with machine learning algorithms that are found in the sciences that are tailored for that a specific analysis and have existed decades before "AI" and LLMs. Said ML algorithms are far more efficient and accurate, able to perform analysis in a short time span on standard desktop hardware. Without specialized AI chips or equipment.

The reasoning behind the Development of an Artificial Intelligence action plan is not driven by the development to build a thinking machine, but utilizing marketing to surreptitiously crush creativity, freedom, worker's rights, and environmental progress.

Art, Music, Literature, Film; all these forms of expression are unique to the human experience, and cannot be made without the human soul - even if you manage to develop a replica, it is one of unfeeling and unthinking stone. It experiences and expresses no love, no joy, no thought, no desire, no inspiration, no beauty. It is an industry meant to ride the train of potential into a self-cannibalizing factory that was built on biting the very hand it feeds from, and will eventually consume those who unwillingly fed it whole; before it must turn upon itself. Artificial Intelligence is the enemy of the Human Spirit, and if I cannot appeal to you on this merit alone; I appeal to you on potential faith: To Sin is not something unknowable and complex, it is to treat people as objects. To uplift these objects over the people they take from is to embody evil in it's purest form.

## **General Comment**

The highest priorities in any plan of action involving AI must include the protections for the rights of the public, not limited to copyright and reproduction. No other industry is allowed wholesale use of public creations without their owners' consent and/or compensation, and AI development must not be any different in this regard. Several industries have already raised significant legal challenges to the creation and use of AI models trained on copyrighted data, and such avenues must remain available in any plan development.

In addition, the plan must include requirements of efficiency and energy consumption. LLMs and other AI systems have an exceptionally high energy usage in both training and everyday use. If left unchecked, this will serve to strain our energy resources as models and their usage grow. The trade war that the administration has instigated against our closest trading partners has already had negative effects for our energy supply - allowing these systems to add more for little gain would be pointless and wasteful in a time where we cannot afford either.

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

When considering an AI Action Plan for the nation, A couple of things that I have to address is the need for proper and ethical training of AI systems and cojoined with that thought is the preservation of Intellectual Property and Copyright.

Any AI system that could have beneficial merit must be trained on data that is owned by the organization developing the technology, or using information expressly given to it by contributors. This training must be rigorous to avoid errors; sometimes taking months or years of development and rigorous testing. Recent events with software technology, such as the 2024 CrowdStrike Incident serves as a grim reminder of what can happen when even seemingly dependable systems have a critical issue. The AI technology must ensure that factual and beneficial information is given at all times. Any AI system that gives out any information that could be considered faulty or spurious casts a dark shadow on the technology as a whole, and there is information publicly available detailing serious errors and omissions made by various AI systems available today that was not thoroughly developed. An expansion of AI into everyday life will impact Americans in more negative ways than positive ones unless there is a foremost effort for all private and public AI technologies to use quality data that is developed by the AI developers themselves or contributed by trusted sources and cultivated for the best uses in stability and security. A major concern that goes along with the previous statement is the potential for any AI developer to use any information without regard for previous established uses of Intellectual Property and Copyright law. Many Americans, both individual and as parts of Corporations, rely on Intellectual Property and Copyright law to protect their intellectual investments. Any AI Action Plan that is developed in this country needs to ensure that carte blanche is not given to any AI developer that would infringe on the rights of practically every American for its own benefit. If Intellectual Property and Copyright law is weakened any way by this action plan, that will cause severe IP issues and set off years of legal strife in many Intellectual fields such as Art, Music, Motion Pictures, Interactive Entertainment, and this would reach into Software Development also, including AI technology, just to name a few industries out of many if any AI developer has overreach into information that it does not intellectually own. The Copyright Office recently has stated as a part of their policy that it must uphold the human requirement for any works created, even if it has been created with AI and that should be upheld and protected for the good of many Americans that have benefited this country through their creative efforts. I strongly urge the policymakers that read this to consider these points to ensure that any AI technology developed in this country is trusted, reliable, and respecting of the rule of law in its ongoing development.

comments.comment_text:
## **PUBLIC SUBMISSION**

**As of:** March 21, 2025 **Received:** March 15, 2025

**Status:** 

**Tracking No.** m8a-wk3z-5qth **Comments Due:** March 15, 2025 **Submission Type:** API

Request for Information: Development of an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-3934

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

I am writing to ask that the government deny OpenAI the ability to train on copyrighted material.

I don't understand why decades of copyright law are suddenly out the window just because one company claims that they can't deliver on their goals unless they're able to violate it. If OpenAI as a company is unable to deliver on its goals, on their own terms, then why should they be given extra help to succeed? Is this really aligned with our country's great history of industry? The core of the American dream is that you're able to make your own way, on your own terms. This is also essential to the spirit of capitalism. But now, again, here is a company like OpenAI claiming that they're incapable of developing an effective product, unless they're able to steal from copyrighted works. This makes no sense to me.

Why can't they source from public works, that have moved out of copyright domain? Why is this brand new industry, which has yet to prove itself, allowed to skirt laws and norms that have applied through copyright law? Can't we at least put laws into place first, where creators can sign an agreement for their works to be used for AI training? Wouldn't it make sense to allow a creator to benefit from their own work, in the same way that movie studios must sign contracts first, before moving forward with an adaptation/production.

I think it's premature, and that OpenAI is overstepping as a company. I think if the government permits this, they open themselves up to additional lawsuits, which could be avoided if they were willing to work with creators first, rather than taking directions from a single company. I will also add that a recent case, Reuters vs. Ross Intelligence, ruled against AI's access to copyright law. There is also currently an ongoing case with Meta. With these as established precedent, I can't see how this doesn't lead to further litigation, and a huge waste of government time and resources while trying to decide on a request that has already been cemented via copyright law.

Please deny OpenAI's request to train on copyrighted material. Please consider the implications of this sort of request, and the amount of power and license you are considering handing over to a single corporation. Thank you so much for your time.

We make some exceptions for criticism, for education, or for significantly transformative work. In my opinion, none of this applies to training generative AI.

I fail to understand the point of allowing these companies to continue to scrape data with impunity. The only point I can see is greed. The greed of taking something that is not theirs and feeding it into an algorithm so it can make counterfeit copies of what they've stolen for profit. I understand that generative AI seems flashy and new and exciting. I find it rather soulless. I find it hard to care at all about books no one cared to write, or about paintings no one bothered to paint.

I do not discount all AI innovation, but I think it could be better served in a position that doesn't drive creatives out of their respective fields chasing the cheapest alternative. If they want to scrape everything off the internet without paying for it, then they should not be able to profit with what comes out of it. Or if they do, then they must compensate all those who were forced unwittingly into their data set.

If it's not clear, I oppose this. These regulations are necessary. If AI is not capable of continuing to grow or advance without mass scraping of copyrighted content, then it is a flaw in their system, not the fault of those who have been stolen from.

This is a blatant violation of the rights of artists to their own work. These generative programs are used in ways that rob Americans of their livelihood and potentially their physical safety. A more appropriate approach would be to dissolve companies such as OpenAI and limit the usage of programs like Midjourney, ChatGPT, Google's Gemini, Microsoft's Copilot, etc., but I am unfortunately extremely aware that asking this administration to take the appropriate approach to pretty much anything is a hard ask.

Also, let's think about this practically for a second: if this passes, do you honestly think big media companies such as Disney will let this stand? They're already responsible for most of how copyright law works nowadays anyway, and while I personally don't care for what they've done I know for a fact that they will absolutely wreck house if something gets in the way of their iron grip on their IPs. As a graphic designer and artist, AI has personally affected me.

Far too many art portfolio and hosting websites have opted many artists into AI scraping without their consent, leaving many designers and artists fearing their work being stolen/scrapped without consent or respect for their boundaries.

Left unchecked, AI will spread to other industries and ultimately be the death knell for our economy and our country. This is a technology we still do not have a full and proper understanding of. AI creators can only see the profit and not the consequences of what they're doing. It will not stop until it consumes every facet of our daily lives.

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) networks poses a significant threat to the climate of our planet and, consequently, to the continued survival of the human race. While AI has the potential to drive innovation and efficiency, its environmental costs are often overlooked, leading to dire consequences for our ecosystems and future generations.

Firstly, the energy consumption associated with training and operating AI models is staggering. Large-scale AI systems require vast amounts of computational power, which translates into substantial electricity usage. According to recent studies, training a single AI model can emit as much carbon as the lifetime emissions of several cars. As the demand for AI technologies grows, so too does the energy required to support them, often sourced from fossil fuels. This exacerbates greenhouse gas emissions, contributing to climate change and its associated impacts, such as extreme weather events, rising sea levels, and biodiversity loss.

Moreover, the infrastructure needed to support AI networks—data centers, cooling systems, and extensive server farms—further strains our planet's resources. These facilities not only consume enormous amounts of energy but also require significant water resources for cooling, leading to water scarcity in regions already facing environmental stress. The environmental footprint of AI extends beyond energy consumption; it also encompasses the extraction of rare minerals and metals necessary for hardware production, which often involves environmentally destructive mining practices.

Additionally, the deployment of AI in various sectors, such as agriculture and manufacturing, can lead to unsustainable practices that harm the environment. For instance, AI-driven precision agriculture may optimize resource use, but it can also encourage over-reliance on chemical fertilizers and pesticides, further degrading soil health and water quality. The automation of industries can lead to increased production rates, which, without proper regulation by a governing body, can result in overconsumption and waste, further straining our planet's ecosystems.

Finally, the societal implications of AI's environmental impact cannot be ignored. As climate change accelerates, vulnerable populations often those least responsible for emissions—will bear the brunt of its effects especially in areas already often battered by severe weather events. The displacement of communities, loss of livelihoods, and increased competition for dwindling resources could lead to social unrest and conflict, and a total collapse of the current United States of America as we have come to know it as its citizens.

In conclusion, while artificial intelligence networks offer numerous benefits, their harmful impact on the climate and the potential threat to human survival must be critically examined. It is imperative that we prioritize sustainable practices in the development and deployment of AI technologies, ensuring that they contribute positively to our planet rather than exacerbate the environmental crises we face. Without a concerted effort to mitigate these risks, we may find ourselves jeopardizing not only the health of our planet but also the future of humanity itself.

Request for Information: Development of an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-4172

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

The AI systems made by tech companies like OpenAI or Google will, with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law, destroy thousands of American small businesses and ruin the ability for American artists to continue to succeed.

AI systems rely on training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of every other everyday American creator who has posted works - written, visual, audio, or otherwise - was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing and cutting us out.

Now these tech companies are asking for exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use". Their belief that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if they are not allowed to, it will stifle American innovation.

It will have the opposite effect; the purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If individuals do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by tech giants, what will be the incentive to create?

If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Protect American creators to protect American innovation. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to tech companies. The government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. The plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just tech companies. Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label AI generated content clearly.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI - I work in tech and rely on it for my creative processes. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of many AI systems, but we should not sacrifice the hard work of thousands of Americans and give it away to tech companies by rewriting copyright law in this manner.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

I think this is a terrible plan for everyone involved. Here is an article that I have written about AI Ethics and Metaethics: https://substack.com/home/post/p-135706040?utm\_campaign=post&utm\_medium=web. The short version is that the plan proposed here violates all the tenets that we as a society claim to value. If you truly believe it is ethical, I will have lost any and all respect for you as pond scum let alone as human beings.

I kindly recommend that you grow a backbone. This will prove disastrous for millions, if not billions, of people. We have tried giving companies with "new" technologies carte blanche before and that went SO WELL every single time. Even accepting an argument that this is necessary for the continued development of AI technologies, which seems like an a priori fallacy in accepting that this is an inherently good thing in the first place, giving private entities this type of power will prove disastrous by concentrating near complete power over all publicly or semi-publicly available information.

Of course, just about everyone in this administration seems to find some perverse joy in contorting themselves to acquiesce to the new corporate power of the week. I hope this does not fall on deaf ears given who could see this comment, but I am not optimistic. On top of concentrating power in the hands of a few people with dubious morality creating an incredibly vulnerable weak point for an entire industry, SUCCESSFUL implementation of this plan would require a complete overhaul of every notion that American society has about copyright. Setting aside the large issue that is the ethical concerns poised by this plan (which, let's face it, if you were truly concerned about that point, this plan wouldn't be a serious talking point right now), the federal government is not in any position where it could successfully implement such overhauls right now. And no, sitting back and doing nothing does not constitute successful implementation; a trained dog can do that.

On the topic of ethical concerns, I do not wish to hear anyone say that they have seriously considered problems poised by this plan and say that they think that there are few to no issues. The livelihoods of creatives will be further destabilized than they already were; entire companies will be put at risk with a lot less options for recourse. In a country that primarily has a service based economy such as America, we could be talking about an apocalyptic scenario within a decade or so.

Lastly, the one thing I want you to consider is the following problem. Think of the absolute worst person you know. The worst person that you could possibly think, that you have ever heard of or interacted with. Now, would you want to give them the type of power that this plan grants? Odds are, you don't know everything about the people in charge of companies like OpenAI. The fact of the matter is that you could be giving power to the worst person you know. Do you want to take that risk?

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan I am an everyday American who works in the entertainment industry. For years I have worked with talented artists who developed their skills and knowledge to build a career and make a decent living to support their families.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. The work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without their consent or any compensation. They ingest their work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to their clients – directly competing with them and cutting them out of the marketplace. Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will creatives possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that creatives can decide when and where creative work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Creatives' work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. The work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest their work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to their clients – directly competing with them and cutting them out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.

If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

Generative AI should not be allowed to train on any art images, literature, or data without the explicit consent of the content creator.

Tools like these (OpenAI) only serve to steal from and further impoverish Americans -especially small business creatives, like freelance writers posting samples for work, or illustrators who need to upload work in order to secure art commissions- when measures aren't taken to ensure people can opt out of having their work be part of the trainable data.

Gen AI innovation doesn't have to and should not rely on theft.

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-4616

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.

If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

This is an overhyped dead-end tech bubble that is destined to go the way of the Segway, Bored Ape NFTs, and Google Glass. I simply will never be persuaded that the future of American arts, letters, and industry is the technology that brought us "Willy's Chocolate Experience."

Artificial intelligence is like artificial lawns: there is no use for it if you have a real one. If I ever decide that I need a chat assistant to overconfidently give me incorrect answers with made-up sources, I can call my ex-brother-in-law.

As Sam Altman has rightly said, "It would be impossible to train today's leading AI models without using copyrighted materials." Well then, it should be impossible to train today's leading AI models, Q.E.D. If it is impossible for someone to get a billion dollars without defrauding working people and stealing intellectual property, then they should not get a billion dollars. This is not a morally or ethically difficult question except to thieves.

The best way to ensure American technological dominance is to see the AI scam for what it is, and instead invest heavily into supporting humans who are able to create and analyze with genuine intelligence and insight. A concrete policy action would be to pull all funding for OpenAI and invest it in education, the arts, and technology that actually has practical applications.

## **Submitter Information**

Name: Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

I am an American who lives for making visual arts, with my own hands, and dreams of making a living through it. I have dedicated my life to honing my craft.

If AI is allowed to run rampant, scraping all works with no regard for American copyrights, turning a profit off of this business model, it would go against the American Dream itself. We have the rights to copyright protection, and thus AI focused companies should respect those rights.

Lack of copyright respect would kill many small businesses, whether it be graphics design or drawing-focused businesses like graphic novels and commissioned artwork. It is antithetical to the American Dream to kill small businesses by fueling one or few giant businesses with work directly stolen copyrighted material from small businesses and visual artists.

The United States of America is built on innovation. Copyright law exists to encourage innovations. What point is there for us artists to innovate if AI models trample our rights and put us out of business? If you wish to maintain innovation, do not infiringe on the rights of creators; protect the rights of creators so that they can comfortably innovate in the first place and potentially give AI technology material that is backed by consent.

I am not against the existence of AI technology. It undoubtedly has important uses. However, it should not be built off the backs of artists who don't consent to having their work scraped by a machine.

## The AI Action Plan should:

- Demand AI focused companies have explicit consent from the copyright holders of any material they use.
- Encourage the existence of a system where copyright holders can license their materials out to AI focused companies for payment.
- Demand transparency from AI focused companies as to what material is in their systems.

A system where AI companies flourish on the backs of artists who give no consent is not sustainable. If artists and small businesses focused on the arts feel secure, they will keep making innovations in the arts, and thus give better quality material to the AI.

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan

I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

Copyright was created to protect creators from the very thing being proposed by these AI corporations.

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-5143

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

It is unfortunate that several different flavors of AI are conflated in the public mind. It us also unfortunate that the non-deterministic output of generative AI makes it difficult even for experts to evaluate it clear-headedly.

However numerous instances demonstrate that generative AI has serious structural flaws which should limit its use for any serious application.

First: generative AI "hallucinates"; that is, it swaps elements from its training data in its output. We have already seen court documents with plausible but fictitious citations, and a wild mushroom identification guide with errors that could cause fatalities. These are not soluble problems, they are intrinsic to the nature of generative AI.

Second: generative AI steals. Particularly when the corpus of training data is shallow, generative AI output infringes upon work - critically, potentially including confidential and sensitive work, if such is available for training. Queries like a request to render art in the style of a particular artist result in infringing output, but carefully crafted queries could also reveal personal identifying information or facilitate corporate espionage.

Third: Generative AI is subject to malicious manipulation of training data. Many of the most embarrassing public failures of gen AI can be traced to a joke site that was interpreted as factual. This can be exploited by websites designed to affect the weighting of training data. Reducing barriers to accessing training data will not help, and will very likely harm, in ways that may be difficult to anticipate in advance.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-5595

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

### **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

#### To whom it may concern:

I am responding to the RFI regarding the development of an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan as directed by the Presidential Executive Order of January 23, 2025.

Generative AI systems are built on the appropriation of human-created content without proper compensation or consent. These systems —particularly the foundation models which under-gird them—consume creative works, professional writings, and intellectual property created by Americans, then produce derivative works that directly compete with original creators. As an American worker and lifelong creative writer, and 1 of 2.32 million American workers holding a degree in computer science, I have witnessed how AI is stealing from my livelihood and profiting from this theft. This represents a massive transfer of wealth from working Americans to technology firms with no fair compensation for those whose work is being exploited.

AI is severely over-hyped and is fleecing the eyes of the American public through inflated promises and misleading claims about its capabilities. Most AI systems fail to deliver on their promises when deployed in real-world settings, suffering from unreliability and incorrectness. The administration should be wary of making policy based on industry hype rather than demonstrated value. Before committing national resources to "AI dominance," we the people should demand rigorous, independent evaluation of AI systems' actual capabilities and limitations.

#### I recommend:

- 1. Implementing strong copyright protections that prevent AI training on creators', artists', and other copyright-holders' intellectual property without permission and compensation
- 2. Requiring transparent labeling of AI-generated content
- 3. Protecting American jobs by restricting AI use that directly jeopardizes the livelihoods of human workers
- 4. Establishing a moratorium on government AI procurement until proper impact assessments can be conducted

In summary, America should prioritize technology that genuinely fosters human flourishing and honors the dignity of work and creativity.

This document is approved for public dissemination. The document contains no business-proprietary or confidential information. Document contents may be reused by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-5746

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

The unregulated scraping of works of art to train AI systems raises significant ethical and moral concerns, particularly regarding the rights and livelihoods of the artists who created these works. Artists pour their time, creativity, and passion into their creations, often relying on their work for income and professional recognition. When their art is scraped without consent or compensation, it undermines their autonomy and devalues their labor. This practice essentially treats their work as a free resource for corporate profit, disregarding the fact that these creations are the intellectual property of individuals who deserve to have a say in how their work is used. You should also think about this: the lack of regulation in this area creates a power imbalance between artists and large tech companies. Many artists, especially independent or emerging ones, lack the resources or legal support to challenge the unauthorized use of their work. This exploitation perpetuates a system where corporations benefit from the creative labor of individuals without contributing to the sustainability of the artistic community. By failing to establish clear guidelines or compensation mechanisms, we risk eroding trust in the relationship between technology and the arts, potentially stifling creativity and discouraging artists from sharing their work publicly.

This unregulated use of art to train AI systems you're aiming for also raises broader questions about the ethical development of technology. AI has the potential to revolutionize many fields, but its progress should not come at the expense of fairness and respect for human creativity. If the foundation of AI is built on the uncompensated labor of artists, it sets a troubling precedent for how we value human contributions in the digital age. Regulating the use of artistic works in AI training is not just about protecting individual rights—it's about ensuring that technological advancement aligns with principles of equity and respect for all forms of human expression.
