**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-5778

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.

If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

We should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

Any AI that requires the theft of intellectual property in order to succeed is completely and utterly unethical. This is not a matter of American superiority in AI, it's a matter of American businessmen wanting to further maximize their profits by replacing skilled American workers with automated replacements. The only people that are uplifted by this is the already wealthy, and provides no benefit for the rest of the country. It, in fact, will only harm them and thus this cannot be allowed to pass.

If an AI system requires training to succeed, it should be on material that has naturally entered the public domain or has been approved to be used by the creators of the material - preferably with some manner of reimbursement to the latter for their assistance. An opt-in approach rather than an opt-out, and should 100% be held to by the law to only use this material rather than giving private companies carte blanche to steal intellectual property - American or otherwise. This would allow the American populace and foreign allies to assist in the improvement of AI development and be properly rewarded for their efforts rather than having their work stolen from them.

In addition, the environmental and energy issues caused by such training need to also be monitored and addressed. Any development should and must include attempts to limit the amount of energy used and the harm it causes to the environment in line with any other preexisting laws and agreements - and perhaps should require additional rules and oversight specific to mitigate its damages. Circumventing these will similarly cause more harm than good to the United States.

If a system cannot function without theft of intellectual property and unnecessary amounts of harm to our country's resources and environment, then that is its own failing and thus should fail. It should not be propped up and granted special privilege to perpetuate its crimes and damage in order to succeed. It imposes and hinders the freedoms and rights of the American populace - past, present, and future. Because while there are already many ways letting this pass will cause immediate harm, there's potential for this ruling to set a precedent that will further impinge upon and reduce the freedoms and the rights of US citizens in the future.

The only correct way to move forward with this - if it should be allowed to do so at all - is with appropriate oversight and laws in place in order to protect the creative liberties and intellectual property of the American populace and its foreign allies, as well as the health and safety of the nation's resources and environment if not the world as whole. Not further elevate only the wealthy and further reinforce the idea that laws and rules do not apply to them, as that only further weakens and harms our nation as a whole.

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-6332

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

LLMs are a fad. They are not useful to consumers, and any attempts to shoehorn them into workflows results in more errors and less accountability for those errors.

However, in an attempt to further develop these models (thus allowing for the creation of hype-building press releases), many AI companies have demanded the ability to scrape data from the entire Internet, with complete disregard for any form of licensing or copyright law. AI training bots already blatantly ignore robots.txt (a manner to tag content as being inaccessible to bots), and giving them an exemption from copyright will destroy the American intellectual property system.

Additionally, it is physically impossible to scale LLM models in a way that will make them profitable -- they require too much data, too much power, and too much hardware. OpenAI is bleeding money. Anthropic is bleeding money. These companies are going to collapse under their own weight, and if the government puts too much money and political power into keeping them afloat, it will be dragged down with them.

In 20 years, do we want to be known as the nation that let an unsustainable business model collapse in on itself? Or do we want to be known as the country that destroyed its copyright system chasing a technology fad?

I'm a writer by trade, and I do not want my writing scraped by generative artificial intelligence. Gen AI is purposely trained on the work of those who have already done the work. This deprives us of the credit for our work, and steals and distorts what we've written. So much so, that gen AI often hallucinates.

This is dangerous, as it can lead people to incorrect conclusions. All the while, our work is used for the basis of a prompt. We don't want to have our work used like this. It deprives us of work, and gen AI will be used to deprive us further of gainful employment.

Particularly for freelancers, like myself, it's already difficult to compete with generative AI, as many companies see it as a "quick fix" for writing. This encourages the stealing of work, not just employment-wise, but also stealing the work we've already written.

This technology needs to be greatly regulated, and LLMs and gen AI should not be allowed to train on already established intellectual properties, as well as individual writing from authors around the country.

There is no need for this technology to exist. It makes using the internet worse, prevents writers from finding work, and is an overall detriment to the intelligence of the American public. When I say I'm scared of future generations growing up with this technology, I'm serious. They're being taught to not think critically, and rely on answers that may not even be true or, worse, hazardous and/or deadly. This prevents the American public from being able to excel in many ways.

Therefore, I ask that large language models and generative artificial intelligence be subject to regulatory guidelines. It poses great and detrimental effects to the US public at large, but more so to those who make their living with the written word.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

AI is an area of technology that has rapidly developed within the last few years, and alongside that rapid development has followed an even more aggressive growth of financial interest in the area. This financial interest has led to an eschewing of caution as the mechanisms of finance continue to invest more and more into a technology that has failed to produce widespread demand from consumers.

Furthermore, AI has the potential to be highly destructive to a variety of industries, and the environment. Generative AI focused on creating text, images, and videos put at risk the careers of lifelong artists and creators. America, as the global leader in film, Television, and music should be doing everything it can to uplift and protect creators, not outsourcing their jobs to machines.

Furthermore, the energy demands of AI can only be characterized as wantonly wasteful, especially in a period of time where we stand at the brink of a climate disaster.

AI is a technology with great potential, and for decades machine learning has been delivering technological advancements that greatly improve the life of everyday people. I am certain that AI will continue to lead to significant technological developments in the future as well.

However, the current push for widespread, unregulated adoption of generative AI risks sapping vitality from the creative workforce of America, and draining America's environmental resources, with no clear benefit beside enriching those who control the technology.

AI must be strongly regulated. Regulation is what forces companies to act in the interest of the American people. While regulation may increase the difficulty of developing value for corporations, that is not the concern of the US government nor the concern of the American people.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

Name: Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

The current generation of privately-owned technology referred to as "AI" is infinitely more harmful than beneficial to the United States due to the lack of intelligent regulation and protection from foreign influence. Any policy put in place should:

- 1. Prohibit ingestion of unauthorized copyrighted materials into AI datasets. It has been proven both in studies and personal use that the current version of "Gen AI" can and will directly plagiarize copyrighted works. By design, it is regurgitating material entered into it, and therefore cannot legally operate within the US copyright system without first obtaining authorization from copyright holders for the reproduction of their work.
- 2. Prohibit "hallucinated" output that is libelous, dangerous, or used in place of a trained human professional where doing so may lead to harm or loss of life. Examples of such dangers include news reports of "AI" publicly accusing investigative journalists of committing the crimes they investigated, "AI" instructing users to add glue to pizza, "AI" being used to deny insurance claims in place of a doctor, or "AI" salespeople offering perspective buyers free vehicles against the wishes of the dealerships.
- 3. Prohibit environmental and personal property damage or eminent domain for the creation, powering, or maintenance of "AI" data centers that will be used exclusively for private profit.
- 4. Prohibit use of "AI" to create deep fake videos or images that are harmful or criminal, including false videos of politicians and perverted videos of living adults and children.
- 5. Ensure all US-authored "AI" is protected from and verified to be clear of manipulation from hostile foreign governments and malicious actors, both at the code and data set levels.

Without these things, the United States has already "lost" the AI battle, as the output of our current models is so faulty and poisoned as to be useless for both private and government use. It cannot reason, it slows productivity, it corrupts existing information, it sews public distrust, it empowers criminals, and it burns resources. In other words: it is snake oil.

Thank you.

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-6522

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues

Request for Information: Development of an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-6610

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

March 14, 2025

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan

I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

Broadly, AI is an over-hyped, over-funded, money pit with precious little real world application (referring to LLMs, generative AI, chatbots and other such models that cannot exist without training data) that steals from my livelihood as an American and profits off of the theft. The vast majority of the major companies investing in these tools are actively and flagrantly violating not only my copyright over my illustrations and designs, but my privacy, and are contributing to the undermining of this country's national security and the safety of our citizens.

It is already known that the environmental impacts of this tech far outstrip the benefits they bring. To ask for even greater latitude over our intellectual property, personal data, and for the freedom to cause greater harm than ever, goes against what America stands for. It is a grift, a con, and a power grab, because they cannot continue to exist without our art, our thoughts, our feelings and our content. Allowing this out of control freight train to steamroll individual liberties is Un-American and grossly irresponsible.

Major companies, such as Microsoft have already seen the writing on the wall regarding AI, quietly scaling back efforts to invest in it and cutting development programs in favor of more profitable endeavors. OpenAI is desperate to suggest we undo our copyright/trademark protections so a handful of companies can run buck wild across our digital landscape. As a concerned American citizen, I do not consent, I do not condone this, and I do not agree with the multi-layered fallacy that unchecked AI development will provide a "better" or "brighter" future for America.

The American people do not benefit from their empty promises of "if we just had more time" and "if we just didn't have to follow the rules". None of these companies owe any loyalty to this country and only care about impossible growth, and endless profits. Make no mistake, they will bleed us dry and then leave for overseas to continue chasing "growth", devastating our economy, hurting our people and loved ones, and betraying any trust we give.

In suggestion for policy, anyone collecting AI training data must properly compensate people for ANY copyrighted training materials or data. This should also include protections that very broadly state WHEN data is being collected, WHERE your data is stored, HOW your data is being used, explicitly, and clearly lay out an appropriate compensation structure for said data. AI-generated materials must not be copyrightable. Furthermore, there need to be laws limiting the replacement of human beings with AI. Lack of human oversight is a recipe for disaster (ask any IT staffer.)

In short, AI needs some breaks, NOW.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

From a concerned citizen and small business owner.

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan

I am an everyday American who runs a small visual design business. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.

If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

AI is not the future of the American economy, it is a bubble that will eventually burst leaving endless debts in its wake, but not before destroying the futures of countless American creatives who could be giving back to the economy instead of the pockets of foreign shareholders once American intellectual properties no longer have any value.

The loss of copyright protections would affect small and big businesses alike, and America would no longer be the world's entertainment capitol.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-6809

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

Since AI is trained on the collective work and languages that humanity has built, any profits from AI should be collectively divided up among all humanity present and future. A dividend of ALL profits stemming from AI should be distributed evenly. There should be no private ownership of AI tools that were trained on data for which they don't have explicit permission from every single source who contributed.

All AI models should be public and non-profit and unable to charge for their use if they are trained by any source for which they do not have explicit expressed permission (not a default option on a public website or the like). I consider anything else plagiarism and theft. Why should someone be able to profit from stealing the collective work of humanity at the expense of others?

I am additionally concerned about biases inherent in the data on which AI is trained and its propensity to generate false answers. We need safeguards in order to ensure we move towards a more true, just and rational understanding of the world.

I think we need to think carefully and deeply about how to support the growth and development of humans in relationship to AI tools. What processes do humans need to engage in to build the kinds of expertise that allow them to critically and creatively assess the output of AI?

I personally do not feel our society is ready to handle the complexities that are emerging with AI, but at the same time I do not believe it is something we can reasonably stop. Thus we need to ensure we have a process for assessing harms (e.g., biased output that leads to increased surveillance of someone,lessens their likelihood to be selected for a job). It is important to recognize that AI is built on the backs of everyone who has every spoken, written or created anything in any language or form and thus any benefits or profits should be distributed evenly and fairly. I am ambivalent about whether AI will be beneficial to society, but I am sure it will not be if we don't actively work to make it free, fair and for our collective benefit not private gain.

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-6977

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

I am not an artist, or author. I am a user, albeit reluctantly, of products presently referred to as "AI."

I think that any policy to foster language and image models should be crafted with great and deliberate care. Recklessness around copyright or trademark, or indeed any generous license to use "training data" without proper consent and provenance, could result in products that are deeply insecure and are banned in other countries.

The United States may find itself so eager to give US technology companies free license to do as they will that the country will effectively eliminate any export potential, thereby ceding the global market to more acceptable products.

Between this and the fostered disregard for privileged information, companies will be less inclined to use such insecure and un-exportable programs.

This is to say nothing of the chilling effect on the creativity and innovation of the American spirit. American creators, authors, and innovators will feel less free to share their creations, for fear of someone else monetizing their hard work and dedicated effort. Intellectual property is a bedrock of American innovation, and shouldn't be sacrificed in a panic induced by industry insiders.

It is the role of government sometimes to dampen the zeal of companies that may do themselves harm in their urgency to compete, the better to sustain a long term healthy competition that lifts all.

## **General Comment**

I strongly encourage the NSF to not relinquish their responsibilities to regulate the Artificial Intelligence industry. Although the industry styles itself as developing artificial intelligence, I say as someone who has studied artificial intelligence in cognitive science and cognitive psychology coursework that these large language models are little more than prediction machines. The programs add little to no insights on what data is entered into them, and on the contrary often result in hallucinations and generalizations that make no sense to subject matter experts. It may seem that these programs are close to making a breakthrough where they will be reliable, and indeed many industry leaders make outrageously rosy claims about what their programs will be able to do, but there is no actual reason to believe that such a breakthrough is close. Allowing these companies to use data/material without paying for it is theft. Allowing the companies freedom to do this will only throw mountains of valuable money and resources (water and land) into a pit. There is no reason to have faith that any of these investments will pay off. Over-reliance on current LLMs is much more likely to lead to error and a stifling of ingenuity and creativity.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

- 1. The combination of unregulated data center growth, cooling demands, and aging electrical infrastructure has begun to cause inconsistencies in utility services that will prove enormously costly to consumers. Data centers and energy companies should not be allowed to offload these costs to the government or pass them on to the American public in the form of higher electrical rates or water costs. Companies seeking to build new data centers should bear the associated costs of those centers to the public, either through taxes or graduated rate differentials.
- 2. AI developers must not be given an exemption from copyright laws. Creating a carve-out from protections that are rigorously defended by corporations and clearly articulated in centuries of case law will weaken the system as a whole. At heart, generative AI does not exist outside of the content used to train it, so to detach that content from the applicable legal framework makes the traditional notion of copyright and protection of the ingenuity of creators meaningless. Developers should negotiate with rights holders, and those negotiations should also include extensive protections for the privacy and safety of individuals connected to the works used, either as subjects or creators.
- 3. Consumers, viewers, and readers should be given the opportunity to make informed decisions about generative AI. Failing to distinguish between the creative output of humans and the derivative products of AI is harmful to communication in general, and to scientific discovery, news media, literature, and education in particular. Just as with copyright declarations of source materials, publication of AI-produced material should include a clear statement of how and to what extent generative AI has been employed.

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-7345

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

Large Language Models and other Generative AI technologies as they are currently being developed and marketed are a dangerous infringement on the rights of writers, visual artists, filmmakers, actors, and musicians.

Allowing for such models to be trained on illegally obtained copyrighted work denies the very essence of copyright protections enshrined in law.

Allowing major corporations to make AI models of existing or deceased persons, sets a dangerous precedent for creative work of those persons. How will a consumer, or regulator know if an appearance in a film is a human actor, or an AI-generated replica? Is the artist who is duplicated allowed recourse?

The potential for misuse in other areas of everyday life is equally terrifying. Imagine a world where because AI replication is of a high fidelity identity cannot be established for someone at the other end of a phone or video call, and the potential for all manner of fraud or security risks. Deepfakes and non-consensual sexual material are areas where we already see rampant abuse of the powers of existing AI tools.

We should not be plunging headlong into embracing these technologies when our social structures struggle to adapt.

Already, too many people try to rely on information "generated" by large language models; those tools are not search engines, cannot understand context, and have no concept of what is real or what is not.

A machine must never be in the position of making a choice that can devastate human lives, especially since they cannot be trusted to be accurate to reality.

AI can do amazing things, and is good at filtering images or testing possible protein folding sequences, or mapping the sky or planet. But it is not yet and may never be in a position to have human-like cognition and may never be able to have the critical human quality of empathy.

I urge the NSF to weigh these factors in designing the regulations for AI tools and technology, and move to restrict the many potential unethical, dangerous, and harmful ways they are already being used in the search for profits at the expense of human beings.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

From: [YOUR NAME] [YOUR PROFESSION] [YOUR ADDRESS OR AT LEAST CITY, STATE]

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan

I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.

If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Additionally it is critical to safeguard the right to refuse access to material where copyright is established - else it enables the use and abuse of copyrighted materials for profit by third parties (i.e. the owners/developers of the AI agents), many of whom have already violated existing copyright law in training their models, and are seeking to whitewash their past criminal actions (described above) by lobbying for this exception.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan I am an American citizen who grew up surrounded by artists who helped shape and guide my life in the best ways possible. Art touches everyone's lives in one way or another – be it through entertainment, architecture, even necessities like the clothes we wear. Copyright laws are in place to protect these people who contribute massively to society, and they will be the first ones hurt if companies like OpenAI get "special allowance" to steal their work.

We need to protect constitutional rights now more than ever, like the rights to our property, which includes intellectual property. Special exemptions for tech corporations is simply allowing them to steal and exploit the hardworking citizens of this country. It has also been proven that generative AI can be extremely dangerous without appropriate oversight, ex. AI written books published with incorrect, dangerous health advice.

The Action Plan moving forward needs solid regulations placed on AI to reaffirm trust and safety, such as requiring consent from creators for materials to be trained on, transparency from these companies on what source material is being used and for what purposes, and legal safeguards for any creative who does not want their property placed in an AI dataset.

AI has tremendous potential to be a very useful tool moving forward, but only if it is handled mindfully and responsibly. Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

I oppose this proposal, which would enshrine organized theft of intellectual property as the basis of national policy. It would also deprive Congress of the power entrusted to it by the framers in Article I, section 8 of the US Constitution to establish copyright protections.

Corporations are supposed to be enterprising, not engines of learned helplessness excused from contributing to the general welfare of the land and people of the United States. Now it appears they can't develop AI without stealing the raw materials - text and content - from the people who created it.

The vast amounts of water needed to generate the energy for an AI project will not be available for any other use, including firefighting, irrigation, and supplying public water systems.

AI has not been shown to be a public good, so this proposal to develop an action plan is premature. Should it ever be established that AI is a public good, the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution prohibits "taking without just compensation" the property, including the intellectual property, of any person, in order to produce a thing alleged to have public value.

This proposal is a broad, reckless license to violate the Constitution on two fronts. It's lawless and should be rejected.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

I am an American citizen who cares deeply about art and human expression. I create digital art as a hobby and know many who's primary income is to create art (of all different sorts). I stand opposed to generative AI as a whole and the companies behind it, both American and foreign.

I believe that AI development has gone far enough and allowing them to ignore copyright is a massive and misguided overstep of power. I do not believe this is a matter of national security and I think this is a fabrication on behalf of companies such as OpenAI to create national fear in order to push their own ulterior motives.

I believe the best thing we can do is put even more restrictions on generative AI products, not remove restrictions but allowing illegal circumvention intellectual property. There is no doubt that artificial inelegance can be an invaluable tool such as in research, but the current state of AI is overbearing and destructive of the carriers of millions of American citizens.

On top of being detrimental to artists, it is destructive to the health of citizens as a whole. Generative AI is touted as something that could thing and act for you and I think giving them total control would be a terrible thing for the intelligence of our country (and frankly the world) as a whole. Less and less people are creating things on their own, not learning why things work the way they do in tasks such as writing, programming, research, painting, et cetera. I believe that if we continue to let this already growing problem fester, no one will know how to do anything. Humans will always push the industries forward, and those who opt to use AI are doing a disservice to themselves to discover things for themself. Consider that maybe who could have been the greatest scientists of our future were held back by the temptation of AI.

In conclusion, I believe we should be restricting generative AI further rather than promoting and giving it unlimited access. I believe that is not only harmful to the jobs of American artisans and researchers alike, but to the populous as a whole by making them less willing to make decisions and learn on their own. I believe that AI companies are disingenuous of the impact this would have and that they are claiming it's a case of "national security" to spread fear.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

## **General Comment**

Subject: AI Action Plan

I am responding on my own personal behalf to the Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan, not as an agent or representative of any institution.

Per the requirements of the RFI response I am stating the following:

This document is approved for public dissemination. The document contains no business-proprietary or confidential information. Document contents may be reused by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.

While AI may prove to be a useful tool in the future, American success to-date has been based on many factors, including our large population of creative people who work across all the arts and sciences. Those people's work is valuable and should not be taken and used without compensation. Current large language models (LLM) have been developed using scraped or pirated data from many sources. The companies developing these LLM are not just taking people's intellectual property without compensation, they are attempting to reverse engineer the thought processes that people put into creating new works with the expressed intent to replace those people in part or entirely in some cases.

First, AI developers must be required to ask permission to include people's work in their model's development. Creators should not have to opt-out; they should be invited to opt-in with compensation.

Second, automated data collection (also known as scraping) must be required to respect requests to not collect data from websites that post such requests.

Third, any data collected by the developer must be anonymized and encrypted while stored, to protect the creators' privacy.

Fourth, AI developers should be charged a surcharge for the electricity and cooling water consumed, along with a charge for the added pollution from the electricity generation. They should be required to follow all environmental requirements for construction and operation of data centers.

Finally, AI models should be treated as potential dual-use technologies and subject to export control (EC) laws and international traffic in arms regulations (ITAR) and thus, review by the Department of Commerce and Department of Defense.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

Enacting this Plan would be a mistake for the United States of America. The current "burdensome" legislative barriers to AI development perform a vital service in ensuring the reliability of American information and in maintaining the quintessential soul and intent of cultural creation.

Social media is already rife with AI generated clickbait content and fake news. A future with unrestricted AI development and deployment would see little authenticity in all facets of life; more than a cultural issue, AI has been known to push incorrect and dangerous information when responding to innocuous prompts. This false information can kill.

With the rise of AI writing tools like ChatGPT, students have every opportunity to cheat the education system. No American will benefit from inflated academic figures. Even if ChatGPT works with educators to safeguard academia, removing restrictions on AI development and deployment will enable competitors to roll out alternative tools which can bypass existing and future academic authenticity checks.

Given current global and economic tensions, it is unwise to lift the set restrictions. These groups dominate a large share of the tech sphere; any interference during unprecedented expansion would be catastrophic. A cyber attack, perhaps, could target a small company to test existing defense measures and plan for a larger-scale offensive. An economic impediment, such as a halt on hardware import or manufacture, would have these companies collapse, leaving consumers without the tools they have potentially built their businesses around. An energy crisis would invite corruption as these AI giants clamored to take what little power there was to go around in order to fuel their incredibly demanding servers and computers.

Many careers are also at risk of being replaced by rampant AI. Artists, musicians, and writers are the backbone of our nation's cultural identity. Given a few years, a single tech-savvy programmer could replace an entire team of career artists to produce a gallery-worthy collection for the highest bidder. Corporations would jump at the chance to cut labor costs by firing writers and other creators in favor of much cheaper AI. Technological advancements have replaced careers in the past, but these replaced jobs were dangerous and taxing: millworkers, assembly line workers, and farmers used to toil for hours in unsafe conditions, but now are working harmoniously with technology that keeps them safe and well. To replace these cultural creators would be to suck the life out of art and media.

There are too many variables and too many dangers. Artifical Intelligence must be watched closely. This Plan must not be enacted. Let America be the premiere in \*safe\* AI development and deployment. Let AI be a tool guided by the government, created by the people and for the people, not for profit.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

I do not believe Large Language Model and Diffusion Model AI has a future as a transformative technology in the United States or indeed, the world. This technology by its very nature cannot ever be reliable or be capable of novel insight or information--all it can do is make probable guesses based on the data it has. Moreover, given the reckless speed with which this technology was released and hyped, there is a large amount of ai-generated data on the internet, which is then routinely scraped and put back into these models. This causes model collapse. This technology is doomed to devour itself and get worse over time, even if the U.S. makes the idiotic mistake of giving Open AI et al carte blanche on Copyright Violations. Does having access to every frame of the Garfield Movie going to prevent cyber attacks from China? Will the contents of every self-published novel on Smashwords predict the next terrorist attack? No, it absolutely will not. I'm sure machine learning has its place in specific applications with carefully curated data sets but attempting to create some sort of computer god by shoving all publicly visible content into data centers that strain the power grid in order to produce functionally useless results like inventing court cases wholecloth or telling end users to put glue on pizza simply isn't rational or necessary. This technology is tremendously expensive in a literal dollar sense and via externalities like power and water. It has not yet given a return on investment, and it's sheer folly for this country to swoop in and prop up this sick horse as it falls to its knees. It's simply not worth throwing the nation's culture in the form of films, art, music, and writing under the bus to do this. Let AI lie in its own grave.

marketplace with competition:

## **General Comment**

I am a Freelance Artist residing in Riverside County, California.

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

AI as a technology is another Dot Com bubble waiting to burst, and I think focusing on AI as something that will uplift American tech is short sighted and mistake. In the current race of companies trying to implement and expand their use of AI, its become clear that AI is full of faults and risks that have yet to be properly addressed by the government.

Outside of the ethical concern, such as the fact that AI has and will be used to replace the jobs of hard working Americans in an attempt to make more profit, there are security risks and flaws that rapid expansion of this technology between various sectors, both public and private, will only make worse. AI is known to have frequent "hallucination," which are instances of AI creating false information and presenting it as fact. Already there have be instances of AI creating false legal cases which were referenced by lawyers in court, putting those cases in jeopardy. There have been instances of AI customer service implemented by companies that have given customers false info about company policy, opening the door for legal action against companies and confusion, dissatisfaction, and weakening trust from consumers when it comes to engaging with companies that heavily us AI. There are also plenty of security risks that AI can pose both for the average user and for a company. I know people personally who have spoken about AI assistants meant to transcribe certain meeting notes, joining meetings on their own and sending transcripts with sensitive information about company workings and workers to people who were not only not part of that meeting, but were not approved to have access to these transcripts in the fist place.

What does it mean if consumer, corporate, and governmentsites start implementing AI rapidly? All I can see is a weakening not only of US internet security but also increasing distrust from Americans. How can a customer trust a site that will give them false information on refunds? How can a company? What legal turmoil will American companies face when AI lies to both them and their consumers? What about government agencies?

As I said at the beginning, AI is a bubble waiting to burst. While there is novelty to it, I and many others I have spoken to have quickly gone from interest and curiosity in this new form of technology, to wariness and distrust, avoid use when possible. Heavy investment in AI by the US, in my opinion, would be wasteful at best, and actively harmful at worst. I ask that you please consider these concerns and how it will adversely effect consumers, US companies, and government agencies should this technology be blindly pushed without proper consideration.

Despite the resources poured into it--billions of dollars, vast quantities of stolen IP and natural human conversation--the technology hasn't meaningfully improved since its public debut and remains so consistently bad at the tasks it's put to that, if it were human, it would've been fired and blacklisted from multiple industries ages ago. comments.comment_text:
## **PUBLIC SUBMISSION**

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-8327

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

Real human artists have taken their entire lifetime to be able to create what they do. Real human artists have invested heavily in their education, their supplies, and the time it takes to refine a skill. And real human artists deserve to have the final say on what is or isn't fair use for their individual works. Copyright holders must have the right to decide for themselves whether their work can be used to train AI models or not. Any law or ruling that takes that choice away from artists, by forcibly allowing AI as "fair use", is unethical and against the spirit of what copyright is meant to achieve. Any law or ruling that removes artists' rights over their own work will have a profoundly negative and lasting impact on the arts, moreso than AI-generative technology already has. What may benefit business in the short term will hobble the creative industries that we all rely on in the long run. There is no modern business that can exist without the arts; art is marketing, packaging, architecture. Everything humans create with intent can be considered part of the domain of art. To allow art to be recycled and regurgitated without any human sensibility, while refusing to pay real human artists for the "fair use" of their work, is profoundly harmful. This has implications far beyond the American border; your international peers will think poorly of you if you choose to support AI over the rights of real human artists.

As an artist myself, and as someone who primarily hangs out with other artists, I cannot begin to tell you how much harm AI generation has already done to the industry. Incredibly skilled artists now find that they cannot get work, because many businesses are too shortsighted to realize the implications of using AI-generated materials in their advertising and branding. But as artists struggle and give up, as artists have to take retail and food service jobs to pay their bills, the supply of artwork for AI models to claim "fair use" of will dry up, until they have nothing to feed on but each other. The quality of what is sold as "art" will plummet, and historians will look back upon this era as a dark age, a blank spot in human cultural progression.

AI has the potential to be something so much better. Imagine what we could achieve if AI models were leveraged by real human artists, instead of against them? We don't need to continue this trend of pitting technology against the arts, when the two are so intimately entwined. But in order for there to be any kind of mutually beneficial relationship between the two, artists need to have the final say on how their own work is used. Copyright documents need to make explicit whether the copyrighted work is fair for AI models to use. I am certain that some artists will choose to make their work available, but it won't be free, and it shouldn't be stolen.

If you have ever enjoyed a piece of art in your life, if you are as human as the rest of us, you know what the right thing to do is. Please make a choice that we can all live with.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

If there is no transparency in how AI is trained and used, then not only will AI development fail, but it will also be a failure to the American people. Copyright laws exist for a reason—to protect originality, creativity, and the rights of creators. While I understand that AI needs a foundation to learn from, it should still be held to the same copyright standards that apply to human creators. Without such accountability, the value of intellectual property could be diminished, making original work feel null and void.

A major concern is that AI, if not properly regulated, may contribute to the erosion of originality. As AI systems generate content based on vast datasets, there is a risk that they will not only replicate but also inadvertently exploit copyrighted material. According to Buick (2024), ensuring transparency in AI training data is crucial for upholding copyright protections and maintaining trust in creative industries. If creators' rights are not safeguarded, the incentive to innovate may decline, impacting fields such as poetry, music, and literature—areas where originality thrives.

While it is true that people sometimes feel discouraged upon realizing their ideas are not unique, this realization often pushes them to refine their creativity and find new approaches. Inspiration fuels artistic and intellectual progress, and without clear boundaries for AI use, this cycle of innovation could be disrupted. Buick (2024) emphasizes that transparency in AI training is essential to mitigating legal and ethical challenges, ensuring that AI does not undermine human creativity but rather supports it.

Transparency in AI development and usage is critical. Without it, we risk devaluing creative work and allowing AI to operate outside of the legal and ethical standards that human creators must follow. Copyright protections must extend into the digital age, ensuring that both AI and human creators are held to the same standards.

## References

Buick, A. (2024). Copyright and AI training data—Transparency to the rescue? Journal of Intellectual Property Law & Practice. https://doi.org/10.1093/jiplp/jpae102

1) The Animation Guild (IATSE Local 839)along with Concept Art Association (CAA), The Human Artistry Campaign, and The National Cartoonist Society Foundation commissioned CVL Economics, a leading authority in economic development and growth, to conduct a comprehensive survey on the profound impact of Gen AI on jobs within the entertainment industry.

The study, conducted between November 17 and December 22, 2023, surveyed 300 C-Suite leaders, senior executives, and mid-level managers across six key entertainment industries to better understand how this technology is being used now, how it will be used over the next three years, and assessing how these technologies will impact creative workers.

About 21.4% of Film, Television, and Animation jobs (or approximately 118,500 jobs) are likely to have a sufficient number of tasks affected to be either consolidated, replaced, or eliminated by GenAI in the U.S. by 2026. As the state with the largest industry employment and industry concentration (or location quotient), California will be impacted the most (affecting 39,500 jobs) both in total job disruption nationwide and with respect to its own economy. New York also has a relatively high employment concentration and will see 15,100 film, television, and animation jobs affected over the next three years.

- 2) Analysts explore the Business Value of Generative AI at Gartner Data & Analytics Summit, July 29-30 in Sydney. They predicted "At least 30% of generative AI (GenAI) projects will be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025, due to poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs or unclear business value, according to Gartner, Inc."
- 3) Goldman Sachs put out a 31-page-report (titled "Gen AI: Too Much Spend, Too Little Benefit?") The report covers AI's productivity benefits (which Goldman remarks are likely limited), AI's returns (which are likely to be significantly more limited than anticipated), and AI's power demands (which are likely so significant that utility companies will have to spend nearly 40% more in the next three years to keep up with the demand from hyperscalers like Google and Microsoft).

comments.comment_text:
## **PUBLIC SUBMISSION**

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-8412

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

By "removing unnecessary burden" you are opening a can of worms that you can not close. Those "burdens" exist to protect the people who were the creators.

Maybe they SHOULD carry the burden; isn't that the price for training these AI models?

In addition, AI safety is a real concern you should be thinking about. I know many people higher up don't understand technology, but the bottom line is that we NEED limitations otherwise things will get out of hand quickly. To be perfectly candid, we don't fully understand how AI currently works; we don't understand its thought process or if it even fulfills the objective we are setting out for it. For more information, I highly suggest Robert Miles at https://youtube.com/@robertmilesai?si=wTfBVFH2nJIuaSWE

Removing this feels similar to removing regulations for medicines; we have these regulations to protect people so that harm isn't done. It's the same here; but instead of protecting people, this plan moves forward with trying prioritize hazardous development.

This isn't even mentioning how these AI's are trained and the social, economic, and environmental costs associated with this.

People should be able to decide how their works are being used; if they don't want it to be used for AI, then they should be allowed to say that it can't be used for training. Just sharing it online doesn't mean they opt in for AI training. If it were, it would be like if you gave your credit card information to buy something online; does that give that website the right to use your credit card however they want? Of course not! Being online shouldn't be an automatic opt in for allowing to work to be used however the viewer sees fit.

Of course, there is also the social cost. There is already an issue with false information being faked by AI; issues like these should lead to more regulation, not less regulation. If you have ever heard of the dead internet theory, then you should already know that this is already an issue.

Of course, the environmental impacts are straightforward; they are just expensive in terms of energy and bandwidth.

Finally, I just wanted to mention the economic cost. The stated goal is to preserve America's AI dominance, but will that really be the outcome? Let's not kid ourselves; even if the companies got all the resources they wanted, will that truly help the US? The AI probably won't be used to help grow the country, but rather to get profit for the company. Note that the company is NOT the US; companies serve to grow themselves, without regard to how they hurt or harm those around them (especially if they think they can make a profit). This is not helping the US economy; it is giving certain companies more power to exploit others around them. If they have the opportunity to make more money elsewhere, out of the US, then they will. Don't delude yourselves into thinking that helping these private companies will help the "US Dominance", because it won't. Technology has never worked that way, especially if it is from a company.

In conclusion, this is a HORRIBLE idea, and you should probably consult actual experts.

## **General Comment**

We created and uphold copyright because we want to recognize that the act of creating is special. That the person who invented the cartoon mouse out of nothing did something more valuable than the person who just photocopied it.

Allowing the AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google to exempt themselves from copyright law is disgusting, chilling, and unamerican.

AI systems cannot create, they can only disassemble and reassemble. They are "trained" by digesting and disassembling the creations of others, actual humans, without their consent, approval, or compensation.

The purpose of fair use is to avoid stifling the rights of the public to comment or report on or satirize copyrighted works. It explicits condemns use intended to replace or supersede the original as piracy.

We allow fair use when the work is substantially transformative, but what does that mean? If I overlay a gif of a dancing baby in the corner of the screen for the entire extended edition of the Lord of the Rings films, I haven't earned the right to send digital copies to all my friends. Transformation requires the same thing as copyright - creation. Human intent.

If I go and tell an AI "art" bot to create an illustration "in the style of" and name a specific artist, it is clearly making use of that artist's work without actually showing any - very clearly replacing and superseding, with no intent on the part of the programmers or owners - SELLERS - of this tool to direct me in any way to the artist whose work I have just appropriated.

If I don't name a specific artist but instead a style, or a subject, it is doing EXACTLY THE SAME THING, replacing the art which has been tagged with those same keywords with the "new" configuration of pixels it has determined to be most similar. That is piracy.

If downloading a copy of a video file containing part of Jerry Maguire is akin to "stealing a car," these companies have just looted the Louvre. Do not let them profit off of this. Hold them accountable.
