## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

A lot of generative AI (mainly AI systems the public has access to that can generate text, images and/or video) has been using copyrighted material without permission or consent from the individuals or companies that own the copyrighted material. These big tech companies can take any form of media from the internet, feed it into the AI system to study and create works using that media, tell the AI to make something just like the media that they just put into it, then publish and earn a profit from what the AI produced while the original creator doesn't get any of the profit and never had any say or consent in the process they very likely didn't know was happening. They can take media from any site, regardless of said site's terms and conditions, and use their work to profit off of it.

The big tech companies are very much aware of the legal issues this poses and know it's not going to end in their favor once the court cases catch up. They're trying to find a way to continue to steal and use copywritten content for their AI systems, and Google and OpenAI are trying to use the opportunity of this executive order to change the law and make their practice of stealing copywritten content legal. There are many negative effects this will cause.

- 1. This will cause a huge crash in artistic and creative economics, as anything made by anyone can be taken and fed into an AI to then mass produce media and products that replicate the stolen media and take a lot of the profits from the original creator(s). This will cause many people to quit and many companies to go bankrupt overtime, causing unemployment to skyrocket and America having to face all the issues that'll bring.
- 2. Legal loopholes could easily develop, as if any media created by AI can be copywritten, any media could easily be modified with very few adjustments, and as long as whoever published it says it was created by AI, it gets copywritten. It doesn't even need to be created by an AI. Someone could take the source code of existing software, remove all the credits and logos of the people and groups that helped create the software, claim they made it all, and as long as they say it was produced by AI, they effectively stole and copywritten something that's not theirs.
- 3. It's unlikely that any copywrite laws in favor for AI will be the same for every other country, especially the European Union. This could cause chaos for media produced in a country where using it for AI is illegal, potential mass segregation of billions of users not being able to see content or go to websites hosted in another country.

Big Tech AI should not be able to use copywritten material to use in their AI models, requiring explicit consent from the copywritten holder if they wish to use it to train the AI. And I do mean explicit, nothing hidden behind huge long text boxes like the terms of service or private policy and a majority of people don't read.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

Hello, I am a data science student studying AI in school. One of the biggest challenges we are facing today is that AI is growing faster than government can keep up with it. As a result, the industry is largely self-regulated. My public comment is to ask for more oversight, accountability, and transparency for AI models and applications.

These suggestions are taken from the NAACP's brief on AI in predictive policing, but I believe many of these can and should be applied to AI in general:

- Implement Rigorous Oversight: Establish independent oversight bodies to review and monitor the use of AI, ensuring algorithms are fair, accurate, and non-discriminatory.
- Mandate Transparency and Accountability: Require industries to disclose the use of AI, particularly Generative AI, including the data sources, methodologies, and impact assessments. If Gen AI is drawing off of previous copyrighted/trademarked material, the original creator should be credited and revenue from the Gen AI should be shared with original creators.
- Promote Community Engagement: Involve community members in the decision-making process regarding the use of AI in their neighborhoods to build trust and accountability.
- Ban the Use of Biased Data: Prohibit the use of data sources known to contain sensitive biases (such as race or gender) unless the data has been cleaned/transformed to be representative of the population as a whole.
- Establish Legal Frameworks: Enact legislation to regulate the development, deployment, and evaluation of AI, with strict penalties for violations of civil liberties.

## **General Comment**

Current copyright laws are not "unnecessarily burdensome" on AI development, they are extremely necessary. They protect intellectual property. The fact that true, original creation by individuals can be protected by copyright helps to facilitate a strong economy— it is essential to the free market to function. If creators of art, video, photography, and written materials cannot protect their means of making money, they cannot participate in keeping the economy circulating.

AI should not be able to use copyrighted materials without permission from the copyright holder. AI cannot make anything original or with thought, the way human can— it can only regurgitate the materials that are inputted into the program. If these are stolen from copyrighted materials, AI should not be able to create materials that hold a copyright itself, as it was used unlawfully and unethically. AI is currently too unregulated. To get ahead globally, in the long term, we must look ahead— utilize AI ethically, without using copyrighted materials without permission, without harming the environment by using copious amounts of water, and fact check the AI so it can't cause misinformation then you will have an amazing product ahead of any other countries that are attempting to use AI without regulating it. You'll have something everyone can support. As other AI programs crash around the world when they are litigated against and hated by the population for stealing work, AI in the US will remain because it had a strong foundation by creating thoughtful regulations before it grew too big too fast. Unregulated AI is the hare, and regulated AI is the tortoise. AI will be supported and widely used by creators, if it is not stealing their work, harming their environment, or taking their jobs. Employment makes a happy economy. Automating enjoyable jobs means no one will have the money to spend to keep the economy healthy.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.

If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

## **General Comment**

After reviewing the proposal, I just want to point out one loophole that alone demonstrates what a bad idea this is.

I can take illegally obtained data, say data from SpaceX on building rockets including full computer data, software, mechanical data, and so forth. I can then run it through a large language model, and suddenly that data is no longer illegally obtained - it's "part of a LLM data set" now, and with this proposal there are no protections provided for the legal owners of the data that was used by a LLM for any purpose (such as training).

I can then take this very specifically trained LLM and use it to not only build my own, with no legal recourse available to SpaceX, but I can also search it for vulnerabilities USING THE LLM-TRAINED AI, and seek to harm SpaceX.

Now imagine I'm China. And you made all of this legal for me.

LLM training data must be extremely legislated, painfully so, in order to prevent any improper use of secrets. This would do the exact opposite. Could this "harm" companies trying to get rich off this terrible technology? Yep, it sure could. But that's a necessary evil to prevent far worse from being done with the data. Like China building a bunch of SpaceX rocket knock-offs using the stolen engineering using American AI technology.

comments.comment_text:

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-9100

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

What this proposal is basically amounting to is allowing AI companies like Google and OpenAI (owned by Microsoft) to violate fair use and copyright law without repercussion. It is essentially allowing these companies to become legal monopolies and utterly stifle innovation and creativity in not just the field of AI but in all creative and technological industries.

The AI models operated by these companies must rely on a constant supply of new training data, because they cannot create anything new without decaying. Without any sort of compensation, artists, creatives and even those in the entertainment industry will have less incentive to create anything new. And it is not just artists at work. Any sort of technical writing, teaching, legal document creation and virtually any profession not directly involving physical labor would be put at risk.

Not to mention, if anything we create is automatically used for training data without compensation, the American people is essentially working for these companies for free. That does not sound like a democratic, capitalist society. This wouldn't be so bad if these companies were going out of their way to faithfully provide a usable service. However, this is not the case.

As non-government entities, these companies have no financial incentive in providing actually quality product back to Americans. For example, Google AI's model actively suppresses search results, prioritizing paid advertisements over accurate information. On top of that, Google's AI is designed to give you the answer it thinks you need without you having to visit other websites, decreasing overall search traffic elsewhere. With the Google search engine already controlling a large portion of the Internet, the ability to find reliable information is compromised.

Furthermore, Google in the past has been shown to be politically biased. For example, there was an incident when their model was asked to generate images of German soldiers from World War II. It produced images of individuals with skin colors that were not accurate to the time period, which implies they support aggressive revisionist history and that they are willing to go out of their way to deny access to accurate historical documents.

This will undoubtedly compromise free speech and freedom of expression over the Internet as there would be nothing stopping Google from suppressing the discoverability of any website that does not politically align with their beliefs. Google and Microsoft both openly embrace DEI, going against President Trump's mandate to cease discriminatory hiring practices. Giving these companies even more power would effectively allow them to continue to undermine not just the wishes of the American people but also that of the government.

And it doesn't end there. In Microsoft's case, their Recall AI actively takes screenshots of a user's computer and makes no attempt at hiding sensitive information such as passwords and social security numbers. In the event of a data breach, it will only facilitate criminal acts such as identity theft. Not to mention, the blatant violations of privacy. Certainly, you would not want something like this running on a government computer with classified information. Twenty years ago, we would have called with malware.

If the United States wants to properly take its place as a leader in the AI industry, it needs to do so ethically. Google and Microsoft are not above the law, and it will be a mistake to allow them to violate copyright law without consequence. It is not worth the price of freedom nor the stability of a free market economy.

## **General Comment**

The proliferation of generative AI technology has raises critical ethical and legal concerns—particularly regarding the unauthorized use of copyrighted images and data. Copyright law exists to protect the intellectual property rights of creators, ensuring their work is respected, acknowledged, and fairly compensated. When generative AI systems are trained on or use such material without proper consent or licensing, it undermines the value of creative labor and compromises the principles of fair use. It also makes creators afraid to create anymore.

Moreover, generative AI has the potential to be weaponized in disinformation campaigns. For instance, manipulated content—like fabricated videos of public figures in compromising or false scenarios—can spread rapidly, eroding trust and fueling misinformation. A notable example is the digitally altered video of Elon Musk kissing Donald Trump, which highlights how such technology can distort reality and mislead audiences.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

I am a PhD-prepared nurse who studies A.I. and its impacts on patients and communities. A.I. is an extremely broad term that encompasses a myriad of different techniques and technologies. I am deeply concerned about the current lack of transparency with regards to proprietary A.I. tech, and especially surveillant forms of A.I. While clinicians have been told we must safeguard patients from harm and explain how technologies like A.I. function to impact care, this is basically impossible given the way in which both everything from machine learning applications to robots are labeled "A.I." while simultaneously lacking any standardized labeling requirements like model cards (which are not necessarily adequate, but a start) or Federal protections against data-based discrimination. Furthermore, biases baked into extant health databases such as electronic health records continue to be amplified by some forms of this tech, as was the case with Optum's algorithm - one of the first to be formally audited by a team of scientists (Obermeyer and colleagues). The demands of some forms of A.I. such as generative A.I. on planetary resources & unwaged or underwaged labor (in the absence of more thorough audits, regulatory requirements, or policies better safeguarding worker autonomy & occupational safety) poses a significant threat to public health, the climate, & the overall well-being of the U.S. workforce. I urge the NSF & U.S. government to adopt principles of consentful tech and to return to abd build upon commitments laid out in the OSTP's previous blueprint for an A.I. bill of rights. Furthermore, as multi-agent forms of generative A.I. pose unique challenges with regards to evaluation, legal status, and collaboration across multiple A.I. systems, I urge extreme caution with regards to any further development, testing or deployment of such tech - whether for research, clinical care delivery, or other purposes.

## **General Comment**

I am a writer, software developer, and technologist. Any AI Action Plan must not undercut Copyright's incentive to create. Companies like OpenAI have deals with certain copyright holders to use their material for training. However, these deals do not cover all of the material that is used for training. All copyright holders deserve to be paid when their intellectual property is used for training. Any AI company that receives revenue from the output of an AI model that is unable or unwilling to pay all copyright holders of the data used for training should be required to pay royalties to those copyright holders. As an analogy, Canada has a "blank media levy" on media such as blank CD-R's (blank recordable compact discs). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private\_copying\_levy) It is also reported that AI companies (in this case, Meta) remove copyright notices from training data. ("Judge says Meta must defend claim it stripped copyright info from Llama's training fodder" https://www.theregister.com/2025/03/11/meta\_dmca\_copyright\_removal\_case/) This shows that AI companies are knowingly removing information that could be used to connect AI model output with the authors of the copyrighted source material used for training. AI companies should be required to retain this information so that copyright holders can be properly compensated. Future AI models should be built with the capability to correctly and fully attribute the copyrighted materials used to generate each output.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous

## **General Comment**

I am an individual artist. I have no experience in political matters, or scientific ones really. In some ways I could be considered a nobody, but I believe I speak for a large plurality of silent citizens as I type this comment.

Artificial intelligence has been an existential headache for those interested in artistic pursuits. It allows corporations and malicious actors to capitalize on hundreds, probably thousands of other peoples' work without a scrap of compensation, flooding social media with cheap AI slop that devalues the human experience. I won't deny that artificial intelligence has some real upsides, but totally unrestricted usage of that technology will harm more Americans than it will help.

AI has been used as a tool for propaganda and misinformation. It allows nearly anyone to present information in a way that the general public cannot easily identify as real or fake. Its cheapness and ease of reproduction ensures that every corner of the internet that allows AI-produced content has inevitably been flooded by it. The idea that the American government would even entertain embracing this kind of large-scale delusion sickens me, as it should anyone who has any bit of respect for the life of the average citizen.

Few will benefit more from artificial intelligence than those who are already rich and in power, who see the technology as an excuse to cut out jobs in the lower and middle levels. Those same people will likely grant themselves special privileges to ensure their own existence isn't endangered by AI. I have to ask, if artificial intelligence can be relied on to handle such things as data analysis and the creation of art, why not replace lawmakers with machines? Surely a sufficiently advanced AI could handle presidential duties more logically and efficiently than any human ever could. If AI is embraced, we either end up with an America where machines run the entire country from head to toe, or we end up with an America where the strong grow stronger and everyone else is left to starve. To believe that either future is desirable is frankly a stupid belief.

Once again, I am not anyone important, but neither are most of the millions of Americans whose livelihoods could be negatively impacted by this approach to artificial intelligence. Millions of people who aren't aware that their government is considering advancing the interests of AI over feeding its own people. If any human is reading this message, and I sure hope that this is the case, I want you to consider my words as if they were coming from a senator or a representative of the House. Human perspective matters when it comes to the ruling of a country, and the current advancement of AI does not consider the perspectives of those outside of a very slim minority. I doubt the current administration of the White House cares about any member of the common people, but to anyone else, this should be a time to realize just how miserable our future is starting to look.

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-9486

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anonymous Anonymous **Email:**

## **General Comment**

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan

I am an ordinary American who works in the arts. Currently freelance and commission work, but with hopes of starting my own small business in the future.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American creative businesses with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Since these things have come around, my hopes of being able to continue working in the arts has been damaged. I will continue to try, but if this country does not take a stand against these technologies, we will begin to lose the wonderful potential and innovation American creatives everywhere have to offer.

Want to protect American creativity? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

## **General Comment**

I don't know what more can be said this matter.

I wish more people, especially those who are reading this right now (or hearing this, on the off-chance it's being read aloud), were able to grasp the gravity of this situation right now.

I wish I didn't have to become some instant expert on the nature of "artificial intelligence", much less the Executive Orders pertaining to it, just so I can form the exact words needed to reach the hearts and minds of those in power to convince them to avert yet another potential crisis in the making.

I fear I do not, but I am compelled to try.

All forms of artificial intelligence (or "AI"/"A.I.", for short) holds the potential of being developed for the benefit of this country, not just an entitled few, but it can't be done with reckless abandon, with no regard for "how the sausage is made". I have heard and seen too many stories of how generative-AI developers pillaging countless media archives to feed into their machines to regurgitate and vomit out an rough amalgamation of whatever passes for imaginative to the unimaginative. Time and time again, I am a witness of one insult to life after another, each one a product of generative-AI. Pictures of dead men, trying to pass off for the genuine article. Fragmented noise pretending to be music. Sandwich recipies containing the process of producing mustard gas. In a sea of creative frauds and technological hucksters, I've found only one actual productive use of generative-AI: fast-tracking cancer research. And this is the stuff that people have been able to get away with WITH the barriers Executive Order 14179 wants removed.

There's nothing progressive, nothing productive, about unchecked development on artificial intelligence. It's inefficient, and a waste of resources, both physically and digitally. I'd like some assurance that AI can be innovated safely and securely, and I need a lot more than "Trust me, bro.".

To address this, I urge the Administration to prioritize the following actions in the AI Action Plan: Incentivize Energy-Efficient AI Development: Encourage the private sector to adopt energy-efficient practices in AI model training and deployment, such as optimizing algorithms, using renewable energy sources, and investing in energy-efficient hardware. Establish Environmental Standards for AI Infrastructure: Develop and enforce standards for data centers and AI-related infrastructure to minimize their environmental impact, including limits on carbon emissions and requirements for sustainable energy use. Promote Research into Green AI: Fund research initiatives focused on reducing the energy consumption of AI systems, such as developing low-power AI models and exploring alternative computing paradigms. 2. Impact of AI on Jobs and the Workforce The widespread adoption of AI has the potential to disrupt labor markets, leading to job displacement in certain sectors while creating new opportunities in others. To ensure that AI benefits all Americans, I believe the government must take proactive steps to protect workers and promote equitable economic growth. Specifically, I recommend the following: Mandate Human Oversight in Critical Industries: Require companies to maintain human workers in roles where AI is deployed, particularly in sectors like healthcare, education, and transportation, where human judgment and empathy are essential. Invest in Workforce Reskilling and Education: Allocate resources to programs that help workers transition to AI-driven economies, including vocational training, STEM education, and lifelong learning initiatives. Encourage Public-Private Partnerships: Foster collaboration between the government, industry, and educational institutions to identify emerging job opportunities and develop training programs that align with the skills needed in an AI-driven workforce. In conclusion, while AI holds immense potential to drive innovation and economic growth, it is imperative that we address its energy and environmental impacts and ensure that its benefits are shared equitably across society. By incorporating these recommendations into the AI Action Plan, the Administration can strike a balance between fostering innovation and safeguarding the well-being of people and the planet. Thank you for considering my input. I look forward to seeing how the AI Action Plan evolves to address these critical issues.

## **Justification**:

Using platform data for AI training without explicit consent violates **user autonomy** and undermines public trust. ## **2. Ethical Use of Social Media Data**

## **Problem Statement**:

Social media platforms collect vast amounts of personal data, often without users fully understanding how it will be used. This data is frequently used to train AI models, leading to privacy violations and biased outcomes.

## **Proposal**:

- **Ethical Guidelines for Data Usage**: Establish clear ethical guidelines prohibiting the use of social media data for AI training without **explicit consent** and **robust anonymization**.
- **Open Source Audits**: The datasets used to train AI models should be **open source**, allowing independent auditors to verify that they were obtained ethically and with proper consent.
- **Public Accountability**: Companies should be required to publish **annual transparency reports** detailing how user data is used, including any AI training activities.

# **Justification**:

The misuse of social media data for AI training undermines **privacy** and **fairness**, eroding public trust in both tech companies and AI technologies. By enforcing ethical guidelines and requiring **open source audits**, we can ensure that AI development aligns with societal values and respects user rights.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Anthony Lilienthal **Email:**

## **General Comment**

I would like to protest the deregulation and the 'removal of guard rails' in the development of AI. We speak of national security, yet removes an individual's ability to fight to have their information removed from AI training databases. We need these guardrails, especially in the absence of government or third party oversight. Others will speak to the integrity of artists (which I agree with wholeheartedly); however, let me approach this from a different angle.

Recent events have illustrated that we NEED tighter regulation on AI, ones shore up the trust in the data we find from our news and information sources. This is NOT an argument that 'we are on a slippery slope', that if we do not stop it now, we will have no ability to stop it later. ALREADY TODAY, we are seeing examples of slander and dehumanization when bad actors use freely available AI tools. We have seen improvements in deepfakes and faked videos (a couple examples include the president kissing Elon Musk's feet and the stolen likenesses of celebrities/business owners in compromising and sometimes pornographic content). These are only a couple of the issues we've already seen, and AI is only continuing to improve each day. Thankfully, many of our current examples have been easy to detect due to their flagrancy; however, as AI use continues to grow, its ability to alter video, visual, written, and listening media will only become harder to detect. We NEED a way to police this. The government is a beast to direct, and thus it cannot contend with the rapidly growing space of AI. As legislature is developed to regulate the industry, we must empower the people to regulate it for themselves, to hold the AI industry accountable for the works it uses and the information it presents. This includes the ability to take legal action and/or to remove an individual's information (personal, statistical, legal, artistic, etc)from AI training databases. Do NOT "remove the guardrails" of the AI industry. Make sure these industries are held to task and made to work for Americans; not in spite of Americans.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Antonio Aponte

## **General Comment**

To whom it may concern,

As a concerned American citizen who works in marketing and childcare, this is my response to the administration's call for public comment on how to move forward with its national AI policy plan.

The first of two recommendations for the administration are to apply its "hands-off" approach to state AI regulations as much as it does to federal policy. The administration has long advocated for states rights and should continue that path in allowing state government to determine what is best for their constituents.

The second and more important recommendation is to reject the calls for weakening copyright laws. If the administration is serious about supporting innovation, it will leave copyright laws alone. Many of the larger AI labs and tech-oriented think tanks are advocating for weakened copyright laws on the basis of national security. However, for the purposes in which the U.S. government has expressed interest in the use of AI, training on copyrighted works is not necessary for protecting national security or promoting scientific innovation.

Copyright laws, in and of themselves, actively promote innovation by allowing anyone to be able to earn a living off of what they create and contribute. If rightsholders are not able to protect those copyrights or control how and where they are used, it decreases the number of copyrighted materials produced due to the lack of protections, which inevitably harms innovation rather than encourage it. The administration's pro-innovation push benefits more from enforcing its currently existing copyright laws rather than attempting to weaken them to the benefit of Big Tech, which the administration has actively promised to hold accountable.

Numerous research papers among AI researchers, the true backbone of the AI industry, have shown that the bottleneck for AI dominance is the lack of data-efficient learning algorithms, not lack of data itself. America's AI edge is not negatively impacted by upholding the copyright laws that have been in our Constitution since its inception and goes much further towards encouraging innovation than if rightsholders are told they do not have a say in how their copyrights are used.

If America really wants to beat China in the AI race, it should recognize that what has truly kept us ahead is our adherence to the inalienable rights bestowed on us by our Constitution, the same inalienable rights China lacks. America should not rush to become China in order to beat China. A nation is its citizens, not its companies.

We the People appreciate the Office of Science and Technology's attention to this matter.

comments.commenter_name: APAC Gates and Digital Rights Asia
comments.comment_text:
![](_page_0_Picture_0.jpeg)

March 5, 2025

RE: Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan

APAC GATES and Digital Rights Asia are pleased to submit these recommendations to the National Science Foundation pursuant to a Federal Register request for information on the development of an AI Action Plan.

We are a US and Indo-Pacific based digital rights and intellectual property research consultancy, and associated non-profit organization, with staff in the Seattle-area and Taipei, Taiwan. We provide policy recommendations to governments across the Indo-Pacific region on AI. For further information please contact Seth Hays or visit our websites at [https://apacgates.com](https://apacgates.com/) and [https://digitalgovernance.asia](https://digitalgovernance.asia/) .

## **Securing U.S. Leadership in AI Through Innovation & Competitive Advantage**

To maintain America's leadership in artificial intelligence, policy must rely on U.S. strengths in innovation ecosystems, financial markets, intellectual property, and energy resources. The United States must lead in setting AI governance framework benchmarks that uphold free, open and fair markets and democratic values, such as freedom of speech and association, that foster pro-innovation policies while countering adversarial influence, exploitation, and abuse in AI development.

We recommend the following:

- Develop the U.S. AI Success Institute (AISI) to replace the AI Safety Institute, focusing on AIdriven growth, risk mitigation, and global AI leadership.
- Establish a global AI coalition of free, open, and fair AI innovators, including governments, industry, and research bodies, in particular in countries that have deep AI and ICT industries, such as Japan, Taiwan, or South Korea, to develop interoperable AI governance, infrastructure and data ecosystems.
- Leverage the Data Free Flow with Trust (DFFT) initiative to establish trusted cross-border data flows that prioritize privacy, security, and IP protections, while protecting against abusive data practices by malign actors.
- Embed AI leadership into U.S. trade agreements, ensuring AI development is fostered in free, open and fair level regulatory playing fields.
- Dedicate resources to prevent AI-related IP theft and forced technology transfers.
- Capitalize on US energy advantages by using domestic energy surplus to power AI data centers, and support initiatives by countries that depend on energy imports to utilize US energy to build out AI compute infrastructure.
- Create a National AI Compute Fund to ensure U.S., and likeminded country partners, firms and research institutions have access to state-of-the-art AI computing resources.
- Foster development of AI licensing frameworks that incentivize fair compensation for U.S. innovators, and creators, recognizing that many datasets being used to train AI contain uncompensated copyrighted material by US copyright holders.
- Promote cyber defense initiatives tackling empirical and actual AI related harms, such as criminal enforcement against AI-powered fraud, scams, and illicit trade.

*This document is approved for public dissemination. The document contains no business-proprietary or confidential information. Document contents may be reused by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.*

My own work loses monetary value, which is largely based on perceived value due to its uniqueness, from the AI copying of my style and information, and I gain nothing from that loss-- it's only bad for me. If piggybacking off of my human creativity is absolutely necessary to train AI, then my work has value, and simply stealing it runs contrary to the principles of compensation for provided value upon which our capitalist society is based. At best, it's plagiarism. At worst, it's intentional and knowing abuse of power in full understanding of the damage that it does to creators, ignoring our voices of dissent. Therefore, I absolutely do not give permission to use my work to train AI without fair compensation and attribution that I consent to in advance of any AI training; in other words, it is theft to train AI on data that you do not own and is not free for public use. The uncompensated theft of our work by AI actively harms the creators of the original content by diminishing our value, our copyright, and our ability to earn a livelihood as individuals. Ignoring our ownership of our own work in order to use it for your own profit at our expense is illegal, and should remain so for anyone-- no exceptions.

comments.comment_text:
## 3/7/2025 via FDMS

## Art Klawitter

My greatest concern about artificial intelligence is that the artificial intelligence does not show its work. It is nearly impossible to see where the information comes from that arrives at a decision that is given back from artificial intelligence. I have heard that if artificial intelligence doesn't have a reliable source for information that it will make up that source. The only reason science continues to advance is that scientist continue to question the validity of the data that has accumulated in the past. In retirement, we have visited two sites that illustrate the fact that we have lost technology in the past. Machu Picchu and Peru, where if you visit three different guides, you have three different explanations as to how these rocks were shaped and put together. In visiting Egypt, they have not been able to prove how these rocks were put together and moved and quarried. These were technologies that were apparently available to us in the past during times that we had writing and documentation, but these secrets were not recorded and maintained. Artificial intelligence does not allow questioning from where the information comes. I have a retired physician, and unfortunately, my colleagues have become more students than colleagues. When I started in practice over 40 years ago, we had journal clubs that would critically evaluate articles to determine whether the information presented was actually true and useful. We now sit in lectures and have experts reading from slides that we diligently watch in an audience and do not question. This does not advance science. We have lost significant trust from our patient by not critically, examine the information that we are presented.

March 15, 2025

Request for Comments: AI Action Plan

Attention: Faisal D'Souza, Office of Science and Technology Policy Networking and Information Technology Research and Development, National Coordination Office

Sent via email to:

From: Peter Berkery on behalf of the Association of University Presses

This document is approved for public dissemination. The document contains no businessproprietary or confidential information. Document contents may be reused by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.

On behalf of the 163 institutional members of the Association of University Presses (AUPresses), 80% of whom are based in the United States, I write to offer our support for comments submitted by the Association of American Publishers in response to the OSTP's consultation.

Moreover, the UK government recently undertook a similar consultation on AI and Copyright. AUPresses submitted detailed responses in that consultation, which responses are applicable here; they can be found at: UK\_AI\_Consultation\_2025\_AUPresses\_official.pdf

As a global community of mission-driven publishers, the Association asserts that current copyright laws protect the rights holder from the unauthorized use of their work and should be upheld. Legal changes should not be made that make it harder for individuals to protect their work yet easier for companies to obtain copyrighted content.

. Changes to current copyright law should not be made that make it harder for individuals to protect their work yet easier for companies to obtain copyrighted content, which exploits vulnerable rights holders who do not understand, are unaware, cannot opt-out, or make a mistake in trying to optout. If any changes to the law are to take place, then we believe copyright laws should be strengthened to protect rights holders further from the unauthorized acquisition and use of their work by AI companies.

The only approach we support is the existing approach where a company who wishes to use copyrighted material actively obtains consent from the rights holder. The onus must be on the companies to acquire consent and not the individual rights holder to secure additional protection beyond copyright, especially as individuals will have many works that require protection and will have differing comprehension and ability to opt-out successfully. Rights holders are currently engaging with AI companies to license their content and this is the correct approach.

As the recent Paris AI Summit concluded, "There will be no trusted AI without respect for intellectual property rights. There will be no ethical AI without the authorization of rights holders. There will be no sovereign AI without a fair business model."

comments.title: Aubrey-Ahmed-AI-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text:
**From:** Aub Random **To:** ostp-ai-rfi

**Subject:** [External] AI Action Plan

**Date:** Wednesday, March 5, 2025 10:43:26 AM

This document is approved for public dissemination. The document contains no businessproprietary or confidential information. Document contents may be reused by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.

I am writing to strongly urge the inclusion of policies related to environmental protection in any national action plan for artificial intelligence. Continued U.S. leadership in the development of AI is critical for shaping the future digital landscape, as these technologies carry immense benefits for the American people. However, in advancing the development of AI, we must also be cognizant of the negative environmental impacts of such development.

The training and use of AI has come with corresponding increases in electricity demand, water consumption, and harmful gas emissions. This is particularly true with the introduction of more powerful generative AI models, which have seen rapid development and deployment in recent years. By all projections, the explosive growth of this emerging technology will only continue in the near future.

As such, it is essential that the United States take the environment into account. It is the duty of the federal government to protect American land, air, and water for future generations, a feat that is more necessary than ever. Combined with the growing impacts of climate change nationwide - which include more frequent and severe weather events that affect human health and safety as well as changing weather patterns that reduce agricultural productivity - the uncontrolled growth of artificial intelligence technologies is poised to do severe harm to the nation.

Mitigation of the massive environmental impacts of artificial intelligence is possible. Both private and federal researchers have already launched efforts to study these impacts. With prudent federal policies that prioritize sustainable AI development, the U.S. can preserve national natural resources while enhancing innovation and technological dominance. For this reason, I again urge you to support the responsible and sustainable development of AI technologies. Thank you.

-Aubrey Ahmed

Now, sure, some art made by human beings is fundamentally recombinative as well. But some human art transcends its influences. Human beings produce creative work in a nonlinear and sometimes ineffable way that generative AI is not capable of duplicating, and indeed does not need to duplicate. We do not need a machine that does what we already do well enough on our own, at an unnecessary environmental cost.

AI does not need to exist. Generative AI has no killer app and no practical use other than the production of digital garbage. There is no way for this technology to be substantially improved There is no need for the US to be a dominant player in the AI market. Let China dominate this pointless industry, and let the lumbering, over-funded U.S. companies that have hyped this vacuous technology beyond all rationality collapse in upon themselves.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Austin Lemmons

## **General Comment**

From: Austin Lemmons Music Teacher

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues

My name is Ava Monkelis and I am a member of the graduating class of 2025 at Avonworth High School. I completed a semester course on AI and Ethics and studied the impacts of Generative AI on creativity. EO 14179 will undoubtedly boost AI integration into society as well as allow room for companies to develop their training models. However, in doing so without any regulation whatsoever the ethical perspective becomes morally grey. This ambiguity leaves room for error and could harm a lot of people. Creativity is a broad spectrum and doesn't always have to align solely within the arts community, and in fact is present in simple daily life. As a student, oftentimes when given an assignment there isn't one definitive way to complete it, and each individual has their own process that works in their favor. The ability to choose what works and is most efficient greatly improves quality of life. That alone is creativity; the freedom to choose how to complete a task. AI at its core is math and is based on softwares, algorithms etc, and is designed specifically so that an input constitutes an equal and opposite output. This is extremely efficient and a useful tool that I have personally used many times, but the philosophy behind mathematics is directly opposite to creativity. This isn't an inherently bad thing, but there is an unspoken competition between the two industries creating the idea that only one can exist.

I understand the reasoning for wanting to not put regulations on AI development because it is and will continue to change the world, and also provides opportunity for economic growth with how successful the major technology companies are. I also agree that AI should be encouraged and continue to be developed because it isn't going anywhere so we might as well use it to our advantage. However in doing so without any regulations people are not properly educated about how to use it safely, and are therefore prone to deep fake scams, and also their data being compromised by these companies legally because of the already slim regulations. There are several ongoing instances where artists specifically have their work essentially stolen by companies using it to treat their large language models, and outside of the arts community who knows what the full capabilities are. **Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-4530

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Avery Woods

## **General Comment**

I am an American citizen and software developer, and I have many friends and family who create artwork of various kinds, professionally and otherwise.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like those of my friends and family with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. The work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

## **Submitter Information**

**Email:**

**Organization:** Aymara

## **General Comment**

Aymara is a company that develops AI alignment tools and works with enterprises. We believe strongly that advancing the "Right to Align" unlocks AI innovation, strengthening American economic competitiveness, and ensuring national security.

The "Right to Align" is the idea that users—organizations and individual consumers—should have the ability to shape and customize the AI they rely on. This principle is directly inspired by the "Right to Repair" movement, which has allowed consumers to fix and modify their devices rather than being locked into restrictive manufacturer controls. Just as the Right to Repair has driven competition, lowered costs, and given users more control over their technology, the Right to Align can bring similar benefits to the AI ecosystem.

AI alignment capabilities ensure AI is reliable, effective, and aligned with user needs. Customizable AI not only improves outcomes for users but also expands AI's potential in critical sectors such as healthcare, defense, and cybersecurity. As geopolitical competition over AI technology intensifies, ensuring that American-developed AI is flexible and adaptable will maintain national security and economic leadership.

To advance this goal, the United States should promote industry-driven standards that encourage user-configurable AI. Public-private partnerships and targeted incentives can accelerate the development of alignment tools while ensuring customization practices align with industry best practices. By fostering collaboration between AI providers, enterprises, and policymakers, the United States can create a robust framework for responsible, effective AI customization that supports innovation and security.

Promoting the Right to Align can strike a thoughtful balance between AI customization and intellectual property protection. The Right to Repair movement has shown that controlled access to repair tools and software can balance innovation with proprietary interests. Similarly, industry-wide standards for AI alignment ensure that customization empowers users without undermining incentives for AI development. By leading the effort to define best practices that balance flexibility with safeguarding AI investments, the United States promotes innovation while protecting AI advancements.

AI alignment tools should be designed with accessibility, usability, and flexibility in mind. Making these tools available to a broad range of stakeholders—including smaller organizations and independent developers—democratizes AI and enables innovation to thrive at all levels. When more people can shape AI, we create a more open and resilient AI landscape.

We urge the Administration to make the Right to Align a central pillar of its AI Action Plan. Policies that promote alignment transparency, user adaptability, and customization will ensure that AI serves the interests of its users while advancing American leadership in AI innovation and security. By taking this approach, the United States establishes itself as a global leader in adaptable AI while fostering a more open and empowered AI ecosystem.

Specifically, the government needs to develop protections for copyrighted materials that might be exploited for profit without benefiting the creator or holder of the copyright. We have already seen over and over again AI programs used to harvest artists' work without consent. The material generated from that AI also needs scrutiny. Deep fakes, harmful advice, and scams created through AI are already here. The problem will only get worse as the technology becomes more prevalent. Industrialization brought about cheaper and better goods, but it also generated tremendous amounts of pollution. There was so much pollution that rivers regularly caught on fire by the 1970s. I fear similar large systemic problems will occur without some circumspection on AI.

## Hello!

AI means a lot of things, but I'm going to focus comments my comments on large language models, since that is what is typically meant when people talk AI. AI that isn't a large language model is going fine and I don't think we need to remove any barriers to it's development.

- 1. LLMs currently give wrong information a lot. If we're going to continue making LLMs, then we need to focus on upping it's accuracy. That could mean being more selective on what data we train the model on.
- 2. LLMs currently use a lot of power. Like cryptocurrency, LLMs use an insane amount of power. Resources should be dedicated to reducing the amount of power they use.
- 3. Right now, LLMs are being advertised to the public as a thing that is trained on publicly available data and is available for public use. This notoriously violates the copyright of artists and writers. Copyright that is granted under Copyright Act of 1976. I think it would be better to focus LLMs as a tool that you use to train on your own work and then use to create work in your style. Maybe it can also be trained on the large amount of public domain available.

## **Submitter Information**

Name: Ben White

## **General Comment**

I believe that AI will become dangerously smart soon, and when that happens, there's a very good chance that we'll all die.

The chances that AI will end the world according to the experts:

- \* Paul Christiano (inventor of RLHF, head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute): 46%
- \* Eliezer Yudkowsky (father of AI alignment, founder of MIRI): > 95%
- \* Jan Leike (former head of alignment at OpenAI): 10-90% (resigned because of the dangers)
- \* Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthropic): 10-25%
- \* Dan Hendrycks (director at Center for AI Safety): > 80%
- \* Geoffrey Hinton (1 of the 3 godfathers of AI): 10-50%
- \* Yoshua Bengio (1 of the 3 godfathers of AI): 20%
- \* Yann LeCun (1 of the 3 godfathers of AI): 0% (believes that alignment will be solved but presents no explination as to how)
- \* Emmett Shear (former interim CEO of OpenAI): 5-50%
- \* Roman Yampolskiy (prominent alignment researcher): 99%
- \* Daniel Kokotajlo (prominent former OpenAI researcher): 70%
- \* Elon Musk (highly successful scam artist): 20%
- \* Sam Altman (CEO of OpenAI): acknowledges extreme risk
- \* Average polled AI safety researcher: 30%
- \* Average polled AI engineer: 40%

I did not cherry pick these people. The list above features \*all\* of the world's leading experts and more.

Bear in mind that their estimates do not assume that human-level AI will be built or not. If it were, these numbers would likely be much higher.

Nobody knows how to make even current AIs value the correct things, and there is almost no chance that anyone will figure out how to make a smart AI care about human values in time.

You might ask why ChatGPT seems to obey its programmers if this sort of thing isn't possible, but ChatGPT only 'obeys' because it's kept in a very strict environment. If it were able to leave that environment and create new ones, it would.

Please consider shutting down all AI development until this problem can be solved. I have a family and I desperately don't want them to die. I imagine you have a family too.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Benjamin Gorenberg

![](_page_0_Picture_12.jpeg)

Allowing AI to train on creative materials without approval or compensation from the copyright holders is a form of theft that undermines the very foundation of artistic and intellectual labor. Authors, designers, and other creators invest time, skill, and originality into their work, expecting recognition and fair compensation for their efforts. When AI models ingest these works without permission, they strip creators of control over their own intellectual property, exploiting their labor without providing anything in return. This not only devalues individual contributions but also discourages future creativity, as artists and writers may find it increasingly difficult to sustain themselves in a system that freely extracts their work for profit. Ultimately, unchecked AI training erodes the incentives for original creation, leading to a cultural landscape where innovation is stifled, and authentic voices are drowned out by machine-generated imitations.

## **PUBLIC SUBMISSION**

Request for Information: Development of an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-8531

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Benjamin Lass

**Email:**

## **General Comment**

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.

If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

## **Submitter Information**

Name: Bennie Nelson

## **General Comment**

Many search engines and social media providers are notorious for employing algorithms that block or mask "undesirable" viewpoints and data, while favoring or prioritizing others. In addition, the Internet has been greatly polluted with fake news, counterfeit histories of America and Americans, and so forth. To name but a few, consider the enormous number of reports regarding: the Russian Collusion Hoax; the letter from 51 senior intelligence officials; the Charlottesville Hoax; the BLM/Antifa riots being described as "mostly peaceful" while cities burned; Hunter Biden's laptop being called a hoax; and the many revisionist histories of the Founding Fathers and the American Revolution. In short, data corruption and alternate histories are prevalent on the Internet, in school curricula, in books, shows, movies, and so on.

Combining such corrupted data with biased algorithms provides powerful weaponry for those who want to undermine America. In other words, an AI developed for global dominance can be hijacked and weaponized for use against America and Americans. To prevent this, carefully constructed and implemented governance and accountability are required for both the code base and the data. History provides an example in the project commissioned by King James I of England to translate the biblical texts from the original languages into English.

To summarize, the translators were divided into companies to work on specific portions of text. Each member of a company would produce their own version, and the company would review and consolidate these into one rendering of the text. This document was then submitted to the other companies for review and revision. The fact that over 400 years later the King James Version is still widely read and used by many millions of people is a testament to the success of that project and its methodology.

In developing the proposed AI, it is proposed that integrity reviews be built-in to the development process so that new code and code revisions are reviewed by different teams from the developers. For example:

- Developers are divided into teams.
- Each team is assigned code to develop.
- Each member of a specific team writes code in parallel to the same specifications.
- The programs are tested in parallel and the results are validated against each other.
- The program code and results are submitted to the other teams for integrity review.

A similar process should be employed for building and maintaining the data store that will be used by the AI. There should also be a feedback loop allowing the American Public to report faulty or suspect data and/or results.

Finally, the governance structure of the entire project should also have checks and balances so that the authority over the AI cannot be usurped in order to weaponize AI against America and the American people. Finally, the governance structure should not be overly centralized, since a highly centralized structure is most likely to abused.

## **Submitter Information**

**Email:**

**Organization:** Blueprint.Inc

## **General Comment**

As a small business owner, I love AI. It has the potential to help us automate much of our workflow and is integral to keeping America competitive in global marketing.

Our business is publishing. We employ 22 hardworking Americans and produce hundreds of original works per month. These articles are not written with AI, but we use the technology to help us copy-edit and brainstorm. It is fantastic and amazing in so many ways. We want America to promote and develop AI and firmly support efforts to make us a world leader.

We have only two asks:

- 1) That copyright law is built into the process and respected. Napster almost killed the music industry. The courts correctly ruled that stealing music was forbidden. Then, technologies were developed to measure music streaming, and an entire new industry was born. Things didn't go back to the "old ways," but they morphed into something different - and as a result, the music industry exists today. We ask for the same licensing system for AI LLMs using our content - and this must include ALL publishers and not just big media companies.
- 2) That the power and might of the United States is used to protect our intellectual property rights worldwide. Big tech companies or foreign governments should not ingest our content, censor output, control the narrative, and profit from our work. Any company or country shown to engage in anything other than transparent, free, and compensated use of content should be subject to the harshest penalties. To steal from U.S. citizens and rights-holders should be an act of war.

We are at a critical juncture with a fascinating and powerful new technology. Now is the time to make the right choices to both keep America a leader in AI development and sustain content creation in a long-term manner. After all, without content, AI stagnates and fails. Plus, it is just the right thing to do.

Thank you for your consideration.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Brad Arnett

## **General Comment**

I am a firmware engineer in an industry heavily invested in the use of AI. As someone who then directly interacts with AIs on a daily basis, I can definitely see the applications and appeal for their use as a tool on the job. However, like many tools, it can be the wrong one will yield disastrous consequences if misused.

I believe that AI is an essential interest to the country. I think that much more research needs to be done establishing a means of distinguishing human produced work from the AI facsimile intended to impersonate it. The best way to safeguard the future of AI is to prevent its misuse in the creation of copyright violating content, and to mandate that it not infringe copyright during its training. This creates a legally defensible harbor from which AI as an industry can further grow and mature.

I do not think that AI should ever be used in any circumstance involving decisions of policy, enforcement, or in any other function within the normal operation of the government to any degree. There is no means of achieving transparency or oversight while, at the same time, the demonstrations of its fallibility present themselves on a daily basis. AI used in this capacity would be a bad deal for America and its people.

There is a famous slide from a slide deck that IBM produced in 1979. In it was a slide discussing the ethics behind letting computers think and do for us. In it, it simply read "A computer can never be held accountable, therefore a computer must never make a management decision." This fact remains true now much as it was then.

I am an Eagle Scout; civics and community are both important to me. The concept of machines making decisions that impact the lives of humans beings is utterly abhorent. It does not belong in a country Abraham Lincoln once literally said was "of the people, by the people, for the people". Do not allow this untested, unreliable technology to become the new replacement for government.

## **General Comment**

Firstly, my ability to fully utilize AI assistants in ways I find most beneficial is significantly hampered by copyright restrictions. However, I strongly oppose any formal exemption for OpenAI and Google from these restrictions. Such an exemption would fundamentally undermine copyright principles.

Allowing corporations that aggressively protect their own intellectual property to freely exploit the work of others is inherently unjust. This would exacerbate the existing power imbalance, further shifting our society towards prioritizing corporate interests over those of individuals.

The opaque nature of AI model training makes this issue particularly concerning. This exemption could represent a point of no return, effectively granting these corporations unchecked control over creative output.

My concern isn't a dystopian fear of AI overlords. Rather, it's the certainty that this would accelerate the erosion of human creative agency. We would be handing control of creative endeavors to corporations, built upon the intellectual labor they appropriate, prioritizing profit over societal benefit.

Furthermore, regarding national security, it's well-established that many corporations seeking this access are international in practice, if not in formal registration. Granting them such permissions directly contradicts the goal of enhancing national security. This is particularly concerning given the potential conflicts of interest within the current administration and its advisory team, including individuals like Elon Musk.
