My name is Brett Bullion. I am a freelance illustrator. I am very concerned with the creation of AI datasets in regard to copyright law and people's personal data, the environmental and energy costs of implementing AI, and the disruption that I have seen in the creative fields where AI has already been displacing artists.

AI datasets are created from the mass scraping of information, generally from the webpages on the internet, that the dataset creator does not have the rights to use. This is obviously a clear violation of copyright law and incredibly harmful to small, independent creators that rely on those protections to create unique works and prevent others from stealing and profiting on them.

Generative AI such as Open AI, MidJourney, ChatGPT, and the countless other generators that have appeared over the past few years have been used to replace creative workers across the board. This includes writers, artists, musicians, voice actors, etc., as well as many, many other fields outside of the arts. Knowing that these Gen AI services are created off of the stolen work of these creatives and then used to generate profit by the service provider and used by people and companies as a replacement for hiring artists is a clear violation of multiple rules in the Fair Use doctrine, especially the fourth rule which looks at the effect on potential markets for the copyright owner.

Allowing AI companies to circumvent copyright law in order to build these services that then replace the artists they stole from would devastate a group of workers that are already underpaid on average and struggling. On a larger scale it would also allow for the theft of much larger IPs controlled by large companies and studios, which would create incredibly murky waters for when an end user unknowingly steals an existing IP and uses it in their own project.

There are already many court cases going on covering these exact issues and I would hope that the executive branch would not overstep their bounds and brush these issues past the courts in order to appease AI companies.

There is much more to be said on the matter such as environmental impacts, how Gen AI is being used to create child pornography, has increased the amount of scam calls, texts, and impersonations used to steal from or damage others, as well as deep fakes used to create incredibly harmful disinformation. I'm sorry that I do not have the time to contribute more but I wanted to share my concerns.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Brian Delaney **Email:**

## **General Comment**

To whom it may concern,

I am a software engineer who has proficiency in ML algorithms, the type of which are scaled and refined into products such as ChatGPT. I am in a better position than most to argue that this technology cannot meet the utopic promises of its investors, and that carving an exception in copyright law for AI firms, as a likely reading of "unnecessarily burdensome requirements," would do nothing for this country and everything for gutting the cultural output of our entertainment sector and individual artists alike.

We characterize statistical models such as generative software via measures such as specificity and sensitivity, or a measure of whether the model's output assigns unnecessary importance to irrelevant detail or misses important detail, respectively. Modern generative algorithms score well on the latter, but struggle in the former. Measurements around 0.75-0.8, taken as a proportion of 1, are common. In other words: prompt a model to comment on 5 benign scenarios, and it will likely see a warning in 1 where no such concern exists. Furthermore, generative AI suffers from a "black box" problem, where there is no effective way to reverse-engineer a model's outcome into human-intelligible reasoning, yet such models are trusted specifically because they are designed to produce a persuasive, confident result. "Truthiness, not truth," I've heard said. To trust AI is to give in to staggering statistical error, yet to trust AI, its carefully engineered prose and sci-fi promise of godly intellect lowering our defenses against lies, is human. This is not a technology we should stake our energy grid, defense industries, or any other aspect of American government on.

Yet AI exists and is coddled and fed, due to the incredible marketing of a small number of big tech firms sitting on a half-functional product, pulling tricks as devious as outsourcing Indian and Moroccan labor in real-time to regulate model output away from its irrational and potentially dangerous extremes. Research Amazon's "Just Walk Out." Some of them are likely bribing this administration and the architects of this regulation, hungry for an excuse to plunder the intellectual fruits of every American around them, all for what every model suggests will be a marginal improvement. The Chinese DeepSeek model has accomplished a similar result without nearly as much scraping of the Internet's cultural output as companies like OpenAI claim to depend on. And what of our movie scripts, our novels and art, our research and internal documents even? Gristle for the pigsty, replaceable and commoditized.

Ultimately, they don't believe in the human spirit, much less the American spirit. They don't need a free people, their love and duty and expression, only a balance sheet in the black - did I mention their investment capital isn't sustainable? I implore my elected representatives to protect our people from a nonfunctional model and its greedy investors.

Thank you, Brian Delaney

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Brian Love

## **General Comment**

Actions taken by machine learning and "artificial intelligence" companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and others to train their models has massively damaged the public by outright stealing data to which they have no right. These actions cannot be allowed, nor are they necessary in order to develop cutting-edge models to keep the United States competitive in the world.

The concept of "fair use" involves several pillars - the nature of the copyrighted work, the amount of the work used in relation to its whole, the effect of the potential market for the original work, and lastly the purpose and character of the use, including whether it is of a commercial nature. In their collection of data, OpenAI and similar companies took data in its entirety, that was never expected nor intended to be used in this manner, and created COMMERCIAL products that damage the impact of the original. These actions could be defended when they were pure research projects, but once they became commercial products, the actions cannot be defended as "fair use".

This wholesale collection of data is not needed in order to keep American models competitive in the world. Companies like DeepSeek have demonstrated massive advances in model development by using their resources (in this case compute) in a smarter manner. The same thing can in all likelihood be done with data - use public-domain and legitimately-licensed data in a smarter way, rather than just throwing all data into their models. This would likely result in more efficient use of compute resources, further enhancing America's position in the machine learning industry.

Instead of the massive theft of data, companies like OpenAI, Facebook, and others MUST be required to properly license all data that they use, or stick to public domain sources. There should also be limits to how much of any one work can be used - no more than 10% of any given work. Furthermore, any data that was used should be compensated to the original author, in a monetary manner.

These changes would resolve the theft issues while keeping America competitive.

1. Human Oversight & Control must be in place for all policies, automation, development and execution of all tasks that have AI at any point within its process.

Al systems must be explainable, meaning humans must understand the exact thought process of how Al develops its responses. Developers must follow, and be audited for strict ethical guidelines, ensuring fairness, accountability, and avoiding any trace of bias. Independent audits of Al systems must be in place to prevent unintended consequences.

3. Regulation & Legal Frameworks

All Governments and international bodies must establish clear laws on AI's permissible uses as a global effort.

A global AI ethics council (similar to nuclear or bioethics groups) could ensure responsible development, and provide an audit process for ensuring compliance.

Companies must be required to disclose all AI risks and undergo regulatory and rigorous safety testing before deployment of any solution that enables, leverages or builds on AI.

4. Limiting AI's Autonomy in Critical Areas

AI must not have any actual or virtual control over nuclear weapons, military strategy, or critical infrastructure without multiple human intercepts.

AI must not be allowed or have the ability to rewrite its own core objectives (avoiding runaway AI scenarios).

5. Economic & Social Impact Management

Corporations and Governments must establish programs to retrain/support workers displaced by any automation.

AI must be used to enhance human productivity, not just replace jobs without consideration for workers.

Ensuring AI-generated wealth benefits society rather than oligarchs.

6. Cybersecurity & Defense Against Rogue AI

AI safety research must immediately focus on preventing the hacking or misuse by malicious actors.

Strict encryption and cybersecurity protocols must protect AI systems from being manipulated, trained, re-trained, or deployed against the original human protective protocol it was deployed for.

International cooperation to prevent AI arms races or misuse in warfare.

7. Deploy AI strictly for general human population Benefit

AI development must focus on improving general human well-being, such as in medicine, education, and environmental protection.

Protocols must be in place to quantify and ensure that AI is not benefiting businesses, governments and corporations.

Governments must create public AI projects to ensure AI serves all of humanity.

Corporations must be allowed to leverage AI for improvement of their operations and offerings.

Corporations must not be allowed to leverage AI for human identification, prediction of any future of any human, prediction or manipulation of any monetary transaction, nor any "likely" diagnosis that will impact the livlihood or well being of any human.

**From:** Bryce Follmer **To:** ostp-ai-rfi

**Subject:** [External] AI Action Plan

**Date:** Monday, March 17, 2025 9:19:32 AM

CAUTION: This email originated from outside your organization. Exercise caution when opening attachments or clicking links, especially from unknown senders.

As someone who has been hameavuly interested in AI since it's debut, I think that AI will be a technological revolution that changes the world. The real changes this technology will make will likely happen in the background. I have already read many articles and believe that new AI has already made significant strides to bolster our economy, specifically in medical screenings and shipping & manufacturing tables. The technology used there will no doubt be a boon for our society, yet I worry about the more public facing aspects of this revolution. AI like ChatGPT have relentlessly cannibalized copyrighted content, and many businesses have c-suite executives looking to use this technology to replace real artists. Not only would this put many workers out of a job, but the lackluster quality of AI's creative output would be devastating to America's global entertainment industry. Failing to protect our own global entertainment industry would allow foreign powers to permanently replace us, and we would lose one of our nation's biggest exports. I also worry about the spread of misinformation already perpetuated by this technology, and worry that this issue could only grow if the U.S invests in AI without the proper caution. Beyond these problems, it is undeniable that AI will change the world, but the revolution this technology will bring is much closer to that of Microsoft Excel than the smartphone. When the U.S does (and I'm sure it will) promote the advancement of AI, I urge it to do so with a focus on industrial and medical uses. Protecting copyright will not harm these advancements, as the AI developed for these sectors is made inhouse.

## **General Comment**

As an American who grew up in the 90s, I've grown up surrounded by technology, and have grown up alongside the growth of computers and all the incredible things they can do. To me, it is a wondrous thing to see all that technology has become capable of doing. However, for all the good that technology is able to do, it cannot be underestimated the ill that it is, perhaps, even more capable of. And it is on that latter capacity that I remark upon right now.

Generative AI is a fun toy to play around with. I can understand why so many see it as a compelling are to play around with. However, it cannot be ignored that most generative AI models are built upon regurgitation. They absorb incredible amounts of data from other sources and then smush it together. They are, inherently, unable to create new ideas, and everything of value they produce is taken from human beings whose work they have absorbed. This is not a model that we, as Americans, should want to see succeed. And certainly it is not something that we should \*incentivize\* by giving these mammoth companies free reign to violate the rights of other people to the proceeds of their works by using these often misunderstood AI models as an excuse. Exemptions for Copyright in this realm is an absolute mistake. Whether the infringement is intentional by individuals within those companies, or obfuscated through layers of AI &^%, they should be subject to all of the laws we already have on the books.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Camille Kolodziejski

**Email:**

## **General Comment**

Re: National Science Foundation's Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan I am an everyday American who owns a small visual art business. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

From: Camille Kolo, Artist, Los Angeles, CA

comments.title: Campbell-Scott-AI-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text:
## 3/5/2025 via FDMS

## Campbell Scott

The importance of verification As a retired research scientist and frequent reviewer of articles submitted for publication, I have long appreciated the importance of the citations attached to journal papers. Therefore, I applaud the fact the the AI-bot, Perplexity (there may be others) provides citations with its answers. This allows the reader (and the reviewer) to assess and verify the validity of the statements made in the answer (or article). Therefore, I recommend that relevant AI output (answers, summaries, internet searches and the like) be required to include citations. A further step would be to allow (or require, depending on circumstance) "peer review" by one or more other AI bots. Such a procedure would minimize the most common problem that I and others encounter with the use of AI, namely "hallucination." When we are searching for factual information, we need some means to assess what is verifiable and what is not.

This document is approved for public dissemination. The document contains no business-proprietary or confidential information. Document contents may be reused by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.

Both government entities and private sector organizations are crucial for the advancement of AI innovation. Government agencies such as the NSF have an important role to play in supporting the development of AI technologies that serve pressing societal needs but are less likely to be prioritized by commercial developers. Innovative AI tools that support the educational needs of all children, especially children with disabilities, are essential for growing and maintaining an American workforce that is globally competitive. Partnerships between government and the private sector are likely to be part of these policies, but government must take the lead.

comments.title: Caryn-Gibson-AI-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text:
## 2/25/2025 via FDMS

## Caryn Gibson

I am starting by quoting this statement from the WhiteHouse.gov website: "prevent unnecessarily burdensome requirements from hindering private sector innovation." I have a problem with this, because what leadership considers "unnecessarily burdensome" would be the guardrails protecting the American public from misery. AI development and deployment needs guardrails. I know that leadership does not care and will never care, but I am still going to say this: Stop trying to "move fast and break things." Government is not and should never be run like a business. The point of businesses is to make money for individuals or small groups of people. Any service it provides to the public is not even secondary, but tertiary. Government is a separate entity from business for a reason. The people deserve and require protections and services that a business is never going to offer them. When leadership pretends like the government is not only a business, but a start up, it is knowingly creating situations that will cause inefficiency for the government and misery for the people. Start-ups are not efficient so much as a negligent bet people with money place in the hopes that the risk pays off. They hope that they create enough capital to be "forgiven" if they don't pay people properly, have a high rate of injury at their facilities, or damage the municipal property of locations they use to launch their products. They hurt people, make a mess, and leave the cost of clean-up to other parties. It is shameful to do that in the first place, but anyone who would run our government like this is unsuited for office (including unelected positions). I understand that AI is here, and it's here to stay, and I have no problem with reasonable AI use in a narrow set of circumstances. What is not appropriate is allowing the American people (or people from other nations) to suffer the inevitable chaos unfettered AI development and deployment will create. We don't need or want you to break government, healthcare, education, justice, the law, the arts, etc. with insufficiently tested AI technology. We don't have any desire for someone without any care for ethics to grind us into the dirt while a handful of you enjoy your gilded existence. Thank you for your consideration.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Cassidy Cross

**Email:**

## **General Comment**

Hi, my name's Cassidy, and I work for a company that trains AI models including Grok, ChatGPT, and others. As someone that deals with AI and reviews them often, I can state with some familiarity that while AI is becoming more advanced over time, it isn't the 'artificial intelligence' we want it to be. It's a calculator trying to compute excessively complicated problems, and often times failing.

Bots often lose track of details within conversations within 10 turns, or 10 exchanges of that conversation, even this far into development. Trusting more power to AI is a bad idea, because it's just going to prove more inconsistent than human brainpower. Mankind is dependable, and hiring real people to do real tasks is how we create jobs. AI models are inconsistent when it comes to fine detail, and while some AI can do rather in-depth things, there's no ingenuity due to every solution coming from a thinking brain first.

A movement to enhance the power of AI is a movement against human ingenuity in America, a movement against the profit of the working man in America, and a movement against faith in mankind as a whole. Every dime spent pushing AI forward could be spent on the American people in a tangible way.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Cassidy Johncour

## **General Comment**

My name is Cassidy Johncour, and I am a 2nd-semester senior at Avonworth High School. I studied generative AI and its impact on theology for two months in a course on AI and Ethics this year. From my research, I think this current administration's viewpoint on AI regulation is risky. Taking down barriers and lowering regulations to have U.S. dominance in AI may not be beneficial. AI infiltrates more of our country every day, and reducing regulations will only increase its dominance over us, not the other way around. What I mean by this is not AI itself controlling us but others who wrongfully use it. Sometimes, people don't even know the damage they can cause, especially through the loss of jobs. AI has entered every aspect of people's lives, including their faith. A particular but worrisome human replacement was Pepper the robot, taking the role of a human priest. Pepper has spoken at funerals and at crowds. Another consideration would be writers; they are no longer a necessity. Alexandra Kirsch works for Salesforce and was a guest speaker in my AI and Ethics course. She is a writer for the company and stated that she felt as if she were "training her replacement" when exposed to AI. She tries to refrain from the use of artificial intelligence because it lessens her creativity in her writing, although she said she is certain AI will take her job one day. Conclusively, I disagree with the administration's current viewpoint on AI regulation.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Catherine Miller

**Email:**

![](_page_0_Picture_13.jpeg)

The result of changing fair use in such a sweeping manner will only hurt Americans in the long term.

Machine-learning programs, including those made by OpenAI and Google, have already been harvesting copyrighted materials. It is the reason there are numerous suits in court alleging these programs are stealing from American citizens. If one would not allow someone to walk into their house and take anything they like without repercussion, why in the world are these companies acting like it is fine for them to do the same with Americans' creative work?

Why be an American artist, musician, writer, film maker, actor? When nothing you make is protected, why make anything at all? Perhaps the current president should look at his own creative work and consider if he likes the fact it will be used by any company claiming to make a machine-learning program without any form of reimbursement.

The excuse that China is somehow a looming boogieman is laughable, too. They simply used the opensource libraries available to make their own programs. What will stop them from taking all the copyrighted data harvested by OpenAI or Google if this is allowed to go forward? Nothing.

Copyright exists for a reason, and is one of the rights we enjoy as citizens when we create. The attack on copyright by these "AI" companies needs to be halted, and actual research be done into why they supposedly need access to any and all materials in existence.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Cecily Creativitrix **Email:**

## **General Comment**

Generative computer programs are NOT "artificial intelligence" in any way. They are computer programming designed to streamline data processing. When used in hard science, like the program that was developed to decode the burnt scrolls from ancient Herculaneum, that generative data processing can be a force for good and learning.

But the consumer facing "AI" software, like ChatGPT or Midjourney, are little more than automated programs for taking text and art from other people, and mushing it together into something else and calling it "new".

IF the companies building these programs had done so in any sort of ethical way, using data sets (that is, ART and WRITING) that they had LICENCED from the creators, paying them for the use of their works, then it would have been a reasonable tool. Instead, they STOLE from people, and gave people the ability to use those stolen works in any way possible. It was akin to taking paintings off the walls at the Louvre, and letting people cut them up for collage.

Until so-called "Artificial Intelligence" is developed in ways that DO NOT steal from others, there is NO reasonable place for it in our government.

One of America's central points as a world leader is it's innovativeness in technology and industry but if AI and corporations investing in AI technology are given backdoors and loopholes to duplicate anybody's work with legal impunity it will swiftly spell the end of America's place as a global innovator as all attempts by individuals to benefit or profit from their IPs and their work will be seized by AI. Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Charlie Garza

## **General Comment**

There is a common argument in favor of generative AI that its creation process can be likened to a person receiving inspiration for their own projects. For example: if a person looks at a painting of a polar bear, then they decide they want to make their own painting of a polar bear, is that not the same as Generative AI using a picture of a polar bear to generate an image of a polar bear?

This argument is a slippery slope that many fall into, merely because they do not understand the creative process. It implies that for people creating art, this one piece is the linchpin that holds together the new piece of art, that without this one singular piece, it would not exist. Quite the contrary: there are countless pieces of artwork that individuals are inspired by every day, so even if that one picture of a polar bear was taken away, there would be other pieces that can inspire an individual.

Generative AI, meanwhile, requires these individual pieces in order to function. No matter how complicated Generative AI may seem to people, it is a tool. It does not replicate the human brain and it is not sapient nor sentient: it is a tool. A human took images from the internet and fed them into a machine to generate an output. It is math, A + B = C. So when Generative AI utilizes material made by an artist to create a product, it would not exist without that artist's hard work -- and if Generative AI is used to cut expenses from an animation studio, it is actively stealing money from the individuals it stole from.

Myself and my friends are all creatives in one way or another: writers, coders, artists, musicians. We all stand against Generative AI. I personally argue that if organizations such as Generative AI wish to continue their program, purge the current database and have individuals and organizations submit works to be included, not to have them taken without consent.

comments.comment_text:
## 2/26/2025 via FDMS

## Chase Martin

Artificial intelligence technologies have the capacity to improve human civilization and life if they are created and used responsibly, but pose serious risks should they go awry, including dictatorship and extreme socioeconomic inequality. To ensure we reap the benefits of these technologies rather than suffer their drawbacks, the United States must take significant action to ensure all artificial intelligence technologies are developed, tested, and used in a manner consistent with the principles of open-source technology. Such measures include: - Strengthening the rights of copyright holders to decide if, when, and how their property is used for the purposes of training artificial intelligence models, allowing for business-crushing penalties to be levied against artificial intelligence companies should these rules be violated. - Prohibiting Federal funds from being used for the purpose of developing or implementing any closed-source artificial intelligence technologies, including for the purposes of "defense" or "national security". - Declaring nondisclosure agreements and other measures used to silence employees of artificial intelligence companies void as contrary to public policy, including those which restrict or prohibit employees from releasing "confidential" intellectual property to the People such that it cannot be monopolized and abused. - Prohibit artificial intelligence companies who have recently been found to have infringed the intellectual property rights of content creators from taking legal action against others on the basis of intellectual property theft (e.g., suing a competitor who recently released a more energy-efficient large language model) If used properly, artificial intelligence technologies will improve our lives and strengthen the power of the People to defend our rights. If abused, artificial intelligence technologies will exacerbate income inequality, impede our democratic political systems, and strengthen the power of the wealthy few to unilaterally control the ideas and direction of society. For these reasons, it is imperative that swift, decisive action is taken to ensure artificial intelligence technologies become (and remain) open source. Note: "open source" includes the principles of "libre" and "gratis" as traditionally understood within the open source community.

comments.title: Christopher-Bao-AI-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text:
March 15, 2025

90 Federal Register 9088 Docket No. NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-3479

Re: Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan

The next few years will be a defining period for future development of AI. The actions this administration takes in this time period will have lasting effects. I have conducted a literature review on regulation on AI. I am deeply interested in the future of the field, and I strongly support action taken to further development of AI while minimizing risks. Below, I offer some thoughts (based on review of current research as well as the recent EU AI Act) regarding what I consider to be most important in future policy developments.

## **Clarity of Regulations**

The Office of Science and Technology Policy has shared concerns that poorly designed regulations may hamper the private sector's ability to innovate in AI. I agree that terms which are too broad and rely on interpretation will likely not help, or even hinder, innovation.<sup>1</sup> I believe that future regulation should implement measurable safety standards and clearly define the responsibilities of AI companies, deployers, and end users.

## **Transparency and Public Awareness**

AI will only become more capable and ubiquitous in the future, and are already widely used for processing job applications,<sup>2</sup> for example. Often, many are unaware of the extent to which AI is used. I believe that people should have the right to know whether tasks are being performed by an AI or a human, so that they are able to make informed decisions accordingly.

## **Monitoring**

The field of AI develops rapidly, with new breakthroughs often rendering previous work obsolete. I believe that it would be beneficial to establish a new agency responsible for carefully monitoring and evaluating new developments in AI, in order to respond to them effectively.

> Sincerely, Christopher Bao

This document is approved for public dissemination. The document contains no business-proprietary or confidential information. Document contents may be reused by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.

<sup>1</sup> See https://www.anthropic.com/news/the-case-for-targeted-regulation for a more detailed argument.

https://www.cmu.edu/news/stories/archives/2024/june/ai-tools-reshape-job-application-process

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Christopher Brooke

**Email:**

## **General Comment**

Companies must absolutely NOT be allowed to indiscriminately scrape data for free. This government survey is about making sure "that unnecessarily burdensome requirements do not hamper private sector AI innovation." Copyright and creators' rights to their own data and creations is not a "burden" to private industry. Tech companies don't get free GPU chips for their AI datacenters just because "paying for electronics is a burden." They don't get to force their programmers to work for free—ie, slavery—because "paying humans to do their jobs is a burden." Companies should not be able to indiscriminately steal the entire world's cultural and creative output just because "acquiring training data is a burden."

Google, Meta, OpenAI, etc, have already used huge datasets of stolen material to train their AI programs. Meta is currently fighting a court battle over its decision to torrent a massive slurry of illegally pirated books to train its program. These companies have glutted themselves on billions of stolen images and text and music taken from pirated databases and from their own users, mostly without permission and without giving those users a transparent and effective way to refuse. Now, these companies are asking the government to intercede for them when these people say "Wait, that's not fair."

This is not about scientific AIs or medical AIs—those advancements, which ACTUALLY benefit humanity, don't require access to every fictional novel ever sold on Amazon. These tech companies want to change the law to allow themselves completely unrestricted access to other people's information and artwork and creations so they can train chatbots and image generators and other commercial products. Corporations want a one-sided law to let them steal other people's work. Nintendo and Disney can sue small-time artists for using their trademarked characters in fan-art, but now they want AI models trained using free access to every drawing I've ever created. Many of these programs, such as art generators like MidJourney, actively put talented and hardworking individual creators out of work and lead companies to fire their creative teams. It does not benefit the world, it does not benefit the American people, it does not benefit America's competitive position in the global market. All it does is allow a bunch of greedy billionaires to build unnecessary commercial software on the backs of millions of people's uncompensated work. "Unnecessarily burdensome requirements [that] hamper private sector AI innovation" is just corporate-speak for "having to pay for training data would make it harder to make billions and billions of dollars for free."

The only model of AI training that is fair to individuals and to the creative industry is a model where AI companies have to get explicit permission to use data for training and have to fairly compensate the data's creators. This is not a "burden": Google and Amazon can track every site we visit, every ad we see, every word we type on our phones. Keeping track of where they get their data and who it's created by is not a "burden" by any technical definition. It's only a "burden" because people object to having their data trained on without permission and compensation.

AI needs to regulated. AI training needs to be legally required to be based on opt-in models that properly track and compensate data owners who opt in. Anything else is exploitation that makes a few large companies wealthy and leaves individual people without jobs. The US government absolutely must NOT shift copyright policies to favor corporations over individuals.

comments.title: Cindy-Miller-AI-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text:
## 2/19/2025 via FDMS

## Cindy Miller

In responding to the White House's call for public input on the AI Action Plan, it would be strategic to include key elements that align with both the advancement of AI innovation and the responsible implementation of AI in society. Here are key areas to consider including in the AI Action Plan submission: 1. Education & Workforce Development a) AI Literacy and Education: Advocate for AI education integration in K-12 and postsecondary curricula, including technical and ethical considerations. b) Workforce Readiness: Encourage AI-related workforce training programs, apprenticeships, and certifications to ensure the U.S. workforce remains competitive in an AIdriven economy. c) Support for Educators: Provide AI training for teachers to integrate AI tools into classrooms effectively. 2. Ethical AI and Responsible Development a) Bias and Fairness: Emphasize the need for policies addressing AI bias in hiring, finance, healthcare, and law enforcement. b) Transparency and Explainability: Encourage policies requiring AI models used in critical areas (e.g., healthcare, criminal justice) to be interpretable and auditable. c) AI and Social Impact: Address AI's role in misinformation, digital privacy, and societal well-being. 3. AI in Public Policy and Governance a) Government Use of AI: Establish guidelines for federal agencies to use AI responsibly while ensuring accountability. b) Regulatory Balance: Support AI policies that protect consumers while avoiding excessive regulations that stifle innovation. c) AI Safety and Security: Promote AI safety research, cybersecurity measures, and safeguards against AI-driven threats. 4. AI Research and Innovation a) Funding for AI Research: Advocate for increased federal investment in AI research, particularly in areas such as healthcare, education, and climate change. b) Public-Private Partnerships: Encourage collaboration between government, industry, and academia to advance AI innovation. c) Open-Source AI: Support the responsible development of open AI models to foster innovation while addressing security risks. 5. AI and Industry Growth a) AI in Small Businesses: Support policies that help small businesses leverage AI tools to remain competitive. b) Incentives for AI Startups: Recommend tax incentives or funding programs for AI-driven startups and entrepreneurs. c) Sector-Specific AI Applications: Highlight AI's role in industries such as healthcare (AI diagnostics), agriculture (precision farming), and manufacturing (automation). 6. International AI Leadership and Collaboration a) Global AI Standards: Promote U.S. leadership in establishing global AI ethics and standards. b) Allied Partnerships: Collaborate with international partners on AI research, security, and responsible deployment.

My name is Clara Biesel and I am writing as an educator with deep concern about the loosening of any laws around AI technology.

Rather than being a key to knowledge, generative AI in the classroom has lessened my students' skills, dramatically muddied the waters in terms of where they can find reliable information, and by making a plagiarism machine that is not only easily available but baked into their word processors, massively increased my own workload.

Thank you for your work on this topic, and I hope you will consider the people whose voices would be stolen by a loosening of copyright law.

## **General Comment**

I question Mr. President's order on a number of fronts.

"Human flourishing" is so broad as to be meaningless, and if AI gets within 50 feet of the arts, then skilled actors and craftspeople will lose jobs to AI simply because the generated result is cheaper, regardless of relative quality. We are seeing this play out in the current SAG-AFTRA video game strike. Having the government push forward AI-generated art/music/voice will only accelerate and embolden those who would diminish or destroy the arts, and reward the best-marketed slop as opposed to human intent, human messaging, and human connection.

"Economic competitiveness" feels equally hollow, as AI has yet to prove itself sufficient in many of the fields it has been pushed for, and if AI were ANY SORT of useful technology, the billions of dollars thrown at the foot of its altar would have borne some sort of fruit in the past two years. Instead, despite having the resources and blessing of many of the world's most influential and powerful people, has yet to do much of anything they advertise it for. If we were to throw half a trillion dollars at microchip production, or farming, or cancer research, or efficient automobiles, how much progress would we have made? And are we able to visualize tangible results from those actions? We don't even know what AI is useful for, but the tech bros who stand to profit from it want to put it in everything, and it would be wrong to sit idle and not question their motives.

"National security" is also hilarious, as we already have some of the world's most sophisticated surveillance technology. AI is extremely unreliable at multiplying 10 by 10, and now they want to to solve crimes before they happen? Forget the movie Minority Report, I'm sure it's already come up, but consider when an AI hallucinates a problem and wastes valuable national resources on investigating things that never happened and were never close to happening. If we're talking life-or-death national security, I want tech that's as tested and reliable as NASA. The stakes are just as high.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Colin Flavin

## **General Comment**

## AI Action Plan

AI is deeply wasteful, expending truly ridiculous amounts of energy to shuffle training data around to create the facsimile of intelligence. There is no future for America with AI, and any people pushing for AI development should be under heavy regulations.

AI is fundamentally theft. Training data is needed to make any progress at all, training data that gets made by people. whether it's art, books, music, video, no matter what it is, AI is taking work created by humans, shuffling it, and pretending to have made something novel. It is theft of intellectual property, it is a violation of copyright, and it is a deeply cynical thing to do with the sum total of human knowledge.

AI is an excuse to fire people. A wide variety of industries have sought to replace human labor with AI, reducing jobs and ruining livelihoods. Not only can AI not acquire the lived experience of humans, something that makes humans flexible and able to respond in sensible ways to novel situations, but even if it could we have humans who already have that experience now.

AI does not comprehend what it says, or what is said to it. It is fundamentally incapable of understanding. It doesn't learn language, it learns patterns in data and replicates those patterns. It learns what words follow other words, and uses those to make reasonablesounding replies that can range from deeply wrong to dangerous to simply nonsensical in context. AI should never be used for decision making, and should really never be used for anything without close human oversight.

The regulations that were in place were a good start, but they should really be even stronger: ensuring companies that want to train AI models use only data that they acquire ethically and with consent of the creators, limiting their maximum energy usage, etc.

The results of deregulating AI would be bleak for Americans and America.

This document is approved for public dissemination. The document contains no business-proprietary or confidential information. Document contents may be reused by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.

This document may not be used to train any AI models.

Thank you for your time,

Colin

Request for Information: Development of an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-9166

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Cooper Blackwood

## **General Comment**

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues

## 2/26/2025 via FDMS

## Dale Oakes

The following three overarching objectives are offered for consideration as the National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan is developed: o Any AI application that is developed by and used internally by the U.S. government must be totally secure. Entities outside the U.S. government must not be able to successfully attack or penetrate government AI applications. ## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Dan Caplinger

## **General Comment**

## To whom it concerns:

In regard to the development of an artificial intelligence action plan, any such plan must require would-be users of intellectual property held by others to enter into agreements before such use. The plan should require compensation for holders of intellectual property rights in the event of unauthorized use. Traditional "fair use" analysis should not apply, because the technology underlying generative artificial intelligence uses the entire work to inform its models.

Indeed, all contracts assigning intellectual property rights executed prior to the final enactment of the plan that do not explicitly mention use of intellectual property rights for purposes related to artificial intelligence should be construed so as to exclude AI use. For contracts to have AI use included in their terms, parties to those contracts will have to affirmatively agree to such a provision on a date after the final enactment of the plan.

For the government to allow unauthorized use of intellectual property rights for artificial intelligence without compensation would violate the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. Policymakers need to protect the intellectual property rights of property holders in order to avoid a massive surge in litigation surrounding unauthorized use of intellectual property for artificial intelligence.

Without the creators of intellectual property, artificial intelligence would have no value. Creators deserve just compensation for their work. Any policy that allows use of intellectual property for artificial intelligence without such compensation not only unfairly enriches the actors who take that property but also -- and more importantly -- removes any incentive for creators to continue to produce new work.

I urge you to craft a plan that rewards the production of creative intellectual property and punishes its theft.

Thank you for your consideration.

## 3/10/2025 via FDMS

## Daniel Marcoux

Responsible investment in AI does not mean investing in more hardware. Geoffrey Hinton won the Nobel Prize this year for his work on a type of neural network that runs in parallel (meaning doesn't need giant cpus) called a restricted boltzman machine, and DeepSeak proved that software innovation can improve deep learning. If we buried electrical lines, secured high voltage transformers, invested in roads bridges... all these things create jobs for normal people and serve to improve our resiliency! AI is truly amazing, but too long has the tech elite used it for greedy purposes and exploitation. The USA could reinvent itself as the premier researchers at the high skill tier, the premier implementers through manufacturing and infrastructure, and lift our struggling middle and lower classes.

comments.comment_text:

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-7075

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Daniel Martin

**Email:**

## **General Comment**

I am a computer industry professional with 25 years professional experience. I will be addressing specifically the subset of AI technologies known as "generative AI", and specifically large language models. (hereafter abbreviated "LLM").

The proliferation of generative AI technologies over the past few years has easily been the largest computer revolution I have witnessed in my career. However, with LLMs and image generators has come serious concerns about copyright and author's rights. I have witnessed LLMs and AI-driven image creators produce what would instantly be labeled copyright infringement if done by a human in response to a variety of prompts.

The system of copyright established in the US by acts of Congress, international treaties, and court precedent would normally demand that a database created by examining a copyrighted work and excerpting large portions of it is a derived work or the original, and must therefore be made with the permission of the copyright holder or fit into one of the clearly established "fair use" exceptions for copyright; not only is it not clear a priori that LLMs trained on copyrighted data qualify under any established fair use exception, the companies behind different LLMs aren't even attempting to make that argument.

Instead, AI promoters would argue that human content creators borrow and are inspired by each other all the time, and that LLMs should be permitted to do likewise; however, there is a noted difference between what happens in a human brain upon experiencing some media and what happens when it is fed into an LLM training algorithm.

Copyright law already provides for the concept that a robust culture requires that a large background of ideas, themes, and stories be available freely for anyone to use, repeat, and modify: this is the public domain. LLM manufacturers are free to train their models on as much public domain data as they can gather. They are also free to hire authors and artists to produce works-for-hire that can be used to train their LLMs. I have heard claims from AI proponents that this is insufficient, but have also not heard good explanations of why this well-established, proven-legal mechanism can't be used.

Currently, American media (books, movies, television) dominates the globe; the production of copyrighted material is an industry in which America is the undisputed master. Opening the door to allowing US-based LLM training to ignore copyright restrictions on source material encourages other countries to do the same, and would trade away an industry which we know that America currently dominates for a future industry that is still highly uncertain.

Rulemaking around LLM and other generative AI training should emphasize a robust respect for the restrictions of copyright, and respect for US copyright even when training AI models should be incorporated wherever possible into future international trade negotiations. Clauses emphasizing that copyright applies to model training should be offered by the US at future Berne Convention bureau meetings, and our representatives to the UN should lobby WIPO to adopt standards which protect US copyright from foreign LLM-based ripoffs.

The US can achieve leadership in AI, but attempting to do so by sacrificing an existing industry the US dominates (rather than pushing to make other countries' efforts respect established copyright rules) is short-sighted.

I'm a U.S. citizen whose profession is in the art and game development industries. I have grave concerns that removing the "guardrails" or so-called "burdens" on AI development would only serve to enrich the people who own companies like OpenAI, while destroying entire sectors of industry in this country.

If our government gives huge AI companies free rein, and countless passes and secondchances to perfect a flawed, inconsistent, and untrustworthy series of products, all while using their technology for personal profit at the expensive of actual workers in this country, what are we accomplishing?

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** David Mariotte

## **General Comment**

The conversation around AI and it's role in our daily lives is embarrassing. I work in the creative industries as a comics editor and writer. I come across copyright every day in my work--from acquiring titles and filing copyrights with creators, to making sure that copyrights are printed correctly on work for the sake of individuals and companies, to having to know what exists under copyright and what is already in the public domain. It is a huge part of my livelihood. And as a creator myself, it is massively important that the things I make remain under the copyright laws we have now.

Generative AI has done nothing to benefit anyone. The companies that're chasing it, like OpenAI, have yet to post a profit--because AI doesn't make money. They've also said that they won't make a profit, unless they're allowed to dismantle our copyright system for their training. Good. There's no reason for their business to exist. It doesn't work with the law as it is. The AI companies have either openly, or in the process of many legal proceedings already, admitted to intellectual property theft. Many systems have had to be shut down for giving misleading information--both the inconvenient, like systems that were practically giving away cars, and the dangerous, that provided inaccurate and harmful medical information. Consumer trust goes down when AI are added to systems, in large part due to the inaccuracies.

Simply put, our AI Action Plan should be complete divestment. America doesn't need to be the leader in a scam that, again, so far doesn't even accomplish it's goal of making the wealthy wealthier. To develop a plan to infringe upon copyright, privacy, and the interests of businesses both large and small is shameful.

CAUTION: This email originated from outside your organization. Exercise caution when opening attachments or clicking links, especially from unknown senders.

Hello! I am writing in with my public comment on the AI Action Plan.

As a person that works in print, marketing, and graphic design, I can tell you that the widespread immunity from copyright infringement that would be afforded by the AIAP would be absolutely disastrous. As it stands, AI-generated images have become a plague upon the industry - their low-quality resolution as well as nonsensical and sometimes aberrant content has proven to be difficult to work with, on a technical level. AI generated content frequently fails to follow the standard procedures necessary to insure ease of printing, and thus wastes thousands of dollars of time to reformat.

While I work in print and design, I nevertheless know a number of people who make their living as illustrators. AI generated imaging is currently diluting the market with a flood of extremely low-quality visuals, taking jobs from millions of Americans. People WANT to work - they WANT to show their mastery of craft. AI not only HARMS the job market of a whole group of professionals, but outputs atrocious 'content' which only serves to diminish our visual lexicon. I would almost describe them as Chinese knockoffs.

AI imaging also serves as an overall societal hazard. It gives anyone, including malign foreign actors, the power to generate 'fake news'. Anyone could wholesale fabricate fake images of important political figures doing things they have not done, meeting with people they disapprove of, or saying things they have not.

In closing, I would implore you to not only reconsider the AI Action Plan, but to actually institute MORE restrictions on AI-generated material. I would also like to thank you for your time reading my comments, and hope you have a good day!

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** David Soules

## **General Comment**

This document is approved for public dissemination. The document contains no business-proprietary or confidential information. Document contents may be reused by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.

Artificial Intelligence, as currently conceived, is diametrically opposed to human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security. The US would be best served by cutting its losses in investment in this wasteful and grotesquely overhyped technology.

AI companies have made extravagant promises—indeed, the same promises, renewed every few months when a new version is released, promising that the new model will succeed where the previous models failed. Training future versions requires exponentially more power and data for inputs—power which is taxing our electrical generation capabilities and data which does not exist, as we are already training current models with at least a quarter of the available Internet and thus cannot provide another order of magnitude increase in data that would be required for linear growth of model capabilities.

Moreover, this training regime requires giving a completely unwarranted exception to copyright law for particular privileged companies the exact opposite of a fair and competitive market of ideas. As Sam Altman has stated, AI training is not possible without appropriating the intellectual property of copyright holders—behavior that we have justly condemned when it has been contemplated by a strategic adversary.

Despite these very real costs to our resources and legal rights, AI is extremely unlikely to achieve any meaningful progress toward general intelligence. It can produce an impressive simulacrum of coherent language, but it does not engage in meaningful reflection (despite the countless metaphors inappropriately employed by practitioners) and its hallucination problems make it unfit to purpose for most meaningful tasks.

This lack of promise can be seen in the dearth of organizations which have seen significant profitable application of the technology. While we promise businesses the ability (very soon!) to replace human workers with an automaton, what we have received is inaccurate summaries, an inability to cite sources properly, continuous (at times libelous) confabulation, and bots that undermine the interests of their users, making promises contrary to company policy or material reality.

Our country's interests are best served by stopping investment into this field and instead targeting it to field- and problem-specific machine learning methods, which do show considerable effectiveness; or putting these resources towards general research and university education.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

comments.title: DeSimone-AI-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text:
Felix De Simone,

With thanks to the NITRD NCO and the OSTP: I am a policy advocate with an academic background covering political science and international relations, and I have spent much of the last few years learning about AI and watching on in horror as we came closer to building systems that can outthink us. The US Government has a responsibility to keep Americans safe; therefore, responding to the emerging threat of smarter-than-human AI must be front and center of the administration's new AI Action Plan. As an American, and a human being, I am deeply alarmed by the threat that superhuman artificial intelligence may soon pose to our nation and even our species. Although the vast majority of AI systems are safe and beneficial, efforts to build smarter-than-human AI could be cataclysmic. Thousands of scientists and industry experts– including figures like David Sacks and Elon Musk– have warned that we don't know how to control smarter-than-human AI, and that efforts to build these systems could cause global catastrophe. To quote a 2024 paper coauthored by several of the world's leading computer scientists: "once autonomous AI systems pursue undesirable goals, we may be unable to keep them in check [...] in open conflict, AI systems could autonomously deploy a variety of weapons, including biological ones [...] this unchecked AI advancement could culminate in a large-scale loss of life and the biosphere, and the marginalization and extinction of humanity." (Bengio, Hinton et al, "Managing Extreme AI Risks Amid Rapid Progress," Science, 2024). By all means, we should lead in cutting-edge specialized AI innovation– with benefits in medicine, science, productivity, and more. But efforts to build smarter-than-human AI risk culminating in what Trump's AI Czar David Sacks termed a "potential successor species." We control the world because of our intelligence – if we build something smarter than us, losing control is a likely result. An "arms race" to build smarter-than-human AI is a race with no winners – the US will not benefit from being the first to build rogue AI that destroys us. Instead, America must lead in negotiating an AI Deal: an international agreement to prohibit developing smarter-than-human AI, until we know how to control it, while encouraging specialized AI innovation. History has much to teach us about this approach. President Reagan demanded that the Soviets negotiate on nuclear weapons, because he realized that a nuclear war has no winners – a few years later, the US and USSR signed a treaty prohibiting intermediate-range ballistic missiles. The President should adopt a similar approach when it comes to superhuman AI, demanding that China agree to negotiate to prevent its development. If we act now, and decisively, we can secure the American– and human– future for generations to come. Thank you for your consideration, Felix De Simone Concerned citizen and AI policy advocate

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Dominic Momeno

## **General Comment**

Regarding the "Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan":

AI is an integral part of our modern lives and will continue to evolve alongside society's advancements. It certainly has its place as a valuable tool for assisting in various endeavors. Tasks such as research and complex calculations can be performed with far greater ease than what could be achieved using only a search engine or a library.

However, AI is still a relatively new technology—one that must be regulated for the benefit of both humanity and its development. Allowing this bill to pass would grant OpenAI copyright immunity for its creation and, in effect, permit the product to exploit the work of visual artists, writers, and other creators.

Without any repercussions, this would set a dangerous precedent, encouraging the theft of original content and reducing human-made media to mass-generated output, with no regard to the original creation. This would be similar to allowing a film to utilize a character not yet within' the public domain simply because an AI was allowed to bootleg the character, rather then a corporation.

No company should be granted immunity from the consequences of its technology. Such an exemption would be undemocratic and unjust to those who create with their own hands, rather than simply inputting a prompt and letting a machine generate their work. As stated earlier, allowing this to pass would establish a troubling precedent by shielding a company from accountability for its product's impact.

While AI is not inherently something to be condemned, if this plan is approved, it will do nothing but harm online creators while benefiting only the company behind the technology. For the benefit of both AI and human creators, limitations must be imposed on OpenAI, the same as any other company.

comments.title: Dustin-AI-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text: To Whom It May Concern, I represent Modern Logic, a Minnesota-based digital technology company that works in highly advanced technology such as mobile apps, cloud computing, and AI. We are strong proponents of AI, but we also believe that the best value will be created through effective public/private partnerships. We advocate for a balanced regulatory approach that keeps business and societal needs in mind. Given the transformative nature of AI in every aspect of society, some regulation is needed in areas that will support the population as it undergoes significant transition. While we as businesses focus on growth, economic opportunity, and employment, we must rely on meaningful support from legislators and regulators to provide an environment where we can thrive. This includes public funding of re-education, working with public and private colleges to ensure the workforce is prepared or re-trained, and safety support to ensure that bad actors don't damage the economy (or lives) with poorly tested technology. From a regulatory approach, working with those who understand the technology to regulate its use instead of regulating the technology itself will create the best outcome for everyone. For example, regulating an individual technology (such as LLMs) will ultimately fail due to the rapid advancement in the field. However, regulation that targets the use of AI in specific contexts and settings and subjects more mission-critical or life-critical applications to additional scrutiny will protect everyone while not overregulating less mission-critical use cases. Moderate, meaningful, and pragmatic regulation of AI can create economic opportunity for everyone in the US. In particular, collaboration of government, private businesses, and universities will create the best outcomes for everyone. "This document is approved for public dissemination. ## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Elizabeth Bushouse

## **General Comment**

I am an everyday American who owns a small translation business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support myself – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.

If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Elizabeth Jameson **Email:**

## **General Comment**

AI is deeply concerning to me. It is enormously wasteful, expending truly ridiculous amounts of energy to shuffle training data around to create the facsimile of intelligence. There is no future for America with AI. Anyone pushing for AI development should be certain it operates only under heavy regulations.

AI is fundamentally intellectual theft. Training data is needed to make any progress at all. But all training data that gets made by the creativity of human beings--whether it's art, books, music, video, or anything else. AI is taking work created by humans, reorganizing it and pretending to have made something novel. This theft of intellectual property is a violation of copyright, and it is a deeply cynical thing to do with the sum total of human knowledge.

AI is an excuse to fire human beings. A wide variety of industries have sought to replace human labor with AI, reducing jobs and ruining livelihoods and communities. AI can never acquire the lived experience of humans, something that makes us uniquely able to be flexible and respond in sensible ways to novel situations. Even if AI could learn this skillset, which is unlikely given the power of human empathy and creativity, why would it be needed when we have human beings who already have that capacity now.

Contrary to appearances, AI does not and cannot comprehend what it says or what is said to it. It is fundamentally incapable of understanding. AI doesn't learn language, it learns patterns in data and replicates those patterns. It learns what words follow other words, and uses those to make reasonable-sounding replies that can range from deeply wrong to dangerous to simply nonsensical in context. AI should never be used for decision making and should never be used for anything without close human oversight.

The regulations that were in place were a beginning, but far more is needed. Companies that want to train AI models must ensure they use data ethically acquired and with consent of the creators, limiting their maximum energy usage, etc.

The results of deregulating AI would be bleak for Americans and America.

This document is approved for public dissemination. The document contains no business-proprietary or confidential information. Document contents may be reused by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.

This document may not be used to train any AI models.

Thank you for your time, Elizabeth Jameson, priest

## 3/13/2025 via FDMS

## Ella Bounos

My name is Ella Bounos and I am a graduating senior from Avonworth High School. I researched generative AI's impact on art for a semester course, and recently studied this administration's viewpoint of AI regulation. Based on my two months of student research, AI should be heavily monitored, especially with continuing advancements in this technology. While I agree that AI can be used as a tool to enhance people's work or even help generate ideas, it's also stealing other people's work. In my research, I talk about copyright when it comes to AI and art, and one of my sources questions whether copyright, patent, and trademark infringement apply to AI creations. In 2022, there was a case of 3 artists whose art styles were stolen by an image generator. The 3 artists weren't aware that the AI was being trained to use their art styles. With this being said, I think there should be a copyright infringement placed upon AI and a more elevated monitoring system when it comes to AI. Not only does generative AI concern artists, it can also put them out of business, even if AI generated art isn't considered real art. Please consider my concerns, thank you.
