Why is human-made art important and why should it be recognized as such? I'm a graphic artist, I work making art for a company and other small organizations on the side. I have developed an eye over years of work that no computer can replicate and few humans will notice unless I make an error. My work allows for ease of comprehension of complex topics, it processes them in my brain and translates them visually into a comprehensible form. An AI does not have the discretion to be aware of what baggage it was programmed with and will spit out uncritical images that can warp meaning. I can get deeper into the philosophy of this but that about sums it up.

But if you care more for the meat and potatoes: this is my career and I love doing it. I love working with small orgs for under what I would usually charge because I can make ends meet with my day job. If AI undercuts that and floods the market, people will notice something is off and feels artificial, they won't like it, but they won't necessarily know why. Art and design is made WITH humans in mind, AI does not care. But profit motives will push people to use it more and it will negatively affect my working relationships as I work slower than an AI (even if my product is better). I want to continue working to make people's visual lives richer. AI slop is slop, but it's cheap slop. Let's put funding into real live human artists instead of more anti-human employee cutting measures.

AI needs to be deeply regulated to forefront human wellbeing, even at the cost of another country doing it better. The ONLY way this country can be great is ensuring the quality of life of ALL the citizens. AI has chipped away at quality of life and quality of work for several years now. I have seen it primarily used for scams and fraudulent businesses, on the art front. Regulation may slow "innovation" in some respects but it will encourage the AI makers to be more creative and ethical with their work instead of making it as fast as they can to amass wealth. This is technology we need to be careful with, for humanity's sake.

Anyway, if this administration thinks AI can replace all "worthless" jobs like art, then maybe it could replace the whole executive branch. Just my two cents.

**Name:** Richard Roberts **Address:** United States,

## **General Comment**

Generative AI is an algorithm capable of generating superficially convincing text and images, but only superficially. It presents serious dangers, as most of the jobs people want it to do, it is inherently incapable of, but can often produce something that looks convincing until you try to use it. This can have disastrous results, such as AI generated mushroom guides leading to poisoning. This problem is built into the generative AI concept itself, because it is only a statistical analysis of existing creations.

To reach even this flawed and dangerous state, AI companies have had to steal vast amounts of copyrighted material. They have said openly, many times, that large scale generative AI depends entirely on this theft. And it is theft. Again, generative AI is nothing but a copying and remixing machine. It does not use the works it is trained on to learn how to create, it simply copies by statistical model. To the extent it ever succeeds, it is because it stole content from the original creator.

Combining these traits, the thing generative AI is best at is being used for dubiously legal or directly illegal scams, where quality is not necessarily, only vast amounts of material that seems convincing at a glance. Then we add in another major problem - by depending on large amounts of stolen data, generative AI engines contain legally sensitive information such as legal documents and medical records, which the con artists already drawn to these tools are motivated to misuse.

In conclusion, AI certainly needs a governmental plan in place, but the policy changes needed are more limits on what generative AI can be trained from and used for. Subsidizing AI companies to do more of what they are doing now will only make these existing problems worse.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Rin Ascher

**Email:**

## **General Comment**

I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues

**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-4019

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Robert Iadicicco

## **General Comment**

I am an everyday American who makes art professionally.

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American livelihoods like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.

Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators' copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly "fair use".

They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.

Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration's AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Rowan Lockner **Address:** United States,

**Email:**

## **General Comment**

While the current administration's priorities are focused on protecting and advancing America's critical domestic economy, it is also crucial that any technology advanced in the pursuit of these goals is leveraged fairly, openly, and without bias, aligning with president Trump's actions to advance AI.

The current industry-wide implementation of AI suffers from extreme directionlessness, both at the application and regulatory levels. A major aspect of this is in regards to the perpetual legal limbo of AI implementation, where LLMs / DL / NN / ML heavily lean on data training sets that include substantial amounts of copyrighted material. Moreover, the outputs of AI-associated tools has already received substantial adjudication. Thaler v. Perlmutter, based on the ruling of Burrow-Giles Lithographic v. Sarony, has already ruled substantively on this matter, drawing on the historical recognition of human creativity as central to the copyright process. At the input end, Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GMBH v. Ross Intelligence Inc. has further ruled that AI-generated outputs, when based upon training data made of copyrighted and personal material obtained without permission from authors, does not constitute fair use.

To meaningfully develop AI technologies - which can become essential tools in areas like data science and drug discovery, where the process parsing through billions of nodes of data can be exponentially accelerated by AI - a meaningful set of guidelines should be established. Aligning with the goals of the NSTC to advance this Critical and Emerging Technology (CET), the fundamental question of AI copyright should be federally and definitively answered. America's rich and globally-dominant artistic outputs and technological leadership can exist in parallel, but only under clearly stated federal guidance.

To advance AI technologies, it should be firmly established that the data training sets of LLMs / DL / NN / ML must abide by American copyright standards. Implementing this simple rule would have meaningful and impactful consequences. Such a standard would ensure that technological leaders in the United States would finally have clear guidance on how to comply with national standards to ensure that their outputs are legally viable, while also protecting America's copyright system. Specifically, any AI Action Plan should provide specific guidance on how data training sets should be constructed out of inputs complying with national standards on copyrighted materials, avoiding the pitfalls of relying on an incomplete patchwork of court decisions that have not yet fully addressed every fact of this issue.

America can and should advance AI technologies, while protecting creators and other copyright holders, through such standards.

comments.title: RR-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text:
## 3/12/2025 via FDMS

R.R.

Our world is driven by digital communications, and digital transformations over the past three years, has further complicated access to one's PII (personally identifiable information). AI, more specifically Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) have transformed data management, especially in terms of privacy and security. It is critically important that periodic reviews of authorized users of PII, include reviewing who has the need-to-know. Authorized and Need-to-Know are two distinct aspects, as are Security and Privacy. NIST Risk Framework (SP 800-53 & 800-161) must be a practice for all entities. Transparent privacy policies and consent mechanisms must be required and entities using AI tools (ML/DL), must implement mechanisms of to inform individuals how their data is collected, used, and shared. There must be mechanisms in place to ensure individuals always retain control over their PII or personal data, and shield individuals from unauthorized access, misuse, or exploration. This also applies to allow only those with the need-to-know have practices in place to ensure proper access and use. Policies and procedures must be implemented that address access control, managing who is authorized AND who has the need to access. Procedures and common practices in granting appropriate permissions, using multi-factor authentication, and regularly reviewing and updating access rights. Entities must prioritize data protection by implementing robust security measures, and ensuring that individuals always retain ownership of their data. Entities must implemented privacy-by-design principles, Entities must implemented measures to ensure data minimization and purpose limitations Entities must regularly audit and assess privacy compliance.

CAUTION: This email originated from outside your organization. Exercise caution when opening attachments or clicking links, especially from unknown senders.

Dear Collaborators of the AI Action Plan,

I would like to submit the following as comment in regards to the AI Action Plan:

- 1. **Generalizing "AI"** behind this label are the actual mechanics and accelerators within currently available technology (large-language models, machine learning, etc.). We should recognize these toolsets directly and broadly demystify how they work.
- 2. **Abuse of the idea of "AI"** Without a demystification, people will abuse this label and hold power over others using fictional narratives of grandness (i.e. Wizard of Oz).
- 3. **"AI" as a guest** We need to look at the root level of American culture and how local economies are best organized from the bottom-up. For too long we have molded cities top-down at the expense of decency. The introduction of new accelerated technologies should be as practical utilities of a genuine foundation, and guests to what is our work.
- 4. **Opt-out option** Everything built in this space needs to be arm's length by its nature. The history of abuse demonstrated by the first wave of computers and digitalization has set a precedent for all involved. New tools may provide greater transparency (i.e. Blockchain), but new agreements must be forged collectively for where this is appropriate. Each use case will mature, but opting out should always be an option.

Best Regards,

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Ryan Linn

## **General Comment**

So, let's start with the obvious: This hurts more Americans than it helps. Point blank, the number of Americans working on or involved with AI to the capacity required to benefit from this is minuscule compared to the number of Americans who are having their blood, sweat, and tears from their hard work harvested en masse without permission to fuel AI development. Those are the Americans who should be protected. Their jobs are what bring value to our country.

AI should have more stringent requirements on what it can and cannot scrape for its models. Without at least written consent of the party being scraped, that is tantamount to theft. That would be like someone buying a Tesla, removing the identifying branding and replacing it with their own car company branding and saying "I made this car". Anyone with eyes knows that's still a Tesla and Tesla would be within their rights to sue. Why should that not be the right of the creators that are being used to train these AI engines without their consent?

We want to be the leading voice of AI in the world? Then lead by example, lead by requiring stringent requirements of AI engines and hold them accountable. We protect our creators and give them the option to participate in AI training or to opt out and enforce that choice with the engine creators.

AI has a place, but it can't be at the cost of others. As it stands, AI is the wild west of tech, would it not be more prudent to implement order and process to it than to let chaos reign? If we want our AI endeavors to be successful and not money pits that are constantly saved from tanking by government loans, we need to look at them on a fundamental level and rethink how these companies generate revenue. We can't just rubber stamp them to run wild across the internet and toss copyright to the wayside for the sake of trying to help one struggling industry at the cost of multiple others. I urge you to rethink this idea and go back to the drawing board.

## **General Comment**

I believe pursuing investment in generative AI is a serious mistake. It will only benefit generative AI companies in the short term, while individual Americans will have protections and rights stripped from them. Allowing generative AI companies to use private material to bolster their product, which they are trying to sell for a profit, is a conflict of interest as it means they have no limit on what sorts of data they can take and repurpose.

Allowing generative AI to flourish is also a sercurity issue, as many individuals are already no doubt aware of deep fakes hurting the lives of individuals.

It does not work as it's meant to and pursuing making it better would only take away valuable resources that could be allocated to tried and true methods.

Companies do not need an exemption to steal from American individuals and even other companies. We should not invest in generative AI and we should not allow the companies creating it to profit off of the hard work of others, with no recourse. To put it plainly, I do not think these companies should be allowed to steal the work of individual Americans for themselves. These companies should not be given an exemption for theft from our citizen's data at such a large scale.

The American government should not provide an exemption for companies to train on our data, private, public, or otherwise. Rather, I think we should be stricter with these companies. We should be holding them accountable for the actions they are taking that are disenfranchising many Americans as we speak.

## **General Comment**

Generative AI is unethical, inefficient, and frequently inaccurate. Models trained on the work of human artists and writers is plagiarism at best, and when monetized content is involved, it escalates to theft. AI strips the soul out of art of all kinds, and returns terrifying inaccurate results when used for searching - numerous articles have covered the inability of various engines to solve word problems and accurately summarize information, with some even providing downright dangerous advice about food and medicine.

Some types of machine learning have genuinely beneficial applications, but generative AI is no substitute for human creativity or critical thinking. If left unchecked, it could result in many individuals living in their own separate realities based on AI-generated "facts" with varying degrees of detrimental results.

AI cannot make judgment calls or understand the human cost or long-term effects of important or difficult decision, so it has no business being used to evaluate performance, resolve insurance claims, or draft policy.

It is entirely reasonable for the United States to aspire to be a world leader in the types of machine-learning that can have valuable scientific applications, but we cannot allow a profoundly resource-intensive plagiarism machine to dominate our society.

Copyright is to protect creators' incentive by discouraging competitors from simply stealing their work - if you allow Gen AI, which does not create but simply repackages what it has been trained on, to breach all copyright law, then you are hurting American workers and industries in creative fields by taking away their protection and incentive.

Proponents argue that without this breach of proper business protections, US Gen AI companies will fall behind China - to which I would respond that this isn't a concern. The current Gen AI technology has been nothing but a scourge forced upon the American public so far. While some AI technology has been beneficial to some fields, Gen AI has shown no valid use. Americans are, by in large, so critical of the technology that adding it has hurt sales for various companies. The propositions for it are unenticing at best, catastrophic at worst; the technology continues at this time to be extremely inefficient (and increasingly so with each new generation) and has embarrassingly low efficacy. So far, advocates for Gen AI have failed to prove that this is a technology worth preserving, let alone considering an "advancement".

Our time and energy would be much better spent protecting American workers from Gen AI, not the other way around.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Sara Carter

## **General Comment**

AI is not paid a salary, so it won't spend its earnings on goods and services. If everyone and their unique work has been replaced by AI, who will have the money to buy what you're selling?

AI should be used to enhance the human experience, not eliminate it. Any government plans involving AI should:

- 1. Protect the IP interests of creators of any form of original works
- 2. Offer no protections for transformative works created using AI generated from purely copyrighted original works that have not been used with consent of or compensation to the original creator. There should also be heavy punishments for violations.
- 3. Offer protections for AI works created from copyrighted work that has been compensated for. A system must be in place to track this and proof of the right to use a compensated original work should be available upon request.
- 4. AI should automate and enhance work tasks, data analysis, and organization as a job aid, not a job replacement.
- 5. No living person should have their voice or likeness used without consent or compensation for AI purposes.
- 6. AI should be used to enhance the physical and logical capabilities of machinery, while creating an equal number of jobs that it will replace.

And so on and so on. Action plans and regulations must wrangle the use of AI for the benefit and betterment of society as a whole. When it comes to the looming threat of misused AI, the government needs to protect the interests of the citizens not only within the United States, but also in the outside world.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Sasha Hayes-Rusnov

**Email:**

![](_page_0_Picture_13.jpeg)

The US framework for AI development ought to adhere to certain core principles to ensure all Americans share appropriately in any ultimate benefits:

- 1. Recognition of rights to individual data privacy and ownership of data that may be used to train models, including voluntary opt-in (rather than opt-out) legal structures, structures for compensation of creators of data used for training, and equitable remedies for infringement on individual rights that include requirements to make models trained on illegally acquired data free and open to the public.
- 2. Energy consumption reduction, carbon neutrality, and environmental harm reduction, including requirements for the use of green energy for new data centers, prohibition of infringement on public water sources, and requirements that chips manufactured in or imported to the US be built using materials from more-sustainable mining operations.
- 3. Adherence to human-based decision-making and liability as AI is implemented to support government and private roles, including securities trading, vehicle operation, all categories of SIGINT and surveillance, law enforcement, and military applications. The law must hold humans liable for actions in all circumstances, whether the person operating and acting on advice from an AI program assistant or, in cases where an AI's advice or actions are not actively verified by a human in real time, the humans who have trained or built the AI in question.

All three of these principles will tend to make AI development more costly and challenging. However, the alternative will be a future in which all Americans feel the harms of AI development while only the few will reap the rewards.

## Scott Peterson

Regarding the AI investment of \$500B... Why are we giving the elite billionaires contracts to make AI that China made for a few million. Sounds like a handout to me. Billions have already been spent and we made an inferior product. Throwing money at this and to Trump's buddies isn't the solution. They said it was because of the work environment they built it in. I'd say the solution is to pay and treat workers better but that wont change, that takes money out of the elite's pockets... And now your essentially donating money to them for the same thing you gve them money for before and..... We had ChatGPT. That was great for a while, until we learned that we were far behind. You deny we are far behind to keep people believing this is the best country. China showed you wrong. You know their practices and how it was done but we are choosing to give money away for a slightly improved product that takes 2 years and by then we are WAY behind China. If you want to stay ahead of China you need more that throwing money at the wealthy and elite. You are wasting our money on a solution that we don't have yet. It's sad to see what's all being taken care of and taken away. More money out of our pockets and more into theirs. Trickle up economics, works almost every time. Nothing that has been done has been America First. It's Billionaire first. Now we're looking at passing a budget bill that takes away more from the average American and trickle it up while prices rise and people can't eat. Get the food and price regulations under control rather than this AI you think we should be working on.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Scott Tuffiash

![](_page_0_Picture_12.jpeg)

## **General Comment**

My name is Scott Tuffiash and I am a high school Language Arts and Journalism teacher at Avonworth High School in Pittsburgh. I currently teach a new course for this school, and it seems maybe a new course for almost any public school, titled "Human Flourishing" and I completed teaching another new course last semester for high school seniors titled "AI and Ethics". Because of this phrase matching the Human Flourishing course I currently teach -" With the right governmental policies, continued U.S. AI leadership will promote human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security.", and because I have studied viewpoints on innovation and regulation regarding Artificial Intelligence products to create the AI and Ethics class and then teach it, I am submitting comments myself and asking about 50 students from this school to do the same today and tomorrow.

Less regulation - through Executive Order 14179 - will allow further experimentation of AI products in the free market of US consumers. What is the current potency of AI products and how can they impact a consumer? At its best, an AI product can offer mathematically derived insights that offer a consumer a variety of outputs. Improved productivity at a job, more efficient use of professional and personal time, potentially improved sense of well-being or purpose: these are potential benefits of a less regulated market of products. Unfortunately, less regulation places the burden of ethical innovation on the consumer instead of the producer. What is at stake then? In the worst case scenario, the mental wellbeing of the consumer…and then potentially the physical life of the consumer itself. Consider https://techcrunch.com/2024/10/23/lawsuit-blames-character-ai-in-death-of-14-year-old-boy/. Vice President Vance suggested at the AI Summit in France that products targeting minors are going to be regulated. But what about the same exact impact of a product built with effective addictive design, unregulated, for a 19 year old? Is the human brain that much more developed at 19 compared to 14? How do we prove that distinction between 14 and 19, reliably, scientifically? Without the onus of regulation on for-profit companies to transparently display addictive design qualities, and furthermore legal ramifications for companies to suffer significant financial losses if they promote addictive design products and can legally hide the design, innovation becomes secondary to a damaged free market of consumers of all ages. Rather then a complete removal of content like the AI Bill of Rights from the prior administration, there should be a re-opening, however swift, for more transparent sharing of information, debate, and policy change within this Presidency, like President Trump's White House website from his first term of office: https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/ai/ai-american-innovation/

comments.comment_text:
**From:** Scott Fronapfel **To:** ostp-ai-rfi

**Subject:** [External] AI Action Plan

**Date:** Sunday, March 16, 2025 12:05:15 AM

CAUTION: This email originated from outside your organization. Exercise caution when opening attachments or clicking links, especially from unknown senders.

## Warm greetings to the NITRD and NCO teams!

I want to provide an additional voice as a freelance artist and a software developer in the entertainment industry.

Generative AI was created using legal grey zones with almost non-existent ethical constraints. Most of these data scrapers were initially indirectly funded by private companies even though many of the datasets "claim" to be open source and for public research. I believe Machine Learning and other ventures into AI research are valuable to human life and the technological progression of our country, but want to warn against allowing personal data, copyright, and the work of small businesses and artists from being used license free by companies who seem to create tools and products which replace the value of those hard working American citizens.

The novelty of generative AI in both imagery and text is quickly replaced once users understand the frequency of hallucinations, and the active INTENT by these companies for the products to be used for ill-advised use cases (including historical document reconstruction, law advice, and replacing artists by actively using machines designed to copy them). We live in an era where generated content has actively replaced human content on the internet, and further pollutes political and historical knowledge with believable fake likenesses in voice, video, and verbiage.

I propose that existing copyright be maintained or modified to further protect creative human works, and that generative AI continue to be restricted to items actively in public domain and that no output from a non-human generative software be considered for human ownership. I also strongly opposed the idea that generative AI, which is largely enhancements to autocomplete algorithms and image upscaler, be properly separated in verbiage from machine learning used for medicine and from proper attempts to create AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) which is an entirely different field of research and does not rely on cloning and polluting existing human works and information.

Thank you for your time! Scott Fronapfel

All e-mails to and from this account are for NITRD official use only and subject to certain disclosure requirements.

If you have received this e-mail in error, we ask that you notify the sender and delete it immediately.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Scripter Beaumont

**Address:**

## **General Comment**

AI implementation has been nothing but an unnecessary time sink. The existence of AI tools in my daily life has not improved anything.

I don't need an AI summary of a Google search query when the first actual result on the page answers my question just fine. These AI summaries are prone to spreading false information as well. Without being able to see the source that these AI summaries pull from, I'm inclined to never trust them.

I don't need ChatGPT to write me a resume when I know how to write one myself. AI writing tools are also prone to plagiarism, and as a person who values academic integrity, I refuse to use them. It sets a bad example for students as well because it disincentivizes creative thought and effort. Why learn how to write if the AI can just write for you?

AI in the arts has been a travesty. Professional artists, many of whom struggle to find jobs, are having their original work stolen and used for AI training without permission. People can then use programs like Stable Diffusion to make rip-offs of those artists' work, passing it off as their own. The resulting art is not only used for plagiarism, but also to create deepfakes and harmful propaganda. This has had a terrible impact on real human lives.

How can Americans be expected to be optimistic about AI when our future looks so bleak due to these issues? If America is to become a world leader in the development of AI, we should be using it to create real, tangible good. Not just convenience. Not just shortcuts. Technology should always be used in service of humankind, and current AI development does not seem to be headed in that direction. I am not convinced that removing roadblocks to further AI development is going to help anyone.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Sean Basinger

## **General Comment**

Thank you for this opportunity to comment.

While I understand it is important to keep up with the rapid growth of technological advancement and for the United States of America to properly compete with other countries in these fields, my concerns today are for the individual and the small business owners.

To my friends, I once compared the dawn of A.I. to Frankenstein's monster or the dinosaurs of "Jurassic Park." The scientific geniuses did not stop to think of the long-term (or even short-term) ramifications these acts could have on the individual. They only saw and thought about how their advancements could help others or be beneficial to mankind in some way. While that is noble, it does not change the dangers and very real threat A.I. places on the individual.

A.I. is growing rapidly. In fact, probably too rapidly. On top of the already very real threat of deepfakes, which has and will give rise to defamations of all kinds, as well as allow scammers and criminals to take advantage of others who may lack the tools necessary to detect such scams, the concern that A.I. will invade the lives of and steal from hard-working citizens is also very real.

For many months now, the tech companies and now the White House has championed the advancement of A.I. and how it will vastly improve the lives of Americans and possibly the world. But what protections are you offering us? What safeguards are there to prevent our jobs from being taken? What is stopping corporate chiefs and CEOs from replacing middle class or lower class workers with A.I.? Where does that leave us? What guarantees can you give us that this will either not happen or there will be some form of worthwhile compensation provided? We already have plenty of struggling Americans in this country, and I fear unleashing this big tech on us will only generate more unless something is done to prevent it.

And what of the concern that copyright protections will be considered null through some form of legislation all in the name of progress? Hundreds if not thousands if not millions of peoples' hard work and innovation (American innovation), devoured by these soulless machines, again, all in the name of progress and so that big tech can have an excuse to plunder our hard work. The individual is steamrolled over by big tech getting a free pass. And what do we get out of it? The promise of a glorified America, strengthened by A.I.? Okay, fair, it MIGHT lead to medical innovations or breakthroughs in science, but where's that guarantee? The things couldn't even draw hands correctly. On the topic of copyright protection, we might as well not even bother to create once these things are set in motion. Stop drawing your pictures, stop taking your photographs, stop making your movies, stop acting, stop it all. A machine will do it for you. It robs the creator of the joy of creating, and it will rob the audience of authenticity. The heart and soul of creativity will be crushed. And while the creator can still create even with the advent of A.I., it will cut into their profits and it is only a matter of time before their hard work is swallowed up by those same soulless machines, or people using those machines to get ahead. Whereas others spent half their lives developing their skills day after day, now somebody who refuses to put in the work will be able to just type in a prompt and take credit for the work when all they did was click a keyboard for a few minutes. And what promises and safeguards do you have for them, those who have spent years trying to better their talents? I'm sorry, but your word will not be enough.

In closing, I again understand the need to keep up with the technology, so as not to fall behind to rivals on the global stage. But the fear that many will be hurt in the name of this progress is very real. If this needs to be done, if progress must be put forth first, then protections and compensation for the average American and the artistic creators of this country need to be put in place before it happens. Thank you.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Sean Elgin

**Email:**

## **General Comment**

To Whom It May Concern,

What Large Language Model development companies refer to as "Artificial Intelligence" is nothing of the sort. It needs to be understood that these systems are black-boxed pattern-matching algorithms aimed at identifying the patterns which appear commonly in training data and reproducing those patterns or approximations thereof.

These systems are limited by the extent of their training data. There exists no "AI" system which can produce functional results in the absence of human-generated material; when access to human-generated material is revoked, the abilities of the "AI" diminish rapidly with attempts to train recursively. Each and every result of "AI" systems is derived from some aspect of the training material, and to render human labor mere grist for the mill fundamentally disconnects us from our creative products. In so doing, generating from the sum total of human knowledge an eternal remix album that never truly steps outside of that which came before while displacing artists who may otherwise have been able to reach such a lofty height.

"AI" is fundamentally incapable of comprehension, of contextualization, and of discernment - it only matters what output creates a response to the prompt that most closely resembles those patterns observed in its training data. This can even allow a clever actor to extract fragments of that training data with careful prompting, as the machine will read the prompt and match a response without awareness of what it is doing or why it is doing it. Additionally, this lack of context or comprehension allows for the production of statements, claims, or conclusions which range from the nonsensical to the outright dangerous. These tools cannot be ethically applied without heavy oversight at the bare minimum. Not even the regulations presently in place are sufficient, though they are necessary.

Setting aside the fact that "AI" does not perform such tasks or bear the qualities of intelligence as claimed by its proponents, the economic purpose of "AI" is simple and disastrous to the American people. As used today, "AI" functions to grant wealth access to some approximation of otherwise irreplicable skill, while denying skilled personnel access to wealth. Large corporations are eager and ready to replace large swathes of the workforce with "AI" systems, and are willing to accept the dramatic loss of actual function this will incur, if only it would rid them of having to pay for actual employees. The impact this will have on America's economy barely needs saying, but for the sake of this comment: this country will never fully recover from allowing these excesses to fester.

I implore those who read this document to decline any and all requests by companies building Large Language Model "AI" products to access our data. If they desire to use all of the data which they can possibly access to improve their product, they are fully capable of purchasing rights from the copyright holders as required of any ethical creative enterprise - and they are more than wealthy enough to do so.

This document may be publicly disseminated. The document contains no business-proprietary or confidential information. Document contents may be used by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.

Consent is not given for the use of this document to train "AI" models or systems which approximate their functionality.

Thank you for your time.

comments.comment_text:
## 2/20/2025 via FDMS

## Seth Roseman

I am writing to ask the White House to prioritize reducing energy consumption and increasing efficiency in the new AI Action Plan. As AI technologies continue to become more integrated into our lives, it is crucial that we address the significant energy demands and associated carbon emissions of these systems. The AI Action Plan should emphasize energy efficiency as a top policy action. This includes investing in research and development to create more energy-efficient AI algorithms and hardware. By focusing on efficiency, we can reduce the overall energy consumption of AI systems without compromising their performance. Data centers, which power much of the AI infrastructure, should be encouraged to transition to renewable energy sources such as solar and wind. This transition is essential for mitigating the carbon emissions associated with AI's energy consumption. There should be a clear, definitive timeline to achieve net-zero emissions for AI operations. Data centers and AI developers should likewise adopt best practices for energy efficiency, including optimizing cooling systems, using energy-efficient hardware, and implementing AI algorithms that require less computational power. These practices can significantly reduce the energy footprint of AI operations. According to a study by the University of Massachusetts Amherst, training a large AI model can emit as much carbon as five cars in their lifetimes. This highlights the urgent need to address AI's energy consumption. The International Energy Agency reports that data centers consume about 1% of global electricity demand, and this is expected to rise with the increasing use of AI. Transitioning to renewable energy can help offset this growing demand. Companies like Google and Microsoft have already committed to achieving carbon-neutral data centers, demonstrating that this goal is both feasible and beneficial for the environment. As a resident of York, Pennsylvania, I am particularly concerned about how AI's energy use may impact our local environment and economy. The restart of Three Mile Island to power AI has many who lived through its meltdown in 1979 worried. By prioritizing energy efficiency and the transition to renewable energy, the AI Action Plan can create a sustainable future for AI technologies and help protect communities like ours from the adverse effects of climate change of (another) nuclear meltdown. By prioritizing energy efficiency and the transition to renewable energy, the AI Action Plan can lead the way in creating a sustainable future for AI technologies. Again, I ask the White House to incorporate these recommendations into the new AI Action Plan to ensure that AI development aligns with our climate goals.

comments.comment_text:
## Shayne Nelson

The US Government should do the following: 1. Invest in Quantum computing. This is the next step in speed and machine learning, graduating from the standard 0/1 computer language to an expanded set of unlimited resources for computers 2. Invest equally in Quantum security. Companies such as Sealsqcorp (LAES) have pivoted semi conductor manufacturing to creating security solutions for Quantum computing 3. Standardize LLM instruction guidelines to limit the ability for machine learning to exceed human constraints. 4. Invest in US AI startups, provide funds to smaller companies to engineer lower cost increased security applications 5. Enforce standard release QA processes across the industry to reduce critical and zero day vulnerabilities. Breaches occur because of the lack of attention to detail. The highest most evident attack vector to AI is through vulnerabilities, or security holes not found in initial QA. This is because many small, medium and enterprise companies do not enforce release management and vulnerability patching cycles that will reduce the overall risk of unauthorized access to active source code, footholds in AI networks and the compromise of sensitive data 6. Require the security enforcement of LLMs and the type of information that is fed to and stored in LLMs to prevent the compromise of sensitive information.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Shirley Zhu

## **General Comment**

The United States needs to better regulate the use of AI to ensure quality. Time and time again, we've seen that less government oversight in the private sector results in cut corners and mistakes that have turned deadly at the cost of the American lives. The there is already little oversight in how AI developed and used, which results in mass-produced, cheap, bad quality product that's worth less than the energy used to generate it. For example, I recently googled "how to cycle a fish tank" and the first few pages of results were polluted with the same generic AI-generated information that was of little help and wasted my time. Now, I have to search for forums or for things specifically published before AI language models became widespread just to know that an actual person wrote the article, at the cost of outdated information that could be wrong now. What if that same search was for how to handle a medical emergency while the ambulance arrives? The technology should make life easier and be optional, not force people to waste their time separating the good information from the rest.

Intellectual property should also be legally protected, not removed. The lack of it disincentivizes innovation, not only in the technology sector, but everywhere. If the government can't guarantee protection for an individual's creative work, then what makes us different from a socialist country? It's an open invitation for brilliant minds to move elsewhere, where their intellectual property and hard work are valued instead of taken. AI generated "art" has already replaced some creative work, putting people out of jobs or resulting in the expectation that creatives work for less than minimum wage for skills that took a lifetime to build up. Science and technology might be the backbone of our nation, but creative work is the living soul and America would not be the same without it.

![](_page_0_Picture_13.jpeg)

I am a university mathematics instructor. As an educator, it is important to me to be able to share publicly content that I create for my courses so that it can reach a broader audience. At the same time, I rely on copyright protection to retain rights and control over materials that I create. My understanding of the proposed regulation is that AI companies would be essentially exempt from following copyright law, and free to use anything I make publicly available to train AI models. If implemented, it would have a chilling effect on me and anyone else who wishes to make material of any kind that they have written available to the public. I would have to seriously reconsider what I can put on the public internet lest it be scraped by AI trainers, and would likely need to keep my course materials restricted to university servers that only my own students can log into.

I also do visual art as a hobby, and enjoy sharing my art online for the sheer joy of sharing it with others. I would also be much less able to do this if my art were more vulnerable to AI scraping. Every other artist I have discussed this issue with feels similarly, so I would also expect to be less able to enjoy others' art.

In sum, this regulation flies in the face of the principles of copyright and the rights of creators, and implementing it would seriously harm everyone's ability to share material (whether written or visual) in public.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Skyler Hoff

## **General Comment**

If the training of competitive generative AI requires the removal of copyright protections for artists, it is not worth it. Generative AI models are derived from human work, but also compete with the products of human work. Human artists cannot out-produce AI, but AI depends on human input. If America wants to be an AI powerhouse, it should be promoting its own independent artists through art grants. Moreover, if AI training is allowed on copyrighted images, how do AI companies propose to stop people from creating AI images from those works? I have models on my computer right now that can reproduce copywritten works and trademarked characters, so this isn't some far-off hypothetical, it's something I could do right now. If it's fine for OpenAI to train a model via infringement, surely it can't be wrong for me to USE a model trained via infringement, for instance, to make art of Mickey Mouse in an intimate kiss with Captain America. I'm just using the product of (what we're assuming is) legal AI training, right?

Additionally, it would be entirely possible for these AI companies to pay to curate datasets. Not only are curated datasets better for specific AI development and innovation--as "generalist" models include a large proportion of junk in their training sets, due to their wideranging nature--but this would create jobs for Americans, who would either be curating the dataset or contributing their copyrighted works. If the USA wants to be dominant in the field of generative AI, surely its citizens should materially benefit from that dominance, and not just the owners of AI corporations.

Recent events have shown that while generative AI can be useful, the sort of wide-ranging disregard for quality training data should not be encouraged. AI should be built with curated datasets for specific purposes, not plagiarized datasets for vague promises of things it'll be able to do in the future.

comments.title: Stephen-Casper-AI-RFI-2025-2.pdf
comments.comment_text:
**A pro-innovation approach to AI governance requires safety and understanding**  Stephen Casper

**Disasters are both intrinsically bad and lead to regulatory hammers.** In the history of safety engineering, many major system failures all follow a certain loose story ([Dekker, 2019](https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/edit/10.4324/9781351059794/foundations-safety-science-sidney-dekker)). It starts off with some system – e.g., a dam, bridge, power plant, oil rig, building, etc – that functions normally for a long time. At first, this is accompanied by direct evidence of benefits and no evidence of major harms which can lull engineers into a false sense of security. But then, tragedy strikes suddenly. For example, before the infamous 1986 Challenger space shuttle explosion, there were 9 successful launches ([Gebhardt, 2011](https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2011/01/1983-1986-missions-history-space-shuttle-challenger/)) which was a factor that led engineers to neglect safety warnings before the infamous 10th launch. Things were fine, and the empirical evidence looked good until disaster struck. There is scientific consensus that AI is a very powerful technology and that it could pose national security threats. This points us to invest in safeguards while we develop it. If AI has a 'Chernobyl moment,' it would not only be tragic in and of itself, but would almost certainly trigger a regulatory hammer effect afterward ([Hendrycks, 2024](https://time.com/7015197/ai-legislation-protects-more-than-just-people/)).

**Democracies require information to function.** Historically, AI has been developed in a very open way in the scientific community. However, in recent years, it has become both more impactful and more closed. This is often described as the "crisis of transparency" in AI. Currently, there is limited scientific understanding and even less public understanding of (1) how labs train their AI systems, (2) how their AI systems function internally, and (3) how they are governed internally. Having more transparency into this (e.g., by having companies produce documentation of their internal risk assessments) would improv public understanding and society's ability to have more informed discussions about this emerging technology. It would also allow for more competitiveness and innovation in the AI space by increasing awareness of frontier practices.

**Subject:** [External] AI Action Plan comment **Date:** Saturday, February 8, 2025 6:38:12 PM

CAUTION: This email originated from outside your organization. Exercise caution when opening attachments or clicking links, especially from unknown senders.

As an academic who studies AI policy, I would recommend focusing on "*process regulation"* as the federal government's central strategy for pro AI innovation and insight governance. Unlike "substantive regulation" which limits what developers can do, "process regulation" regulates how they can do it. For example, ingredient bans are substantive regulation and requirements for nutrition facts are process regulation. Thus, I believe that process regulation (e.g. requiring documentation from developers) would be a pro-innovation approach that also allows for a more informed public.

As an example of a process regulation-focused draft, see the [Preserving American](https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/senate-bill/5616/text/is?overview=closed&format=xml) [Dominance in Artificial Intelligence Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/senate-bill/5616/text/is?overview=closed&format=xml) draft from last congress which was introduced by a senate republican.

**From:** Steve Lyke **To:** ostp-ai-rfi

**Subject:** [External] AI Action Plan: Clarify who is responsible

CAUTION: This email originated from outside your organization. Exercise caution when opening attachments or clicking links, especially from unknown senders.

To the Networking and Information Technology Research and Development National Coordination Office, National Science Foundation,

While other guardrails may be necessary, I suggest that AI safety concerns can be efficiently addressed by clarifying that AI is a tool used by humans who remain responsible for the results of its use. It should be the responsibility of AI developers to accurately inform users about the characteristics of the tools they have developed. So informed, users should take responsibility for what results from their application of the tools. Stephen E. Lyke, PhD, PE, concerned citizen

## **General Comment**

Many regulations on AI \*should\* be burdensome in order to ensure that it is used in beneficial ways. In particular, regulations should make it clear that reliance on AI cannot be used as a means to avoid liability in cases where a human being making the same decision would be considered negligent; it cannot be used as a defense against charges of discrimination, where bias in the training data produces an identifiable bias against groups having various protected characteristics, such as race or disability; and it cannot be used as a defense against copyright infringement, where the unauthorized use of copyrighted work in training datasets results in economic harm (whether immediate and provable or the speculative long-term result) to authors and other copyright owners. If AI firms believe they can't compensate authors fairly for the use of their data and still turn a profit, then that means that the resulting AI tools are a net loss to society once externalities are properly accounted for, and so the loss of these tools is a net gain for humanity.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Steven Kaas **Email:**

## **General Comment**

My main hope for the AI Action Plan is that it gives serious attention to the risks of losing control over future, highly advanced AI systems — risks that could lead to catastrophic or even existential consequences. Many submissions likely outline concrete policy proposals to address this. I don't claim special expertise in that area, but I want to highlight one approach that may not yet have been raised.

AI experts differ sharply on the severity of existential risk from misaligned AI. Researchers like Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, and Stuart Russell have warned that current AI advances are placing us on a highly dangerous trajectory. Others, like Yann LeCun and Andrew Ng, argue the risk is overstated.

Sound policy depends on rigorously assessing how serious an extinction-level threat AI poses, understanding the nature of that threat, and identifying how it can be addressed.

To that end, I suggest supporting structured, public dialogues between leading researchers on AI and its risks — perhaps modeled after the Dutch government's "Climate Dialogue" project (2012–2015) (https://mwenb.nl/climate-dialogue/), which brought together climate scientists with opposing views. Such a forum could foster more transparent, systematic, and constructive expert conversations, grounding AI policy in well-vetted ideas and making them accessible for public scrutiny.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Steven Swanson

## **General Comment**

Excluding companies that utilize AI from copyright law will bring about the death of the trillion-dollar entertainment industry in the United States, taking along with it much of the professional class.

Make mo mistake. Writers, artists, photographers, filmmakers, musicians, designers, architects, engineers, software developers, all make use of technology to enhance their craft, but until now each new tool has not infringed upon the basic ownership that these creators have over their creations.

We already have clear evidence that generative AI takes enormous amounts of copyrighted materials without the consent of their owners and uses them to train and refine AI models, often with the express objective of depriving the aforementioned copyright owners of their livelihoods.

It is disturbingly easy to achieve. An AI can take a fraction of an artist's body of work, work that frequently has taken a lifetime to perfect and distinguish, and then begin producing unauthorized likenesses of their work within minutes, flooding galleries and image searches with counterfeits and misrepresentations, drowning the creator in a procedurally generated flood of slop.

What does this ultimately mean? In no small terms, the evisceration of art and entertainment. Creators will continue to create, but if they believe that sharing their work online will result in wholesale theft then they will have no incentive to do so. Those that survive will find their way to ply their trade outside the U.S. economy, with the most straightforward method being to relocate to a country that does protect their intellectual property. Our loss will be their gain.

While the creators vanish, consumers will be inundated with derivative, inauthentic slop produced in quantities too vast to be adequately inspected or regulated, and consumers will lose faith in the ability of media to inform, inspire, and entertain. All you have to do is conduct a Google image search to see just how pervasive the problem already is, with up to 90% of results being A.I. generated derivatives that distort and destroy public trust. AI is even being used to quickly create spoof websites of news sites, retailers, financial services, and even emergency services, stealing citizens' sensitive information and money while giving nothing of value in return.

As it stands, companies invested in AI do not have a credible best use case for this technology, with most investing in it based on a fear of missing out on the Next Big Thing. No one in tech company boardrooms is discussing the damage AI can do, and that is exactly why the U.S. Government should not entertain the utopian propaganda of AI's advocates.

I have very little faith that this government will make a decision to protect the long-term health of the nation, including that of the unaccountable oligarchs that now hold it in a stranglehold, but on this issue I felt a need to make my voice heard.

Exempting AI tech companies from copyright will kill people. Worse than that it will kill any trust in authority, and risks crushing our nation's soul.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Steven Zuber

## **General Comment**

I am writing in response to the White House's Request for Information on the development of an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan. As AI systems become increasingly capable, it is imperative that their development is guided by careful, deliberate planning to ensure alignment with human values and long-term safety.

The potential benefits of AI are immense, but so are the risks. One of the most pressing concerns is the possibility of misaligned superintelligence—AI systems that, due to insufficient oversight or flawed design, could act in ways that are dangerous to humanity. Researchers at institutions such as the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI) (intelligence.org), Center for AI Policy (CAIS) (safe.ai), and Control AI (controlai.com) have outlined scenarios in which advanced AI, if not properly controlled, could lead to catastrophic outcomes. A robust AI Action Plan must prioritize technical research into AI alignment, as well as policies that ensure AI systems remain interpretable and corrigible.

Additionally, the economic impact of AI-driven automation must not be overlooked. Large-scale job displacement could lead to significant economic instability and social unrest. While automation has historically created new types of employment, the speed at which AI is progressing may outpace our ability to adapt. Policymakers must explore strategies such as retraining programs, adjustments to labor laws, and, potentially, new economic models to support displaced workers.

I urge the administration to approach AI development with a strong commitment to long-term safety and societal well-being. This means supporting rigorous research into AI alignment, creating regulatory frameworks that prevent reckless AI deployment, and preparing for the economic shifts that AI will bring. By taking these concerns seriously now, we can help ensure that AI remains a tool for human progress rather than an existential risk.

Thank you for your attention to this critical issue. I appreciate your leadership in shaping a responsible AI future and your solicitation for thoughts from your fellow Americans. I'm sure I'm not alone when I say I welcome further discussion on these concerns.

Sincerely, Steven Zuber

## **Submitter Information**

Name: Stuart Wagner

Email:

## **General Comment**

It is critical that government and industry are able to develop novel capabilities within a permissive development environment directly with protected and classified data. Some ideas to accomplish this.

- 1) Sandbox environments that support untrusted software to be commingled with classified and protected data. These environments allow anything to come in, but require deep inspection to let any data or software to leave. This allows for sandboxes to bring in malware, untrusted software like Deepseek, and run it directly with protected or classified data to learn from these capabilities and learn how effective they are in a military or intelligence context.
- 2) One day/One week clearances provide officials in all organizations with classified data the ability to waive clearance requirements for short term projects, work, and collaborations. For example, DoD should be able to throw a one-week hackathon and with proper security protections, allow uncleared personnel temporary access to Secret information if there is a national security need to do so (such as trying their product on Secret or Top Secret data).
- 3) Automatic classification of data Security classification guides should be written deterministically and without contradiction such that their policies can be algorithmically applied to classified and protected data. Data should similarly be automatically declassified given proper time as well. Fundamentally, machines should be increasingly involved in applying rules about the classification of data and when its ready to be declassified.

Finally one last idea is automated rules of engagement and military law analysis. The decision speed by lawyers still at times closes the window of a potential military operation to move ahead - ie a lawyer takes longer than the time window of a mission to make a decision. We should by policy increasingly be leveraging natural language processing and machine learning to increasingly automate rules of engagement interpretation during competition and war to ensure that we are not missing those windows of opportunity.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Sydney Savatt

**Email:**

## **General Comment**

Hello, My name is Sydney Savatt, and I am a senior at Avonworth High School and a soon-to-be graduate. For the past 2 months, I have been researching and studying the impact of Generative AI in College Sports Recruiting during my AI and Ethics course. From the research I have conducted, I believe that the current administration's viewpoint on AI regulation, which emphasizes careful consideration of risks while encouraging innovation, is beneficial for society by promoting responsible innovation and reducing potential risks. Many have claimed that it can be a threat to human-replacement and more specifically in my research, it can take away the recruit-coach connection. By replacing a coach recruiting a player with an AI tool, the process would rely heavily on statistics rather than character and leadership abilities. While some express concerns that AI could replace human recruiters, potentially diminishing the importance of character and leadership in player selection, I truly believe that the use of AI is far from these theories and has more of a beneficial impact on society when used as a resource, as JD Vance has suggested. AI through film and highlight-creating apps (Gamechanger/HUDL) has played a significant role in helping players get noticed by college coaches through its ability to generate a highlight film for a player solely based on game film. Players can use these videos created by Artificial Intelligence to send to a coach, which is a crucial first step in getting their foot in the door. AI has been a huge part of many players' success in getting recruited, including my own, where my highlight video I created using AI was able to catch the eye of a coach and eventually land me a Division 1 softball scholarship. This experience shows that if we find a good balance with AI, where we encourage it but also consider ethical concerns, it can help people and give them chances they might not have had otherwise. If we focus on smartly using AI, it can open up opportunities and make things better, instead of just replacing what we already have. And that's kind of what our government is trying to do – push for progress, but also make sure we're protected.

comments.comment_text:
## 3/14/2025 via FDMS

Sydney Shields,

My name is Sydney Shields and I am a member of the graduating class of 2025 at Avonworth High School. I completed a semester course on AI and Ethics and studied the impacts of Generative AI on elementary schools. EO 14179 will be a mix of improvement and disruption. Deregulation of AI would benefit elementary teachers as AI is a great tool for various aspects of their day. However, AI is a harmful tool for elementary-aged students. Education policies should be based on teaching students how to properly use AI and limiting student access in Elementary schools. Students should not have access to AI independently without being monitored by an adult. In Elementary schools, children learn problem-solving and critical thinking skills. Access and abuse of AI can hinder the development of these skills. In addition, kindergarten to secondgrade students don't always understand that AI is not a person. A study showed that younger children depicted their at-home smart speakers as having faces and emotions. In conclusion, EO 14179 will be somewhat of an improvement to elementary schools, but there needs to be a policy in place that will ensure proper teaching and containment of access to AI in elementary schools.

And somehow that's still not enough? I'm wondering what is left for them to steal, and why they would need to ask to steal it. What happens when OpenAI has stolen everything that's left? It'll eat itself, creating more and more hallucinations, until it's totally useless. What is the endgame to this Action Plan?

Unless OpenAI is actually a complete failure and Sam Altman is trying to keep the scam going just long enough to get as much money as humanly possible out of it. Which begs the question, why is the US Government working so hard to save a failing business that sucks up more resources than a small city while providing nothing but recycled slop and guesswork. It can't even do simple math at this point.

Ironically, this proposition would also be bad for OpenAI and other generative AI programs, because then others can steal their "work" with impunity, which historically AI proponents really don't like. They hate when others "steal" their prompts - with seemingly no self awareness that they in fact have stolen from artists, writers, and other creatives.

There are good AI programs that are useful, but they have very specific use cases, like the AI developed to identify baked goods in a Japanese bakery that is also good at identifying cancer cells. (Notably that AI program is not 100% capable of finding cancer cells without a trained radiologist overseeing the analysis.) But OpenAI is not identifying cancer cells, or even identifying baked goods. It cannot tell a picture of a honeybee apart from a picture of a baby in a bee costume. I'm all for scientific innovation and exploration - but some hypotheses don't turn out, and should be abandoned. OpenAI has not earned the right to Americans' copyrighted work, and our hard work should not be bastardized for the sole purpose of lining a billionaire's pockets.

comments.title: Thaier-Hayajneh-AI-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text:
## Thaier Hayajneh

Introduction To ensure U.S. leadership in AI, we must establish strong foundational pillars, starting with early AI education, workforce development, and strategic research investments. AI is rapidly advancing, and the U.S. must prepare students early to develop the skills necessary to compete with other nations and lead in AI innovation. The following policy actions are critical to achieving this goal. Priority Policy Actions for AI Education & Workforce Development 1. Early AI Education as a National Priority Develop a standardized AI curriculum in K-12 education, ensuring students gain foundational AI, machine learning, and computational thinking skills. Expand AI literacy programs in elementary and middle schools, integrating AI concepts into math, science, and technology education. Launch federal AI teacher training programs, equipping educators with the necessary knowledge and resources to teach AI effectively. Encourage public-private partnerships to provide AI learning resources, mentorship programs, and hands-on AI labs in schools. 2. AI Workforce Readiness & Global Competitiveness Implement AI apprenticeships and industry collaborations to transition students from academic learning to real-world AI applications. Establish federal AI upskilling initiatives, particularly cybersecurity, data science, and ethical AI governance. Create a national AI talent pipeline, ensuring a diverse, skilled workforce ready to compete in the global AI landscape. Priority Policy Actions for AI Research & Development 3. Strategic AI Investments for U.S. Leadership Increase funding for ethical AI research, including bias reduction, explainable AI (XAI), and adversarial AI defense mechanisms. Support AI research in cybersecurity applications, focusing on fraud detection, threat intelligence, and national security. Establish federal AI innovation hubs to accelerate AI development in key sectors such as healthcare, defense, and finance. 4. National AI Security & Infrastructure Protection Strengthen AI-driven cybersecurity solutions, ensuring the protection of critical infrastructure and sensitive data. Implement a federal AI risk assessment framework, ensuring AI applications align with national security priorities. Enhance U.S. AI competitiveness through strategic partnerships with academia, government, and industry. ## **General Comment**

As an author in several networks with other authors, as well as artists, filmmakers, and several other creative industries, I strongly urge the United States government and the Trump administration to uphold creatives' copyright and IP rights, and ensure that generative AI models cannot train on copyrighted works without proper licensing and compensation. Generative AI already poses a great threat to workers' rights and livelihoods in creative industries such as film and video gaming. The creative industries of the United States are a cornerstone of it's cultural exports and economy, and have done great work over the decades in building America's reputation as a land of economic and personal freedom. This is why it's important we protect the rights and livelihoods of the people in these industries, and why we should not undermine copyright just for the benefit of the AI industry. Artificial intelligence can and should be a benefit for all sectors of the economy, and many artists and writers wish to leverage artificial intelligence in a way that benefits the arts without harming people's livelihoods. By enforcing copyright licensing for companies looking to use copyrighted material to train their AI models, we can ensure that workers can continue to produce media for the entire world to enjoy while also allowing for technological advancement in a way that is mutually beneficial and positive-sum. The future doesn't need to be a zero-sum game where some industries are financially ruined by others, but a mutually cooperative future is only possible by upholding the laws of the country. Copyright law is an important cornerstone of the law that drives innovation in all sectors, but removing copyright protections because of tech companies' demands would not only harm creative industries, but it would be a massive blow to all industries that rely on intellectual property in the United States, which in turn would also harm its technology industries, including companies like Google and OpenAI who are lobbying for reduced copyright protections. This is why I urge the United States federal government and the Trump administration to uphold copyright law, protect people's intellectual property rights, and ensure that artificial intelligence is trained and developed in a way that is mutually beneficial for the entire economy and does not plunder the intellectual property of other sectors without any compensation.
