**Document:** NSF\_FRDOC\_0001-DRAFT-2930

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Thomas Davidson

## **General Comment**

Training AI on copyrighted works should not be considered fair use. Allowing companies to continue this practice would be disastrous both for the economy and for the individual lives of countless creatives across many fields. Further, I believe it is unethical, inconsistent with legal precedent, and would lead to further long-term consequences.

Consider what would happen if these AI models were to continue improving, and were legitimized by this "action plan." Profit-driven companies would not pay human artists, musicians, writers, etc. when AI can do the job quicker and cheaper. People who had something unique and valuable to contribute to society would no longer be able to do so; instead they would be forced to do unskilled work or be unable to find work at all.

AI will not create new jobs anywhere near the scale of the jobs lost. When the economic activity of human creative work disappears, that also means less tax revenue to fund the government. It's only a matter of time before this extends to nearly all jobs, creative or otherwise, as businesses seek to cut costs with AI. What happens when the majority of Americans are unemployed?

Generative AI does not come up with its own ideas; it adds nothing new that it didn't take from humans. However, it will have fewer new ideas to consume when human artists are pushed aside. Humankind will creatively and culturally stagnate when we rely primarily on AIgenerated works to inform, entertain, and inspire us.

Finally, I would like to address the criteria typically used to evaluate fair use today as I understand it.

- 1. Regarding the purpose of the use, it is commercial a point against fair use.
- 2. Regarding the nature of the works used, many of them are novel, copyrighted, and otherwise not helping the case for fair use.
- 3. Regarding the portion of the work used, the nature of the technology makes this impossible to measure. However, it has been demonstrated that AI sometimes reproduces images it has been trained on nearly identically. I think this should be a point against fair use.
- 4. Regarding the effect of the use on the market for the original work, generative AI unquestionably devalues the works it is trained on.

I hope given these factors, the economic consequences, and the potential degradation of what makes us uniquely human, you will agree that training AI on copyrighted works should not be considered fair use.

Thank you for your time.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Tim Susman

**Email:**

## **General Comment**

In the development of large language models (LLMs) that generate text in response to a prompt, and the development of generative technologies that create images and other creative output in response to a prompt, all generally lumped under the category of "AI," the developers have admitted that they cannot create useful products without training them on copyrighted works that they have not been given permission to use. Eliminating the requirement to compensate the copyright owner for a for-profit use of their work undermines the entire US copyright system. It is not an "unnecessarily burdensome requirement" to require that a copyright holder be compensated when someone else uses their work for profit. That is what copyright means.

What's more, the product these companies are making using copyrighted work is in direct competition with the creators of the work they're stealing. The companies are creating a product that competes in the same space as the copyright holders, who will see their revenue suffer as a result. We have already seen the harm that AI-generated work can do in spaces such as Amazon's self-publishing, magazines that have been forced to shut down submissions because of AI-generated entries flooding their portals, and even Facebook's feed, crowded with AI-generated text that destroys the point of a social media feed.

An initiative such as this one prioritizes corporations--and the CEOs, as the people who profit the most--over the well-being of the American people. It would be a huge mistake to move forward with it.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Timothy Miller

## **General Comment**

Per the requirements of the RFI response I am stating the following:

This document is approved for public dissemination. The document contains no business-proprietary or confidential information. Document contents may be reused by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.

I have deep and abiding concerns over the executive order and subsequent directives regarding the Development of an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan.

Section 2 of the executive order, "Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence," stipulates the following: "It is the policy of the United States to sustain and enhance America's global AI dominance in order to promote human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security." However, the deployment I've seen of current AI technologies, particularly what's known as "generative artificial intelligence" (alternatively, "generative AI") seems antithetical to promoting "human flourishing" in any form.

The "training" of generative AI models requires the massed scraping and analysis of human-created works, particularly writing and visual art. To date, AI companies have point-blank refused to pay anyone who wrote anything that was used for AI training, instead trying to defend their massed theft as "fair use."

Generative AI systems have also required huge expenditures of energy and water, imposing new strains on American electrical grids and water systems. Further, the highest-profile attempts to deploy generative AI at scale have posed a direct threat to human employment, denying people the ability to earn a living on their own terms.

AI developers must be required to ask permission to include people's work in the development of their models. Creators should not have to opt out; they should be invited to opt in, with suitable compensation.

Automated data collection (also known as scraping) must be required to respect requests to not collect data from websites that post such requests.

Any data collected by any AI developer must be anonymized and encrypted while stored, to protect the creators' privacy. AI developers should be charged a surcharge for the electricity and cooling water consumed, along with a charge for the added pollution from the electricity generation. They should be required to follow all environmental requirements for construction and operation of data centers.

Last but not least, AI models should be treated as potential dual-use technologies and subject to export control (EC) laws and international traffic in arms regulations (ITAR) and thus, review by the Department of Commerce and Department of Defense.

While I remain an AI skeptic, I acknowledge that artificial intelligence may reach a point where it can indeed be used for the betterment of humanity. In the present, though, I hold that AI must be developed in forms which respects and upholds the dignity of humans in all walks of life, and that where AI development would run counter to the well-being of any human, human rights and dignity must be given priority over corporate interests.

comments.title: Tom-H-AI-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text:
## Tom H

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan. The rapid evolution of AI technology demands that we ensure advancements do not compromise user privacy or the protection of intellectual property (IP) rights. The rate at which AI technologies are advancing in capability is too significant to gate from use in any contexts. The lack of control over flow of information when using an AI tool not only jeopardizes user privacy and IP but also severely restricts critical research opportunities—especially in clinical settings where patient data is involved. As it stands, the amount of information that the AI tools and/or their company extracts from user input is not transparent whatsoever. The current lack of transparency regarding the data extracted from user inputs is deeply concerning. AI tools should include a verifiable "private mode" that prevents data from being transmitted, stored, or used for training by the company or any other entities unless the user explicitly opts in. This option must be easily accessible and provide complete control to the user, ensuring that both individuals and organizations can safeguard their sensitive information. Moreover, complete legal assurance is essential for the handling of personal, proprietary, and clinical data. Without robust privacy controls, there is a significant risk that confidential information may be exposed to unauthorized parties. In the case of clinical data, for instance, the absence of clear safeguards prevents researchers and clinicians from confidently using AI tools. Compliance with HIPAA guidelines is crucial here; any AI tool handling patient information must guarantee that such data is fully protected and not compromised in any way. Aligning these privacy measures with existing legal frameworks - such as GDPR and HIPAA - would provide a strong legal and ethical foundation for these requirements. The present lack of these measures include restricted research opportunities, stifled innovation, and a general fear amongst individuals and organizations of data misuse that could ultimately hinder the broader adoption of AI technologies. In conclusion, I urge the agency to mandate that all AI tools offer a complete, and legally VERIFIABLE 'private mode.' This requirement will not only protect user data but also foster responsible innovation across all sectors, ensuring that the benefits of AI technology can be fully realized without compromising privacy or security. Thank you.

Allowing the use of copyrighted works to train AI would be an unmitigated disaster, both for the nation and for me personally as an artist.

The entire point of copyright is to prevent unauthorized use of creative materials, isn't it? Carving out an exception for the largest companies in the world defeats the entire purpose. Furthermore, the idea that art can be stolen and plagiarized at any time will actively depress the motivation of artists to create. Less creation means less innovation, across all creative fields, from writing to visual arts to filmmaking. That has a direct impact on our own ability to compete with other nations, in terms of economics and forward-thinking ideas.

This is all before getting to the fact that the benefits of generative AI are VASTLY overestimated. After several years and tens of billions of dollars invested in the technology, there is yet to be a single actual use case that solves some kind of problem. It has gotten to the point where companies are shoving their AI tools into unrelated products, making them less reliable, just to claim that more people are using AI. This is an enormously expensive solution in search of a problem, and just like NFTs before, the bubble will burst and leave economic disaster in its wake.

Please don't add to this disaster by undercutting one of the only protections that artists and creatives have under our current system. The bottom line is that allowing AI companies unrestricted access to our work will do incalculable damage to an already unstable industry while offering absolutely nothing in return. Artists don't want it, consumers don't want it, the American people don't want it.

comments.comment_text:
**From:** tony zigelman **To:** ostp-ai-rfi

**Subject:** [External] Comments regarding AI action plan **Date:** Saturday, March 15, 2025 11:39:30 PM

CAUTION: This email originated from outside your organization. Exercise caution when opening attachments or clicking links, especially from unknown senders.

## Hello,

It is my understanding that AI models compress training data down to a matrix that they then use to generate responses. Those responses, for some queries and some training data, may reproduce the contents of the training data.

This is not ok.This is a clear violation of copyright law. You are not allowed to make a thing that has a chance -- any chance -- of intentionally reproducing someone else's copyrighted work.

Should you doubt the validity of my claims, I would ask you to investigate OpenAI's implementation of a secondary layer on ChatGPT that checks to see if their AI model is dumping large quantities of copyrighted text to the user and stops the response mid-way if it detects said copyrighted text. This suggests to me that modern AI models do, in fact, have the ability (and the propensity!) to distribute copyrighted work.

It is my belief that the government should strongly investigate one or both of the following stances: AI models should be treated as compressed data, and that all of their training data should be considered to be in their data, and/or all AI-generated data should immediately enter the public domain.

AI is directly responsible for a loss of American jobs, American productivity, and in a handful of cases, American lives. it is astoundingly good at generating things that \*look\* correct but aren't. We do not need to protect American AI interests. We should instead be looking to protect American intellectual work and prohibit the use of AI for tasks where it purports to present factual information.

If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to get in touch.

## Tony Zigelman

comments.title: Travis-Park-AI-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text:
## 2/25/2025 via FDMS

Travis Park

The United States must remain at the forefront of artificial intelligence (AI) development to ensure economic growth, national security, and technological innovation. In response to the Request for Information (RFI) on the AI Action Plan, I propose the following key areas of focus: 1. Research & Development (R&D) Investment Increase federal funding for AI research in universities and publicprivate partnerships to drive innovation. Expand grants through the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Department of Energy (DOE) for AI advancements in key industries such as healthcare, cybersecurity, and manufacturing. Support AI ethics and safety research to ensure responsible AI deployment. 2. Workforce Development & Education Implement AI-focused curricula in K-12 education to build foundational skills in coding, machine learning, and data science. Provide federal incentives for AI training programs in higher education, vocational schools, and apprenticeships. Expand funding for AI workforce reskilling programs to prepare workers for AIdriven industries. 3. AI Infrastructure & National Security Strengthen AI computing infrastructure, including cloud computing access and high-performance AI chip manufacturing in the U.S. Enhance AI capabilities in defense and cybersecurity to protect national security assets. Establish public-private partnerships to ensure U.S. firms have access to cutting-edge AI tools and research. 4. Ethical & Regulatory Frameworks Develop voluntary AI guidelines that promote ethical AI use without stifling innovation. Encourage transparency in AI decision-making processes while protecting intellectual property. Implement policies that prevent AI bias and ensure fairness in automated decision-making. 5. AI Integration in Government Agencies Federal Efficiency & Automation: Use AI to modernize government processes, automate administrative tasks, and reduce operational costs in agencies such as the Social Security Administration (SSA), Internal Revenue Service (IRS), and Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). AI-Driven Public Services: Implement AI for improved public services, such as chatbots for customer support in federal agencies and predictive analytics to enhance public health and disaster response efforts. AI for National Security & Law Enforcement: Expand AI applications in the Department of Defense (DoD), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for threat detection, cybersecurity, and border security. Data Management & Decision-Making: Develop AIpowered data analysis tools to improve decision-making in agencies such as the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Department of Energy (DOE). AI in Research & Space Exploration: Enhance AI applications in NASA for deep space exploration, climate research, and autonomous robotic systems. 6. International Collaboration & Leadership Strengthen alliances with global AI leaders to set international AI standards that align with U.S. values. Lead efforts to counter foreign adversaries' use of AI for cyber threats, misinformation, and economic espionage. Promote AI diplomacy to maintain U.S. influence in global AI governance. By prioritizing these strategic initiatives, the United States will maintain its position as a leader in artificial intelligence while ensuring economic prosperity, national security, and technological excellence.

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Trevor Morgan

## **General Comment**

Hello OSTP, NITRD NCO, et. al,

I'm a professional video game developer of 6 years who has a vested interest in AI as a future potential aide in development. My job necessitates I work with a lot of artists, programmers, and designers with various opinions on the subject. The biggest controversies over AI has been the lack of transparency on dataset contents, training models for profit on data without express permission or license to do so. This should be made more clearly illegal, that AI works are not implicitly original works. Continuing to keep this question in legal limbo without enforcement hurts the copyright interests of domestic small businesses and individuals by allowing massive conglomerates to circumvent copyright law by feigning ignorance about where their training data comes from.

I think the best way to tackle this issue is to tackle the causing issue - the lack of privacy protections online. A common proposal is stricter tracking laws in the US similar to the GDPR in the EU which would empower the freedom to privacy and keep Americans' copyright rights intact. Part of my job is working with Personally Identifiable Information, and as I have customers across the globe I comply with the GDPR. The burdens on services are negligible compared to the benefits the average citizen gains. I would go further and say that we should codify DoNotTrack options as a mandatory compliance rather than a suggestion to the website.

Another concerning issue on the infrastructure side is the power consumption of training models. We need to change how we price electricity to a more common-sense approach. If a facility requires a ton of power, they should be eating the cost of producing that power, not having it distributed to all grid uses. This could be handled by utility companies directly if given the proper authority.

## **General Comment**

As someone with a Ph.D. in Computer Science, it has been truly shocking to see how big tech has pulled the wool over the public's eyes with regards to Generative AI. Generative AI has been oversold and and it has drastically under-delivered. There is no product.

There is no reason for AI training to be exempt from legal copyright restrictions. AI is profiting off the backs of hard-working Americans at no cost. These large companies, like OpenAI and Google, are aware that they are stealing and this is why they are pushing for deregulation. If the shoe was on the other foot, they would sue individuals into the ground over this.

We are due an inevitable economic crash over AI, and this is an attempt to offset that. Continuing to push this off will just deepen the damage. Hold AI companies accountable, pay workers a fair wage, stop gutting the American Economy for a fraud.

It is obscene these companies ask the US Government for \$5 Trillion on one hand, and then beg to be able to steal data on the other hand. Meanwhile, they cry fowl when AI output is used to train other models. You cannot have it both ways.

If anything, there should be further regulation and restriction on AI to prevent it from causing the kind of damage it has already caused to our economy. Training these models for academic purpose has always been fair use, but pretending that trillion dollar companies are being "disadvantage" because they might have to pay for use of data like everyone else is disgusting.

I urge the rejection of all of these proposals. Let artists and creators own their work, as has been the precedent for over a century.

comments.title: Vanessa-Amayo-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text:
## 3/13/2025 via FDMS

## Vanessa Amayo

My name is Vanessa Amayo, and I am a graduating senior from Avonworth High School. I researched the impact of generative AI on the music industry for a semester course, and I recently studied this administration's viewpoint on AI regulation. Based on my two months of student research and 12 years of studying music, I think that AI regulation must be consistent with existing policy (such as copyright law) to protect human American creators. Tennessee's Ensuring Likenes Voice and Image Security (ELVIS) Act introduced novel legislation protecting artists specifically from nonconsensual AI usage, and similar policies should follow. Nonconsensual AI usage could be socially and financially devastating for artists, particularly small or independent artists without the resources to protect their work. Policy makers must hold AI developers and the music industry accountable to protect human artists. Music and art are such vital components of human culture, but performing and creating at advanced and professional levels can be limited by socioeconomic factors. AI-integrated platforms have the power to give beginner musicians access to music and enhance professionals' capabilities. However, these tools must not be used as a replacement for human artists in the name of economic gain, for it will harm human culture and joy. As a musician and student, I believe that AI has the power to make both extremely positive and negative impacts, and it is the responsibility of the user, the developer, the government, and society as a whole to decide if we will leverage AI for good or let it devastate human artistry.

In fact, this won't even be about AI anymore if the claim can be made that something came from AI but is really just plagiarized without it.

The term "AI", as its currently used, is little more than a search engine. The training data is fed into a large probabilistic model that free associates words together.

These tools have little, if any, value. They frequently "hallucinate" due to their probabilistic design. They have no notion of truth or accuracy. Their only value is to create a list of words that approximate a sentence to the reader.

That said, what they're good at is regurgitating the input that they receive. This input is the real contributions of human effort. The allowance of fair use to their training on copyrighted material is an affront to the human effort used to create what they receive.

Furthermore, what we're seeing in the market has the classic signatures of a speculative bubble. The "AI war" is nothing more than a competition between the hucksters vying for supremacy in the eyes of the investors. The only way to win is not to play the game.

I do not support changing copyright law to favor AI use. And I do not support assigning copyright protection to the output of AI models. This is a flawed business that shouldn't be allowed to exist.

## **General Comment**

## Dearest reader,

I have followed the development of AI (specifically, generative AI models) since the first ever public release of Dal-E. At first, the concept of generative AI as a whole, a process that could aid in human creation was groundbreaking. I and many in the field of technology were very interested in what potential paths this could open for not only those interested in computer science, but artists and musicians as well. At first, I used these generative AI models to create inspirations for cityscapes, skylines, etc. It made the creative process fun and inspired, but that all changed as generative AI became more widespread. We saw AI turn from a simple tool for inspiration, to a force that eliminated the jobs of millions of artists, both professional and aspiring, and flooded not only the online, but the physical world with "art" that lacked the very essence of human creativity and labor as a whole. Art is what makes us, as a species, unique. When we look at past cultures, one of the biggest ways that we see their existence is through their art. Consider the ancient Roman and Greek empires, with paintings and books that laid the groundwork for our current movies, films, and more. Without art, humanity isn't so human. And that is what currently is happening. I'd estimate that about a quarter of the internet, its videos, images, and texts, are generated entirely from AI. When we have that big of an influence, who knows what could happen if the smallest mistake happens in relation to the "thought-process" of AI (which, as a reminder, we haven't the slightest clue of how it might work. See the "Black Box" effect). As a 17 year old perusing a career in cybersecurity, my, and many other's perception of the future is bleak. It is more than a possibility that, if it continues on its current trajectory, AI will steal jobs from not only art majors, but from computer science, journalist, English, architecture, music, and math majors as well. I beg you to consider this; if tariffs are being placed to increase jobs and prevent external importation, AI should be restricted as well. If AI continues to grow, eventually it will consume all jobs, leaving America, and possibly the rest of the world, in a state of poverty with a few select elites, primarily those behind gen AI, at the top. If we continue to create flawless, intelligent beings, what will happen to those who have flaws? What will happen to the entire, human race. We are going beyond technology at this point. Please, listen to the people of America. We are scared, concerned for not only our future, but the future of humanity itself. And there is nothing we can do but hope and pray.

## **General Comment**

To whom it may concern,

Generative AI and computer learning models are fascinating technologies with multiple applications that could benefit the United States. However, I think the technology should be handled in a safe and ethical manner. To me this means a few things:

- All training data should be owned or licensed by the creators of the learning model. The use of unlicensed data should not be allowed.
- The use of data and works as training data should not be considered under the "fair use" exception to copyright law.
- The use of personal data should always be opt-in, not opt-out. Changes to licenses on websites and software to retroactively attempt to license user's data for use as training data should not be allowed.
- The use of AI outputs without human review in government and business decision making (such as hiring decisions, medical claim rejections, applications for government grants, etc) should be disallowed.

Thank you for considering my response.

comments.title: Wu-chang-Feng-AI-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text:
## Wu-chang Feng

The non-stop and rapid pace of change in technology and AI has made education and workforce development challenging. Courses developed years ago are now obsolete, leaving students illprepared for a job market that has seen rapid change over the last several years. In our experience attempting to deliver a course applying advances in generative AI towards solving problems in cybersecurity (Labs are available at https://codelabs.cs.pdx.edu), we have seen that a different approach is necessary when attempting to prepare students for an AI-enabled future. We believe that such an approach will allow the US to remain competitive in the technological future. Our approach embodies the main aspects below: 1) Creativity. AI has reduced the importance of the mechanics of technology. Impactful solutions are now driven as much by the ability for someone to imagine an application as it does actually being able to build one. Towards this end, an approach where students learn a breadth of topics and then practice creatively building AIenabled applications that apply them will be paramount. 2) Skepticism. AI and reports of its capabilities can lead many to believe that models can solve problems well beyond their ability to do so. It is important that students are continually exposed to problems with known solutions that AI can not solve at all or can not reliably solve. 3) Change. New AI models are released and deprecated over a period of months. Tasks that models failed at before, may be reliably solved with newer models. It is important that students develop an agile mindset, understanding that a narrative they believed about AI previously, may no longer apply currently. 4) Security. Most developers of AI applications have no formal training in cybersecurity. As a result, simple vulnerabilities such as prompt injection, excessive agency, insecure tools, insecure output handling, and over-reliance are proliferating the marketplace of AI applications. It is essential that students get practice exploiting vulnerable AI applications in order for us to ensure that our AI future isn't controlled by adversaries able to exploit insecure applications. 5) Cost. One of the problems with AI applications is that models are being used to solve problems that they are not trained to solve or that can be solved more efficiently with alternate approaches. Rather than throw everything at the model to perform, it is essential that students understand and be able to apply the range of technological tools, both AI and non-AI ones, to build robust, cost-effective solutions. comments.comment_text: I appreciate the opportunity to provide input on the development of an AI Action Plan. As a researcher in computing, AI, and cybersecurity, I would like to emphasize the critical role of federal funding for fundamental scientific research in ensuring the continued advancement and responsible development of AI technologies. One of the most concerning trends this year has been the erosion of federal support for fundamental research, particularly within the NSF. AI research does not occur in isolation; it relies on a strong foundation of discoveries from mathematics, physics, cognitive science, cybersecurity, and computer systems research. Reductions in funding for NSF and other federal research agencies jeopardize this ecosystem, limiting the potential for breakthrough innovations and hindering the United States' ability to maintain global leadership in AI. AI research does not exist in a vacuum. Its success depends on interdisciplinary collaboration with fields such as neuroscience, linguistics, material sciences, and cybersecurity, among many others. Without sustained investment in these interconnected disciplines, AI research will face significant barriers in areas such as explainability, robustness, and security. Moreover, policy discussions on AI funding should not be confined solely to AIspecific initiatives but should also include substantial investments in basic sciences, highperformance computing, and research infrastructure. AI models are increasingly reliant on advancements in quantum computing, semiconductor technology, and biological computing, all of which require strong government-backed research support. If the U.S. government is serious about maintaining AI leadership, it must reverse the trend of funding cuts for fundamental research and commit to a comprehensive, long-term AI research strategy that strengthens investments across multiple scientific domains. This approach should include: Increased NSF funding to support foundational AI and interdisciplinary research. Sustained support for highrisk, high-reward research that industry alone is unlikely to fund. Enhancing collaboration between academia, government, and industry while ensuring open access to critical AI research findings. Investment in AI infrastructure, including secure and ethical data-sharing platforms to facilitate cutting-edge research. Conclusion The success of AI research and its responsible deployment depend on broad-based scientific investment and an interdisciplinary approach. The U.S. government must prioritize funding for basic research through NSF and other agencies rather than cutting critical support for the broader scientific community. Without this commitment, the long-term sustainability and competitiveness of AI research in the United States will be at serious risk. I appreciate the opportunity to contribute to this discussion and strongly urge policymakers to reaffirm their commitment to federal funding for fundamental research as a cornerstone of the national AI strategy.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305

## **Submitter Information**

**Name:** Zach Thompson

## **General Comment**

As AI tech advances and we consider adopting it more broadly, it is essential that we first protect copy-written content, and any content that has value, from authorized use in training models. This tech has already brought in hundreds of billions in funding, and, if the projections are to be believed, will bring in billions in profit. AI does not work without the data supplied to its models, and if AI is going to profit from that data then it must compensate those who produced the data.

Furthermore, AI model input needs to be tracked to address biases and potentially hazardously in accurate information, especially in areas of medicine and moral action, as people will come to trust these algorithms, thus we must make every effort and take every precaution to guarantee that they are, in proven fact, trustworthy.

Intense attention must also be paid to consideration around those who AI intends to automate away. Society is made of people, not corporations, and so societal benefit must be the primary goal of AI, NOT profit. AI also has great potential to create a dystopian future where it is used as a tool of oppression. It cannot be used to track the lives of individuals, nor in any capacity to single out individuals for punishment - whether that be criminal or persecution - freedom and privacy must come first. There is likely no end to the way this tech can be abused - often justified as serving the greater good - but as the everyday power we wield increases, and so also its destructive capabilities, we must safeguard ourselves against it. We learned this lesson with nuclear weapons, but "weapons" of the future will not look so crude. They will be subtle, and masquerade as anything but a weapon, yet that is what they will be no matter their name.

If we move forward with eyes open, honest about the dangers and risks, and do not make naive decisions about others may use AI, then we may well arrive at a future that benefits all of use and moves forward into a new age.

## **General Comment**

As a somewhat recent graduate of a creative writing program, I find it critically important that the allocation of using copyrighted works to feed into generative AI is highly unethical and should not be permitted. The creators of such work have not given their permission for their work to be stolen to create inferior products that would ultimately lead to their replacement in the creative fields that showcase the truest creations of humankind. Artificial intelligence is just that, artificial. It cannot replace the human spirit when it comes to creating art, stories, essays, or any other creative endeavor. Generative AI is not the future, and further development into it would be a waste of time and resources. The companies saying otherwise are merely trying to profit off of stolen work. The advancement of AI will not benefit national security, and would more than likely harm it as it has been shown time and time again that generative AI is unreliable and extremely error prone. Allowing AI training on copyrighted works without permission would exacerbate this, as many copyrighted works contradict each other and would lead to "hallucinations" or false information generated by the AI. Additionally, AI generated content has been seen by the majority as lazy or subpar, further emphasizing that training on copyrighted material is a waste of time and resources. People would much rather see the creations of fellow people, not machines regurgitating stolen work. Furthermore, training AI on copyrighted work could leak sensitive information about businesses and institutions for anyone to see. Such secrets could be stolen and used against such businesses and institutions. Any promises of long-term profit are false. AI may seem like the hot new thing, but I find it comparable to cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Those technologies ballooned with countless resources being poured into them only for them to fizzle out and fall into relative obscurity. Generative AI is just the second coming of that. Sooner or later, the AI bubble will burst and any resources put into it will be wasted as the markets chase another trend. And in chasing the current trend, it hurts artists and creators as companies try to cut corners by eliminating them for a short-term profit. The technology is too unstable to invest in, and training it on stolen work would ultimately undermine the copyright system. It's already been ruled that AI generated content isn't subject to copyright, so why should AI generation be allowed to train itself on copyrighted work? The humanities were meant to be human, and they should remain that way.

comments.title: Zack-Davis-AI-RFI-2025.pdf
comments.comment_text:
## RE: AI Action Plan RFI

While the development of articial intelligence applications has and will continue to unlock economic value, it's critical that government decisionmakers don't lose sight of the more far-reaching implications. Today, AI is a useful tool for the automation of cognitive tasks, much like any other computer program. In that context, far too many concerns about "AI risk" from misinformation or misuse of existing systems are overblown. Nevertheless, in the limit of arbitrarily powerful AImachines that can do everything humans can do and morethere's a serious risk of humans losing control of our own creations.

However strange the idea might seem at rst, the arguments are so overwhelming that hundreds of qualied expertsincluding, notably, Turing Award winners Georey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio and the CEOs of frontier AI companies Demis Hassabis, Sam Altman, and Dario Amodeisigned a 2023 statement proclaiming that "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war" (https://www.safe.ai/work/statement-on-ai-risk).

It's hard to judge exactly when in the future trajectory of AI development the truly existential threats will emerge, and harder still to judge what the optimal policy response should be. (A theoretical argument about what should happen "the limit of arbitrarily powerful AI" doesn't say much about how that limit is approached.) But the stunning advances of deep learning over the last dozen years (and, notably, large language models over the past six) present clear evidence that it's not too early to act in some way.

As a mere concerned citizen (a computer programmer by profession, having studied the issue as a private individual), I'm not sure I have the expertise to say exactly what ought to be done, but one obvious suggestion is that the U.S. AI Safety Institute should be well-funded and its recommendations taken seriously. Also, mandatory reporting requirements for frontier AI training runs would provide critical visibility without unduly burdening innovation.

As Paul Christiano of the U.S. AISI points out (https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/Hw26MrLuhGWH7kBLm/aialignment-is-distinct-from-its-near-term-applications), the technical project of guring out how to build secure AI systems is distinct from the passing political fads of the moment. This is not a partisan issue. I am,

Faithfully yours,

## Zack M. Davis

AI is a remarkably nebulous term still. As such, it is difficult to call superiority, or even really cite truly ethical use, of AI as a whole. What we do know of AI currently is that it swept the internet, taking in copyrighted data and built itself up illegally using that information for profit. As such, until such a time that all AI is put through rigorous examination to remove all of the data that isn't used with permission, this executive order is pushing technically illegal activity.

In order to push this part through, AI has to be defined better, and refined to be fully legal and ethical.
